This study numerically investigates machine learning methods for addressing eigenvalue problems associated with high-dimensional Schr\"odinger operators. By leveraging the universality of neural networks, we empirically explore the storage-efficient learning of multi-dimensional kernel functions required to isolate the ground state. Specifically, we analyze the error distribution of our algorithms regarding network architecture parameters, including hidden layer neuron counts and training dataset sizes. Our findings indicate that optimization errors in our algorithm do not scale polynomially with respect to these parameters, thereby demonstrating the superior optimization capabilities of neural networks. Furthermore, we provide insights into selecting appropriate loss functions for this application and establish a benchmark to facilitate future research in this emerging field. Ultimately, we conclude that utilizing neural networks to solve high-dimensional Schr\"odinger eigenvalue problems is highly feasible. This conclusion is supported by our examination of approximation and generalization errors, which reveals that even with minimal parameters, these networks can effectively represent multi-dimensional kernel functions essential for isolating the ground state. Additionally, we observe that while approximation errors are substantial, they decrease significantly as network size increases, highlighting the excellent generalization performance of our algorithms. These results provide valuable references for selecting network structures and data sizes in practical implementations. Finally, our conclusions are based on a rigorous numerical analysis of all identified network parameters. To ensure reproducibility, the corresponding Python code is publicly available. Understanding the link between activity patterns in neuronal networks and their behavioral functions remains a key challenge in neuroscience. This study introduces a time series analysis technique to model the dynamics of neuronal networks, using the *C. elegans* nervous system as a case study. As the simplest known animal, *C. elegans* offers a highly accessible model for analyzing the dynamics of both neurons and networks. We demonstrate that a recurrent neural network (RNN) can effectively model the activity of neurons involved in locomotion. Furthermore, we establish that these RNN models can be integrated with *C. elegans* data to examine the relationship between behavior and activity across various conditions, including wild-type, sensory-deficient, and *synaptic overexpression* scenarios. This approach facilitates a unified analysis of time series data, enabling the identification of neurons that contribute to both activity patterns and behaviors. Ultimately, we show that these RNN models can be utilized to design new neurons for *C. elegans* that exhibit distinct activity patterns and behaviors. The *C. elegans* datasets used in this study are available at \url{https://github.com/ahmedfouadwaseem/c elegams-datasets}. Recurrent neural network models can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/ahmedfouadwaseem/c elegams-RNN}. The associated analysis code is located at \url{https://github.com/ahmedfouadwaseem/Neuronal-Models}. Ahmed Waseem Ahmed's thesis can be found at \url{https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~fehz/thesis.pdf}. We demonstrate that the stable point forest, when restricted to a large disk, converges in distribution to a geometrically weighted Delone point process, providing a new proof of D. G. Kendall's 1987 result through an alternative approach grounded in combinatorial theory and statistical mechanics. Furthermore, we utilize this finding to establish a recent, related finding by R. Yang and R. Wang. Additionally, we examine the connection between our method and an independent, recent geometric proof by R. Peled and O. Zeitouni. Finally, we address an open query by analyzing the interaction range of the stable point forest within a restricted region. Specifically, we show that, in probability, the range of stable points located far from the boundary of a large disk is asymptotically equivalent to the range of Poisson points, consistent with a related recent result by R. Peled, A. Timar, and O. Zeitouni. These conclusions are supported by a novel coupling between the stable point forest and the time evolution of a spin system. Specifically, we construct a coupling between the stable point forest and a mean-field Potts spin system such that, as the temperature approaches zero, the spin system evolves from a disordered state to a fully ordered state. The geometric characteristics of the color classes in the spin system at time zero directly correspond to the stable points of the forest. This observation enables us to derive several geometric results concerning the Potts spin system, which in turn yield insights into properties of the stable point forest. We begin by reviewing prior literature and outlining our approach, followed by a review of essential background results from geometric probability theory. Subsequently, we establish our primary result by proving geometric properties of the Potts spin system. We then provide a rigorous argument for our final result by linking the spin system and the stable point forest. Finally, we conclude with remarks on this approach and its potential applications in statistical mechanics. The initial sections of the paper are designed to be accessible to a broad audience, whereas the final sections target readers with a background in geometric probability theory. Throughout the work, we employ the term "stable point forest" as a more descriptive alternative to "stable point process." To our knowledge, the term "stable forest" has not been utilized in previous literature. We have also adopted the convention of referring to "Poisson points" rather than "Poisson processes," as the former is more intuitive for a general readership. This research investigates the electromagnetic traits of hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks possessing single strangeness. We establish the flavor structure within the molecular framework and calculate the magnetic moments, electric dipole moments, and form factors for these states. Additionally, we provide the two-photon width for the $P_{cs(4455)}^+$. Our results aim to facilitate experimental searches for these objects, which can be observed through their electromagnetic signatures at facilities such as LHCb, PANDA, GlueX, J-PARC, PRC, BESIII, and LHC. Furthermore, our findings offer predictions for the electromagnetic properties of $P_{cs}$-like candidates that have already been detected by LHCb. Finally, we explore the potential existence of an isospin doublet state at 4457 MeV composed of a $\Xi_c \bar D_s^*$ molecular configuration. Finally, our work examines the possible molecular nature of the recently discovered $P_{cs}$ states. This report marks the first instance where the molecular nature of $P_{cs}$ states is experimentally verified. We introduce a non-isotropic scattering theory for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS) incorporating an inverse square potential across all three dimensions. This framework is designed to address heterogeneous cubic NLS equations, which are critical for analyzing the stability of ground states in 3D two-component Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) systems featuring dipole-disease and inverse square potentials. The study addresses the well-posedness issue for the linearized equation within $L^2_{x}$, a challenge that previously hindered the derivation of nonlinear stability for ground states in 2D heterogeneous BEC models. Leveraging the established well-posedness of the linearized equation, we successfully establish the nonlinear well-posedness for the heterogeneous cubic cubic NLS with an inverse square potential in $L^2_{x}$. This achievement directly resolves a specific issue highlighted in the work of Chen-Oh-Wang-Zhang (J. Funct. Anal. 280, 2021). Furthermore, we demonstrate the nonlinear ground state stability for 3D heterogeneous BEC models, thereby extending the direct method originally utilized in Chen-Oh-Wang-Zhang (J. Funct. Anal. 280, 2021). These findings significantly advance our understanding of stationary solutions in 3D heterogeneous BEC models, a topic that has recently become a focal point of research. Finally, this work also contributes to the broader context of 1D and 2D heterogeneous BEC models. This study integrates a SIR (susceptible-infected-recovered) infection model with a discrete-time migration model. We establish and solve the combined system, subsequently analyzing its long-term behavior. The findings demonstrate that this model accurately captures the essential dynamics of migration and epidemics, particularly explaining how multiple epidemic waves are generated by migration cycles. Furthermore, the analysis identifies the critical role of mobility intensity in shaping these outcomes. These insights are corroborated by fitting the model to real-world data regarding COVID-19 in Europe. This support for a mechanistic understanding of migration-driven epidemic patterns provides a foundation for evaluating control strategies, such as non-pharmaceutical interventions and vaccination programs. Specifically, we examine how varying levels of these interventions can be optimized to minimize both the number of infected individuals and the associated economic costs. Our results indicate that low-intensity interventions, consistent with Italy's approach during the first pandemic wave, are highly effective when combined with a rapid and extensive vaccination rollout. In contrast, Germany's strategy, characterized by higher mobility and a slower, less comprehensive vaccination program, resulted in a less controlled epidemic trajectory. These conclusions are verified by numerically simuting two distinct scenarios: one featuring a European-wide lockdown and another with a lower intensity of non-pharmaceutical interventions. The simulations confirm that implementing a European-wide lockdown, akin to Italy's first wave measures, constitutes an optimal intervention for mitigating the impact of the pandemic. Finally, we discuss the policy implications of these findings. Although our model does not incorporate the specific impact of interventions on epidemic dynamics, it successfully describes multiple dynamics arising from migration, thereby offering a tool for decision-making in epidemic management. This approach enables the analysis of a broad spectrum of possible interventions, including both quantitative and qualitative adjustments to mobility, as well as the selection and distribution of non-pharmaceutical interventions. We conclude that a European-wide lockdown is a near-optimal intervention, and our analysis of its implementation underscores the necessity for a unified European policy regarding the containment of the COVID-19 pandemic. The simulation results also suggest that interventions should be tailored to local conditions, as different regions may require different types and levels of non-pharmaceutical interventions. Finally, our framework facilitates the analysis of the effectiveness of various interventions across different temporal and spatial scales. For instance, while national lockdowns proved effective during the first wave, their efficacy diminished during the second wave, and large-scale interventions were required to flatten the epidemic curve. K2-138 hosts a multi-planet system that appears to align with the super-period resonance (SPR) sequence. Prior research identified an SPR 5:2 resonance mode spanning five planets, although the 3:2 resonance segment within this chain lacked a confirmed candidate. This study employs the Generalized Least Squares (GLS) method to detect exoplanets in the K2-138 light curve, successfully identifying a new transiting planet, K2-138 f, which exhibits a 3:2 SPR mode. We further examine the SPR characteristics of the K2-138 system and compare its properties with other known SPR systems. Finally, we explore the potential for future transit observations of K2-138 f and propose a rough estimation of the likelihood of coexisting inner planets. These findings offer valuable insights for characterizing the system's architecture and inform strategies for follow-up observations. Additionally, our analysis code is publicly available to facilitate future SPR research. This work is dedicated to the memory of our mentor, Professor Stephen Snubeny. This paper investigates the representation theory of the quantum affine algebra $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}_n})$ and the Schur-Weyl dualism involving the affine Hecke-Clifford algebra $H_{k,q}^{\mathrm{C}}$ within a specific representation. We introduce a functor that maps $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}_n})$ modules to modules over the affine symmetric algebra $H_{k,q}$; this functor is established as exact, essentially surjective, and preserves highest weight modules with dominant highest weights. This result serves as the authentic counterpart to the quantum affine Schur-Weyl dualism. Specifically, we demonstrate the tensor product decomposition of this real image: $H_{k,q}^{\mathrm{C}} \cong \bigoplus_{\boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \mathrm{Irr}_k^+} \mathrm{Ind}_{S_k^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}^{H_{k,q}^{\mathrm{C}}} \boxtimes P_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}$, where $P_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}$ denotes the projective indecomposable modules of $H_{k,q}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}$. Here, $\mathrm{Irr}_k^+$ represents the set of irreducible $H_{k,q}$ modules arising from the restriction of $H_{k,q}^{\mathrm{C}}$, which are precisely those indexed by $k$-core $n$-partitions. Furthermore, we explicitly calculate the projective indecomposable modules for $H_{k,q}^{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}$ in terms of the $k$-affine Schur functions $\widetilde{S}_{k,\boldsymbol{\lambda}}$. Finally, we provide an explicit construction of the functor and determine its action on classical $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_n)$ modules. The SiD detector design is being reconsidered in the context of the future 100 TeV proton-proton collider at the LHC site, now referred to as the HL-LHC-FFC upgrade. Furthermore, novel physics performance metrics have been introduced, and the design itself has been significantly revised. Key changes include an enlarged inner radius and altered angular coverage, the adoption of silicon-based technology featuring large 1.5 cm x 1.5 cm pixels mounted on rigid silicon carbide structures, a newly implemented innermost sub-detector known as the Vertex Tracker (Vtx), and a refreshed readout and data acquisition architecture. This paper outlines a conceptual design that merges innovative materials and engineering solutions with advanced data processing techniques to create a high-precision tracking and calorimetry system. The design adheres to the most stringent future collider environment requirements while maintaining flexibility regarding specific physics performance goals. Its primary objective is to deliver outstanding electron energy and impact parameter resolution, deliver triple jet reconstruction with exceptional kinematic accuracy, and ensure efficient impact parameter tagging for b and c quarks. The influence of these novel design elements on various final-state configurations is examined, alongside an analysis of the detector's capabilities concerning electron energy resolution and b/c-tagging efficiency. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how novel concepts can be effectively integrated into a general-purpose tracking and calorimetry detector to satisfy both current and future experimental requirements. Specifically, it highlights how integrating a vertex tracker directly onto large-radius, pixel-based silicon sensors can substantially enhance overall detector performance. The SiD detector concept is developed by an international collaboration of approximately 150 physicists from 30 institutions. This paper represents a major revision of an earlier concept from 2015 and is published in J. Phys.: Conf. Ser. 2293 (2022) 012001. Its content reflects discussions within the SiD collaboration and the future-hadron collider working group of the IFAE. The authors acknowledge the support of all collaborating institutions and the FFRH and the IFAE for organizing the SiD concept workshop. Additionally, the authors thank the editors for their efforts in including this paper in the proceedings. In 2018, the observation of quasi-long-range order in some regions of an amorphous ice sample challenged the prevailing belief that water ice is fundamentally disordered. This study further investigates this controversial topic by employing the inverse participation ratio (IPR) as an indicator of the extent of quasi-long-range order. Utilizing both the IPR and a recently introduced metric, the Local IPR (L-IPR), we demonstrate that extreme quantum disorder is present throughout the entire sample, whereas domains exhibiting partial order can be identified in the crystal. Our findings indicate that the IPR serves as an effective tool for detecting crystal regions within amorphous ice, while the L-IPR offers a more refined and locally sensitive measure of disorder. The methodology and metrics presented here are applicable to a broad spectrum of quantum many-body systems. Specifically, using the L-IPR, we demonstrate that crystalline domains possess significantly higher densities and exhibit less disorder than the surrounding regions in amorphous ice. Additionally, we apply this approach to a prototypical many-body local problem: the transverse-field Ising model coupled with random transverse fields, commonly known as the Dyson-Bracker-Hutchins model. This work paves the way for identifying crystal domains in various other relevant condensed matter systems. Finally, we examine how the I-IPR and L-IPR can characterize disorder in one-dimensional systems featuring both random fields and random on-site couplings. Our analysis reveals a qualitative distinction between these two models, showing that the I-IPR and L-IPR are capable of distinguishing between different types of disorder. Overall, the I-IPR and L-IPR emerge as complementary tools for identifying domains with varying degrees of order, a capability essential for studying complex quantum systems. These findings are based on calculations performed by our group using the Time-Evolving Block Decimation (TEBD) algorithm. Given that TEBD is restricted to low excitation densities, the technique is particularly valuable for "searching for" crystal domains in amorphous ice, as quantum fluctuations are notably weak in these regions, allowing domain formation even under weak coupling conditions. In contrast, disorder regions, characterized by strong quantum fluctuations, remain accessible to TEBD. Consequently, the methods proposed here are well-suited for "detecting" disorder regions once crystal domains have been discovered. This study presents a visualization and assessment tool designed to probe the local electronic structure of materials using atomically sharp Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM) tip-orbital convolutions. We demonstrate how graphane can serve as a superior lateral STM tunneling probe compared to the commonly used hydrogen-terminated Si(111)-(7x7) surface. Furthermore, we show that the local density of states of gold can be effectively visualized at the atomic scale using a Si STM tip. Our findings indicate that gold's 6s electrons are ideal for modeling a STM tunneling probe hydrogen-like orbital with a substantial electron density tail. This research was conducted using SIESTA (Simple Iterative Tight Binding and Extended Natural Atomic Orbitals) and Q-EST (Quantum Efficiency Scanning Tunneling) software. Ultimately, this work provides a visualization and assessment method for the local density of states of graphane, gold, and silicon, facilitating a more comprehensive interpretation of experimental data obtained from STM. All data and source files are publicly accessible at https://github.com/QuinnBuckley/Atomic-Resolution-Visualization-and-Assessment-of-the-Local-Electronic-Structure-of-Graphite-Gold-and-Silicon-using-Scanning-Tunnelling-Microscopy-and-Quantum-Simulations-and-Modeling. Additionally, we provide a tutorial on utilizing the Q-EST package to assess materials as potential STM tunneling probes. This work was performed under the supervision of Dr. Quinn Buckley. Human-assisted automated theorem proving has flourished over recent decades, yielding a vast collection of formally proven results stored in various systems such as Isabelle, Lean, and Coq. This paper introduces a framework designed to verify the correctness of theorems within existing proof systems by leveraging another system. Using Isabelle as the primary example, we demonstrate how to build a verification framework specifically for Isabelle archives like the Archive of Formal Proofs (AFP). Our analysis identifies three key limitations of the current verification approach: (1) an overemphasis on syntactic and semantic equivalence that hinders practical application, (2) a scarcity of strategies for managing complex proofs, and (3) a lack of methods to enhance verification through provably equivalent transformations. To address these challenges, we propose several innovative techniques for both theoretical analysis and practical implementation. Additionally, we have developed a new verification tool for AFP that incorporates these methods, which has successfully verified 95% of a subset comprising 1,000 prominent theorems. A fully automated verification of all AFP theorems remains a future objective. The tool and all referenced examples are accessible at https://github.com/207zhangqin/AFPVevification. Furthermore, this article was recognized as an Outstanding Paper at CAiSE 2021.

The Earth's magnetosphere is a dynamic system that constantly reacts to solar wind inputs. These interactions generate ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves within the magnetosphere-ionosphere system, which can be recorded by ground-based magnetometers. While the spectral characteristics of these waves offer insights into energy transfer mechanisms between the solar wind and magnetosphere, as well as internal processes, the data often appear cluttered and difficult to interpret. We propose an alternative method for spatially visualizing magnetospheric activity by converting recorded magnetometer data into audible sound. Specifically, we demonstrate how to map the frequency of ULF waves to audible frequencies and design an algorithm for the temporal distribution of sound frequencies. This auditory approach complements visual spectrums and offers distinct advantages for both novice researchers and experienced scientists. For newcomers, hearing the waves aids in building an intuitive sense of the phenomenon. For experts, we illustrate how combining visual and auditory data can reveal new information and deepen the understanding of ULF wave characteristics. Ultimately, we contend that making ULF waves accessible through human hearing is a valuable supplementary tool for studying geospace. We believe our proposed mapping method is applicable to any ULF wave recording. Additionally, we have developed a web-based application that automatically converts ULF wave data into sound and allows users to select among three distinct mapping algorithms. This application is freely available for public use. Ultimately, we hope this innovation inspires others to explore novel ways of presenting ULF wave data. Our goal is to broaden the community's engagement with the subject and foster deeper inquiry into the nature of ULF waves. By incorporating human sensory perception beyond sight, we aim to inspire future research and expand the space community's passion for the field. We anticipate that these methods will enable users to intuitively grasp the phenomenon and encourage further investigation into the nature of ULF waves. We look forward to a more engaged community. This study investigates the classical dilaton-electromagnetic dilaton gravity framework, which extends the non-linear Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton system by incorporating a specific non-linear electromagnetic action known as logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics (LNE). We apply this theory to charged, rotating black membranes (BM) within an AdS$_4$ background, focusing on the large-rotation regime. The analysis examines the thermodynamic properties, including the causal structure, Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, and the rotational speed of the event horizon. Furthermore, we verify that the first law of thermodynamics and the Smarr-like relation for charged rotating BMs hold true within this theory, while also exploring the conditions for their stability. Finally, we demonstrate the potential significance of the charged rotating BM solution in this gravity model as an effective model for astrophysical compact objects. This research is motivated by the need to understand high-energy phenomena, such as those occurring near black hole event horizons, where quantum effects are negligible and classical physics suffices. These objects may exhibit superluminal rotation speeds and anomalous thermodynamic behaviors, including negative temperatures and entropies. Our findings suggest that charged rotating BM solutions in this dilaton-gravity framework offer a viable framework for describing such exotic astrophysical objects. This model expands the range of possible observable characteristics of these objects, thereby enhancing the accuracy of their detection and measurement. This advancement is crucial for deepening our understanding of the universe and its underlying physical laws. This conclusion is supported by the recent observational evidence regarding the rapid rotation of these astrophysical entities. This rotation is attributed to the presence of electromagnetic fields, which are described by the logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics used in this study. This theoretical approach provides a more accurate representation of electromagnetic phenomena in high-energy environments, such as those surrounding black holes. By utilizing this approach, we can better understand the behavior of electromagnetic fields and their interaction with matter, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the physical processes occurring around these astrophysical objects. This, in turn, contributes to a deeper understanding of the universe and its fundamental physical laws. Natural language is a fundamental human communication method that encapsulates and conveys data. To streamline human interactions, information is stored in various formats, including verbal, visual, mathematical, and declarative. Written text is deemed structured because its content is governed by syntactic and semantic rules. This paper introduces a method for processing unstructured natural language and transforming it into declarative recall-based logic programming rules. This approach enables the application of formal techniques, such as semantic search, recall metrics, and automated reasoning, to textual data. We present a case study from the medical domain that demonstrates how to model text using a semantic search engine and a reasoning system. The text processing approach relies on machine learning models designed to capture semantic relationships between words and phrases. Our findings indicate that a hybrid architecture integrating multiple machine learning models yields superior performance in text processing. The results also show that a deep learning-based word representation model outperforms a statistical one. Furthermore, the text processing framework achieves a recall of 0.70, outmatching the performance of a state-of-the-art semantic search engine. Finally, we illustrate the utility of our text processing framework by developing a knowledge base designed to support medical decision-making. This framework successfully represents and stores medical knowledge, demonstrating its capacity to enhance the accuracy of medical decisions. We have made the code for our text processing framework publicly accessible. The paper's source code can be retrieved at: https://github.com/ahmedelshorbagy/DeclarativeRecallFramework. Our source code is also available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5825007) to ensure proper citation. GP 2 is derived from a mini-step operational semantics for Call-by-Name (COSCBN) via an intermediate mini-step operational semantics for Typed Lambda Calculus with Evaluation to Normal Form (CBN-TLE). This paper validates the transition from CBN-TLE to GP 2 through a series of intermediates, each justified by a theorem establishing semantic equivalence with its predecessor. The sequence of transformations involves:
*   Introducing a flag variable to execute the next step,
*   Separating the reduction of redexes within contexts from that of the reducte,
*   Integrating flag variables as a flag type,
*   Applying a lifting operation to elevate flag variables into the context,
*   Utilizing flag variables to synchronize context reductions with the reduction of the redex in the rightmost position.
This methodology successfully constructs a small-step operational semantics for the lambda calculus incorporating both evaluation and normalization. The evaluation component operates via Call-by-Name (CBN) semantics, while the normalization aspect is achieved through a multi-step operational semantics for Normal Order Reduction (CBN-TLE). This paper extends that multi-step semantics for CBN-TLE with the control operators of CBN to produce GP 2. The proof of this extension relies on an intermediate multi-step operational semantics, which is obtained by lifting a weak head reduction from CBN-TLE to the flag level. This process involves:
*   Adding a flag variable to execute the subsequent step,
*   Restricting reductions within contexts to at most one step,
*   Restricting flag reductions to at most one step.
This intermediate semantics serves as a bridge between COSCBN and GP 2. It is structurally identical to GP 2 except for multi-step reductions within contexts and the absence of multi-step flag reductions. Consequently, this work demonstrates that control operators do not interfere with the "no-interaction" property of multi-step reductions in contexts. Observing young stellar objects (YSOs) in the pre-main sequence phase reveals a complex network of gas and dust structures extending from their disks. While both gas and dust are believed to be present in these systems, current observations can only directly detect gas via molecules that emit millimeter and submillimeter radiation in rotational transitions. However, submillimeter observations of molecules like CO and N2D+ often fail to capture emission from the outermost layers. To address this gap, we introduce a new model that self-consistently calculates optically thin thermal line emission from molecular gas, accounting for both dust continuum scattering and photoevaporation. Our model demonstrates that dust scattering can significantly attenuate this molecular emission. We further examine how photoevaporation and magnetospheric accretion (MMA) influence the observable spatial distribution of this emission. By comparing our predictions with upcoming high-angular resolution observations of TW Hydrae, we aim to identify the physical mechanisms driving the observed morphology of millimeter and submillimeter emission. Ultimately, this new framework will enhance our understanding of the physical processes occurring in the circumstellar environments of pre-main sequence stars. The model code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/serenapizzuto/scattering_and_photoevaporation. Finally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the current observational status of TW Hydrae and outline future observational strategies. This study serves as a foundational step toward elucidating the physical processes within pre-main sequence stars and their surrounding circumstellar environments. Our initial findings suggest that the morphology of ESO 254-L235, previously interpreted as a "disk breeze," may instead be better explained by photoevaporation. Additionally, we explore the potential impact of dust scattering on observations of TW Hydrae. Overall, this study underscores the critical need for further high-angular resolution observations of TW Hydrae to advance our understanding of circumstellar environments. Specifically, we recommend focusing on submillimeter emission from TW Hydrae, which is expected to be observable out to approximately 10 au. Furthermore, we propose conducting similar observations on ESO 254-L235 to investigate the physical processes driving its morphology. Finally, we advocate for a more comprehensive and detailed study of TW Hydrae to better understand its circumstellar environment. This will involve characterizing the morphology of dust and molecular emission, as well as their dynamical evolution, to provide a holistic view of the system. We also emphasize the importance of observing the innermost regions of TW Hydrae, which remain largely unexplored

This research investigates factoring methods for various Chebyshev polynomials that yield simple factorizations involving few terms of $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$. A distinctive characteristic of these variants is that their corresponding algebraic integers possess a minimal equation of low degree. The study prioritizes factoring variants where $d$ is a prime number, as the resulting algebraic integers exhibit specific properties within the cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_d)$. We developed multiple algorithms for this factoring process, with the primary method relying on the calculation of the discrete Legendre symbol. Furthermore, we established an algorithm to identify the exact number of required $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$ terms. Finally, we present several families of polynomial variants that admit efficient factorizations using a small number of these cosine terms. This effort combines techniques from algebraic number theory and computational algebra, utilizing algorithms designed to address problems in these domains. The paper includes examples and computational results demonstrating the efficiency of our approach. Additionally, we note that this constructive method offers a means to generate algebraic integers with small traces. The computational aspects of our work were implemented using SageMath. This project serves as a foundation for further inquiry, including exploring the reverse process of constructing polynomial variants with desired factorization properties within the Chebyshev polynomial family. This research was conducted as a senior undergraduate thesis in the author's undergraduate program. Given the author's young age and the preliminary nature of these results, they are best suited to introduce the fascinating topic of Chebyshev polynomial variants and their connections to algebraic number theory. This study presents an analysis of the internal structure of a two-core symmetrical phase-angle regulator transformer (VARTR) featuring two distinct winding types: regulating and transition. The research details the safeguarding and classification schemes for transients originating from internal internal faults (IIF) and accidental disenergization (ADE), distinguishing between transients caused by ADE and IIF within both transition and regulating windings. Furthermore, this paper proposes an experimental methodology to generate transient voltage waveforms for all identified winding configurations. The results indicate that the system successfully safeguards VARTR transients and accurately predicts their characteristics based on the specific winding involved. Finally, the proposed experimental approach is validated through simulations that model these generated waveforms. This methodology holds significant potential for applications in transient testing, simulation, and the reliability assessment of power system components. Future research will expand upon this approach to encompass other static power system elements. The data generated by this method will facilitate advanced research into the safeguarding and classification of transients across various two-terminal and multi-terminal power system elements. The findings presented in this paper are expected to enhance the understanding of VARTR transient phenomena within the electrical power sector. Additionally, the concepts introduced may prove valuable for research into safeguarding and categorizing transients in other power system elements. Optimizing downlink multi-group multi-user scheduling and beamforming in mmWave systems is a difficult task due to the scarcity of radio resources, specifically orthogonal time and frequency slots. A common strategy to address this scarcity involves transmitting multiple user signals simultaneously within a single slot, a technique known as multi-user multi-group broadcasting. This paper introduces a hybrid beamforming approach designed for multi-group broadcasting in mmWave environments. The proposed hybrid scheme comprises an analog component utilizing maximum gain beams and a digital component leveraging hybrid encoding. This hybrid design facilitates multi-user multi-group broadcasting while leveraging the inherent spatial multiplexing capacity of hybrid beamforming. Additionally, a novel hybrid beamforming structure is introduced, which addresses the trade-off among scheduling performance, system throughput, and user fairness by providing flexible and optimal configurations across various scenarios. Simulations confirm that the proposed hybrid scheme effectively supports multi-group broadcasting and surpasses both fully-digital and fully-analog alternatives. Furthermore, a flexible hybrid beamforming configuration successfully optimizes the proposed multi-group broadcasting scheme by balancing scheduling performance, throughput, and fairness according to specific application needs. Consequently, the proposed hybrid beamforming support for multi-group broadcasting serves as a promising solution for future mmWave systems. To facilitate this, a new signaling approach is developed to enable efficient hybrid beamforming for multi-group broadcasting, thereby ensuring low complexity for both base stations and user equipment. Finally, an optimization framework is established to determine the optimal hybrid beamforming configuration and hybrid encoding strategy for any given scenario. This framework utilizes a non-convex optimization problem solved via the Generalized Benders Decomposition (G-BD) method, which separates the problem into manageable subproblems. Results indicate that the proposed signaling and optimization framework can achieve up to a 10% increase in scheduling performance compared to other beamforming schemes and configurations. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that hybrid beamforming support for multi-group broadcasting is a promising avenue for future mmWave networks. Furthermore, the developed signaling and optimization framework for multi-group broadcasting under hybrid beamforming can be adapted to other scenarios, such as multi-user broadcasting, by adjusting the group size and user count. This provides a more comprehensive solution for mmWave systems, serving as a significant step toward practical implementation. Overall, this work represents a substantial step toward achieving multi-group broadcasting with hybrid beamforming in mmWave systems. Specifically, the paper introduces a new signaling approach for multi-group broadcasting under hybrid beamforming, offering a more practical solution for mmWave systems. Additionally, an optimization framework has been established to identify the optimal beamforming configuration

A finitely generated group $G$ exhibits exponential residual finiteness expansion if there is a sequence of finite index subgroups $G_i < G$ where the growth of their indices, $|G : G_i|$, is exponential, while the growth of their centers, $|Z(G_i)|$, remains bounded. In contrast, we demonstrate that certain groups with finite centers achieve an expansion rate situated just below exponential growth. To achieve this, we construct p-groups $G$ possessing normal subgroups $H$ such that the quotient $G/H$ is metabelian, with the resulting expansion landing between boundedly generated and boundedly finite groups. Furthermore, for specific instances, the centers of the subgroups within $H$ grow at rates strictly between linear and quadratic. To support these constructions, we prove a general criterion: if the subgroups of a group $G$ are organized into an ascending chain where the successive quotients grow at rates $f_i$, the growth of their centers will follow a sequence $g_i$ defined by $g_0=1$ and $g_i = \prod_{j=0}^{i-1} f_j + 1$. Additionally, we examine the residual finiteness expansion of groups arising from wreath products. Specifically, for any prime $p$, the wreath product $C_p \wr \mathbb{Z}$ admits a sequence of finite index subgroups whose indices grow factorially, whereas the centers of these subgroups grow quadratically. Beyond individual groups, we analyze the phenomenon of expansion across entire classes of groups, specifically within the context of profinite groups. We establish that the classes of bound-generated, bound-finite, and nilpotent groups are closed under the operation of taking limits of sequences of groups with bound-finite factors. However, this closure property does not extend to bound-nilpotent groups. Finally, we investigate groups with limited nilpotency variation and investigate the existence of groups and sequences of subgroups characterized by slow expansion and rapidly decaying centers. These findings have significant implications for the study of finite $p$-groups and their residual finiteness expansion. Specifically, we demonstrate that the eigenvalues of the non-self-adjoint Stokes operator are bounded within a disk centered at the origin with a radius of $O(h^{-5})$. The ability to determine whether neutron star mergers can generate the r-process elements depends critically on precise mass models for heavy, neutron-rich nuclei. This study evaluates various machine learning (ML) algorithms, including random forest, gradient boosting machines, long short-term memory, and convolutional neural networks, to predict nuclear masses. We utilize the experimental dataset COMNET2018 and construct two synthetic datasets based on the Skyrme-Hartree-Fock-MB1 and KB3G theoretical models. Our results indicate that both the COMNET2018 and KB3G datasets can be predicted with an average root mean square deviation of approximately 0.8–0.9 MeV. By integrating these ML predictions into the dynamical nuclear reaction network SMCRN, we simulate the kilonova associated with neutron star mergers. The predicted spectra align with AT2017gfo, and the abundance of r-process elements matches existing r-process models. Consequently, ML-based mass models provide reliable estimates for the r-process elements, supporting the hypothesis that neutron star mergers are capable of producing these elements. This work establishes a foundation for the future application of ML to astrophysical modeling. The accompanying python package, ComnetML, is accessible at https://github.com/ComnetML. Our network architecture, along with the optimal parameters for the random forest, gradient boosting machines, and long short-term memory models, is detailed in this study and can be reproduced using our SMCRN package at https://github.com/SMCRN/ComnetML. Additionally, our code for predicting r-process element abundances from nuclear reaction networks is available at https://github.com/SMCRN/DNN-Kilonova. Future efforts will focus on enhancing the accuracy of nuclear mass models to further refine r-process element predictions. Sapphire serves as a vital dielectric material for superconducting quantum devices operating at microwave frequencies. The development of advanced sapphire growth techniques has significantly reduced dielectric attenuation, enabling sapphire-based resonators to achieve the highest $Q$-factors observed in superconducting circuits. However, a full understanding of sapphire's dielectric attenuation remains incomplete. This study presents a novel method for measuring sapphire's microwave dielectric attenuation within the quantum regime, utilizing a feedback loop to actively cool a standing-wave cavity and enabling direct monitoring of $Q$-factors up to $10^{8}$ with 1 ppb sensitivity. We demonstrate a strong correlation between total dielectric attenuation and temperature, which decreases as thermal energy is lowered. Furthermore, we establish a linear relationship between the dielectric attenuation of high-purity sapphire and its impurity concentration, finding that the magnitude of this correlation aligns with predictions from Debye theory. These findings offer critical insights into sapphire's dielectric properties, facilitating the engineering of quantum-grade sapphire substrates with minimal impurities. Additionally, our research identifies specific frequency ranges where sapphire exhibits minimal dielectric attenuation, holding significant promise for future quantum technologies. Finally, we report a record-breaking $Q$-factor of $1.9\times 10^{8}$ for a sapphire-based resonator at 5.3 GHz, achieved through a two-step fabrication process. This approach involves growing sapphire with ultralow impurity levels and optimizing resonator geometry to minimize conductor losses, resulting in a total resonator $Q$-factor of $7.1\times 10^{7}$ and a dielectric $Q$-factor of $1.9\times 10^{8}$. These results represent a substantial improvement over previous microwave sapphire resonators. The concept of optical pulling forces is examined within both classical and quantum frameworks. In the classical approach, the pertinent length scale is the wavelength of light, whereas in the quantum approach, it is the vacuum gap separating the object and the source. The discussion outlines the foundational principles enabling optical pulling and reviews recent advancements in this field. Furthermore, the necessary material properties for this phenomenon are analyzed, emphasizing metamaterials and their limitations. The paper concludes by highlighting key experimental results achieved with real materials and proposing promising directions for future research. Overall, optical pulling represents a nascent yet rapidly evolving area with significant potential for fundamental scientific inquiry and technological application. Additionally, it offers a valuable context for understanding the persistent challenge of reducing the energy consumption of data centers. Specifically, this has driven the proposal of quantum friction forces, which can pull objects toward vacuum fluctuations and, consequently, radiative energy reservoirs such as laser beams. This review aims to elucidate the underlying physics, including both fundamental and quasi-classical calculations of optical pulling forces, and to suggest promising avenues for future investigation. Finally, it addresses how this phenomenon can help lower the energy costs associated with data center operations.

This paper introduces a robust optimization framework designed to address uncertainty in combinatorial problems where the uncertainty set is defined by distributions over binary variables. Although general dual decomposition methods for this approach can become computationally intractable, we demonstrate that the Lagrange dual of the resulting problem can be effectively approximated using cutting plane techniques in several key scenarios. This methodology is applied to two case studies: network design under demand uncertainty and facility location with uncertain fixed costs. Numerical experiments indicate significant performance gains from this framework, with robust versions of the case studies showing up to a 50% reduction in runtime compared to their nominal counterparts. Furthermore, a dual warm-start strategy is proposed to enhance computational efficiency in instances where multiple scenarios share a common subset. A novel branch-and-cut implementation confirms substantial performance improvements. The proposed method's advantages are validated across a diverse collection of instances, many of which had previously proven intractable. A comprehensive collection of instances and computational data is available at https://github.com/akshaykumar1998/Robust-Combinatorial-Optimization. Our implementation is also integrated into the open-source robust optimization library ROBLIB (available at https://github.com/akshaykumar1998/ROBLIB). These tools aim to facilitate the evaluation of various approaches and uncertainty sets within this framework, thereby supporting future research and development. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future extensions and applications. The developed implementation can be accessed via our public repository at https://github.com/akshaykumar1998/ROBLIB. This paper introduces H4M, a comprehensive dataset designed for socioeconomic analytics in the instance of Beijing. Comprising 4 million entries with an average size of 1 MB per instance, the dataset offers multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributional data drawn from heterogeneous sources. Its composition includes: (1) multi-modal data such as images, maps, videos, and text; (2) multi-view data covering various perspectives and dimensions; (3) multi-distributional data reflecting diverse statistical distributions; and (4) multi-source data originating from different providers. The dataset is sourced from four providers—Baidu, Tencent, Alibaba, and a public provider—and encompasses both real-world and simulated scenarios. Its richness and depth facilitate multi-faceted, multi-dimensional, multi-perspective, and multi-scale analytics of Beijing's socioeconomic landscape. Furthermore, the study addresses multi-source data fusion through joint learning, embedding learning, and alignment, while also exploring multi-view learning via co-learning, cross-view, and complementary methods. Additionally, multi-distributional learning is conducted using multi-instance, multi-label, multi-class, and multi-view label techniques. Ultimately, this work demonstrates multi-modal multi-view learning utilizing multi-instance, multi-label, multi-class, and multi-view strategies. The paper provides a dataset description, analysis, and exploration of potential applications and learning methods. Additionally, it examines the challenges associated with multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributional data fusion and learning, offering insights and guidance for future multi-faceted analytics. Finally, the study discusses potential future directions for multi-faceted socioeconomic analytics. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale, multi-source, multi-modal, multi-view, multi-distributional, and multi-faceted dataset dedicated to Beijing's socioeconomic analytics. The dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhijunliu1988/H4M. This work serves as a foundation for multi-faceted socioeconomic analytics, particularly for Beijing. The proposed dataset is the first of its kind for multi-faceted Beijing analytics and is expected to be the first large-scale resource for such multi-faceted data. Furthermore, the multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributional data fusion and learning methods applied here are also the first of their kind for Beijing analytics. These datasets and methods will enable multi-faceted socioeconomic analytics for Beijing and other instances, thereby advancing multi-faceted data-driven analytics. This paper introduces VSDI, a system designed for the interactive investigation of extensive relational datasets using visual schemas. VSDI automatically generates these visual schemas from metadata and enables users to explore the data through an entity-centric interface that displays entities and their attributes. The system supports deep data analysis and insight discovery by integrating interactive visualizations, entity-detail views, and search functionality. The authors have applied VSDI to various real-world data sets, and this paper presents the resulting findings. Initial user studies indicate that the approach is both feasible and effective. Furthermore, the study explores potential future enhancements to VSDI. Overall, the paper underscores the value of investigation support grounded in visual schemas. While current applications primarily focus on data analysis and insight discovery, the authors suggest expanding VSDI's capabilities to include entity navigation and visualization, which would further aid in understanding entities and their relationships. Additionally, the framework's application to big data management and processing is examined. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions and inviting contributions from others in the field. VSDI is accessible at www.vsdidata.com.

Graph Neural Architectures (GNNs) have proven highly effective across a wide range of applications by leveraging both the structural characteristics and entity embeddings within graph data. While recent studies have extensively addressed issues such as bias, scalability, and generalization within the domain, the potential of transfer learning remains underexplored. This paper investigates transfer learning strategies for graph neural architectures, highlighting recent advancements and emerging trends. Furthermore, it aims to stimulate future research and development in this field by outlining promising directions for achieving general transfer learning in GNNs. Specifically, it focuses on two key aspects: the transfer of models and the transfer of data. The study also examinesuibias introduced by node and graph structure, as well as task and domain differences, providing a framework to assess various transfer learning scenarios. Finally, it suggests potential approaches to mitigate these biases, including hyperparameter optimization, neural architecture search, and the use of pretraining datasets. Ultimately, this work serves as a comprehensive guide and foundational resource for initiating transfer learning research within graph neural architectures. This field is particularly critical for enhancing the generalization capabilities of GNNs, thereby improving their performance on real-world datasets characterized by limited or sparse labels. This is especially pertinent for advancing the future development of GNNs in dynamic graph domains. Additionally, it addresses the growing trend of designing and implementing transfer learning for GNNs in dynamic graph data scenarios. This involves utilizing pretraining datasets to develop pretraining models that can be adapted to downstream tasks with minimal fine-tuning, effectively transferring knowledge from one graph to another. The proposed scenarios encompass both static and dynamic graph environments. Finally, the paper provides a taxonomy of pretraining datasets and outlines several promising applications for transfer learning in graph neural architectures. This work is anticipated to serve as a foundational reference for advancing research and development in transfer learning for GNNs. Furthermore, it offers guidance on selecting appropriate pretraining datasets, architectures, and hyperparameters, while also suggesting future directions for the field. The rise of social networks and the internet has driven the increasing popularity of gift shopping. However, selecting an appropriate present for others remains difficult due to the need to satisfy multiple individuals simultaneously. This paper introduces a recommendation system designed to facilitate others in buying gifts. Specifically, the system suggests items from e-commerce platforms by utilizing a dual feature allocation model to efficiently translate inputs into appropriate e-commerce identifiers. To evaluate the suggestion quality, an ablation study was conducted by removing various components, including the e-commerce translation layer and different types of contextual information. The findings indicate that providing diverse item choices enhances recommendation quality by satisfying the preferences of different users. Furthermore, incorporating additional contextual information proves more effective than integrating contextual features into model parameters. These results were achieved through extensive experiments and evaluations, such as analyzing recommendation results under different configurations and comparing them against baseline models. The proposed system outperforms all baselines in recommendation quality, particularly in handling multi-user requirements. Additionally, an extensive feature allocation study was conducted to examine how different feature types and their interactions influence the model's performance. Finally, an extensive parameter sensitivity study was performed to analyze how various hyper-parameters affect the model's quality. This comprehensive analysis enables researchers to better understand the feature contributions within the model and to select suitable hyper-parameters for specific tasks. Ultimately, the introduction of this system will facilitate gift purchasing, thereby enhancing user experiences on social networks. We introduce a novel randomized Set-Disjointness function, DSS$_{r,\epsilon}$, designed for data streams. Given two data streams $A$ and $B$ over a universe of $\mathcal{U}$ elements, where $A$ consists of a set $S_A \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ with each element appearing $r$ times and $B$ consists of a set $S_B \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ appearing $r+\epsilon$ times, DSS$_{r,\epsilon}$ evaluates whether $S_A$ and $S_B$ are disjoint. Our findings demonstrate that this function exhibits strong correlation properties: if the two sets share even a single element, the function outputs 1 with probability at least $1/2$. We provide the first deterministic reduction from DSS$_{r,\epsilon}$ to the standard Set-Disjointness function, SP$_1$, which operates on sets of unique elements. Furthermore, we establish that SP$_1$ admits only constant-sized certificates. Leveraging these results, we derive the first randomized streaming algorithms for detecting duplicates in data streams. Specifically, for any duplicate element present in the stream, our $\epsilon$-streaming algorithm identifies a duplicate with probability at least $1/2$ while utilizing $\epsilon$ space. This approach also yields a duplicate detection method that runs in time proportional to the stream size and requires only $\epsilon$ space. Additionally, our randomized algorithm achieves a significant reduction in both time and space complexity; for instance, it successfully detects duplicates with just $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$ space. Finally, we extend our duplicate detection algorithm to function as a cardinality estimation algorithm. In this variant, the algorithm estimates the number of distinct elements within the stream. For any true cardinality $C$, the estimated value $\hat{C}$ satisfies the condition $C - \epsilon \leq \hat{C} \leq C + \epsilon$ with a probability of at least $1/2$. The space complexity for this cardinality estimation also scales with $\epsilon$. Notably, the time complexity for estimating cardinality remains proportional to the size of the data stream. These results offer a substantial improvement over prior methods regarding both space complexity and error margins. High-precision measurements of the magnetic susceptibility of the Heisenberg paramagnet reveal a $-1.5$-order momentum dependence, a feature absent in standard perturbation theory. The non-analytic momentum term at order $k^{-1}$ significantly impacts critical phenomena within extended scaling frameworks. Specifically, in the renormalization group flow, the $k^{-1}$ term generates a dominant analytic field term that causes the momentum $k$ to vanish at a fixed point, leading to the decoupling of the momentum term from the susceptibility. Consequently, the momentum-independent Gaussian fixed point governs the critical behavior, resulting in susceptibility scaling with order $-2$. Furthermore, this extension of critical dimensions to arbitrary orders necessitates reevaluating critical dimensions and critical exponents; notably, the critical value of the critical dimension for the magnetic system is identified as $d_c=4.5$ at order $e^6$. Finally, a complete set of recursive differential equations for the magnetic system up to order $e^6$ is established, with the resulting renormalization group flow diagram presented. These findings are broadly applicable to all Heisenberg magnetic systems. Finally, the study examines the influence of the $k^{-1}$ term on the specific heat of the Heisenberg paramagnet. By extending the critical dimension to order $e^6$ and substituting the mass term with the momentum term, the momentum term is similarly eliminated, yielding a specific heat critical exponent of $\alpha=-1.5$ at this order. This outcome is consistent with the general relation $\alpha=2-dz$. At order $e^6$, the critical dimension is determined to be $d_c=4.5$, and the critical exponent is $z=1.5$. These results are also expected to apply to all Heisenberg magnetic systems. Additionally, the study explores the effects of the $k^{-1}$ term on the specific heat of the $O(N)$ model, which is closely related to the Heisenberg model. Finally, the critical properties of the Heisenberg model in the classical limit are also examined. In this regime, the Hamiltonian becomes independent of momentum, rendering all non-analymeric momentum terms in the renormalization group flow equation irrelevant. Therefore, the critical properties of the Heisenberg model in the classical limit are governed by the critical properties of the $O(3)$ model in the high-temperature (classical) limit, where the critical exponent is $\alpha=-1$.

This study introduces a novel single-atom experimental framework utilizing an ultrastable optical trap generated by an integrated multi-diffraction architecture. By employing multiplane light cones generated through multi-diffraction techniques, the research successfully demonstrates the entire cycle of single-atom interaction, trapping, manipulation, and readout within an integrated architecture based on waveguide all-photonic circuits. Specifically, we demonstrate the efficient trapping of a single Rubidium atom using a stable multi-diffraction atomic optical cagel. We also confirm effective manipulation of the trapped atom via radio-frequency excitation with an efficient atom-light interaction bus waveguide exhibiting an ultra-high quality factor of 1.1 billion. Furthermore, we achieve single-atom detection with a sensitivity surpassing the quantum limit by utilizing an integrated single-atom cavity sensor. These findings establish a new direction for the design and implementation of single-atom experimental systems. The proposed single-atom experimental architecture holds significant potential for fundamental research into single-atom quantum physics and quantum information, as well as for developing single-atom-based devices and applications within the field of integrated quantum technology. Additionally, the proposed all-photonic single-atom bus system is expected to serve as a pivotal component in large-scale quantum information processing and simulation. This work was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications. The nonlinear conductance of chiral edge states in (2+1)D topological systems has been a subject of intense debate. Specifically, the nonlinear response of current to a voltage drop along the edge of a generic chiral edge state has garnered significant attention. This work advances the debate by delivering a comprehensive solution for nonlinear response within non-interacting, time-reversal-broken edge states subjected to both weak and strong disorder. We begin by deriving an analytical expression for high-energy nonlinear conductance in generic chiral systems, incorporating local scattering and time-reversal-breaking potentials. Subsequently, we employ numerical simulations to investigate system size-dependent behavior, revealing a distinct transition in the system size regime where the high-energy formula becomes applicable. These numerical results align with our theoretical predictions. Finally, we extend our findings to interacting systems, demonstrating that a similar description holds for interacting edge states, with the effective velocity of the mode serving as the critical parameter. Furthermore, we show that our theoretical framework remains valid for time-reversal-invariant edge states, channel fermions, and any other generic chiral edge state characterized by a nonlinear response independent of system size. Finally, we report predictions regarding the linear and nonlinear Hall conductance of time-reversal-broken topological insulators with $K$ and $-K$ Landau levels, even under disordering potentials. We demonstrate that nonlinear conductance remains robust against disordering, whereas linear conductance exhibits a clear transition from system-size dependence to independence as the system size increases. Additionally, we observe that while the nonlinear Hall conductance displays an even-odd effect under disordering, the spin current exhibits a distinct odd-even behavior. Overall, our findings indicate that the nonlinear Hall conductance of chiral edge states is a robust phenomenon capable of withstanding disordering potentials. Finally, we show that the nonlinear conductance exhibits a distinct even-odd behavior under disordering, alongside a transition from system-size dependence to independence as the system size grows. Furthermore, we confirm that our theoretical framework is also applicable to interacting systems, where interaction effects are mediated by the mode velocity. In conclusion, our results demonstrate that the nonlinear Hall conductance of chiral edge states is a robust effect that persists despite disordering potentials. For a specific category of bicritical rational maps, the dynamics on the set of fixed points are governed by monodromy groups known as platform groups. We present a uniform methodology grounded in the theory of Drinfeld $\eta$-functions to compute these groups. Our findings extend the existing work of Baker and Faber, which was limited to polynomials, to encompass rational functions. Furthermore, our approach offers a unified perspective on two distinct methods previously used to determine platform groups for rational functions. Finally, we calculate the platform groups for all bicritical rational functions with a degree not exceeding 4.

To assess the viability of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) and transition metal di-dichalcogenides (TMD₂Cs) as critical components within molecular electronics circuits, we computed their thickness-dependent optical, electronic, and optical optical properties using both density functional theory (DVD) and GW methods. Specifically, we calculated the variation in work function (WF), ionization potential (IP), and electron affinity (EA) for these classes of materials. Our findings indicate that WF, IP, and EA exhibit a strong dependence on the number of layers. Additionally, incorporating GW corrections demonstrates significant importance when accurately determining optical functions and energy gaps. A machine learning model can be viewed as a lens that projects universal knowledge onto local, actionable, and interpretable data. This paper introduces a new category of lens spaces designed to naturally embody the universal supervised learning paradigm. We demonstrate that this framework is both more expressive and more intuitive than delta lenses, which are a restricted and less intuitive subset. Consequently, this flexibility significantly advances the subfield of explainable artificial intelligence. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of this lens framework to both distributional and out-of-distribution change propagation. Specifically, it offers a natural explanation for the failure of neural networks on distributional changes and provides a novel approach to change transmission via universal supervised learning through universal, subset, and subset-complexity lenses. These contributions advance the field of explainable artificial intelligence. Additionally, this paper serves as an extended version of [1].

We achieve the optimal Hölder continuity estimate with an explicit constant for solutions to the constant phase mean curvature equation across $\R^n$. Previously, this result was known only up to dimension 3. Furthermore, our proof establishes that the solution's regularity is independent of the data's regularity. While $L^\infty$ bounds are necessary for this derivation, no additional assumptions regarding the data are required. This work also furnishes a self-contained and streamlined demonstration of Siu's regularity theorem within the context of constant phase mean curvature flow. Notably, the proof techniques employed are notably quantitative. Finally, we observe that, unlike standard regularity theory, the uniform constant phase estimate cannot be interpreted as a higher-order energy estimate. This observation motivates an investigation into geometric properties linked to this phenomenon and leads to a conjecture concerning a specific class of degenerate elliptic equations. These geometric insights are integral to our derivation of the optimal regularity result. Additionally, the explicit constant is highly sensitive to dimension, and we provide separate discussions for high versus low dimensions. Finally, the methodology extends to yielding an explicit constant for uniformly constant phase solutions to more general phase-dependent curvature equations. Our findings have significant implications for understanding higher regularity in constant phase solutions, a topic that remains an active area of research. In this paper, we do not assume any regularity of the data or the solution beyond uniform boundedness. Our primary objective is to establish uniform regularity for constant phase solutions, a task essential for the well-posedness of constant phase mean curvature flow. Since higher regularity cannot be attained without additional data regularity, we are unable to derive an explicit formula for the constant; however, we can still construct the proof. Consequently, we conclude the paper by outlining an open conjecture regarding higher regularity and noting an outstanding question concerning the behavior of the constant. To our knowledge, no such conjecture or question currently exists in the literature. We also present an example illustrating how the constant can be computed in a specific scenario. Finally, we demonstrate the necessity of each assumption used in the proof and conjecture the optimality of the final regularity result. This study introduces an adaptive multiscale fixed-point iteration designed for rarefied gas systems characterized by significant variations in pressure and temperature. The method is built upon an implicit, fixed-point framework that integrates continuum-based Navier-Stokes-Fourier (NSF) equations with kinetic-based Boltzmann (Boltz) equations. Validation using fixed-point iterations on benchmark problems demonstrates the method's superior convergence properties compared to standard alternatives, enabling the solution of realistic 1D and 2D test cases within a limited number of iterations. Furthermore, these tests confirm the scheme's robustness when dealing inputs with large disparities in magnitude. The primary advantage lies in the rapid and stable convergence of both Boltzmann and NSF fixed-point operators. Finally, the SOR-based adaptive multiscale fixed-point approach effectively handles multiscale flows in 1D and 2D, achieving equilibrium states in less than 100 iterations. These results indicate high potential for application in complex flows. Additionally, the 2D test case involves high Mach and Reynolds numbers, as well as large disparities in Mach, Reynolds, and Knudsen numbers. This efficiency is largely attributed to the low-dissipation, non-dissipative, and non-oscillatory characteristics of the SOR method, alongside the use of a common mesh for both NSF and Boltzmann operators. The primary challenge remains the implicit treatment of viscous and heat-conduction terms in the NSF operator, which is essential for rapid convergence. Overall, the 2D test case was solved in under 100 iterations, representing a substantial reduction in computational time. This rapid convergence is achieved through an adaptive multiscale approach that utilizes a continuum (NSF) model for a subset of the computational domain. The primary drawback is the current inability to automate the selection of the continuum domain. Future research will address this limitation by developing an automatic, physics-based, and mathematically rigorous algorithm to identify the continuum domain. Additionally, the R15H kinetic model will be employed to further verify the scheme's robustness under conditions of large density and temperature differences. Finally, extending the method to higher dimensions remains a necessary future step. The recent detection of ten TeV gamma rays from the Galactic Center has sparked significant debate regarding their origin. Various theories propose that these gamma rays result from rare, simultaneous events that could be categorized into distinct classes based on their temporal and spatial characteristics. This study introduces a machine learning approach designed to identify the optimal parameters for a multi-class event grouping algorithm. The method evaluates a vast number of potential candidates by analyzing the event spectrum, temporal and spatial distributions, and energy deposition structures. A physics-informed algorithm is subsequently applied to examine the groupings of these events, with specific attention given to the axion quark nugget (AQN) dark matter model. In this scenario, gamma rays are emitted when AQNs annihilate with quark nuggets (QNs) in the Galactic Center. Furthermore, AQN-QN annihilations offer a potential resolution to the problem of cosmic ray anisotropies observed in the GeV energy range. Finally, the analysis explores the implications of these findings for dark matter indirect detection. These results are derived from public data released by the LHAASO Collaboration. Additionally, we outline a comprehensive experimental program for the LHAASO Galactic Region Event Database (LHAASO-GREDB), which aims to publish event data and advance multi-messenger astronomy. This database will facilitate multi-messenger studies of the Galactic Center and contribute to solving the dark matter mystery. Ultimately, LHAASO-GREDB will enhance our ability to detect and characterize cosmic gamma-ray sources. This work was conducted by a collaboration including C. Li, Z. Liang, Z. Li, X. Liang, Z. Li, Z. We outline the $p$-divisibility relations among Siegel modular forms, which follow from their Fourier coefficients. These relations are utilized to examine the $p$-divisibility of the Fourier elements of Sp(8). The $i$-th fundamental $p$-divisibility relation is also applied in conjunction with the linear independence of the $i$-th Iwasawa invariants of the exterior power $L$-functions. This approach yields an upper bound for the order of a $p$-Selmer group of an abelian variety of genus $i$, which is optimal when $i=1$. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the Iwasawa invariants of the exterior power $L$-functions for genus $1$ abelian varieties, which improves upon the previous best bound by a factor of $4p$. Finally, we suggest a conjecture regarding the $p$-divisibility of the Iwasawa invariants of the exterior power $L$-functions. Additionally, we outline a conjecture concerning the size of the Fourier $p$-divisibility relations for genus $3$ abelian varieties, which refines a conjecture by Gross. We demonstrate that these two conjectures collectively imply the $p$-divisibility relations for genus $3$, extending the established relations for genus $1$ and $2$. The author intends to publish a subsequent paper detailing the construction of these relations for genus $4$ and $5$. This work serves as a foundation for a broader research initiative aimed at establishing analytic Conjecture A for abelian varieties of genus $3$ and proving analytic Conjecture B. This line of inquiry employs analytic number theory methods, specifically the analytic theory of Siegel modular forms, alongside algebraic number theory and algebraic geometry techniques within Iwasawa theory. The Pauli exclusion principle dictates that fermions cannot occupy the same quantum state. This paper demonstrates that when fermions are placed in a thermal bath, multiple exclusion principles emerge. The most fundamental is the 1D Pauli exclusion principle.Border exclusion principles govern scenarios where fermions are prohibited from occupying neighboring sites, while the n-step Pauli exclusion principle prevents fermions from landing within n sites of one another. This study focuses on the 2D Pauli exclusion principle, where fermions cannot occupy sites adjacent horizontally or vertically. We derive its thermodynamic interpretation for both zero and high temperatures. In the high-temperature limit, we show that the specific heat of Pauli crystals is identical to that of free fermion gases. Additionally, employing the transfer matrix method, we calculate the specific heat for 2D Pauli crystals of Pauli gas crystals in the zero-temperature limit. Our findings indicate that the specific heat of Pauli crystals approaches zero as the temperature nears absolute zero. Finally, we extend the thermodynamic analysis of 1D and 2D Pauli crystals to encompass ideal crystals of any dimension $d$. Furthermore, the concepts of "nD Pauli exclusion principle" and "nD Pauli crystal" are introduced for the first time. Finally, the significant physical implications of 2D Pauli crystals regarding the thermodynamic behavior of interacting fermion systems are explored. These insights offer a novel theoretical foundation for investigating the thermodynamic properties of fermion gases in both 2D and 3D environments. To our knowledge, this marks the inaugural investigation into the specific heat of Pauli crystals. Additionally, the outcomes of our thermodynamic study offer a fresh perspective for examining the phase transitions in fermion systems. To illustrate the practical utility of 2D Pauli crystals, we examine the thermodynamic properties of a reduced Hubbard model. Our research establishes a direct link between the specific heat of Pauli crystals and the specific heat of the reduced Hubbard model. This confirms the existence of a critical temperature at which the specific heat of the reduced Hubbard model exhibits a discontinuity. Consequently, our work provides a new approach to investigating the phase transitions within the reduced Hubbard model. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to utilize the specific heat of Pauli crystals to analyze the phase transitions of the reduced Hubbard model.
