This paper addresses time-vaulting matrix problems that are critical across diverse fields such as computer science, control engineering, and physics. While various methods exist to handle these issues, most rely on simulations that do not inherently yield predictions for time-varying data. Furthermore, existing solutions often suffer from computational inefficiencies and a lack of comprehensive theoretical frameworks. To overcome these limitations, we propose an optimized framework based on Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNNs) for calculating forward and backward neural network outputs. The forward ZNN approach enables the rapid generation of temporal forecasts for time-varying data, while the backward ZNN (BZNN) scheme ensures the convergence of the solution process. The development of novel x-ray optical components is currently driving advancements in both laboratory experiments and astrophysical observations. However, as the x-ray wavelength range utilized by these devices shifts from meters to nanometers, significant challenges arise in achieving broad-field use with high sensitivity and resolution. This review examines current methods for boosting the optical performance of wide-field x-ray devices, addressing three primary categories of imperfections: intensity variations, spatial distortion, and blurring. We specifically focus on x-ray grazing incidence technologies, which are essential for both astrophysical missions like Chandra, XMM-Newton, and future successors such as Athena, as well as for ground-based research. Ultimately, we analyze the most effective strategies for enhancing the optical specifications of these devices. Given the growing interest from commercial entities in producing x-ray optics, we also provide an overview of the underlying physical principles and the mathematical tools required for characterization. Furthermore, we explore methods for simulating the performance of these devices. A key finding is that while Monte Carlo simulations offer the highest accuracy, they are computationally intensive and often impractical for characterizing complex devices; consequently, we advocate for a hybrid approach combining Monte Carlo methods with ray tracing to balance precision with computational efficiency. Finally, we outline an open-source Python-based ray-tracing package that facilitates characterizing and optimizing grazing incidence devices. This tool is freely available to assist researchers in advancing x-ray technologies. By integrating this software with Monte Carlo simulations, users can achieve the highest level of detail possible. Additionally, we present a dedicated website dedicated to x-ray device characterization, which serves as a valuable resource for those interested in the field. This platform provides access to the software, along with extensive information on device performance, imperfections, and improvement techniques. We believe this comprehensive online resource will be highly beneficial to the x-ray community. A full version of this review is available as a white paper. This paper introduces a Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) based algorithm designed to learn the structure of a target network in a distributed setting while maintaining data privacy. This work extends our previous research documented in arXiv:2006.01010 and arXiv:2006.01011, which utilized singularly private and federated GW-based learning methods for graph metric alignment. The primary innovation of this study is the integration of local differential privacy (LDP) into the GW algorithm. In a distributed environment, communicating private edge features between agents and a central server poses significant privacy risks. To mitigate this, we apply LDP, a privacy guarantee where each data holder encrypts their local data before transmission. This is achieved by perturbing edge features with noise during the algorithm. We demonstrate that the proposed GW algorithm preserves graph isomorphism and effectively identifies correct neighbors. Furthermore, we prove that the distributed GW algorithm with LDP offers $\epsilon$-graph differential privacy, establishing a relationship between sample size and privacy leakage. Finally, experiments on real-world datasets confirm that the algorithm successfully learns graph structure, meeting both privacy and accuracy requirements. These findings indicate that the proposed algorithm can identify correct neighbors even under strict privacy constraints. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi-1995/DLGP.

Double beta decay stands out as a premier field for investigating fundamental weak and strong interactions within nuclear matter. This study reports both direct and indirect constraints on the double beta decay of $^{204}$Pt $\rightarrow$ $^{204}$Pb, covering the process, its associated weak-axion potential, and dark matter-induced mechanisms. Notably, the $^{204}$Pt $\rightarrow$ $^{204}$Pb channel offers a unique pathway to detect dark matter via coherent elastic scattering, owing to its exceptionally low threshold energy of 1.1 keV. Furthermore, the analysis examines the previously proposed $^{204}$Pt $\rightarrow$ $^{198}$Os channel, which was earlier dismissed due to an inaccurate Q-value. The resulting limits are significantly more restrictive than prior findings, with the new $^{204}$Pt $\rightarrow$ $^{204}$Pb constraint improving over the old limit by two orders of magnitude. These results are compared against other established limits and projected future sensitivities, including those from upcoming experiments. Additionally, the study explores the potential of $^{204}$Pt as a viable channel for dark matter searches using existing high-purity germanium detectors. The work concludes with a discussion of the channel's advantages and the experimental advancements necessary to achieve optimal sensitivity. All calculated half-lives and matrix elements are provided in an associated repository for future investigations. The findings suggest that $^{204}$Pt is a promising channel for double beta decay research, and its full potential can be unlocked through dedicated experiments utilizing large quantities of this isotope. Specifically, the study recommends the development of a novel experimental approach to the $^{204}$Pt $\rightarrow$ $^{204}$Pb channel, which could achieve sensitivity orders of magnitude beyond current limits. This could be accomplished by deploying a large array of high-purity germanium detectors at a dedicated dark matter facility, where the low energy threshold would enable sensitivity to both the $^{204}$Pt $\rightarrow$ $^{204}$Pb double beta decay channel and potential dark matter interactions. The paper also addresses the challenges of isolating and enriching $^{204}$Pt, the complexities of setting up the experiment, and the necessary steps to achieve the desired sensitivity. Ultimately, the $^{204}$Pt channel holds great promise for advancing double beta decay research, and its full potential can be realized through further experimental efforts.

These contributions represent a significant advancement in the theory of the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system. We demonstrate that in any local, continuous, and non-reversible symmetry within a many-body quantum system, there must exist a low-energy excitation located at zero momentum. This phenomenon serves as a form of Spontaneous Non-reversible Symmetry Breaking. Our finding extends the Generalized Nonrenormalization Theorem from superfluid helium, originally derived by Hohenberg and Halperin for systems with spatial translation and rotation invariance, into a purely quantum framework applicable to any many-body quantum system, including isolated atoms and ions. Furthermore, we show that the wavefunction of this low-energy excitation is directly proportional to the generator of the non-reversible symmetry, a relationship that constitutes a manifestation of the Cottingham relation. This insight is corroborated by both numerical and analytical studies of non-relativistic free fermions and bosons. Additionally, we examine the possibility of Spontaneous Time Reversal Symmetry Breaking in quantum Hall states and free fermion systems. A key distinction from relativistic field theory is that the low-energy excitation need not be unique; it may possess a non-trivial degeneracy at zero momentum, a characteristic particularly relevant for non-reversible symmetries. This study introduces a novel analytical framework for modeling intermodal forward Brillouin scattering diffusion within solid-core photonic crystal fibers. The interaction between two spatial modes is characterized by four distinct energy transfer coefficients, which are calculated using the interaction integral method. These coefficients are conditioned on the relative orientations of the involved polarizations and the spatial profiles of the modes. Furthermore, an analytical solution is derived for the evolution of power differences between the two interacting modes over time and along the fiber. This theoretical approach eliminates the necessity for numerical computation of interaction coefficients and provides immediate access to the system's dynamics. The validity of this theory is confirmed through comparisons with results obtained from finite element method simulations and experimental data. Finally, successful demonstrations of energy transfer between two modes and the observation of periodic power exchange in a practical experimental setup using a Photonic Bandgap Hollow Fiber are presented. The proposed theory is applicable to any fiber supporting multiple spatial modes and can facilitate the design and analysis of advanced devices capable of generating multiple copies of a pump signal. Additionally, it enables the investigation of complex dynamics in multi-mode, multi-brillouin systems, which are currently beyond the reach of existing analytical methods. This study introduces a new metaheuristic designed to address two closely related optimization problems: the Set-Union Knapsack Challenge (SKU) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Issue (BMC). In the SKU problem, a decision-maker selects items with associated costs from a costed set, ensuring that the total cost does not exceed a specified budget. The goal is to maximize the number of distinct sets covered by the chosen items, where coverage is determined by the union of selected elements. The BMC problem is a specific variant of SKU that further requires all selected items to have a cost of exactly 1. Both problems are provably NP-hard, and existing literature has developed metaheuristics for them; however, these methods often struggle with intractable runtime complexities. Our proposed approach employs local search, which is renowned for its strong performance on optimization tasks. To enhance efficiency, we implemented several modifications, including a preprocessing stage, optimizations for the local search component, and a novel clustering technique. The efficacy of this algorithm is validated through numerical experiments on synthetic datasets. Results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in both problems, achieving superior solutions within significantly shorter computational times. Additionally, the paper provides insights into the utility of the preprocessing and clustering algorithms. Finally, we outline future research directions that leverage the properties of SKU and BMC as applications of the broader Set-Union Selection issue.

Gauging the transverse momentum distribution (TMD) of gluons is essential for addressing certain experimental and phenomenological challenges. In proton-proton collisions, specific observables in vector-boson production and coherently diffractive physics are sensitive to gluon TMDs. Additionally, certain features of the back-to-back dijet distribution at moderate vector-pair $q_T$ in hadron colliders may arise from the gluon Sivers function. This study demonstrates that the TMD of gluons, $f_{\scriptscriptstyle{g}/\scriptscriptstyle{g}}(x,k_T^2)$, can be derived from the parton distribution function of the transverse momentum-dependent generalised leading twist, $F_2^{(n,k)}(x, Q^2)$, a well-established structure function in deep-inelastic scattering. Utilizing the $n$-th moment of $F_2^{(k)}(x,Q^2)$ within large-momentum effective theory, we successfully recover the parton splitting function $P_{gg}(x)$ and the gluon TMD $f_{\scriptscriptstyle{g}/\scriptscriptstyle{g}}(x,k_T^2)$, even at low $Q^2$. This approach offers a new method for determining the gluon TMD from deep-inelastic scattering data, which is anticipated to become available in the near future. Furthermore, this technique may prove useful for extracting light-quark and gluon TMDs in the future. A python-based public code, \texttt{GM-PDF}, is provided to facilitate these calculations. This tool is currently being utilized to extract the gluon TMD from the HERA deep-inelastic scattering dataset. The paper also examines the prospects of employing the LHC vector-boson and dijet datasets for gluon TMD extraction. Finally, the study explores the implications of the small-$x$ limit of the TMD for the longitudinal structure function $F_2^{(n,k)}(x,Q^2)$, which is closely related to the generalized hadron orbital angular momentum distribution. This work may have broader applications in the field of hadron physics. The paper includes several appendices covering topics such as the derivation of the splitting function from the moment of the structure function, the derivation of the TMD from the moment, the vector-boson and dijet moments, and a discussion on the non-moment of the structure function. Cycling is a popular mode of transport, particularly in dense urban areas, though accidents remain a significant concern due to high injury and mortality rates involving cyclists and pedestrians. Utilizing computer vision, the method analyzes video footage to generate a real-time, context-sensitive risk indicator. When a user activates the indicator, the system examines the current video frame to evaluate collision risk by measuring the distance between the cyclist and other road users, such as cars and pedestrians. This descriptor is integrated into the Cyclist Risk and Accident Predictor (CRAP) application, enabling users to monitor their instantaneous risk exposure. Furthermore, the method can be extended to evaluate environmental factors influencing risk exposure. The approach is validated using over 1,000 cyclist crash records from Barcelona, Spain, and tested across various urban settings. Deep neural networks (DNNs) achieve remarkable performance across numerous real-world applications, yet they remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we show that the AN framework is compatible with model ensembles, offering a straightforward and effective strategy for further strengthening resilience. Nonlocal transport models, frequently utilized in particle physics, fluid dynamics, and continuum mechanics, can be viewed as a perturbation of classical local models. This perturbation exhibits singular behavior when the model parameters approach zero. This study rigorously analyzes the singular limit for a class of nonlocal transport models that encompass the standard linear models as a specific instance. We demonstrate the entropy admissibility of these models and establish a convergence rate for the sequence of solutions to the local transport equation as the perturbation parameters vanish. The proof relies on a maximum principle applied to the difference between nonlocal and local solutions. Furthermore, we examine the case of periodic boundary conditions and address several open questions. Notably, our findings regarding the convergence rate are optimal when local transport models are unique, meaning they cannot be improved upon. However, in scenarios where local transport models admit multiple solutions, resolving the issue of convergence rates remains an open problem. Finally, we present a new class of nonlocal transport models where the proof of the convergence rate relies on novel techniques. To address the issue of entropy admissibility, we employ two novel concepts: entropy defect measures and the entropy defect function. This approach is particularly valuable for verifying the mathematical well-posedness of nonlocal transport models that cannot be reduced to local transport models with standard defect measures. Additionally, we establish the uniqueness of this class of models. The paper concludes with an outline of the numerical implementation. We begin with a numerical implementation of entropy defect measures, demonstrating that the defect function remains non-negative in the case of periodic boundary conditions. This study demonstrates that every Morse-Smale dilation surface containing this horizon saddle link is a covering surface for either regular heptagonal or triangular tilings of the plane as observed from the Poincaré disk. Furthermore, we establish that all such surfaces are affine surfaces and propose a method to construct a closed surface with these horizon saddle links as closed geodesics within any given genus. Finally, we present examples of surfaces featuring multiple disjoint horizon saddle links and conjecture that, although these horizon closed geodesics are not necessarily stable, they constitute the stable closed geodesics of all Morse-Smale dilation surfaces. The proof of this conjecture relies on a key result by Athanasiadis and Goodwillie. This study introduces a total association matrix that synthesizes strong, weak, and zero correlations to more comprehensively characterize the functional connectome. By integrating this matrix with a low-rank representation through rank-preserving Riemannian dimensionality reduction, we successfully extract the core structural components of the functional connectome. This methodology is applied to analyze the functional connectome of 28 healthy individuals using task-based fMRI data, revealing an association network with a one-dimensional topological structure. The network's endpoints correspond to the visual and motor cortices, which are hypothesized to be the primary drivers of the brain's functional association network during cognitive tasks. Furthermore, we reconstruct the functional connectome using a low-rank matrix composed of cortical principal components, demonstrating that this approach effectively captures the fundamental brain structure while filtering out noise. Finally, we establish the efficacy of the proposed method for dimensionality reduction and its superiority over traditional techniques in this context. In Reinforcement Learning, Variance Decrease Learning (VDL) was originally proposed to accelerate convergence by minimizing post-decision variance. This study investigates a modified version of VDL, termed PEP-VDL, which incorporates prior knowledge regarding the impact of actions on states. We demonstrate that PEP-VDL can serve as a policy improvement step in Policy Gradient methods, thereby enhancing their performance. For experimental validation, we utilize the Lunar Lander environment, comparing our approach against prior versions of VDL and established policy-improvement techniques. These results provide empirical support for the efficacy of PEP-VDL, particularly in promoting safe actions during critical episodes. Additionally, we present theoretical findings for on-policy policy improvement, analyzing the necessary conditions for convergence. Finally, we evaluate the approach in a real-world scenario involving a robotic arm tasked with opening a child-proof medicine cabinet, aiming to minimize attempts at opening the door incorrectly. Video demonstrations are available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=14222222222. The code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/PEP-VDL. Our findings indicate that PEP-VDL achieves significantly more successful unlearning attempts and requires fewer unlearning attempts overall compared to other methods. Furthermore, the proposed approach surpasses existing techniques in safety, as evidenced by lower average total rewards per episode. This success is attributed to the method's ability to encourage safe actions when the task is unlikely to succeed. The accompanying code enables the replication of these results and facilitates the exploration of new possibilities. We have also empirically demonstrated the effectiveness of PEP-VDL in learning to walk on uneven terrain, successfully navigating without falling. This success is evidenced by the agent's ability to move forward without attempting to correct a fall. The code allows for the replication of these results and for investigating how the method performs across different terrains. When two objects are imaged under conditions where diffraction is significant, their combined image results from the convolution of the individual object images with the point spread function (PSF). A common simplification assumes that the PSF remains unchanged for objects of different brightness or color. However, this study demonstrates through examples that the PSF can vary with intensity and wavelength. Such changes are most pronounced in the core of the PSF, which corresponds to the Airy disk, whereas the Airy rings remain approximately constant. The varying behavior of the central peak stems from the aperture's diffraction characteristics, specifically the amplitude transmission, and consequently impacts the central intensity and full width at half maximum. These findings are illustrated using several examples. The proposed model proves particularly valuable in astronomy for analyzing images of point-like stars, where variations in the central peak's shape are more detectable due to lower image intensities. The methodology is also applicable to other imaging systems. The examples provided highlight the distinct behaviors of the PSF in both its core and its rings. This distinction is crucial when analyzing images of compact, extended, or mixed sources, as it allows for the accurate estimation of the relative contributions of individual objects to the combined image. This capability is essential for determining the physical properties of the objects and the parameters of the imaging system. Additionally, the study examines how to quantify the differences between PSFs, noting that while a standard chi-squared test is applicable to the Airy rings, it is not suitable for analyzing the central peak. Finally, the paper outlines the specific characteristics of the center and the rings. To facilitate the analysis of combined images, a Python package named \texttt{psf} is provided, which includes a function to calculate the varying PSF and its parameters. We introduce an analytical approach grounded in linear elasticity and statistical mechanics to investigate the resilience of crystalline materials against fracture. Our method incorporates energetic defects, specifically dislocations, and evaluates resilience using energetic and geometric criteria. The primary findings are: (i) when a material is loaded near its dislocation source strength, the proposed energetic metric predicts a significantly higher resilience exponent—aligning with experimental data on metals and ceramics—compared to the geometric metric, which relies on mechanical stress; (ii) incorporating dislocation relaxation effects into the analysis reveals that resilience becomes tunable, depending on the specific arrangement of crystal defects; and (iii) our theoretical resilience estimates for brittle materials exceed those for ductile materials. These results advance our understanding of how atomic-scale phenomena govern bulk material resilience and highlight new avenues for enhancing it. Furthermore, this framework offers a novel paradigm for fracture resilience that complements the conventional distinction between brittle and ductile behaviors. We have made our predictions and simulations accessible through an open-source resilience calculator available at resilience411.org. Ultimately, this research demonstrates a pathway to improved structural integrity in materials and structures. We investigate statistical mechanics frameworks featuring Gaussian free fields interacting with random curves, specifically Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs) driven by random points. Within this context, we propose a novel random log-gas comprising two components: SLEs at capacity $\gamma^2$ representing the SLEs fields, and points at activity $2\sqrt{2}\alpha$ representing the conditioning fields. Focusing on a unique equilibrium state known as the Borodin-Petrov state, we demonstrate novel determinantal structures using Jacobi processes and establish broad scaling limits as the domain expands. These findings imply that the field configurations of the gas scale jointly with the domains in hydrodynamic limit. Furthermore, we illustrate applications to an infinite strip and propose an $\mathrm{SL}(N)$-generalization of the Borodin-Petrov state. This work extends our prior research [10, 11] and stands as the first instance of modeling a gas of random curves via a random log-gas. Additionally, it offers an alternative characterization of Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surfaces, as the conditioning field can be linked to Liouville theory [16, 20, 21]. Finally, our methodology may hold promise for studying more complex stochastic geometries, such as multiple SLEs or random surfaces. This study establishes new bounds for the solution norms of the Navier-Stokes equations using the maximum norm under periodic initial conditions. These findings suggest that regularity can be managed more effectively in this scenario compared to other initial value problems. The derivation relies on a technique by Kato, applied here within a Fourier setting to achieve Fourier-based anisotropic estimates. Additionally, we explore alternative resolution methods and provide several useful observations. As practical applications, we offer specific examples demonstrating that the derived estimates are effective. The computer code employed for these calculations is made available. Furthermore, we present a novel result confirming the logarithmic optimality of our findings in the case of $L^3$ data, extending the work of S. Kato and P. G. Constantine. Our maximum norm estimates could also hold significant value for addressing turbulent flows with periodic disturbances. For instance, in a shear flow scenario, a sufficiently strong transverse perturbation can trigger instability, leading to the generation of streamwise vortices and streaks. Our analysis indicates that for small Reynolds numbers, this perturbation effect diminishes rapidly, whereas it may be significantly amplified at higher Reynolds numbers. Similar conclusions can likely be reached for other periodic problems, potentially offering valuable insights into various physical phenomena. We anticipate that the earlier mentioned turbulent problems will also benefit from our maximum norm estimates. Traditional verification of quantum computations has primarily depended on downloading the full quantum state for analysis. This paper introduces a method to validate the final states of N-qubit systems in linear time (O(N log N)) using substantially fewer measurements, thereby enhancing verification efficiency. The approach utilizes classical shadows to construct high-caliber estimators for Pauli coefficients, which are then compared against the known coefficients of the target final state. We demonstrate the universality of this technique by testing the generation of various multimode Gaussian states—such as single-mode squeezed, two-mode entangled, two-mode squeezed vacuum, and two-mode cluster states—using Gaussian unitary evolution on Gaussian input states. Experimental results indicate that this method supports high-caliber fidelity analysis for these states within linear time. Furthermore, traditional verification is shown to be more time-efficient than downstream methods for tasks like fidelity estimation and hypothesis testing. These findings lay a foundation for achieving time-efficient fidelity analysis and resource-efficient quantum verification. The code supporting this work is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/Time-Efficient-Verification-of-Quantum-Calculations. Additionally, we have developed a free package named TEVQA (Time-Efficient Quantum Assessment) to facilitate practical implementation of traditional verification for quantum computations. The package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install TEVQA. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/Time-Efficient-Verification-of-Quantum-Calculations. TEVQA is also accessible on Zenodo at 10.5298/zenodo.8178775. Future updates to the package will include an automated protocol design feature that allows users to input a quantum circuit, after which the program will automatically generate a verification protocol using traditional verification. This functionality is currently available only for circuits that produce multimode input states. We anticipate that traditional verification will prove valuable for assessing the performance of various quantum computing platforms. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness against noise, enabling the accurate analysis of final states produced by noisy quantum circuits. This capability is particularly significant for near-term quantum processors, such as superconducting quantum computers, that are susceptible to circuit depth limitations. Consequently, traditional verification serves as a practical tool for evaluating the performance of quantum computing platforms within linear time. Finally, we propose extending traditional verification to support the verification of quantum operations. This paper focuses on traditional verification methods tailored for quantum computations. We introduce a deep generative framework designed to produce realistic 3D cell shapes. Our approach is built on the concept of implicit representations, which are defined as the zero-level sets of continuous functions. Specifically, we utilize a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to learn a continuous implicit shape function from real cell images, modeling the cell boundary as the interface where the function's output equals zero. This learned function is capable of reconstructing various cell forms, even those that differ significantly from the shapes observed in training data. By employing the implicit Hamilton-Jacobi formulation of level-set methods, we demonstrate that the proposed model can generate forms that are creative and bio-physically plausible for cell dynamics. Furthermore, we present a method to induce anisotropy in synthetic cell forms by integrating a pre-defined elliptical shape with the generative model. Our experimental results indicate that the model can produce novel, realistic cell dynamics and forms that diverge from the input dataset. Additionally, we show that the model can recover synthetic cells generated by ground-truth dynamics, as well as input cells that exhibit partial resemblance to the synthetic dynamics. Finally, we find that the model is robust to variations in training parameters, even when cell morphologies vary widely within the training set. This model holds promise for applications in cell form synthesis, interactive shape design, and the investigation of generic properties and constraints inherent to cell shapes and dynamics. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/akimasa/SIGGRAPH-Asia-2020-implicit-cell. This work is supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 19K14208.

The surge in digital content has created a pressing and often overlooked necessity for accessibility, which this paper addresses through a multi-faceted, mixed-method approach combining literature review, case studies, and interviews. Drawing on concepts from computer science, education, and sociology, the discussion centers on access barriers faced by non-native English speakers, children, and print-impaired individuals, with a specific emphasis on the latter group. The primary argument contends that documents accessible to print-impaired users must be structured in machine-readable formats, such as HTML or XML, rather than static ones like PDF or PPTX. Supporting this claim, the paper examines the distinct challenges faced by screen reader users, alongside the secondary and tertiary arguments that formatted accessibility serves non-print-impaired users (specifically learners and non-native speakers) and constitutes an ethical imperative. Finally, the conclusion explores the potential consequences of neglecting this necessity and offers suggestions for advancing the field of document accessibility. A key contribution of this work is its synthesis of diverse literature across disciplines to construct and support accessibilty claims, while its case studies provide fresh perspectives on applying accessibility principles to education and language learning. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that accessibility extends beyond being a necessity; it is an ethical obligation. Supporting materials are available at https://github.com/Divyansh-1999/document-accessibility. The paper's title is Document Accessibility: A Necessity for Non-Print Impaired Users. We introduce XLNet, a generalized pre-training approach designed to address the limitations of current autoregressive Transformer baselines in language modeling and comprehension tasks. Specifically, we replace the fixed autoregressive structure with an XLNet order based on \textit{next token} prediction via \textit{mutual information} maximization, initiate the self-attention mechanism through an out-of-vocabulary token, manage mutual masking to resolve conflicts between attention and masked language pre-training, and propose a linear transformation to capture mutual information across diverse token types. Consequently, XLNet achieves superior performance in both language modeling and downstream tasks compared to existing methods. Specifically, it gains +2.3/+1.9 F1 points on SQuAD, +1.3/+0.9 on WikiText, and an additional +2.7 F1 point on RTE, while utilizing 1.6x fewer pre-training tokens. Furthermore, we conduct an empirical analysis of mutual information objectives and their connection to information theory. Exoplanet atmospheres are typically studied through transit spectroscopy, which analyzes changes in a planet's transit depth across different wavelengths. However, stellar activity introduces significant noise into these measurements, making it difficult to distinguish between stellar and planetary signals, especially when using low-resolution spectra. This study simulates spot-crossing events in both low and high-resolution spectra of an active star transiting in front of it. By comparing these events to low-resolution data, we can determine if high-resolution spectroscopy serves as an effective mitigation strategy. Our simulations indicate that high-resolution spectroscopy does not eliminate spot-crossing events from low-resolution spectra; instead, it allows for the precise tracking of spots to better characterize them and improve the correction of their effects. Consequently, combining high and low-resolution spectra offers a more robust approach to transit spectroscopy than relying on low-resolution data alone. We conclude that utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy will substantially reduce the noise in transit spectroscopy over time. Additionally, we introduce the Open Source Python package `spactran`, which employs the Ray tracing library `libart` to simulate these events. The package includes a sample active star and provides a method for interpolating observed spectra to match simulated spectra, facilitating easier comparison. The package can be accessed at https://github.com/SpencerKraemer/spactran. Our findings also have implications for exoplanet atmospheres with low signal-to-noise ratios, such as Kepler-13b. We demonstrate that spot crossing events in Kepler-13b's spectrum are likely responsible for the absorption features detected in low-resolution data, and that high-resolution spectroscopy will aid in mitigating this contamination. Ultimately, we argue that transit spectroscopy should be conducted simultaneously with high-resolution spectroscopy to effectively account for stellar activity. This approach will enhance our understanding of exoplanet atmospheres and our success in detecting biosignatures. While hydrodynamic theory offers a well-developed framework for predicting the movement of self-propelled objects across liquid surfaces, its applicability to fluid bio-locomotion remains uncertain. This study examines fluid surface interactions using both experimental and numerical methods to evaluate existing hydrodynamic models. We present the *Helophasa* centipede as a novel self-propelled object on a water surface, detailing its morphological and physiological adaptations for surface travel. By measuring key physical parameters of both the centipedes and the water surface, we analyze their surface locomotion dynamics. Our findings indicate that *Helophasa* centipedes generate significant surface ripples during movement, causing them to displace substantially more water mass than predicted by classical hydrodynamic models. Consequently, we propose a new theoretical framework for fluid bio-locomotion that integrates biological traits with advanced hydrodynamic principles. This work establishes a foundation for investigating biological systems and their interactions with hydrodynamic forces. Furthermore, the body plan of *Helophasa* centipedes holds potential for bio-inspired bio-robots, which could aid in environmental remediation and serve as bio-sensors. We present early JWST NIRCam imaging of 12 optically faint yet luminous ($L\gtrsim L^*$) galaxies at $z\sim 2-3$, which were previously obscured by dust extinction ($A_V\gtrsim 2$ mag) and thus missed by optical surveys. By analyzing these images, we determined the rest-frame UV surface brightness ($S_{UV}$) and examined how it varies with redshift, extinction, and star formation rate (SFR). Our results indicate that these galaxies are compact, with $S_{UV}$ values ranging from 100 to 1000 $L^{\odot}_{UV}$ pc$^{-2}$. We demonstrate that $S_{UV}$ correlates with $A_V$ and $z$, but remains independent of SFR. The $S_{UV}$ values observed in these dusty galaxies are comparable to those found in massive starbursts at $z\lesssim 1$ and in local starbursts and star-forming galaxies. This implies that the star-forming regions in these dusty, optically dim galaxies are likely small-scale and virginal, rather than being composed of larger regions with lower surface density. Furthermore, we estimate that these optically hidden, infrared-bright galaxies account for approximately 10% of the total $L^*$-normalized SFR density at $z\sim 2-3$. This finding suggests that traditional optical surveys have significantly underestimated the SFR density of star-forming galaxies during the cosmic epoch of peak star formation. Finally, we conclude that JWST's ability to detect the $S_{UV}$ of galaxies behind high $A_V$ will be essential for uncovering the true nature of star formation. Ultimately, this study highlights the critical role of JWST in revealing the physical characteristics of galaxies that were previously invisible to optical observations. Future work will be conducted on the remaining sample once JWST capabilities are fully utilized. This study examines the impact of external electric fields on non-covalent interactions within the S66 basis set test set. The investigation relies on symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT) test calculations to assess how field-induced changes in interaction energy components correlate with variations in molecular orbital phases. While applying an external field of 0.005 au along the molecular axis results in a significant reversal of highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbital phases, it causes only a negligible alteration in the total interaction energy for any molecular pair. In contrast, perpendicular application of the same field magnitude generates a comparable orbital energy gap but produces a distinct shift in orbital phases. This phase shift correlates with a more pronounced change in interaction energy, particularly for dispersion, which is identified as the primary contributor to the field effect. The research further confirms that this phenomenon is more significant in weak interactions and that its magnitude varies based on the specific axis orientation used to apply the external field. Finally, the study demonstrates that such non-negligible effects on molecular pair interactions can occur even at relatively high external field strengths. These findings are further validated by comparing the spectroscopy of benzene and toluene under similar conditions. Overall, the research indicates that while external electric fields do not drastically affect interaction energy, they are capable of inducing significant shifts in orbital phases and electron density distributions. Consequently, this underscores the necessity for high-accuracy quantum chemical methods when modeling molecular systems subjected to such fields. Additionally, the study explores potential applications of these findings in understanding non-covalent interactions in external field-assisted processes, such as molecular separation. Specifically, it is shown that an external electric field can enhance the selectivity of field-induced alignment for certain dimers, including benzoic acid dimers. Furthermore, under these conditions, benzoic acid dimers exhibit a stronger preference for alignment parallel to the dimer axis compared to dimers formed by structurally similar molecules like phenol. These results suggest that external electric fields could play a crucial role in influencing benzoic acid dimerization and alignment, a factor that must be accounted for in future research on benzoic acid crystallization. Finally, the paper addresses the potential significance of this phenomenon in understanding non-covalent interactions in benzoic acid dimers within strong electric fields, such as those present at the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope. The inherent non-determinism and ambiguity in Industry 4.0 cyber-physical systems make meta-heuristic approaches insufficient for generating high-quality schedules. Consequently, this study focuses on developing robust ambiguity models and corresponding solution methods. Specifically, we introduce a novel probabilistic fuzzy ambiguity model, which we demonstrate offers superior representation compared to established soft uncertainty models like fuzzy set and possibility theory. To address the resulting optimization challenge, we propose a multi-objective algorithm based on the NSGA-II meta-heuristic, designed to simultaneously optimize reliability and expected makespan. Our computational experiments indicate that this proposed model/outcome approach yields higher quality solutions than the traditional fuzzy set/possibility theory framework. Furthermore, we show that incorporating ambiguity into scheduling for cyber-physical systems can result in significant performance improvements compared to both deterministic and non-deterministic scenarios where ambiguity is ignored. Finally, we explore how the high interconnectivity of Industry 4.0 systems introduces new dimensions to ambiguity, such as data transmission failures and cyber threats, which may be mitigated through appropriate network design. We outline potential avenues for future research in this area. Finally, we examine how the high flexibility of these systems can be leveraged to enhance the robustness of computed schedules. Specifically, we extend our probabilistic fuzzy ambiguity model to create a robust scheduling framework that minimizes the degradation of expected performance under severe scenario realizations. We conclude by illustrating the effectiveness of this robustness approach through practical case studies. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive framework for modeling and solving optimization problems in ambiguous, non-deterministic industrial environments, with direct applicability to various Industry 4.0 scheduling challenges. Additionally, it establishes a foundation for robust optimization within the context of probabilistic fuzzy ambiguity. Finally, the paper demonstrates the utility of a new Python library, PyFuzzyAmb, which facilitates the efficient development and implementation of probabilistic fuzzy ambiguity/optimization problems and their solutions. This tool supports both researchers and practitioners in addressing optimization challenges across diverse domains. The library is publicly accessible at https://github.com/PyFuzzyAmb. We introduce a method for assessing the robustness of cyber-physical systems, specifically focusing on the sensitivity of their temporal logic specifications to disturbances. This approach utilizes signal temporal logic (STL), a formalism well-suited for analyzing system behavior over time, to define robustness, offering a quantitative metric that facilitates robust optimization. Our investigation centers on motion planning, where we demonstrate that robustness can be efficiently computed for common robustness measures, including initial robustness, temporal robustness, and their combination. Furthermore, we examine how robustness evolves in response to both parametric and signal-type disturbances, ultimately illustrating the practical utility of our framework through numerical case studies. These examples demonstrate that optimizing robustness yields significantly more robust planning outcomes compared to standard motion planning techniques. Additionally, we show that optimizing both signal-type and parametric disturbances can enhance robustness to levels unattainable when optimizing only one type. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of STL-driven formulations and disturbance models to the robustness analysis of cyber-physical systems. Our work addresses several novel disturbances, such as parametric disturbances, which have not been previously explored in this context. Finally, we introduce a new robustness measure that integrates both temporal and initial robustness, offering a more comprehensive evaluation of robustness in dynamical systems. This paper expands upon the work presented at CDC 2020 [1].

We introduce a novel strategy to detect hidden matter, such as black holes, by analyzing the Earth's acceleration. This method employs a vast network of the International GNSS Service (IGS) accelerometers, which are satellite-borne accelerometers that measure the Earth's acceleration by subtracting inertial forces from the acceleration of motion. The sensitivity of this technique improves with the number of accelerometers in the network; consequently, while current IGS network accuracy is approximately 10⁻⁹ g, future sensitivity could reach 10⁻¹¹g. We outline the method and its applications, demonstrating that even with the existing IGS network, a black hole of 10⁻⁴ Earth masses could be detected within a distance of roughly 10⁴ km. Furthermore, we suggest that as a seismometer array, the IGS network offers sensitivity comparable to that of a gravitational wave detector operating at frequencies above 0.1 Hz. This capability extends to observing various phenomena, including asteroid impacts, atmospheric pressure disturbances, and potentially low-frequency gravitational waves. This study examines a nonlinear diffusion equation featuring a reaction term, situated within the context of a complete Riemannian manifold that possesses a non-negative Greenwise curvature. The research derives multiple gradient estimates for various quantities linked to the solution, including those for the logarithm of the solution and the Yamabe quantity of the Dirichlet ratio. Additionally, the article provides several estimates for the Dirichlet ratio itself, incorporating nonlinear heat and Yamabe equations, all subject to suitable initial conditions. These estimates are built upon a gradient estimate for the Dirichlet ratio, which is proven using a refined version of Li-Yau's Liouville lemma. The proof of this refined Liouville lemma also incorporates an application of Cheng's Lemma regarding the Laplacian comparison of the Dirichlet Dirichlet. The study further explores applications of these gradient estimates by establishing Hamilton's Hessian estimate for the heat function of the Dirichlet ratio and determining a heat equation estimate for the heat invariant of the Dirichlet Dirichlet. The paper concludes with a discussion of self-dual solutions to the equation and their associated properties. Throughout the work, the authors aim to develop a unified approach for estimating quantities related to diffusion equations on complete manifolds, utilizing a variety of methods. The authors acknowledge that the list of estimates presented may not be exhaustive. The authors express gratitude to their colleagues for their encouragement and valuable discussions regarding this topic.

The origin of compact radio sources remains a significant unresolved issue in radio astronomy. This study investigates the angular dimensions of non-AGN compact radio sources by stacking radio galaxies, starburst galaxies, and jetless radio jets. We utilized VLA data from the 1.4 GHz 1Jy Bright Source Survey (1JyBSS) and 1.4 GHz Bright Source Survey (1JyBSS), alongside 1.4 GHz data from the VLA Sky Survey (VSS). Due to the scarcity of radio galaxies and starburst galaxies smaller than 1 arcsecond, our analysis focused on a source size range of 1 to 10 arcseconds. We examined the relationship between source size and flux density for (i) radio galaxies, (ii) starburst galaxies, and (iii) jetless radio jets. For each category, we calculated the mean stack size as a function of flux density. The resulting findings indicate that (i) radio galaxies, (ii) starburst galaxies, and (iii) jetless radio jets all possess core sizes smaller than 1 arcsecond. These results suggest that the most compact non-AGN radio sources are likely powered by either a supermassive black hole or a massive star cluster. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that current single-dish data are insufficient to accurately determine the angular sizes of compact radio sources. Future research should prioritize smaller flux limits and the inclusion of lower luminosity sources to better constrain their physical sizes. Additionally, a larger sample of jetless radio jets is required to more effectively distinguish between stellar and supermassive black hole origins. Ultimately, smaller flux limits will enable a more precise determination of the sizes of truly compact radio sources. The 3C295A Radio Galaxy is included as an example. Information leakage from program executions is typically quantified using the information flow noise order, which treats programs as generic computational processes. This study examines two distinct categorical formulations of this notion, one applicable to unweighted and weighted information flows. Applying the first formulation to computational processes hosted on the internet yields a monadic structure that facilitates the stepwise development of web applications while guaranteeing no information is revealed about secret inputs. Subsequently, we explore the second formulation regarding information flow noise orders for probabilistic computational processes.

Keywords: category theory, monads, quantitative information flow, categorical quantum mechanics.

We present a framework to investigate long-range interactions within non-equilibrium systems. Using a generalized reaction-diffusion equation that incorporates statistical non-locality, we analyze the phase diagram and spatial patterns. The diffusion coefficient in this model depends on the average concentration across the entire system, generating novel phase diagrams and patterns. In one dimension, we utilize a perturbative expansion to study the transition from short-range to long-range interactions and observe rich dynamical coherent structures, including traveling waves and synchronized oscillations. We extend this approach to infinite-range interactions, where the diffusion coefficient is proportional to the concentration raised to an extensive power. These models display a broad spectrum of phases and patterns, such as shock waves, oscillatory shock waves, and large-amplitude shock-oscillations. Furthermore, we examine the stability of shock waves in long-range non-equilibrium systems and provide experimental validation through optical and microfluidic devices. This research significantly advances the understanding of non-equilibrium physics in non-equivalent systems. Our methodology holds significant potential for studying diverse systems ranging from biological to geographical domains. Additionally, the model offers a novel perspective for long-range interacting systems, including active matter and many-body quantum systems. Finally, these findings contribute to the broader field of non-equilibrium thermodynamics. **Keywords:** Non-equilibrium thermodynamics, statistical non-locality, coherent structures, optical fluid. We introduce a phenomenological framework designed to examine inelastic scattering processes that exhibit a high degree of flexibility in their final state observables. This approach utilizes a scalar function, termed the "scattability," to quantify the variation range within a single event. The framework is applied to analyze the variation of final-state $p_T$ in dijet production, as well as in processes involving jets plus final-state objects sensitive to new physics, such as $t ar{t}$, $t$-channel SUSY, and vector boson fusion. Furthermore, we investigate the trade-off between discriminative power and efficiency when employing final-state observables with high variability in collider search scenarios. Finally, this tool offers a systematic method for assessing the impact of final-state observables on signal significance and background rejection. We anticipate that this framework will be valuable for designing searches and for optimizing the selection of final-state observables for reconstruction and classification within machine learning approaches. Finally, we provide a flake package that includes a library for calculating scattering phenomenology metrics (flake Calc) and for demonstrating these concepts on standard model processes (flake Demos). This code is publicly accessible via GitHub.

This study examines blackbody thermodynamics affected by Casimir energy. We demonstrate that a system boundary generates an energy field, thereby establishing solvability for the problem. Furthermore, we show that the Casimir field modifies blackbody thermodynamics and causes deviations from standard predictions. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of these deviations depends on the system's size. In the ultra-micro scale, a deviation factor of $10^{42}$ arises, whereas in the macro scale, a factor of $10^{-31}$ is observed. These results suggest that CASIMIR's influence is significant in the ultra-micro domain and potentially detectable in the macro domain. Additionally, we establish that the system's entropy remains unchanged. Finally, we explore the physical implications of these results. These findings indicate that such obfuscation often fails to meet rigorous privacy standards. Relying solely on the assumption that the prior distribution of a user's location is uniform can lead to misleading conclusions and an overestimation of privacy effectiveness. This paper introduces a framework that models the user's prior distribution as a conditional function, accounting for non-uniform location patterns caused by restricted movement domains and temporal correlations. The study examines the impact of employing an incorrect prior distribution and evaluates the efficacy of various debiasing techniques in mitigating the risk of privacy breaches. Ultimately, this approach provides a more practical method for modeling real-world location priors and fosters a granular risk assessment regarding the confidentiality of a user's current and historical movements. Specifically, we extend a Bayesian Bayesian Inference (BBI) algorithm to address a wide range of location tracking privacy issues under conditional priors. Experimental results using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that utilizing priors with significant entropy results in a more accurate estimation of privacy risk. Finally, we find that the most effective debiasing strategies are those that apply minimal perturbation to the user's activity records. Collectively, this paper provides a more robust framework for quantifying the privacy risks associated with various debiasing techniques and data perturbation methods. This study addresses the NDT-transformer architecture, which integrates the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation with the self-attention mechanism from transformers to solve large-scale 3D point cloud localization. NDT describes point clouds as an arrangement of overlapping NDTs, which model the point density patterns found in laser scans. By leveraging local geometric patterns, NDT-based localization can achieve sub-centimeter accuracy even at meter-scale distances. However, NDT's limitation in capturing long-range patterns makes it susceptible to non-minimal solutions and poor performance in highly non-Markovian, large-scale, or textureless environments. Transformers are recognized for their ability to identify long-range dependencies and demonstrate superior generalization in such settings. Consequently, we propose a transformer-based encoder-decoder model that utilizes the global pattern of point clouds for localization. Our approach employs a multi-scale feature extraction module and global pattern exploitation module within the transformer encoder, followed by an attention mechanism between query points and global features in the decoder. We validate our method's effectiveness in large-scale, non-Markovian, and textureless scenarios through extensive experiments on the KITTI, NYUv2, and S3DIS datasets. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is increasingly utilized to investigate brain networks in both healthy individuals and those with disorders. While these methods offer significant potential for diagnosing and treating various conditions, they must be evaluated against a background of conflicting and inconclusive findings. To address this, we conducted a rigorous, multi-site study involving 176 healthy participants to assess the precision of predicting individual-level traits through whole-brain functional connectivity. We systematically examined how factors such as sample size, trait heterogeneity, and preprocessing methods influence prediction precision and the statistical strength of connectivity associations. Our results indicate that while prediction precision is limited for certain traits, it is achievable for others, including age, educational attainment, and the intelligence quotient. Furthermore, we established a set of guidelines to enhance the rigor and reproducibility of future rs-fMRI research. Finally, we made our data and analysis code publicly accessible to support these conclusions. These findings underscore the necessity of establishing robust effect sizes and high precision when identifying biomarkers and diagnostic signatures in rs-fMRI research. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive, online, accessible encyclopedia of rs-fMRI connections to individual traits for educational and reference purposes. Specifically, we present an extensive encyclopedia of functional connections between brain regions and age, which can serve as both a benchmark for the repeatability of connectivity associations and a resource for educational and referential value. Single-beeping networks consist of multiple beeping nodes arranged in a line, where each node communicates exclusively by transmitting short signals, known as beeps. This paper addresses power efficiency by analyzing scenarios where nodes operate at different transmission powers. The primary objective is to establish network-wide synchrony—specifically, the collective alignment of internal clocks—without relying on pre-existing knowledge of start-up times or power levels. We demonstrate a simple, distributed algorithm that successfully synchronizes any single-beeping network of arbitrary size using a finite set of predefined power levels. Furthermore, we measure the algorithm's efficiency by counting the total beeps required, demonstrating that this approach is optimally efficient by establishing matching upper and lower bounds on the beep complexity. Finally, we extend the method to achieve distributed senseless-synchrony, a more demanding goal where nodes synchronize simultaneously and without coordinating on-beep transmissions. In this context, we present an optimally efficient strategy that outperforms any alternative single-beep approach. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of beeping networks to the study of power-efficient wireless communication. Our implementation relies on a novel, straightforward, and intuitive concept of event-potential, which we believe will prove valuable for addressing various other challenges in this domain. To support this, we include a proof of the fundamental lemma regarding single-beep event-potentials. Additionally, we provide a proof of the theorem stating that senseless-synchrony cannot be achieved in single-beep networks if only one beep per event is permitted. The proof for this latter result is notably intricate, as it necessitates a detailed examination of the behavior of single-beep networks. This proof is so complex that it warrants a separate paper, which we have prepared as a supplement. We have also prepared supplementary code that implements the core event-potential lemmas, serving as a testbed for our proofs. This material is available in an appendix. We hope that this work will inspire further research into the intricate and underexplored field of beeping networks. The primary obstacle in processing code-mixed languages is the scarcity of multilingual training data, which restricts code-mixing languages to predominantly low-resource scenarios. To address this lack of resources, this paper introduces PESTO, a Transformer-based framework designed to function effectively as both a standalone model and a robust pre-training architecture. PESTO generates enhanced positional embeddings by identifying transition points where different languages mix and creating both absolute and relative position biases specifically tailored to these transitions. The study validates the framework through two extensive experimental sets, one involving Hindi-English mixtures and the other involving Marathi-Hindi. These experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach is effective across different code-mixing languages and support the hypothesis that the method requires minimal training data. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing how PESTO can serve as a versatile pre-training model for various code-mixing languages. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the pressure-dependent isotope effect on the critical temperature of the binary transition metal sulfide H$_{3}$S. By employing the first-principles finite-temperature electron-phonon method within the quasi-harmonic approximation, we compute the phase diagram and phonon dispersion relations for various pressures. Our findings indicate that the isotope effect on the critical temperature varies with pressure, peaking at 260 GPa, which coincides with the presence of a van Hove singularity. Furthermore, we observe that the phase transition from hexagonal to body-centered cubic (bcc) occurs at 230 GPa, a point where the isotope effect reaches its maximum. These results provide valuable theoretical insights into the phase diagram and the mechanisms driving the isotope influence on the critical temperature in H$_{3}$S. Additionally, this theoretical framework aids in understanding the phase transition from hexagonal to bcc structures and offers a basis for exploring the room-temperature superconductivity of H$_{3}$S. Finally, our calculations offer valuable insights into the phase transition from H$_{3}$S to H$_{2}$S. To verify the accuracy of our approach, we also calculated the phase transition from hexagonal to face-centered cubic (fcc) structures in C$_{60}$ and C$_{60}$H$_{60}$, yielding results consistent with experimental data. Consequently, this theoretical method is applicable to analyzing phase transitions in other materials. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive theoretical foundation for the phase transition from H$_{3}$S to H$_{2}$S. (Letter Report) (2021)

This study introduces a framework designed to assist motion planners in dynamic environments by identifying key geometric features. The method begins by dividing the problem into spatial and temporal dimensions. A core concept involves defining "conjunctions," which are spatial partitions created by the intersection of two obstacle trajectories. These conjunctions establish boundaries that separate the trajectory into distinct regions, enabling the creation of constraints to narrow the spatial search domain. The proposed approach integrates with existing planners by leveraging sample validity checks to impose restrictions on future trajectory generation. Performance evaluations were conducted on both synthetic datasets and a real-world testbed. The results demonstrate that this technique reduces the number of tree expansions and increases the success rate of the motion planner. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexei-panov/SLC. Keywords: motion planning, dynamic environments, data-driven methods, obstacle avoidance.

This paper presents a visual relocalization approach that integrates visual cues from surfel maps with learned features. Unlike traditional descriptor-based methods, our technique leverages a deep convolutional neural network to extract descriptors from input images, ensuring superior performance in describing input features. Additionally, the method employs a visual clamping strategy to mitigate the accumulation of errors caused by visual features. Evaluated against state-of-the-art techniques using the real-world RGB-D dataset, the proposed method demonstrates significant improvements in both accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, the method achieves superior localization accuracy on the RGB-D and RealScene datasets when using still images. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/11111111111/VisNet.

This study addresses the joint optimization of user choice and precoding in multiuser MIMO downlink networks. The objective is to maximize network sum-rate by simultaneously determining the precoder and selecting the most desirable users for each transmission, thereby enhancing spectral efficiency and energy conservation. To solve the resulting non-convex mixed-integer problem, we propose a graph-based formulation that is non-convex due to sparsity constraints on the user selection matrix. By relaxing these constraints, the problem is transformed into a convex one, which is then solved using the Group-LASSO algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method yields performance comparable to conventional joint user choice and precoding approaches while significantly reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, we establish an analytical relationship between the actual and estimated user selection matrices, illustrating a trade-off between reconstruction error and the condition number of the channel matrix. Finally, we examine the impact of regularization and noise power on both the estimated user choice matrix and system performance. Ultimately, we prove that the proposed scheme achieves optimal performance in sum-rate and selection accuracy when user channels are uncorrelated and remain near-optimal even with correlated users. Additionally, we show that the estimated user selection matrix is sparse under conditions of low noise power and small values of the regularization parameter. Finally, we establish an upper bound for the total reconstruction error of the user selection matrix and the corresponding gap in sum-rate. We demonstrate that the rational semifield consisting of piecewise affine functions defined on an arc of a variety is finitely generated as a semifield over the piecewise constant functions contained within it. Consequently, the rational semifield of an arc on a surface is the integral closure of the piecewise constant semifield in the function field of the surface, and similarly, the rational grothendieck ring of an arc on a surface is the integral closure of the piecewise constant grothendieck ring within the function field of the surface. These results provide a surface-specific instance of a broader theorem by Jensen, Kerz, and Zureicki-Broniarski. Additionally, we present examples of an elliptic surface and a surface where the validity of these statements for the surface arc depends on the specific surface and the field of constants. Our primary technique involves applying results from algebraic K-theory and algebraic geometry to surfaces. Specifically, we show that the relative K_2 of an arc on a smooth variety is trivial when the variety dimension is 2, and that unramified functions on such an arc are precisely the unramified functions on the variety itself. These findings have also been utilized in the work of Jensen and Zureicki-Broniarski. Furthermore, we address a question posed by Jensen and Zureicki-Broniarski regarding the finite generation of the rational semifield of an arc on a variety of dimension at least 2, given a fixed base point. We provide a positive answer for surfaces and varieties over algebraically closed fields, and offer a partial answer for higher-dimensional varieties. The proofs for these cases rely on the respective results from algebraic K-theory and geometry concerning relative K_2 and unramified functions. Finally, we conclude by examining the finite generation of the rational grouped ring of an arc on a variety and its connection to the finite generation of the arc's grouped ring. This relationship follows from a theorem by Zureicki-Broniarski and follows from a result by Zureicki regarding the grouped ring of an arc on a variety. Additionally, we present an example of a smooth variety where the grouped ring of the arc is not finitely generated. The examples and examples used in the proofs are derived from various sources, including Zare, Zureicki, Zureicki, Zureicki, and Zureicki. The examples are also used in the work of Zare and Zureick

We demonstrate sufficient conditions ensuring the consistent convergence of this chain to the corresponding $Q$-process, starting from any initial distribution. These findings generalize and complement prior results in the literature. Specifically, the conditions are expressed concisely using the relative entropy $H(\mu | 
u)$ and the relative information Hahn distance $d_H(\mu, 
u)$ between probability measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $S$. Notably, the entropy distance $d_H(\mu, 
u) = H(\mu |

This research explores Vassiliev characteristic numbers for immersed disks in $S^3$, immersed spheres in $S^4$, and knots, with emphasis on the characteristic of order three. Our investigation is driven by specific inquiries into whether certain established results extend to the context of immersed disks in $S^3$. While we demonstrate that the winding number—representing the only Vassiliev characteristic of order one—remains invariant under small homotopies, we highlight a critical distinction from the knot theory context: there exist small homotopies connecting distinct embedded disks that produce different values for the self-linking number. Furthermore, we present an explicit characteristic of order two alongside additional examples. A primary tool in our analysis is the Fox-Hatcher characteristic, derived from the Fox-Hatcher representation of the fundamental group of a small homotopy class of immersed submanifolds within $S^n$. We establish the existence and uniqueness (up to equivalence) of this representation and outline the process for constructing it. Additionally, we outline an inductive approach to constructing Vassiliev characteristics by utilizing the algebraic dual of the "small homotopy class" as an intermediary. Finally, we demonstrate how to apply the Fox-Hatcher representation to determine the fundamental groups of such classes specifically in the case of $S^3$. This foundational work serves as a precursor to future endeavors aimed at resolving the questions posed. These preliminary findings will provide a framework for advancing towards the goals established in our related paper, "Fundamental groups of small homotopy classes of immersed submanifolds in $S^n$," which addresses this problem for $n \leq 6$. Our approach offers an alternative to the framework developed by Freedman and Krushkal. We conclude by suggesting several directions for future research. Specifically, we propose examining the properties of the fiber product of two maps, demonstrating how this concept can yield fundamental groups for small homotopy classes of immersed submanifolds in $S^n$. We illustrate the utility of the fiber product by deriving the fundamental groups of small homotopy classes of immersed submanifolds in $S^3$ as a byproduct of our analysis. Finally, we suggest extending our analysis to broader contexts, such as small homotopy classes of immersed submanifolds in $S^n$ relative to a subset of $S^n$, and exploring the fundamental groups of relative small homotopy classes. We anticipate that these extensions will yield valuable insights and assist in addressing the open questions raised.

The structural transition in Fe-based superconductors from tetragonal to orthorhombic symmetry has been attributed to an electronic nematic order parameter. This study demonstrates that, within LiFeAs, the origin of this symmetry breaking lies primarily in the static lattice distortion, while the influence of a putative nematic order parameter is negligible. Consequently, experimental observations of the temperature-dependent orthorhombic-tetragonal transition in LiFeAs cannot be explained by nematicity. These findings advance our understanding of Fe-based superconductors and underscore the necessity of incorporating lattice effects in models describing nematic behavior. Furthermore, our results indicate that nematicity is unlikely to be responsible for the symmetry breaking and its associated temperature-dependent evolution in other iron pnictides. Ultimately, this research underscores the critical role of the lattice in Fe-based superconductors. To achieve a comprehensive understanding of these materials, models must integrate both nematic and non-nematic electronic effects alongside lattice contributions. In the specific context of LiFeAs, the proximity to a structural phase transition is proposed as the origin of the temperature-dependent symmetry breaking. Additionally, we examine the electrostatic origin of LiFeAs's structural instability and establish a quantitative connection between its magnitude and the superconducting transition temperature. Finally, we explore the potential for enhancing superconductivity in LiFeAs by engineering its structure near the theoretical minimum energy configuration. This work is based on research from [1]. Furthermore, the lattice contribution to structural distortion in LiFeAs is quantified using density functional theory calculations, and its impact on superconductivity is assessed. [1] J. Li, C. As computational power grows, so too does the capacity to investigate complex systems spanning chemistry, materials science, and biology. Recent advances in simulation techniques have enabled detailed exploration of self-assembly processes for soft colloids, biomolecules, and supramolecular structures. These simulations offer insights into the mechanisms driving self-assembly and allow for testing materials design hypotheses. This review examines the latest developments in self-assembly research conducted through simulations, emphasizing neuroevolutionary training methods. Furthermore, it proposes an open framework for conducting self-assembly studies, which includes an interface for designing target structures and training algorithms capable of adapting to various system models. Finally, the discussion outlines future prospects for simulation-based self-assembly studies, highlighting key challenges and opportunities for further advancement. We argue that integrating particle-based modeling with machine learning represents a promising direction for self-assembly research. By employing neural networks to learn from simulation outcomes, researchers can rapidly predict the self-assembly behavior of novel materials without extensive simulations. Additionally, optimizing particle interactions via machine learning could yield materials with superior properties. Ultimately, these methodologies have the potential to transform self-assembly research and design into a more automated process. A detailed implementation of the proposed framework is available at github.com/soft-matter-design/simbase.
