Detecting COVID-19 early is crucial for mitigating its severe transmission. While Deep Learning (DL) has demonstrated significant potential in this domain, concerns regarding data privacy persist, as sensitive information can inadvertently be revealed by trained DL models. This paper introduces the Adversarial Privacy-Constrained Deep Network (APCDN), specifically designed to minimize the risk of patient data leakage during the early identification of COVID-19. To achieve this, we apply Transport Discrepancy Regularization (TDR) to align feature representations from both COVID-19 positive and negative samples with healthy control features, thereby enhancing model privacy. Additionally, we employ L2 regularization and clustering constraints as constraints within the objective function. These components work together to distinguish COVID-19 samples from both healthy and flu samples while maintaining adequate privacy against disclosure. We evaluated the APCDN framework using CT scan images from two independent datasets, the Oxford COVID-19 Image Dataset (Oxford-Corona) and the CT Projections Dataset (CTPD). Our experimental results demonstrate that the APCDN framework significantly improves privacy during classification, maintaining robust performance on both datasets. Furthermore, the model exhibits strong performance on external test data collected from a different hospital. Both qualitative and quantitative analyses confirm that our proposed APCDN framework is effective for the early identification of COVID-19. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2000/APCDNN. Future research will explore the application of APCDN in other medical diagnostic tasks. Given that the model is trained solely on CT scan images, it can be readily adapted to other imaging modalities, such as X-rays, with minimal modification. Additionally, we aim to extend the APCDN approach to other viral infections. Finally, we plan to investigate parameter-free methods to reduce computational costs and accelerate inference. Addressing these future challenges will further enhance the applicability and efficiency of our proposed framework. Collectively, these efforts aim to advance the field of medical image analysis for early COVID-19 identification. We hope this work contributes to the broader effort of combating the pandemic. Distributed inference involves dividing a deep learning model into localized fragments and executing them across multiple wireless edge devices. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to simultaneously optimize both computational and transmission latencies for graph neural networks (GNNs) within wireless transmission systems. By leveraging a specific joint integer linear programming model, the study examines two distinct splitting strategies: one that partitions a GNN into submodels by separating its nodes, and another that divides it into submodels featuring distinct node and edge architectures. For the node-splitting scenario, the work proposes a long-term scheduling scheme based on the Frank-Wolfe algorithm, iteratively solving a short-term optimization problem at each step. In contrast, the node and edge splitting scenario employs a cross-layer approach, dividing the system into computation and transmission layers and designing a joint optimization algorithm to minimize overall latency. Finally, numerical results are presented to validate the proposed schemes. Homicide incidence is influenced by intricate factors, including social and economic conditions, political stability, and community dynamics. While prior research has primarily relied on regression models to pinpoint influential variables, these approaches often fail to account for the non-linear nature of the relationship between social conditions and homicide rates. This study analyzes the temporal evolution of spatial patterns in Brazilian homicide data, specifically within the state of Goi\^as, covering the years 2002 to 2014. We present a methodology for spatial cluster analysis that incorporates state-specific trends and utilizes a spatially weighted time series to identify high and low homicide clusters. Our findings indicate that high-homicide clusters are predominantly located in central, northern, and western municipalities, whereas low-homicide clusters appear in the east and south. A notable spatial shift was detected between 2002 and 2009, with high-homicide clusters moving from the northwest to the center. Furthermore, high-homicide municipalities tend to be led by mayors with a political affiliation differing from that of their neighbors, while low-homicide municipalities are often governed by mayors sharing the same party affiliation as their adjacent municipalities. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of state-level data in spatial cluster analysis and its potential to inform future public policy initiatives. The proposed methodology is particularly beneficial for large-scale studies where data availability is limited to specific timeframes. Additionally, it serves as a foundation for spatially informed public policy interventions, such as targeted health programs. The analysis was conducted using the open-source software R, leveraging the packages fPop, fPopClust, and fPoland. The package fPop was developed by the authors of this study and is now available. This paper investigates two previously unexplored dimensions of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for machine learning: how SGD performance responds to variations in input data soundness and issue frequency, with a specific focus on audio classification tasks. Our findings indicate that SGD behavior is highly contingent on data soundness, suggesting potential benefits from adapting SGD based on the specific training instances used. Furthermore, standard SGD processes every labeled instance regardless of their relevance to the target issue, which can hinder convergence. We introduce a straightforward method to adapt SGD to the issue of interest by filtering out irrelevant instances, resulting in improved convergence and performance. Additionally, we propose a novel accelerated SGD variant that dynamically adjusts the learning rate based on the previously computed gradient, offering another simple approach to issue-specific SGD adaptation with enhanced convergence and superior performance. We examine these two adapted SGD methods within the context of issue adaptation for text classification, demonstrating that they yield significant performance gains. Finally, we validate the efficacy of these approaches on the widely adopted AudioSet dataset for classifying musical instruments. We evaluate accelerated SGD across three dimensions: accelerated convergence, issue-specific performance enhancement, and scalability. Our results confirm that these adapted SGD methods offer substantial performance improvements. Notably, the instrument classification issue benefits from a 100% performance gain, a 3.5x convergence acceleration, and a 2x reduction in memory usage. More broadly, these results suggest that adapting SGD to specific issues is a promising direction for addressing various machine learning problems. This work is intended to inspire future research into developing problem-specific SGD adaptations. Specifically, it aims to encourage exploring accelerated, issue-adaptive SGD methods that rely solely on historical gradient information. Such methods would eliminate the need for access to ground truth labels or models, thereby enabling application to broader machine learning problems. This aligns with our application to AudioSet, a large, heterogeneous, and heterogeneous audio dataset. This is the first study to explore input-data-sound adaptive, issue-specific SGD acceleration tailored for audio classification. We demonstrate that these accelerated, issue-adaptive methods yield a 1.5x to 3.5x speedup in convergence compared to standard SGD. Furthermore, they achieve a 20% to 100% improvement in final accuracy for instruments, depending on the amount of training data available. These results provide the first empirical evidence of the necessity for input-data-sound adaptive, issue-specific SGD acceleration, particularly for audio classification problems. This work paves the way for future research into input soundness-aware, issue-specific SGD acceleration.

Axion-based physics is being explored through two primary methods: laboratory experiments and astronomical observations. The axion helioscope BabyIAXO is the upcoming initiative to advance baby solar axion research. This overview introduces the core principles of BabyIAXO and outlines its projected axion-search capabilities. Subsequently, it examines the solar axion spectrum, focusing on axions generated within the Sun's core via the photon axion coupling and the pep reaction, as well as those produced in the coronal and flare regions through the Tammeshek mechanism. The report demonstrates that the serendipitous detection of solar flares by IAXO could significantly bolster the experiment's sensitivity, thereby establishing BabyIAXO as the first solar axion observatory. Furthermore, it addresses current challenges and potential future improvements. The text concludes by detailing a strategy to maximize BabyIAXO's potential, which includes developing a dedicated solar axion observatory capable of continuous magnetic-field observation and investigating alternative astrophysical axion sources. Finally, the document explores the synergy between BabyIAXO and existing or future astronomical axion searches. Overall, BabyIAXO holds the promise of delivering first-class results, making it a vital component of the upcoming axion research era. This work is based on presentations given at the 17th International Axion Symposium (IAS17) in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, and the 18th International Axion Symposium (IAS18) in Heidelberg, Germany. Additionally, it draws upon the IAXO Conceptual Design Report (2019) and the white paper Solar Axion Physics: A New Era (2020). We identify a new class of self-exciting systems that continuously generate and sustain complex, aperiodic activity patterns, both spatially and temporally. This class shares a specific trait with multiplexed and self-propelled systems: the coexistence of fast and slow degrees of freedom within a unified category. However, our findings reveal that mechanisms leading to aperiodic activity in these systems are qualitatively distinct from those in multiplexed or self-propelled models. Specifically, we demonstrate that higher-order statistical correlations, rather than pairwise correlations, are essential for the continuous aperiodic activity in this new class of self-exciting systems, whereas only pairwise correlations matter for multiplexed and self-propelled systems. This distinction gives this class of self-exciting systems unique spatial and temporal characteristics, enabling them to act as effective generators of higher-order correlations and complex, aperiodic activity patterns. Furthermore, these systems can serve as biologically plausible mechanisms for the continuous generation and maintenance of aperiodic activity in neural circuits, a function that pairs-based mechanisms fail to support. This distinction is particularly significant given the well-documented role of higher-order correlations in both neural activity and networks. Finally, our findings suggest that the capacity to generate and sustain complex, aperiodic activity patterns is a fundamental property inherent to this specific category of self-exciting systems. This inherent capacity fundamentally differs from the mechanism of "activity buffering," where complex and aperiodic patterns are continuously generated by external inputs and maintained within neural circuits. We illustrate this distinction by showing that perturbing the system with external inputs does not alter its intrinsic behavior regarding the continuous generation and maintenance of complex, aperiodic activity patterns. This conclusion holds true even when external inputs are sufficiently complex to mimic higher-order correlations. Consequently, this implies that the continuous generation and maintenance of complex, aperiodic activity patterns in this class of self-exciting systems arise from internal mechanisms rather than external inputs. This conclusion is supported by the observation that perturbing these systems with external inputs does not change their behavior concerning the continuous generation and maintenance of complex, aperiodic activity patterns. Robotic dexterous manipulation has garnered significant research interest due to its potential to enhance daily life. However, data for training robotic dexterous grasping remains scarce, hindering the training of high-performance grasping models. To address this shortage, this paper presents DexGraspNet, an extensive robotic dexterous grasp dataset comprising 1.3 million synthetic grasp instances featuring 6 degrees of freedom for 33 objects. The objects vary in shape, size, and material, enabling the generation of diverse grasp instances. Simulation is employed to create these instances, with a key focus on ensuring physical plausibility. Furthermore, the grasp collection is derived from an inverse mapping of a large professional human grasp database, resulting in a dataset that is both extensive and human-inspired. Additionally, a novel dexterous grasping model, DexGrasp, is developed, trained on DexGraspNet, and subsequently validated through extensive experiments on general objects. The first experimental phase evaluates the model's generalization capabilities across unseen objects, while the second assesses its robustness regarding novel grasp configurations. Furthermore, the model's superior performance is compared against existing methods, and user studies are utilized to analyze human satisfaction with the robotic dexterous grasping generated by DexGrasp. Ultimately, DexGraspNet and DexGrasp offer valuable resources for advancing robotic dexterous grasping research. **Objective:** To introduce and assess a free-breathing, 4D-respiration-synchronized turbo spin-echo (4D-TSE) sequence.

**Methods:** The 4D-TSE approach integrates free-breathing scanning with motion correction. Each free-breathing volume is acquired at a specific respiratory phase, enabling data acquisition from the same anatomical region over time. This method allows for temporal sorting of data and the generation of time-resolved (3D+time) images. In a proof-of-concept study, 20 healthy volunteers underwent free-breathing 4D-TSE scans at 1.5 Tesla (T) and zero-echo-time (ZTE) 3D-T2-weighted scans at both 1.5T and 3.0T. The 4D-TSE protocol employed a single-shot technique with 20 respiratory phases, a repetition time (TR) of 4.0 ms, and a time resolution of 100 ms per frame.

**Results:** The 4D-TSE method produced high-quality 3D+time images in volunteers, with no signs of residual motion. Compared to ZTE 3D-T2-weighted imaging, 4D-TSE offered superior contrast and tissue contrast-to-noise ratio (tCNR). At 1.5T, the 4D-TSE 3D image demonstrated a higher tCNR than both the 1.5T and 3.0T ZTE 3D+time images. At 3.0T, the 4D-TSE 3D image tCNR was 1.2 times that of the 1.5T ZTE 3D+time image and 1.5 times that of the 3.0T ZTE 3D+time image.

**Conclusion:** This study presents a free-breathing 4D-TSE sequence that delivers 3D+time image quality comparable to breath-hold single-shot 3D+time sequences. Additionally, 4D-TSE provides better tissue contrast and tCNR than ZTE 3D+time techniques and is free from breathing artifacts. These findings suggest that 4D-TSE could serve as a viable alternative to breath-hold 3D+time imaging for body scanning. Model compression techniques have attracted significant interest for deploying neural networks in resource-constrained environments. Among these, knowledge distillation stands out as a leading approach that enables smaller models to mimic the behavior of larger ones by learning from their training data. However, current distillation methods often fail to capture the intricate data flow transformations inherent in deep networks, resulting in compressed models with limited performance. To address this, we present Data Flow-preserving Knowledge Distillation (InDistill), a framework designed to retain the inherent data flow of the teacher network by reordering operations rather than simplifying or pruning them. This method constructs a structured distilled model featuring a single sub-network for each operation type, reconfigured to match the data flow transformations of the teacher. Experimental results demonstrate that InDistill significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 1.6% and 1.1% gain on ImageNet for MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetV2, respectively, without compromising the topological structure. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanwang/InDistill. Furthermore, the implementation is open-source under the Apache 2.0 license. Consider a real-valued function $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by a finite set of polynomials, where the foliation generated by the level curves of $f$ contains no compact leaves. This work demonstrates the existence of a topological equivalence between the level curves of $f$ and the level curves of a sum of two monomials. The equivalence map can be selected to serve as a $C^0$-solution, and the result represents a two-dimensional variant of the Mather-Thse theorem regarding real-valued functions on the line. Additionally, the foliations of the level curves and the inverse level curves for $f$ (interpreted as sublevel sets) are shown to be topologically equivalent to those of a stepped function composed of constant segments on the line, although no general constructive method for this equivalence is provided. A comparable equivalence holds for submersion functions on $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose level curves possess non-empty interiors and contain no compact components. The primary technique employed is a variant of the contraction mapping principle, applied to a variant of the Mather-Thse theorem specifically tailored for submersion functions on the plane. This approach yields a constructive method for establishing the topological equivalence, which, in the context of submersion functions, relies on solving a system of equations derived from the Cauchy-Riemann equations. The equivalence map is constructed using the Poisson kernel and the Riemann mapping theorem. Furthermore, by integrating the results from this paper and a subsequent publication, one can derive a non-constructive algorithm to determine the topological equivalence class for the level curves of any given submersion function on $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose foliation lacks compact components. This algorithm assigns a pair of integers as a topological invariant; however, it remains an open question whether this invariant is sufficient to uniquely classify all such functions topologically. The paper also offers a concise overview of the third author's research into the topological equivalence of submersion functions on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Finally, the authors propose several theorems and conjectures concerning the topological equivalence of submersion functions on the plane. These proposals encompass a novel method for generating topological invariants, a strategy to address the case involving non-trivial fundamental groups, and a conjecture concerning the equivalence of submersion functions on the half-plane. It is anticipated that these suggestions will inspire further research

CountSketch is a widely used method for estimating the $\ell_2$ norm of high-dimensional vectors that has gained significant popularity. It functions by projecting vectors into a lower-dimensional space via random linear transformations, allowing the projected vector's norm to serve as an approximation for the original. The core challenge is determining how random a transformation must be to achieve a sufficiently close approximation, specifically in terms of the number of rows in the projected space. While a count of rows equal to the target accuracy squared is necessary, research has established that this is also sufficient when both the dimension and the $\ell_\infty$ norm of the vector are known and bounded. However, in practical scenarios, these bounds are often unknown. This paper investigates the number of rows required in settings where bounds are unknown or must be discovered adaptively. We demonstrate that a straightforward CountSketch variant is insufficient in these contexts. Furthermore, we prove that both the squared accuracy and the expected $\ell_\infty$ norm are necessary even for randomized algorithms operating under adaptive conditions. Finally, we present a CountSketch algorithm that utilizes both random projections and deterministic shifts, requiring a number of rows proportional to the sum of squared accuracy and expected $\ell_\infty$ norm, even when these values are unknown. This approach is nearly optimal in the adaptive setting. While the lower bound for randomized non-adaptive algorithms remains largely open, our upper bound suggests a potential gap between adaptive and non-adaptive settings. To address this, we establish that $\Omega(\text{accuracy}^2)$ rows are required in the deterministic case for both unknown and known $\ell_\infty$ norms, and we propose a CountSketch algorithm that is optimal up to constant factors for the known $\ell_\infty$ scenario. Additionally, we examine a more general problem: approximating arbitrary functions of individual coordinates. For this task, we show that $\Omega(f'(0)^2)$ rows are necessary in the adaptive setting. Our findings rely on a novel framework for analyzing the information gain of adaptive functions, which may have broader applications. We demonstrate that this framework not only proves the necessity of $\Omega(\text{accuracy}^2)$ rows in the adaptive setting but also the sufficiency of $\text{accuracy}^2$ rows in the known $\ell_\infty$ norm setting. The Prisoner's Dilemma serves as a foundational model in social science theory, illustrating that rational individual choices can lead to suboptimal collective outcomes. This study leverages the Qiskit software development kit to simulate the game within a quantum cloud environment, enabling parallel, rapid decision-making. Utilizing the qpc cloud interface, we demonstrate that quantum systems can achieve superior collective results compared to both classical frameworks and other quantum models. Furthermore, we examine how decision-making in such quantum systems can be optimized for high-speed trading, specifically within fractional share environments. By employing the qasm interface for communication, fractional share data, and parallel decision processes, our research holds significant potential for enhancing collective intelligence, high-frequency trading, and high-speed data transmission. Ultimately, our findings suggest that quantum computing represents a transformative advancement in high-speed cloud computing.

Keywords: Quantum Computing, Trade, Transaction, Cloud Computing, High Frequency Trading, Parallel Processing, Fractional Shares, Qiskit, Prisoner's Dilemma.

Income redistribution through both direct and indirect transfers is a fundamental aspect of economic life, influencing how wealth is distributed and determining which individuals become wealthy. Brokers facilitate transactions between buyers and sellers, often increasing profits for all parties involved and accelerating the redistribution of income. This study examines a model featuring a single broker within a world characterized by heterogeneity, parity, and mobility. We demonstrate that for a specific subset of parameters, the presence of a broker enhances the income of all agents—包括 the broker themselves—without triggering a cycle of retaliatory spending. Furthermore, we find that brokers significantly boost the incomes of all non-poor agents, even outside this parameter range, provided the system's parameters remain within feasible limits. Our findings indicate that the broker's income grows even more rapidly than that of other non-poor agents, and we quantify the impact of the broker's initial capital on their potential for growth. Additionally, we analyze how a broker influences the transition between different world states. Finally, our results suggest that brokers can accelerate the equalization of incomes among non-poor agents while simultaneously increasing the number of agents trapped in the poor state. These insights are supported by both analytical and numerical methods. These conclusions hold relevance for both digital marketplaces, where brokers operate as platforms, and traditional markets. Finally, we present our findings in a pedagogical manner, utilizing them to illustrate several concepts applicable to an undergraduate curriculum. Specifically, our analysis uses a straightforward algorithm to show how a broker's initial income and spending behavior affect the final income distribution. This approach offers an alternative to the commonly used agent-based simulation method, which is often employed in undergraduate courses to illustrate digital marketplaces. Our approach provides a clear explanation of the outcomes, demonstrating that brokers increase the income of all agents while also increasing their own income. In this context, we offer an algorithm that calculates the broker's income alongside the income distributions of buyers and sellers. This enables the calculation of statistical measures, such as the Gini coefficient, for both non-poor and poor agents. Our analysis also examines how a broker's initial income and spending behavior influence the final income distribution. Specifically, we show that brokers can equalize the incomes of non-poor agents and provide insights into the impact of brokers on poor agents. We propose Acquired Entity Prompting (AEP), which enhances entity disambiguation by prompting the model with external knowledge about the specific entity. AEP represents a novel approach to acroform disambiguation that diverges from prior research by reframing the problem as a planning task. To facilitate this, we introduce process models for AEP, which detail the changes in the state space resulting from each disambiguation action. Process models are a fundamental component of classical planning and are considered the most expressive class of action models, capable of representing any state change. We present a novel planning algorithm, Shortest Path Planning (SPP), to solve process-model-based disambiguation problems. We demonstrate that AEP surpasses state-of-the-art methods on a real-world dataset. Our analysis reveals that AEP is particularly effective in scenarios involving rare entities and those sharing common homonyms. Additionally, we find that the order in which acroforms are disambiguated significantly impacts the likelihood of generating a valid story graph. Finally, we show that AEP successfully generalizes to datasets not present during training, such as moving to new datasets and solving out-of-domain disambiguation challenges. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first application of classical planning to the ABSTRACT dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/ashish-agarwal17/PlanningWithEntityPrompts. Human interaction is largely social, often beginning with dialogue. During conversation, entrainment refers to the process where partners adjust their behavior based on their partners' actions. This study introduces a computationally efficient approach to model vocal entrainment, emphasizing the role of dynamic acoustic features like formants and spectral centroid. The proposed method utilizes Gaussian Mixture Models to characterize these formant and spectral centroid features, alongside the auto-correlation of envelope energy. Evaluated on a dataset of 1,000 English dyadic conversations, the study demonstrates that including group-level features enhances dialogue modeling. Furthermore, results indicate that grouping dyads by their conversational style yields more distinct entrainment models than assigning specific models to individual speakers. Finally, the research shows that entrainment metrics can effectively distinguish between dyads with varying conversational styles and identify similarities among individual members within the same group. The article concludes by discussing how these findings can advance computational models of social behavior. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/entrainment. This paper introduces a categorical model for full lambda-S1 with explicit names, where lambda-abstracts represent isometries within the unitary sphere. We demonstrate that this model satisfies the fundamental properties of the quantum-S1-calculus, including the exchange, generation, eta, and completeness rules. Additionally, we establish the model's consistency by proving the fundamental theorem and verifying the necessary conditions for the parallel reduction relation. The constructive nature of our definitions and proofs ensures that all operations required to construct isometries in the unitary sphere are available. Furthermore, we examine the model's capability to serve as a framework for formally verifying quantum programs. We successfully illustrate this by formally deriving two well-known quantum programs: the Hadamard gate and lambda-manipulation, both of which are fundamental components of quantum computing. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the model can derive the corresponding quantum programs in a straightforward and natural manner. These findings provide a foundation for developing a programming language and a development environment featuring formal verification tools for quantum programs. In this context, the programming language would serve as the syntax of the quantum-S1-calculus, and the development environment would consist of the categorical model paired with a proof assistant. Together, they would enable the formal derivation of all essential combinatorial rules for quantum manipulations in the quantum-S1-calculus. Finally, we show that the model can derive the Dijkstra and Sarkar's constructive solution for the controlled-NOT gate, a critical element of quantum computing. In this case, the programming language corresponds to the quantum-S1-calculus extended with a constant for the controlled-NOT gate. By formally deriving the controlled-NOT gate, we can subsequently derive its transpose, a fundamental operation in quantum computing. This case study underscores the model's effectiveness in deriving essential quantum gates and operations. Through these examples, we have demonstrated the model's utility in deriving fundamental quantum gates and operations, thereby providing a solid foundation for the formal development of quantum programs. Ultimately, this approach represents a significant step toward achieving formal verification for quantum computing. Specifically, it provides a foundation for developing formal verification tools for quantum programs, an essential requirement for the field of quantum computing. Thus, these results constitute a fundamental contribution to the advancement of formal verification within quantum computing. We introduce two novel quasiparticle excitations driven by correlated density-density interactions within a two-dimensional electron system under a strong perpendicular magnetic field. These interactions arise from exchange and Coulomb forces, which become significant at high electron concentrations. The resulting quasiparticles, labeled QP1 and QP2, differ from traditional charge-carrier excitations; specifically, QP1 involves the creation of two electrons alongside two holes, whereas QP2 generates three holes alongside one electron. Both QP1 and QP2 can be partially filled by varying electron-hole ratios, enabling an analysis of multi-component two-dimensional electron gases and their associated anyonic excitations. We derive exact, precise analytical expressions for the energy-momentum dispersion relations of these quasiparticles, identifying critical phenomena including absolute minimum energy states, maximum energy states, and critical points where energy-momentum curves exhibit inflection points. Furthermore, the model demonstrates how adjusting interaction strengths can manipulate hole-electron interactions, facilitating hole condensation, hole superfluidity, and potentially a hole-superfluid phase transition. Additionally, the framework accounts for both nonretarded and retarded interactions, with a comparison made between the fractional quantum Hall effect driven by Coulomb interaction versus exchange interaction. Finally, we discuss the stability of these quasiparticles and propose a method for their experimental observation. This study extends the understanding of the FQHE beyond weak interaction regimes, offering a pathway to construct a highly tunable quantum simulator for investigating strongly correlated electron systems. Ultimately, these findings may contribute to the development of quantum computing technologies. **Keywords:** Coulomb interaction, exchange interaction, quasiparticle excitation, quantum Hall effect, quantum computing. **PACS:** 73.43.-r, 73.43.+f, 72.10.-g, 72.10.-d, 73.21.-f, 73.21.La, 73.43.Lp, 73.43.Na, 73.43.mn, 73.43.mn, 73.43.+n, 73.21.+f, 73.21.+l, 73.21.+p, 73.21.+q, 73.21.+r, 73.21.+s, 73.21.+t, 73.21.+u

We introduce DUVET, a project investigating how galactic outflows regulate star formation, utilizing a combination of *Hubble* and *JWST* imaging alongside new *HST* UV imaging of the bursting disk galaxy A2390-IT. Our analysis reveals that A2390-IT exhibits a massive outflow with a blue-shifted outflow-to-disk mass ratio of 0.25, alongside distinct spatial variations in star formation efficiency (SFE) and SFE surface density (SFE_s), which align with the outflow's morphology. Specifically, SFE reaches 0.01 Gyr$^{-1}$ in the outflow's path, compared to 0.003 Gyr$^{-1}$ in regions intersected by the outflow's tail, and drops to 0.001 Gyr$^{-1}$ in areas outside the outflow's influence. These findings support the hypothesis that outflows suppress star formation. Furthermore, A2390-IT demonstrates a strong correlation between SFE_s and UV surface brightness, a relationship absent in star-forming regions shielded from the outflow. This correlation indicates that the outflow suppresses star formation in dense, bright molecular gas clumps, while unimpeded star formation proceeds in dense gas lacking sufficient UV brightness. These results are consistent with prior observations of outflow-affected galaxies and align with theoretical models of star formation. Additionally, we identified a compact, UV-bright star-forming region within the outflow's trajectory that shows no significant star formation activity over the past 100 Myr, providing further evidence that outflows suppress star formation on timescales of tens of Myr. Finally, A2390-IT displays a strong correlation between SFE and the [OIII] 5007/4959 emission line ratio, suggesting that outflows suppress star formation in regions where the emission line is optically thick. Collectively, these results support the conclusion that galactic outflows significantly suppress star formation. This study is the first to employ *Hubble* and *JWST* imaging to characterize star formation in outflow-affected regions, offering the first spatially resolved comparison of star formation properties in these versus unimpeded regions. This study analyzes the impact of the phase boundary on the triangular flow $v_3$ using the sPHMiT multiphase transport framework. By adjusting the equation of state (EoS) through variations in the phase boundary, we observe that $v_3$ is more sensitive to EoS adjustments than transverse flow $u_t$. Specifically, a stiffer EoS, characterized by a more gradual increase in the speed of sound near the phase boundary, results in higher $v_3$ values. These findings are supported by application to experimental data from Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200–50 GeV. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of initial geometry on $v_3$ sensitivity, determining that a more irregular initial geometry, such as that found in Cu+Cu collisions, leads to a more pronounced dependence of $v_3$ on the EoS. Our results demonstrate that $v_3$ serves as a valuable observable for exploring the QCD phase diagram, with these insights being particularly relevant for upcoming measurements at the RHIC Beam Energy Upgrade. Finally, we conclude that the ratio $v_3/u_t$ offers enhanced sensitivity to the QCD phase boundary compared to $v_3$ alone. Overall, these observations highlight the value of combined $v_3$ and $u_t$ measurements for mapping the QCD phase diagram. We anticipate that future measurements of $v_3$ and $u_t$ will significantly advance our understanding of the QCD phase diagram. We have also made our $v_3$ sensitivity results accessible via an online tool. This online tool will be a valuable resource for the upcoming Beam Energy Upgrade (BE Upgrade) experiments, enabling researchers to efficiently determine the optimal beam energy for investigating the QCD phase diagram. Additionally, we plan to make the $v_3$ sensitivity results available as an add-on analysis for BE Upgrade data. We strongly encourage BE Upgrade experimental collaborations to include $v_3$ and $u_t$ measurements in their data analysis plans to facilitate this investigation. We believe that incorporating $v_3$ and $u_t$ measurements into BE Upgrade experiments will substantially contribute to the exploration of the QCD phase diagram. This paper introduces a new method for creating simultaneously robust and reconfigurable robotic structures using 3D printing. We have developed structure variants that exhibit both robustness and reconfigurability by employing two key strategies: the integration of a 3D truss model into the structure and the use of a novel, non-symmetric, unbalanced rocking mechanism. Our findings demonstrate that these two strategies can be combined to achieve higher unbalanced rocking amplitudes. Additionally, we present simulation results that validate the function of the structures across a broad range of random inputs, such as base excitations. The proposed structure is highly flexible and can be easily adapted for various applications, including protection systems for sensitive payloads and haptic devices for virtual reality. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first fully 3D printed structure capable of reconfiguration. Recent research indicates that pre-training on monocular depth estimation tasks yields superior results for semantic segmentation compared to control classification tasks. This study investigates whether the enhanced performance stems specifically from classifying depth bins or from the inclusion of continuous depth values. We evaluated a pre-training strategy utilizing a linear layer to map network outputs to continuous depth scores, rather than predicting depth bins. Experimental results show that this depth assessment method fails to outperform classification in boosting semantic segmentation performance. Furthermore, we observed that performance gains are specifically linked to the use of continuous values; while bin-based results exceed those from binless classification, they do not match the performance achieved by monocular depth-assessed networks trained on depth continuous scores. Consequently, we hypothesize that the primary benefit of depth information in deep networks stems from the continuity of depth values, which constrains and refines semantic segmentation predictions. Finally, we propose a novel and straightforward post-training strategy that effectively integrates depth networks by adjusting class predictions based on local depth changes. This approach enables networks pre-trained with depth continuous scores to achieve performance rivaling network pairs trained on separate tasks. Overall, our work demonstrates that depth information enhances semantic segmentation performance, regardless of whether the network is trained or post-trained to output depth scores. Additionally, we introduce a new PyTorch implementation that is straightforward to implement and provides competitive performance. Let $\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})$ represent the space of analytic functions defined on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. Consider the linear operator $T: \mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D}) \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})$ defined by $f(z) = az^n + bz^m$ with $m > n \geq 1$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{C}$. This paper demonstrates that if $[0, \beta)$ is the Bohr radius for the class of normalized log-harmonic mappings $\mathcal{SLH}(\mathbb{D})$, then $\beta$ serves as the enhanced Bohr radius for the operator $T$ restricted to this same class. Furthermore, we extend this finding to bounded normalized log-harmonic mappings, denoted by $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}^{h}(\mathbb{D})$. Additionally, we derive sufficient conditions for starlikeness and boxikenness for log-harmonic mappings. Finally, we examine the Bohr radius of starlike log-harmonic mappings and provide an outline of its connection to the Bohr radius of pseudoconvex domains.

Keywords: Logarithmic harmonicity; Enhanced Bohr radius; Starlikeness; Boxikeness.

Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation. We demonstrate that its sampling distribution approximates a normal distribution with sufficient accuracy even at small sample sizes, provided the intra-class correlation is low. This insight reveals the optimal configuration for array experimental designs aimed at maximizing the statistical power to detect a specified effect, a setup that is notably more efficient than the current standard. Furthermore, we introduce a series of computationally efficient approximations for the variance and higher moments of Kendall's tau, enabling rapid calculation even when the statistic is derived from multiple samples of varying sizes. Consequently, these methods facilitate new avenues of inference and computation regarding Kendall's tau that were previously unattainable due to its high computational cost. Simulations indicate that utilizing these formulas results in procedures with significantly reduced false rejection rates and markedly shorter computation times. Finally, we apply these techniques to a large-scale epidemiological dataset to demonstrate their practical utility. Overall, our findings offer substantial computational and practical benefits, particularly for researchers employing array experimental designs. Additionally, our code is modular and extends readily to other correlation estimators, such as Spearman's rho, which shares a similar large-sample behavior. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where analytic expressions for the variance and higher moments of these rank-based correlation measures are made available. The code is accessible at https://github.com/tpg212/EffectiveKendallsTau. A primary contribution of this work is providing users with options that enhance the reliability of statistical inference when using rank correlation. Given that thousands of scientific publications currently rely on default settings, the potential impact of these improvements is significant. We anticipate that our findings will inspire further methodological advancements and encourage the scientific community to critically evaluate conclusions drawn from previous studies. We aim to assist the community in assessing the validity of such inferences and offer practical solutions to mitigate any identified biases. Our code serves as a starting point for users to explore these enhancements. We hope these findings spark additional research into the finite-sample properties of rank correlation, as current theory is limited to large samples, and to novel inference techniques that leverage the existing asymptotic properties more effectively. To ensure privacy and security in privacy-preserving edge intelligence (PP-EI) for vehicular networks, this paper proposes a practical and secure Unified Framework for PP-EI (UFP-EI). The framework comprises two primary components: the first addresses the challenge of malicious attacks during the learning phase by introducing a novel Byzantine Robust PP-EI (BR2) scheme; the second component focuses on the communication phase, presenting a new Practical and Secure PP-EI (PSP-EI) scheme that enables secure, privacy-preserving information exchange between vehicles and the base station (BS). Simulation results demonstrate that the BR2 scheme offers superior robustness against attacks compared to existing schemes. Additionally, both the PSP-EI scheme and a baseline achieve high accuracy in location prediction tasks while effectively safeguarding user privacy through secure multiparty computation. Furthermore, both proposals are highly communication-efficient, making them well-suited for deployment in vehicular networks. Finally, both schemes are resilient to a passive BS that cannot compromise user privacy. These findings indicate that the proposed schemes are suitable for real-world implementation in practical edge intelligence applications within vehicular environments. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first scheme that simultaneously ensures security, privacy, and practicality in PP-EI for vehicular networks. The advent of photorealistic face image generators has made it increasingly difficult to distinguish between real and synthetic faces. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) models are widely applied across various domains, including game design, robotics, and autonomous vehicles. However, most existing research in self-driving cars utilizes simulated environments, such as those provided by CARLA, due to the significant computational resources required for real-world training. This paper investigates the application of DRL models on actual driving scenarios involving human occupants. To address issues like sparse rewards and overfitting, a novel architecture named Deep Q-Multihead Network (DQMN) was developed. This model integrates the multi-output capabilities of a DQN model with the error-backpropagation technique from a multi-loss error model. The study involves three core components: an encoder for state representation, a controller for action selection, and an output layer for reward generation. Experimental results indicate that the proposed DQMN architecture achieves superior performance in both simulation and real-world scenarios when compared to the widely used Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) model. Furthermore, the paper explores the application of DQMN in a round-robin testing scenario for self-driving vehicles. Finally, the authors conclude by discussing potential avenues for future research. Keywords: Deep Reinforcement Learning, Autonomous Driving, Self-driving Vehicles, Deep Q-Multihead Network.

Asynchronous parallel (AP) Parallel Deb Sobes (PDS) evolutionary algorithms enable substantial reductions in runtime and increases in efficiency for multi-objective evolutionarily algorithms (MOEAs). However, because AP-PDS algorithms evaluate candidate solutions at varying times, high-quality outcomes are often discovered later than anticipated, leading to an underestimation of their true quality and a bias toward early evaluations. This introduces a risk that superior solutions may be overlooked. To address this evaluation time bias in AP-PDEOs, we introduce a novel parent selection mechanism designed to mitigate temporal biases. This mechanism integrates an apriori parent selection strategy with a subsequent frequency-based correction step. Empirical evaluations on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach enhances the overall performance of AP-PDEOs. Additionally, the proposed algorithms have been shown to outperform standard MOEAs, including NSGA-II. The complete source code is accessible at https://github.com/evolutionary-algorithms-and-machine-learning/PyAPDEO. The microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 was initially identified through photometric monitoring of the Magellanic Clouds by the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment. Subsequent analysis using high-resolution near-infrared imaging from Keck Adaptive Optics (KAOS) and Gemini South Adaptive Optics Imager (GAIA) confirmed the presence of a point-like source located approximately 2.8 arcseconds from the lens. This object was identified as a host star supporting a planet with a mass of 4.8 Earth masses ($\pm 1.3$) and a semi-major axis of 0.14 AU ($\pm 0.03$). The planet's equilibrium temperature is calculated to be 200 K, classifying it as a super-Earth. The host star is likely a K or M dwarf with a mass of 0.44 solar masses ($\pm 0.08$) and a luminosity of 0.046 solar luminosities ($\pm 0.008$). This system is situated in the Galactic disk at a distance of 3.6 kpc ($\pm 0.7$) and is expected to be approximately 10 billion years old. The discovery of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 confirms that microlensing is highly effective for detecting cold, low-mass planets orbiting low-mass stars in the Galactic disk. Additionally, the system's age and the characteristics of its planet contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of planetary system formation and evolution. This study represents the 1434th microlensing planetary system identified to date. This work investigates the high-rate behavior of time-oscillating Lindblad generators, yielding multiple findings and insights. First, by employing a rigorous resolvent method, we demonstrate that the dynamics associated with these oscillating generators converge to a deterministic limit as the oscillation rate increases; this limiting dynamics corresponds to the solution of a stationary Lindblad master equation, where the effective time-independent generator is derived from the resolvent expansion of the time-oscillating one. Second, utilizing the resolvent method, we establish a second-order rate of convergence for the strongly symmetric case and provide an explicit form for the leading error term in the imaginary part of the spectrum of the time-oscillating Lindblad generator. Finally, within the context of a three-level system, we illustrate the results of this method through two applications. Furthermore, by integrating the resolvent method with the multiple scales method, we derive an alternative proof for the main results, thereby validating the resolvent-based approach and highlighting the distinct advantages of the multiple scales method. Notably, the resolvent method is more effective in quantifying the rate of convergence. The methodologies and results presented herein are applicable to quantum control, quantum computing, and quantum simulation. Specifically, the findings regarding the rate of off-resonance excitation are particularly significant for quantum control applications. Additionally, the insights into error analysis for Lindblad diagonalization can facilitate the development of quantum algorithms. The discussion on three-level systems may offer valuable perspectives for the design of quantum circuits. Finally, the insights into multiple scales methods could aid in simplifying complex quantum systems. Overall, this research aims to provide valuable insights and tools for advancing quantum technology. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the Lindblad equation and Lindblad generators; Section 3 presents the main results; Section 4 offers two applications within three-level systems; Section 5 discusses the implications of these results; and Section 6 concludes the study. The depolarization signal recorded at the Ce site in Rh-rich compositions confirms the formation of a ferromagnetic structure below 19 K, which aligns with neutron diffraction findings. Additionally, the signal reveals a complex phase diagram characterized by competing phases: a ferromagnetic state coexisting with a ferromagnetic-spin solid phase, as well as the emergence of ferromagnetic-ordering-induced nuclear-solidification in CeMgS-type rare-earth compounds. These results offer new insights into the phase competition within this specific class of materials. Furthermore, depolarization at the Rh site indicates a phase transition in CePd$_{0.9}$Rh$_{0.1}$ at 19 K, likely corresponding to the onset of ferromagnetic ordering on the non-magnetic Rh sites. Finally, depolarization at the Pb site demonstrates that the magnetic moments at the Ce site remain relatively stable throughout the entire temperature range. These observations are discussed in the context of the proposed ferromagnetic structure for CePd$_{0.9}$Rh$_{0.1}$. The successful application of neutron depolarization in this work establishes a new method for studying magnetic ordering in rare-earth compounds. This novel depolarization signal observed at the Ce site could serve as a valuable alternative to traditional diffraction methods for examining magnetic ordering in similar materials. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction for classifying graphs and generating node or subgraph representations. However, decoding these representations requires careful design of interpreters to ensure GNNs function as reliable and trustworthy tools. Since current decoding methods lack a unified framework, we propose a parameterized framework for GNN interpreters. This framework offers a systematic approach to modeling interpreters and provides practical guidance for their construction. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to parametrize various components of an interpreter using this framework, revealing its flexibility and potential to produce novel, improved interpreters. Additionally, we present a comprehensive suite of non-trivial test cases for evaluating GNN interpreters, which can test these frameworks and parametrizations on diverse and challenging problems. Our extensive experimental evaluation shows that these approaches yield significant improvements in accuracy, faithfulness, and stability across a wide range of graph problems. We have open-sourced our framework and testing framework to facilitate the development of future GNN interpreters. We hope this resource will help the community advance the field of GNN interpretation. The complete implementation is available at: https://github.com/epfl-lgl/gnn-interpreter.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are widely used to solve partial differential equations, yet their training via the least squares residual often suffers from slow convergence due to spectral bias. While spectral bias can be mitigated through the use of higher-order Adams methods, these introduce numerical instability. In this study, we demonstrate that adding a second-order Adam optimizer effectively addresses spectral bias without compromising numerical stability. We validate this finding across various high-dimensional partial differential equations. Furthermore, we analyze the underlying reasons for this improvement and establish a link between progressive training via Adam and spectral bias utilizing the singular value decomposition matrix of the linearized training process. These findings offer valuable insights for training PINNs on complex problems. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/kevinhcheung/Momentum-Spectral-Bias. Additionally, a supplementary video is available at https://youtu.be/4211111111. Finally, our results indicate that momentum-based optimization enhances both the training and generalization performance of PINNs. This study examines a phase-tripling system featuring a thin, dissipative layer with locally varying Kelvin-Voigt attenuation. The model is represented by a system of wave equations for $u$ and $w$ connected via complex-valued functions $G$ and $H$, where $w$ is confined to a small interval $(c,d)$ and includes a locally defined Kelvin-Voigt attenuation term. A key assumption involves a specific growth condition for the derivatives of $G$ and $H$, which becomes critical for systems lacking self-similarity. This condition is linked to the existence of stable linked waves—solutions to the undamped system with real phases and amplitudes that may differ by a constant phase factor. The primary objective is to establish local-in-time damped exponential stability for the system, contingent upon the damped linked-wave condition, which asserts that all linked waves possess constant magnitudes across the domain and vary only in phase. This condition serves as the dissipative counterpart to the spectral damped phase condition found in prior literature. Additionally, we demonstrate that the damped phase condition implies the spectral damped phase condition, thereby validating the applicability of existing results from previous studies. Our findings also highlight a significant distinction between attenuation models based on the Kelvin and Voigt approaches within dissipative layers. Notably, under certain growth constraints on the derivatives of $G$ and $H$, the spectral damped phase condition is not necessary for exponential stability; instead, it can be substituted with the damped linked-wave condition. Furthermore, these results offer an alternative perspective on the distinction between the damped linked and spectral conditions previously documented. Finally, we outline an open question regarding the necessity of linked-wave conditions for exponential stability in systems where the dissipative layer's position varies with position and/or time. To address this, we provide an explicit counterexample of a symmetric linked-wave system that exhibits subexponential growth despite having a stable spectrum. This counterexample arises from a condition where the real parts of the linked-wave eigenvalues approach zero at a rate slower than the rate at which imaginary eigenvalues grow, a scenario that can occur in non-self-adjoint systems. Our approach involves constructing linked-wave solutions with vanishing amplitudes, a method that also facilitates the derivation of spectral conditions for exponential stability. This study addresses two key challenges in reinforcement learning (RL): the need for human-interpretable policies and the difficulty of balancing exploration and exploitation when action semantics are unclear. To tackle these issues, we introduce a hierarchical RL framework that treats high-level actions as high-level observations, enabling the learning of low-level policies associated with each high-level action. The high-level policy is represented as a set of logic programs derived using Inductive Logic Programming. By interpreting high-level policies as disjunctive logic programs, the resulting policies are inherently human-interpreertable. Furthermore, providing high-level policies as actions allows the agent to infer their meanings during exploration, thereby refining the balance between exploring and exploiting actions at both hierarchical levels. Experiments on two continuous control tasks with distinct semantic structures demonstrate that our approach outperforms both standard deep RL methods and other hierarchical RL variants. Additional results on discrete gridworlds and a robotic arm task highlight the versatility of the proposed two-level hierarchy. The code and videos are accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/explainable-model-driven-hierarchical-rl. Finally, this work shows that even when exact models are unavailable, learning models that capture the semantics of actions remains possible. The paper concludes by discussing the advantages and limitations of this two-level hierarchical model-based RL method for learning interpretable policies. Finally, the article emphasizes the interpretability of the resulting policies, which is crucial for applications such as autonomous driving and robotic surgery. The authors believe that rigorous research into the trade-off between performance and policy interpretability is essential for developing safe and trustworthy AI systems. Given the significant impact of policy interpretability, we argue that it should be treated as a third pillar of RL research, alongside sample efficiency and generalization. Data compression is widely used to reduce storage costs and transmission times, typically relying on redundancy within source ensembles. In the quantum realm, however, the uncertainty principle prevents straightforward applications of classical methods. This study investigates the intersection of quantum nonreversibility and compression within a biphoton system. We introduce a nonreversible compression protocol for biphoton pairs and demonstrate that even though the entanglement between spatial modes remains reversible during the process, the physical configuration of the compression device induces nonreversibility. Specifically, after compressing one subspace, the state cannot be perfectly decompressed into its original form without access to the specific parameters of the device. We validate this finding by showing that the output state after compression and subsequent expansion is not a pure state, despite the expansion itself not directly collapsing the state. Furthermore, we establish a link between this phenomenon and quantum irreversibility. Finally, we illustrate that this effect can be observed in experiments conducted at the two-photon level using spontaneous parametric down-conversion. These findings hold significant implications for the quantum information domain, particularly regarding quantum error correction and cryptography. For instance, in cryptography, the possibility of compressing quantum states renders the original protocol vulnerable to eavesdropping attacks. In contrast, within the quantum error correction framework, this effect enables the design of new codes capable of correcting both amplitude and logical-damping-dissipative errors. Additionally, our results open avenues for developing new quantum algorithms that simulate the compression and expansion of quantum states. This study introduces minimax (SOT) challenges derived from a broad category of functions exhibiting sum-of-translates characteristics, founded on the relative entropy of Gaussian distributions and its variants. These problems extend the Fenton approximation framework beyond the specific scenario involving the average relative risk of a mixture Gaussians. Significant progress has been achieved regarding convex hull properties, structural insights, and the rigorous existence and uniqueness of solutions (up to permutation). Additionally, large deviations asymptotics involving linear scaling of variances are examined within two distinct regimes: constant means and equal means. Dark matter may interact with nucleons via spin-dependent forces, necessitating both direct detection experiments utilizing heavy target nuclei and a thorough investigation of $^6$Li's role within such targets. This study presents the most precise measurement of spin-dependent interactions with $^6$Li to date, achieved through a thermal neutron capture study on enriched $^6$LiF. The resulting direct and indirect constraints on spin-dependent interactions are significantly tighter than previous limits derived from $(\gamma,n)$ and $(n,p)$ reactions, as well as other recent thermal neutron research. Furthermore, our findings offer a direct validation of the $^6$Li transfer operator formalism, which has previously been tested only indirectly. We also compare these results with those from other direct detection experiments that utilize $^6$Li, highlighting a marked discrepancy that demands resolution. Finally, we explore the potential of neutron capture reactions as direct detection experiments, specifically examining the capture of thermal neutrons by $^{129}$I. This approach could enable the study of spin-dependent interactions with iodine nuclei, a capability currently lacking in other direct detection methods. Additionally, this represents the first such investigation into spin-dependent interactions with iodine. We also examine the technical challenges associated with conducting this experiment, including achieving sufficient sensitivity and managing background radiation. Ultimately, we conclude that a dedicated neutron thermal capture experiment is essential to fully exploit $^6$Li in direct detection research and to establish a robust framework for evaluating new proposals in this field. This includes assessing proposals that employ $^6$Li in direct detection setups alongside $^{129}$I. We demonstrate that this would be feasible within a year using existing $^6$LiF target material and the existing NIST HFIR facility. However, achieving the necessary sensitivity to fully explore spin-dependent interactions with iodine would require approximately a decade of data from a more powerful neutron source. We have identified two suitable sources for this purpose: the proposed ESS in Sweden and the proposed MSRE in China. We strongly advocate for $^6$Li research to be prioritized at these facilities. We anticipate that this initiative will significantly advance the field of direct detection, particularly regarding spin-dependent interactions. We anticipate that the resulting constraints will be competitive with, and potentially exceed, those from other direct detection experiments, thereby playing a crucial role in the search for dark matter. Blind image restoration (BUR) addresses the challenge of recovering high-quality images from low-quality sources by simultaneously estimating the image and the degradation model. This paper introduces a novel approach for single image restoration that treats the image as a superposition of multiple patches, where each patch is modeled as a linear combination of basis images. The basis images are iteratively updated using a conjugate gradient algorithm, while the mixture weights and degradation model parameters are inferred through a variational Bayesian (VB) framework. The proposed VB algorithm is applied to image restoration, demonstrating effective recovery of images corrupted by various models. Experimental results indicate that the method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhenghaochen1992/BlindImageRestoration. This paper presents a formal validation framework for reasoning about programs specified in logical form languages that combine first-order logic with temporal assertions. Our approach builds on the Hoare logic formalism but is specifically adapted to accommodate rich, expressive specifications written in these languages. To address the challenge of managing large conjunctive/conjunctive-like formulas common in such contexts, validation is conducted via rule induction on the FOL sub-formulas. Furthermore, to support temporal assertions, additional rules are constructed based on SMT solvers dedicated to temporal reasoning. Ultimately, validation is achieved through fully automated proof generation using our specialized Coq library. We demonstrate the framework's applicability by validating examples drawn from existing literature within our tool system. This system comprises a Coq library featuring an extended Hoare calculus tailored for first-order logic and derived from Hoare's original formalism, as well as an SMT solver library built upon the Interpolation library. Finally, we illustrate how valid theorems can be proven using our tool system in conjunction with the specified Coq library. Our work represents the first fully automated validation of Hoare logic applied to first-order logic formalisms utilizing a Coq library that extends standard Hoare calculus with support for first-order logic. Additionally, we provide an auxiliary Coq library that interpolates the proof rules derived from the SMT solver library; this library enables the validation of proofs generated by our tool system through fully automated proof generation. Our method employs first-order logic formalism to articulate rich specifications and utilizes fully automated validation of Hoare logic via Coq to ensure reliable verification of these specifications. This capability facilitates the automated analysis of complex software systems, delivering more robust and dependable solutions. Canopus is a Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replica state machine (RSM) designed for distributed systems. It features a streamlined protocol that reduces network communication overhead by leveraging asynchronous broadcast channels and minimizing the frequency of synchronous interactions. Furthermore, its replica implementation is optimized to enhance scalability. Canopus has been successfully deployed in various cloud environments, including AWS, Azure, and GCP, where it manages the serving of application data. However, current Canopus deployments are constrained by storage and computation bottlenecks. Canopus stores all received application messages in memory on every replica to maintain consistent ordering for the construction of deterministic state. Consequently, applications generating many small messages face significant computational overhead due to the sequential processing required for these messages in Canopus. This paper demonstrates how these Canopus-specific characteristics can be exploited to scale Canopus replicas, thereby addressing both computation and storage constraints. We introduce several techniques to scale Canopus based on these opportunities. Our evaluation results indicate that these techniques can reduce storage and computation bottlenecks by up to 4x and 2x, respectively. Furthermore, bottlenecks related to slow application functions can also be mitigated. Overall, Canopus can achieve 2x to 4x higher throughput compared to other BFT systems. Research on biological lipid membranes has demonstrated significant variations in bending modulus measurements for specific lipid types, with some studies indicating a negligible change in this property when cholesterol is added. To investigate the impact of cholesterol on membrane deformation and mechanical properties, we employed the coarse-grained MARTINI lipid model. Our simulations utilized an ensemble of laterally heterogeneous membranes containing varying concentrations of cholate as a model for cholesterol. We calculated the spring constant for various planar and spherically symmetric geometries, accounting for both lipid tilt and curvature. Our findings indicate that including cholesterol does not alter the MARTINI model's bending modulus; this result holds true regardless of whether cholesterol is distributed uniformly or unevenly. Furthermore, our computational approach enables the simultaneous analysis of multiple membranes, facilitating a statistical assessment of membrane properties under varying conditions. These results align with several experimental measurements regarding the effect of cholesterol on bending modulus, while contradicting others. Our analysis of the conflicting experimental data reveals that the observed discrepancies may stem from: (i) the coarse nature of certain experimental methodologies, (ii) potential artifacts arising from the purification process used to isolate pure lipid types, and (iii) the inherent laterally heterogeneous nature of lipid distributions in membranes. Finally, we demonstrate that both the spatial distribution of cholesterol and the fluidity of the membrane influence the area per lipid site and the tilt angle, even though they do not affect the bending modulus. These conclusions are consistent with prior experimental findings. This paper examines the application of the loop quantum gravity formalism to an ADM system characterized by a single radius and a scalar field. Although this model is not a true boundary case, it serves a significant pedagogical role by contrasting with the well-known "minisuperspace" version derived from the Connes form of the LQG Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that this alternative model provides a more accurate test of the formalism and, more importantly, yields a more realistic description of the quantum evolution of the gravitational field. Specifically, it reveals a more intricate relationship between field momentum and density, leading to a more complex evolution of the field's zero mode. Most notably, the model indicates that the field momentum can reach arbitrarily large values, potentially resolving certain conceptual ambiguities. This study presents Phase I of the 10-year data collection from the Pierre Auger Observatory, focusing on the most energetic cosmic rays detected during this initial period. This dataset encompasses events with energies exceeding 5×10¹⁹ eV, including the three most energetic ever recorded. We analyze the energy distribution and explore potential correlations between the energy and zenith angle of these ultra-high-energy events. Additionally, we examine the potential for clustering in the northern sky, which aligns with the Virgo Supercluster, and report on the first four decades of the observed flux distribution. Finally, we discuss the quality of the data and identify specific events that warrant further investigation. These findings will be utilized in Phase II of the Auger Observatory's science program. The catalog includes events with energies above 5×10¹⁹ eV, featuring a total of 1,150 events, with 26 exceeding 5×10²⁰ eV. Key information for each event includes the measured energy, shower axis direction, shower size at the fluorescence detector level, and the number of surface detector stations that registered the event. Additionally, two supplementary catalogs are provided, offering reconstructed event properties derived from combined analyses of the Auger data and simulated showers. One of these supplementary catalogs includes all 1,196 events with energies above 5×10²⁰ eV. The three most energetic events identified in this study are designated as the Auger Tritent, the highest-energy event ever observed, the Auger Triplet, a multi-TeV photon candidate, the Auger Trinary, the highest-energy event above the horizon, the Auger Tractant, and the highest-energy event below the horizon. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision applications; however, their deterministic nature prevents users from evaluating prediction uncertainty. We introduce BayesOD, the first Bayesian approximation tailored for object detection, which utilizes Monte Carlo dropout to quantify uncertainty in localization and classification. By employing a Monte Carlo-based formulation, BayesOD can estimate uncertainty metrics for both bounding boxes and object categories. In our experiments, we utilized the COCO dataset to train and evaluate the method's performance on detection accuracy, localization uncertainty, and classification uncertainty. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these uncertainty estimates enable uncertainty-guided detection, yielding additional improvements in overall detection accuracy. Our results indicate that BayesOD outperforms existing object detectors in achieving higher accuracy while maintaining uncertainty scores at comparable levels. We introduce a novel classical pigeonhole phenomenon by employing transversal modes within multi-qubit systems. Our findings indicate that the probability of finding two distinct qubits in the same computational basis state can approach zero, even when three or more qubits are involved. Additionally, we demonstrate experimentally that the count of potential collisions is limited by both the count of available states and the number of qubits, thereby refuting the original conjecture by Adamek et al. (2021). This serves as a significant step toward developing an efficient parallel replication of unknown quantum states. The proposed method holds potential applications in fundamental quantum information tasks, such as quantum state cloning and indistinguishability testing. Furthermore, we suggest exploring this phenomenon across diverse quantum encoding schemes and physical platforms. Finally, drawing inspiration from the classical two-pigeonhole scenario, we design a game and investigate strategies that exploit this new phenomenon, revealing a fundamental conflict between quantum and classical approaches to pigeonholing. These contributions may inspire further research into fundamental issues regarding the replication of classical and quantum information. This study utilizes a Monte Carlo code to simulate the trajectory of once-a-year CRAND particles (OYP) caught at low Earth orbits (LEO), where trapped particles cannot complete a full orbit due to the influence of Earth's magnetic field. The code calculates the gyro-radius, drift-radius, and bounce-radius for each simulation step, accounting for variations in magnetic field intensity caused by the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF). Results indicate that the IMF significantly affects trapped particle motion. The IMF Y-component determines the orbital plane of the trapped particle, while the X-component dictates the direction of the interplanetary convection, causing the orbital plane to rotate around the Y-axis as the particle is carried away from Earth by the solar wind. Furthermore, trapped particles are captured with velocities that closely align with the velocity of the IMF. These findings suggest a specific mechanism for particle capture at LEOs: as a particle enters the interplanetary convection flow, it begins to rotate around the IMF Y-axis. During this rotation, the particle may become trapped if it crosses to the other side of the magnetic bottle at a position with a weaker magnetic field. Additionally, the IMF Z-component causes the orbital plane to rotate around the Y-axis, with the rotation direction determined by the sign of this component. Consequently, the model demonstrates that the capture of once-a-year particles at LEOs is highly dependent on the IMF. These outcomes offer a new perspective on the capture mechanism of CRAND particles at LEOs and may aid in predicting particle trapping events. Finally, the study confirms that the intensity of the particle flux is closely related to the magnitude of the IMF. A stronger magnetic field produces a larger particle flux, as the particle's drift radius becomes more constrained by the magnetic field. This relationship can be expressed as $J \propto B^{1/3}$, where $J$ represents the particle flux and $B$ denotes the magnetic field intensity. The model also indicates that the flux of OYP is greater than that of non-trapped particles. These results are consistent with the capture of relativistic electrons at LEOs, as previously proposed by [1]. Overall, the findings suggest that the capture mechanism of CRAND particles at LEOs is similar to that of relativistic electrons. Specifically, the capture of CRAND particles at LEOs is primarily caused by the interplanetary convection flow. This study aims to enhance the efficiency of existing LLM-based NLU applications by utilizing a pre-trained model, specifically OPT-350M, which comprises 350 million parameters.
