Recent research has demonstrated that self-supervised language pre-training can substantially advance conversation understanding. However, existing self-supervised methods often yield suboptimal results in this domain because they rely on generic natural language objectives that fail to capture the specific features relevant to conversations. To address this, we introduce a self-supervised pre-training approach grounded in meaningful-based concepts, which focuses on the meaningful relationships between conversations and questions. This method pre-trains the Transformer-XL model using the Meaningful-based Pre-training (MBPT) algorithm on a large, diverse dataset, followed by standard Supervised Conversation Pre-training (SCP) and fine-tuning. Our results show that MBPT consistently surpasses the baseline SCP approach across multiple metrics, achieving significant improvements in question answering accuracy (F1 scores rising from 47.0 to 54.3 and 48.9 to 54.0 on two large-scale datasets) and enhancements in conversation summarization and dialogue state tracking. Additionally, evaluations on eight domain-specific datasets indicate that our model yields superior performance compared to the baseline in these fields. Given that MBPT leverages meaningful associations between conversations and questions as its self-supervised objective, it demonstrates that such associations are transferable to domain-specific tasks, thereby validating the efficacy of our proposed algorithm. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhenghaozhang1993/meaningful-based_pre-training. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical component of machine learning, facilitating an in-depth understanding of how models function, their efficacy, and their potential biases or errors. Despite the proliferation of various methods and metrics proposed over the past few decades to quantify this interpretability, there remains a lack of consensus on a single, unified definition and measurement standard. This paper introduces a novel framework for evaluating algorithmic interpretability through the lens of human learning, a domain where cognitive science and psychology have established comprehensive definitions and cognitive scores to assess learning processes. We demonstrate the application of this framework to address and refine the concept of interpretability. Furthermore, we introduce the cognitive intricacy score as a new metric for quantifying an algorithm's interpretability. By applying this score to a suite of classification models trained on the Iris dataset, we illustrate its practical utility. Finally, we validate the proposed framework and score using both algorithmic metrics and human studies. Our results indicate that models with higher reported interpretability scores are more easily understood by people, and that the cognitive intricacy score effectively captures the difficulty of this learning process. These findings provide robust evidence supporting the efficacy of the proposed framework and metric. Overall, this work offers a fresh perspective on and tools for defining and measuring algorithmic interpretability. The associated code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/CognitiveIntricacy. Deep learning has become a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, enabling machines to excel in complex tasks by identifying patterns within vast datasets. However, many real-world applications are constrained by limited computational resources, preventing the deployment of large-scale models. To address this challenge, we introduce TiWS-iForest, a novel isolation tree designed for small machine learning environments. TiWS-iForest constructs trees more efficiently by utilizing fewer data points per node and by dynamically selecting optimal split features and indices based on specific optimization goals. We evaluate its performance across three distinct scenarios: (1) small datasets, (2) highly constrained hardware, and (3) edge devices. Our results demonstrate that TiWS-iForest outperforms existing anomaly detection methods, offering superior accuracy while significantly reducing data transmission and storage requirements. The implementation is accessible at \url{https://github.com/DeepEdgeResearch/TiWS-iForest}. This research was conducted within the Deep Edge Laboratory at the University of Surrey. Further information can be found at \url{https://deeledge.org}. Given the universal constraint of limited computational resources in many practical tasks, TiWS-iForest serves as a valuable resource for the broader machine learning community. The authors are members of the Deep Edge Laboratory at the University of Surrey. Additional details regarding this limitation are available at \url{https://deeledge.org}. For insights into why TiWS-iForest constitutes a valuable contribution to the machine learning field, visit \url{https://deeledge.org/contribute}. Poisson processes serve as a foundational framework for modeling extreme values. This paper proposes a reparameterization of a standard Poisson process model that aligns more closely with the parameterization found in Archimedean Copula models commonly used for multivariate extremes. By integrating these two prominent frameworks within a single structure, this approach facilitates the analysis of both marginal and dependence parameters using distinct sets of expert knowledge. A key benefit of this method is its capacity to produce a more reliable estimate of the tail index in the marginal distributions. We examine this reparameterization within the context of the bivariate Hüsler-Reiss distribution and the bivariate Gumbel-Singh-Mitra distribution. In a simulation study, we compare the performance of this reparameterization against traditional methods. Finally, the methodology is illustrated using two datasets: one related to financial returns and the other to environmental data. Throughout the paper, we rely on Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to execute the Bayesian analysis. A key finding is that, under this framework, shape parameters can be reliably estimated even with a relatively small number of observations. Additionally, we demonstrate that shape parameters in these models are not necessarily constrained to be non-negative. Finally, we show that this model serves as a viable competitor to existing methods available in popular statistical software. All analyses are supported by a comprehensive R package that we provide. A detailed tutorial will be published as a monograph. Furthermore, we have made available a new R package that incorporates all techniques discussed in this paper. To ensure reproducibility, we have also released an R notebook containing all relevant code. We have also published a review of all these techniques, which will serve as the foundation for a doctoral dissertation. The review paper, along with the software and related materials, will be accessible via our university's institutional repository. The software is available on CRAN. The tutorial, along with other supplementary materials, can be downloaded from our GitHub repository. The tutorial is also accessible via an RStudio cloud environment. Our approach is also applicable to multivariate extremes. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of Poisson process models to financial returns. In this application, we estimate the tail index at specific points in the unit interval and along the line connecting these points. Our findings indicate that the resulting estimates are more reliable than those produced by traditional methods. Furthermore, we have developed a new R package that incorporates all techniques discussed in this paper. A detailed tutorial will be published as a monograph. This study examines the problem of minimizing the average cross-sectional area of a convex body $K$ using a parallel projection. The result indicates that such "critical" bodies must possess a specific structural property: their surfaces must be composed of two families of developable surfaces. Conversely, "critical" convex bodies with this structural characteristic were demonstrated to indeed minimize the average cross section. Notably, the regular polyhedra, which belong to this class, achieve the minimum average cross section. In the context of $n$-dimensional space, the average cross section of a regular polyhedron is calculated as:
$$ \frac{2^{n+1} (\sqrt{2} + 1)^{n-1}}{n! (n+1)} $$
Additionally, the average cross sections for regular simplices and cubes were also derived. A significant theorem by Khachin was refined, and the authors propose the hypothesis that the regular polyhedron provides the minimum average cross section for convex bodies inscribed within it. Furthermore, it is proven that the minimum average cross section of a convex body inscribed in a given circumscribed regular polyhedron is attained by a polyhedron sharing the same symmetry as its circumscribing body. The paper also presents several constructions of such "critical" bodies. Finally, the authors extend their conjecture to higher dimensions, suggesting that a regular simplex yields the minimum average cross section. The text concludes with an English translation of Minkowski's conjecture.
Keywords: convex body; cross section; average cross section; regular polyhedron; regular simplex; circumscribed regular polyhedron; developable surface; developable fragment.

This paper outlines our system for the Common Sense Evaluation (COMET) task, which was co-organized with SemEval and IWT for ICAIR at ACL 2020. The goal of COMET is to assess large-scale common sense knowledge networks. Our approach concentrates on two tasks: (A) identifying genuine instances of abstract concepts within corpus-specific instances, and (B) evaluating the confidence of a knowledge network regarding a specific relation between predefined entities. To address Task (A), we developed SiNET, a hybrid network that integrates resources from ConceptNet and Wikipedia. For Task (B), we introduced a knowledge augmentation strategy that enhances the symbolic knowledge network's coverage and reliability by incorporating additional information from WIKIpedia. The evaluation environment for SiNET is detailed in our technical report, which also covers Task (B). SiNET achieved state-of-the-art results across all metrics, securing the first place among 27 participating systems. A thorough analysis of the results is provided. The code for SiNET is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/comet-atomic-2020.

**1. Introduction**
Recent years have seen a surge in interest in large-scale symbolic knowledge networks designed to represent common sense knowledge. These networks, or knowledge graphs, consist of relation triples—statements about entities such as "the Eiffel Tower is in Paris." Prominent examples include ConceptNet (Durrett et al., 2019) and NELL (Srikumar et al., 2017). While these networks have demonstrated remarkable growth over the past decade, their completeness remains a significant challenge. This limitation is particularly acute for abstract concepts, such as "kindness," which lack a fixed physical form. Consequently, the community has recently focused on two critical issues: (A) generating valid instances for abstract concepts tailored to specific corpora, and (B) assessing the confidence levels of symbolic knowledge networks regarding specific relations. Hi-GAL is a survey designed to map the Galactic plane within the 450, 25, 160, and 850 $\mu$m bands, covering a 30$^{\circ}$ x 30$^{\circ}$ area at a resolution of 10$^{\prime\prime}$. This pipeline is engineered to process data from the Hi-GAL experiment, which utilizes the HAWC+ and TESCA heterodyne and bolometer instruments mounted on the 6.5-meter James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. It employs a straightforward yet effective data reduction strategy, allowing the pipeline to generate maps and spectral line data within days of observation. Consequently, Hi-GAL has successfully completed two full surveys of the Galactic plane, delivering maps of unprecedented quality and sensitivity. This method has proven highly adaptable, recently being extended to the Hi-GAL successor survey, MaPP, which offers even greater sensitivity and utilizes a larger field of view. This paper outlines the Hi-GAL data reduction pipeline and its underlying strategies for data processing. It details the various steps involved in reducing and combining data from both HAWC+ and TESCA, as well as the methods employed to produce MaPP data. The resulting products include calibrated, combined maps and data cubes, alongside point source catalogues and spectral line extraction tools. These outputs are accessible via the Hi-GAL Data Archive. The paper concludes by summarizing the scientific outcomes derived from the two Hi-GAL surveys and the emerging MaPP survey. Finally, we discuss the future of the HAWC+ and TESCA instruments and the anticipated products from the MaPP survey. The code is publicly available on GitHub. The globular cluster NGC 2808 is renowned for its multiple-population structure and a wide range of helium abundances. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of 13 red giant clump stars from NGC 2808, utilizing a deep, wide-field V-band image alongside Hubble Space Telescope (HST) V606 and W659 filters. By employing the color-magnitude-diagram (CMD) method, we determined the stellar parameters and derived abundances for these stars. Our results reveal a significant spread in C and N abundances, while O and M show only minor variations. Crucially, we confirmed a substantial variation in iron abundance (Fe) among these stars, consistent with earlier findings by Brocato et al. (1982) and Zibetti et al. (2000). Furthermore, we identified a strong correlation between Fe and N abundances, suggesting that the formation of N is driven by the metallicity of the stars. Additionally, the data supports the existence of an anti-correlation between O and N. These results indicate that NGC 2808 exhibits a broader variation in nucleosynthetic yields compared to other globular clusters. Finally, we propose that the stars with the highest Fe abundances likely formed from material enriched by core-collapse supernovae, whereas those with the lowest abundances originated from material processed by low-mass stars. This conclusion is reinforced by the observed correlation between M and Fe abundances. Overall, this study provides a detailed examination of the initial population in NGC 2808, confirming significant variations in Fe and N levels. These findings offer valuable insights for understanding the nucleosynthetic yields of massive stars and the cluster's evolutionary history. The data utilized in this work is accessible via the Mendeley data repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7100009. The code can be requested from the corresponding author.

We investigate single-file particles constrained to move along one dimension by analyzing their single and two-body entropies. Focusing on the dynamic entropic sorting phenomenon—where slower entities overtake faster ones—we define the "initial exit" as the event where a faster entity, previously trapped behind a slower one, escapes from a shared confined region. We demonstrate that the duration of this initial exit can be modeled as the output of a Poisson process, where the rate depends on both entropic and viscous factors. Specifically, we find that the probability distribution for this duration follows an exponential form determined by the product of entropic forces and the relative viscosity of the colliding pairs. We validate these findings by calculating initial exit durations for systems involving free diffusion and diffusion within finite domains, using particle chains composed of single-file free range hard-cores and generalized Langevin single-file particles as specific instances. Our findings offer both qualitative and quantitative insights into single-file dynamics, facilitating the creation of intuitive and quantitative metrics for characterizing initial exit durations. Furthermore, we provide a quantitative approach to estimating useful metrics for applications involving file-based data transfer. These results establish a foundation for developing efficient initial exit strategies in data transmission, where the "duration" represents time, and "entropy" and "viscosity" reflect time-dependent data transmission constraints. Additionally, we propose a framework for quantifying relative viscosity and entropy based on prior research into free-range and single-file diffusion. Ultimately, we conclude by outlining potential future research directions and practical applications of these results. Specifically, we detail how our methodology can be applied to establish an efficient initial exit strategy for file transfer, thereby significantly reducing transmission times. We also demonstrate the method's utility in data transmission by applying it to free-range and single-file transfers of both discrete and continuous data. We anticipate that our findings will facilitate the development of efficient initial exit strategies for data transmission, thereby reducing transmission times and enhancing the efficiency of file transfer processes. Measurement inferences in quantum physics typically involve applying Bayes' theorem to update the state $\rho$ of a quantum system following a projective measurement $M$ with outcome $m$. However, standard applications often overlook the Bayesian prerequisite that prior and posterior judgments exist within the same information framework. This paper introduces the Quantum Bayes' Theorem (QB'T), a necessary condition for inferring a post-measurement state that updates across consistent frameworks defined by commuting von Neumann algebras. The QB'T establishes an equivalence between two procedures: (i) updating the state and performing measurement $M$, versus (2) carrying out a pre-measurement check $C$ that is strictly implied by $M$, then updating the state based on $C$. This process facilitates state inference across different description frameworks, a capability that QB'T renders consistent. Specifically, if a researcher intends to update the state after a projective measurement $M$ without explicitly executing $M$ first, QB'T mandates that they conceptually perform $C$ and subsequently update the state based on $C$ rather than $M$. We provide illustrative examples from our prior work to demonstrate that QB'T is essential for ensuring consistency in such state inferences. Furthermore, we apply the QB'T to the problem of back action evasion in continuous-variable quantum physics, deriving new results that generalize our previous findings. A key advantage of this approach is that it eliminates the need for an auxiliary unperformed ideal measurement, which was previously required in standard state inference procedures. Additionally, the QB'T offers a novel perspective for establishing necessary conditions for the continuous variable back action evasion. Finally, we propose a protocol for state inference in quantum physics that is strictly aligned with Bayesian principles, contingent upon the application of QB'T. The parametric Lyman-alpha Filter Model (LAFM) describes the transmission spectrum of a ground-based Lyman-$\alpha$ filter designed to facilitate astronomical photometry of high-redshift objects in the Lyman-alpha forest region. By employing standard parametric equations, the model captures the transmission curve's shape and narrow aperture, allowing the transmission values at the edges of the aperture to be defined by a single free parameter. The model was validated against observed transmission curves from the ALPACA filter, which exhibits a free-parameter transmission at the aperture edges ranging from 0.11 to 0.40. This model is intended to support cosmological simulations and investigate the neutral hydrogen distribution within the intergalactic medium. Additionally, it serves as a tool for researchers to assess the capabilities of current and future optical and optical/near-IR telescopes for high-redshift astronomy. The model is accessible as a Python module at https://github.com/akshaykumar123/LAFM. Furthermore, a series of Jupyter notebooks is available at https://github.com/akshaykumar123/LAFM/tree/master/Notebooks to illustrate the model's application in high-redshift cosmology and to outline the necessary modifications for adapting it to various filters and telescopes. This paper introduces and analyzes ideal synchronization controllers designed for network-wide state estimation in graph-filter symmetric networks (NFSNs), focusing on continuous-time linear time-invariant (LTI) systems. By leveraging the specific structural properties of these systems, we demonstrate that a centralized controller can achieve finite-time convergence of state estimates with exact precision. We then develop filter-based synchronization controllers (FSSCs) capable of achieving near-identical performance to the centralized approach while enabling distributed implementation. Utilizing the nested-sinusoidal (NS) technique, we prove that a properly designed FSSC converges within finite time and remains exact, with its design relying solely on the system structure and parameters. Furthermore, we establish the existence and uniqueness of these FSSCs. Finally, we extend this research to discrete-time LTI systems, presenting an analogous FSSC design and confirming its ability to achieve synchronized state estimate convergence. To validate our theoretical findings, we present simulation results. The core contributions of this study are twofold: (i) the demonstration that FSSCs can synchronize state estimates in NFSNs, and (ii) the provision of explicit, closed-form design formulas for both continuous- and discrete-time scenarios. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive analysis of synchronization performance, stability, and robustness against disturbances. The proposed methodology is applicable to a broad spectrum of graph-filter symmetric networks, including graph-filter complete networks, nested-sinusoidal networks, and nested-sinusoidal trees. Our approach enables precise synchronization of state estimates, thereby facilitating accurate network-wide information recovery. This advancement holds significant potential for enhancing the precision of information recovery in various NFSNs. The paper is structured as follows: Section II presents preliminary background and notation. Section III defines NFSNs and their associated structural properties. Section IV details the design and analysis of FSSCs, supported by numerical examples in Section V. The paper concludes with a summary of our main contributions. Multimedia content, particularly video, is increasingly consumed on mobile devices, yet searching for multimedia remains a challenging endeavor. A viable solution involves employing dynamic indexing for multimedia streams. This article introduces a method for dynamically maintaining an index of video frames based on visual descriptors. It defines image similarity via geometric transformations and presents algorithms to populate and update this geometric similarity index. The approach utilizes local feature descriptors, specifically ORB, which are geometric invariant. The index is constructed using a feature signature and achieves rapid lookup through geohashing. The proposed technique has been implemented in C++ and assessed on both mobile and desktop platforms. Experimental results indicate comparable performance on mobile devices relative to desktops. Furthermore, the method demonstrates the ability to maintain an index for a video stream with minimal memory consumption. However, matching image similarities relies on the presence of a sufficient number of feature descriptors within each image. The study presents both successful and failed retrieval examples. Overall, the method proves highly effective for dynamic picture indexing. Future enhancements could involve using more robust descriptors like SIFT or ORB-SIFT, though this would necessitate increasing the computational resources available. Additionally, color and motion information could be incorporated into the visual descriptor to enable richer similarity measurements. The index supports multiple similarity metrics, including geometric invariants, similarity invariant geometric transformations, and projective transformations. While projective transformations incur higher computational costs, they offer the greatest flexibility. The index successfully retrieves images under both rigid and non-rigid transformations. Although full projective invariance is achievable, some minor retrieval errors occur due to scale limitations in descriptor matching. To address this, a novel method for detecting and correcting camera rotation could be developed to automatically adjust camera parameters. Furthermore, a mechanism to dynamically select the most appropriate similarity metric based on available computational resources would be beneficial. Finally, the index can be extended to handle higher-dimensional data, such as 3D models or audio. Implementing this multivariate approach would require a different geometric similarity definition, potentially involving geodesic distances on a sphere for 3D data, alongside the current application to 2D images. Alternatively, the index could be utilized for content delivery networks. In this scenario, servers could maintain copies of videos indexed in this manner, enabling users to search for videos they are currently watching or to recommend new ones. This solution would require only a small initial indexing cost, with subsequent updates occurring asynchronously. The keyless communication framework eliminates the need for a secret key by utilizing a common random seed shared between the transmitter and receiver. However, the transmitter's output must still satisfy specific statistical constraints to ensure the receiver can adequately exploit the seed. This paper introduces a keyless verification protocol suitable for general continuous-alphabet channels, consisting of two steps: first, the channel output is tested against a uniform distribution; second, if the test passes, the output is used to generate a secret key via a randomness extractor. We analyze the security and efficiency of this protocol for the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. Our findings indicate that a constant amount of key material can be extracted when the transmitter operates at power $P$ above the threshold $2\sigma^2+\sigma\ln\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)$, where $\alpha$ denotes the significance level of the first test. This efficiency surpasses that of recent seed-based schemes and approaches the theoretical maximum derived from intrinsic randomness. Additionally, we demonstrate that a moderate power increase significantly enhances security. These results are achieved with only a negligible degradation in average rate. Finally, the protocol's performance is evaluated through simulations. (Extended abstract)

Keywords: keyless communication, hypothesis testing, uniformity testing, intrinsic randomness, secret key rate, seed-based schemes, AWGN channel.

Washboard potentials serve as simplified representations of various physical systems, including electrons moving through a periodic crystal lattice under an external electric field. The dynamics of charged particles interacting with optical or terahertz fields are frequently modeled using the Lorentz electron within an energy-dissipative washboard potential. Although the standard washboard potential dissipates energy via friction proportional to velocity, a generalized form employing the square of velocity is frequently utilized to represent Josephson junctions and self-consistently coupled plasma systems, such as sum-frequency generation near a metal surface. The one-dimensional generalized washboard potential exhibits two equivalent minima separated by a saddle point, with the distance between saddle and minimum scaling with the external field amplitude. When this distance exceeds the uncertainty principle's limit, the potential facilitates tunneling between equivalent minima, forming a metastable double-wound structure. In the limit of negligible tunneling, the generalized washboard potential mimics a double-wound system where the particle resides in one of the equivalent minima. This study investigates uniform transport in these potentials, contrasting them with the well-established linear washboard model, which offers an analytical solution for uniform velocity. We demonstrate that for sufficiently strong external fields, a threshold amplitude exists below which uniform velocity is impossible. Furthermore, we analyze the conditions required for tunneling between equivalent minima and quantify the reduction in the field-amplitude threshold for tunneling compared to the linear washboard potential. Finally, we outline applications of these generalized washboard models to the velocity of Lorentz electrons and surface currents generated by surface plasma waves. Specifically, we show that external fields with higher frequencies result in greater velocities across the same range of amplitudes. Additionally, we illustrate that uniform acceleration is achievable for external-field amplitudes that preclude uniform velocity. These findings may inform the design of systems aiming to achieve high electron velocities. To facilitate future research, we provide a numerical solver for the generalized washboard potential. This tool enables the calculation of uniform acceleration, determination of external-field amplitudes for tunneling between equivalent minima, and the estimation of threshold amplitudes for uniform velocity. The numerical solver is available as an open-source repository at https://github.com/alexei-ivanov/washboard-transport. The proposed approach is also applicable to investigating transport in systems described by the Schrödinger equation with a generalized washboard potential. We present a new framework for estimating impulse response functions (IRFs) based on local projections. This approach classifies IRF estimates as either linear or nonlinear and applies tailored smoothing techniques to achieve optimal performance in each scenario. For linear IRFs, the method offers optimal estimation by implementing a study-specific banding strategy that accommodates varying signal-to-noise ratios across equations. Regarding nonlinear IRFs, the approach utilizes kernel-based smoothing with an adaptive bandwidth selection mechanism inspired by the local linear regression method ADOLPACK. Simulations demonstrate that this procedure delivers superior performance compared to existing methods available in the R package LPIR. Furthermore, an application to local labor markets reveals distinct patterns of IRF spillovers between linear and nonlinear cases. Specifically, linear IRFs exhibit stronger positive spillovers from the Federal Reserve's large-scale asset purchases, whereas certain industries and states display significant negative spillovers in specific lags under nonlinear IRFs. These negative spillovers are economically substantial and suggest that large-scale asset purchases may have reduced the severity of the recession in these sectors. Finally, the paper includes a tutorial on implementing the methodology using a simple example. A comprehensive GitHub repository is available to facilitate the reproduction of all results and to serve as an accessible introduction for readers. Momentum and energy flow through spacetime are governed by the stress-energy tensor. In the context of angular momentum, this role is fulfilled by the angular momentum tensor, a quantity that exists in classical physics but remains ill-defined in quantum theory. However, the quantum Landau problem reveals that introducing a magnetic monopole renders the electromagnetic angular momentum tensor incomplete. We demonstrate that supplementing it with the quantum angular momentum of the electromagnetic field—described by a non-trivial wave function—yields a consistent quantum mechanical total angular momentum tensor, termed the angular Casimir momentum. This concept is illustrated through an example involving the electromagnetic field between a point charge and a perfectly conducting sphere. Notably, this momentum is intrinsic to the quantum state of the electromagnetic field; it is not merely quantum in nature but fundamentally intrinsic to it. Furthermore, this angular Casimir momentum plays a crucial role in ensuring the conservation of total angular momentum within quantum electrodynamics. Finally, we explore a novel connection between the quantum electromagnetic vacuum and the topology of its configuration space. This phenomenon manifests in the electromagnetic angular momentum of the Landau problem, which is quantized and non-zero, despite the electromagnetic field being completely specified by its classical zero-point components. These quantum effects are anticipated in other systems, such as the Dirac monopole, where they may be experimentally observable. Specifically, the total angular momentum of the Dirac monopole field, which includes the angular Casimir momentum, serves as a fundamental element in the quantum mechanical conservation laws of total angular momentum. Consequently, the total angular momentum operator, when applied to the monopole field, yields an eigenvalue that is quantized in units of $\hbar$. This confirms that the monopole field carries intrinsic angular momentum, a conclusion that contrasts with the standard interpretation of the canonical angular momentum $p_\phi = 0$ in planar quantum mechanics. The canonical angular momentum $p_\phi$ represents the kinetic angular momentum of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field, whereas the intrinsic angular momentum of the particle is absorbed by the electromagnetic field. The electromagnetic angular momentum of the Landau problem, therefore, represents the intrinsic angular momentum of the electromagnetic field, a quantity that may also be experimentally detectable. The proliferation of fine-grained information on the web has sparked significant interest in utilizing textual data for various applications, including search engine rankings, news aggregation, and recommendation systems. However, standard NLP models often overlook unique attributes within texts, leading to the failure of conventional NER models in classifying fine-grained entities. Furthermore, Euclidean space is often suboptimal for representing named entities, as semantic relationships such as hypernymy and hyponymy are more accurately modeled within a hyperbolic framework. This study introduces FGNET-RH, a hyperbolic NER model designed for fine-detail named entity recognition. By leveraging the characteristics of hyperbolic space, the model effectively captures semantic relations, allowing for the construction of a hierarchy among named entities. Consequently, FGNET-RH achieves a substantial performance boost on existing NER datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art models by an average of 10.6% in F1-score on the search benchmark. The code is accessible at https://github.com/taehyuklee/FGNET-RH.

Virtual machine (VM) provisioning is a common task in cloud data centers. Current load and resource management systems handle new requests by either placing VMs on the first available host or, in some cases, distributing them across all hosts based on the specific resource type. However, these mechanisms fail to account for upcoming host additions or removals. When a new host is added, it is often under-provisioned relative to others, while an existing host approaching capacity can render previously valid locations invalid. This leads to increased local migrations and a loss of load-balancing efficiency. To address this, we introduce Prepartition, a new load-distribution strategy. When a pre-provisioning request arrives, Prepartition allocates the required resources across a selected subset of hosts, guided by an allocator that balances current and future capacities using an optimization-based model. Upon receipt of actual reservation requests, these pre-provisioned VMs are migrated using an efficient assignment algorithm. We evaluated Prepartition using the DClouds2.0 simulator, which models pre-provisioning requests alongside standard reservations. Our results demonstrate that Prepartition significantly reduces the number of migrations compared to first-fit allocation and achieves more equitable load distribution across all hosts than load-balanced allocation. Furthermore, the Prepartition allocator adapts to future load changes with minimal computational overhead. Finally, we analyzed the impact of migration delays caused by pre-provisioning, showing that the proposed solutions remain effective for both immediate and delayed migrations. Overall, this paper validates the feasibility of accounting for future events during present decision-making and establishes a foundation for developing next-generation load-distribution strategies for VMs. This approach is particularly relevant for virtualized environments where future hardware resource changes are frequent. Additionally, the pre-provisioning concept is applicable to container-based systems, where containers serve as lightweight alternatives to VMs. Although the Prepartition allocator is not optimized for real-time processing, it can be deployed as a background service to handle pre-provisioning requests, ensuring that actual provisioning requests are still processed in real time by the underlying partitioner. This allows Prepartition to deliver the benefits of forward-looking load distribution without incurring additional delays. The pre-provisioning concept is also applicable to offline reservation systems that receive requests periodically. Finally, we have developed a complete pre-provisioning solution that outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of migration count and load distribution quality. This paper introduces the Anticipation Network (ANET), a novel architecture designed to forecast Nash equilibria in extensive-form games. We first demonstrate that the reinforcement learning (RL) process within a single agent, when interacting with a fixed policy of others, naturally converges to the trajectory leading to a local Nash equilibrium. To accelerate this convergence, we incorporate the concept of "gradient flow" from continuous optimization, allowing an agent to adapt its strategy toward the equilibrium more rapidly. Building on this, we develop ANET, which utilizes this rapid adaptation capability to learn how to anticipate equilibria more effectively. Our validation results demonstrate that ANET significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and inference speed. This study examines the research of Bareinboim and colleagues (2016, 2018, 2020), which establishes identification conditions for inferring causal relationships from observational data using observational graphs augmented with front-door and backdoor variables. These conditions guarantee that a specific instrumental inequality (for front-door variables) or a confounding inequality (for backdoor variables) accurately reflects causal impact within a discrete additive noise model. Our work first derives general identification conditions for arbitrary observational graphs, unifying and broadening the results from these papers. Furthermore, we establish identification conditions for a novel class of graphs involving confounding inequality, and demonstrate the application of these findings to continuous and Gaussian noise models under a sign constraint on the causal graph. Finally, we develop novel upper and lower bounds for causal impact in high-dimensional settings where data limitations prevent causal functions from being expressed through a single variable. These bounds utilize the total correlation of the treatment and confounded variables, offering an analysis of how causality can be quantified using mutual information-based metrics in high-dimensional contexts. We illustrate these results with causal analysis examples involving both simulated and real-world data, highlighting the advantages of the proposed bounds. Specifically, we analyze the impact of social media on political elections and demonstrate that the total correlation between vote shares and social media activity can serve as a reliable proxy for the causal impact of social media on voting behavior. Additionally, we show that mutual information between social media activity and candidate performance scores effectively captures causal impact regarding voter performance. To facilitate these findings, we also introduce a new Python library designed to support causal inference using instrumental inequalities and total correlation-based bounds. This library includes functions for calculating identification conditions, visualization tools for identification paths, and computational methods for both exact and approximate calculation of total correlation-based bounds. All code required to replicate this study's findings is available on GitHub. This paper introduces a new class of algorithmic tools designed for effectively predicting linear time-invariant systems while remaining immune to stealthy attacks. Within the linear system framework, attack resilience in predictive algorithms is essential for maintaining robust system performance. However, existing literature on this topic is limited, and current approaches often suffer from either low prediction accuracy or high computational complexity. To address these limitations, the study first reformulates the attack resilience problem into a more tractable form by leveraging the concept of effective predictability. Subsequently, it proposes a novel algorithm based on linear programming that guarantees attack resilience without increasing computational complexity, regardless of the attack model used. Finally, the approach's efficacy is validated through a simulation case study. The results demonstrate that this proposed method achieves superior prediction accuracy compared to existing techniques. Notably, the algorithm maintains its attack-resilient properties even in scenarios where other techniques fail to do so. Furthermore, the tool exhibits excellent scalability across various attack models and computational complexity levels. Additionally, the approach is applicable to linear time-varying systems and linear parameter-varying systems. Current automatic text summarization systems function primarily with dominant languages, such as English, and are largely ineffective for non-dominant or under-resourced languages. This paper introduces the first large-scale Indian language dataset designed for automatic summarization. We present the GAE-ISumm dataset, constructed from the Indiabix website, which includes 100,000 document-article pairs in 11 Indian languages: Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Hindi, and Urdu. GAE-ISumm offers significant value for future research by enabling the creation of automatic summarizers without the need for human annotation. To evaluate unmonitored models, we conducted experiments using both a Transformer-based architecture and a Graph Auto-Encoder, comparing their performance against a rule-based method. Our analysis reveals that a deep learning approach grounded in deep contextualized language representations surpasses traditional rule-based techniques. We further highlight the challenges of building a robust, generalizable summarization system and outline potential directions for future research. The dataset and associated code are accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/GAE-ISumm. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) serve as a robust method for unsupervised representation learning, offering an alternative to traditional deep network training that relies on large datasets and specific task definitions. However, the success of this approach is highly sensitive to hyperparameter selection, particularly regarding network architecture and prior distributions. While previous studies have explored hyperparameter optimization, they often overlooked the impact of regularizing prior distributions. This work investigates the effects of regularizing these priors and introduces a novel technique to incorporate minimum distance regularization directly into the cost function. Experimental results demonstrate that regularizing the posterior distribution substantially enhances representation quality, whereas regularizing the prior distribution has a more limited effect. Furthermore, we develop a minimum-variability regularizer to penalize excessive model flexibility. Our optimized VAE architecture achieves competitive performance on MNIST and CIFAR10 tasks, matching state-of-the-art results. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexei-tsv/variational-autoencoder. We provide detailed insights into the influence of regularization on the learned representations. Our findings indicate that minimum-variability regularization produces circularly distributed representations, while a combination of regularized priors and reconstructed data costs yields grid-like patterns. These regularized representations exhibit superior suitability for downstream tasks, such as classification and clustering. Additionally, we demonstrate the utility of these representations in few-shot learning scenarios. Overall, our work underscores the critical role of regularization in VAEs for effective representation learning. We argue that VAEs should be evaluated based on their representational capabilities rather than solely on reconstruction accuracy, thereby encouraging further research into the properties of latent spaces. Finally, we emphasize the necessity of developing interpretable regularizers to facilitate deeper understanding of the features within these spaces. To address this, we propose extending current regularization approaches to enable the assignment of semantic labels to specific features. Our findings regarding the circular and grid-like structures of representations support this proposed direction for future research. We conclude by advocating for a shift in focus toward representational understanding and exploring the application of these learned features in low-data regimes. The Internet of Things (IoT) has become a pivotal technology for enabling communication between physical objects, driving innovation across various industries. Within IoT systems, devices exchange data via the Internet; when localization techniques are employed, this communication occurs over local networks. However, as IoT adoption grows, so do security threats, prompting researchers to propose blockchain-based solutions to mitigate these risks. Concurrently, there is increasing interest in integrating intelligent agents into home appliances to enhance security and automate control. This paper proposes a novel blockchain-based security framework designed for home gadgets, specifically targeting intelligent devices such as home fans. By combining a blockchain application with a localization technique at the MAC layer, the study aims to secure communication between objects while optimizing bandwidth usage. Evaluation through simulation using the NS2 platform demonstrates that this method not only strengthens blockchain communication but also conserves bandwidth. The findings indicate that the proposed approach enhances the reliability of home gadget communication networks. Finally, the paper concludes by identifying remaining challenges in the system and suggesting future research directions. Keywords: Blockchain, Home Automation, IoT, Localization, NS2, Security.

The performance of a digital communication system is fundamentally constrained by the reliability of its decision device. While maximum likelihood detection offers optimal reliability, its computational complexity renders it impractical for real-time use in modern systems. Consequently, a widely adopted compromise involves replacing probability of error values with logarithmic metrics, known as L-values, which can be processed by a binary decision device. However, the high complexity of calculating L-values remains a significant bottleneck. This paper introduces a deep learning-based method to efficiently reduce the computational complexity of L-value computation. By framing the task as a single-bit decision problem, the approach minimizes complexity while preserving near-optimal reliability. Furthermore, a novel deep learning architecture is proposed that ensures constant complexity regardless of codeword length. The method is applied to two mainstream coding schemes, turbo codes and LDPC codes. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a significant complexity reduction with only a negligible degradation in performance. The core strategy relies on a dynamic programming technique for tree-decompositions, yielding an algorithm with running time $O(c^d \cdot n)$, where $d$ represents the degeneracy of the undirected underlying graph and $c$ is a constant. By integrating this approach with graph modifications, we developed a family of algorithms for various UFE problems, achieving $k$-fixedpt constants. Applying these methods to the Upward Planarization with Minimum Feedback Arc Set (UPMFBAS) problem—finding the smallest set of arcs to reverse for upward planarity—specific instances yield $k$-fixedpt, $(k+\Delta(G))$-fixedpt, and $(k + \sqrt{8k} + 2)\cdot \chi(G)$-fixedpt constants for graphs with tree-width $k$, feedback vertex set size $k$, and clique cover number $\chi(G)$, respectively. Furthermore, utilizing dynamic programming on tree structures, we established parameterized algorithms for the Hasse Diagram problem, specifically the existence of a linear extension and the minimum number of "double edges" (pairs of adjacent elements oriented toward each other), producing $k$-fixedpt and $(k+\Delta(G))$-fixedpt constants. This paper introduces a framework, termed the Human Max-Bound (HMB), designed to address challenges in noisy, crowdsourced datasets. By examining human-provided labels through a probabilistic lens, we develop a theory that combines ensembles of deep learning models with the metrics described in our prior research. Our approach employs a quantile regression wrapper to fit a distribution over model outputs, thereby establishing an error-bounded interval around the "true" softmax distribution of class probabilities. This distribution serves as a proxy for human perceptions of uncertainty. We demonstrate the HMB method's effectiveness across three case studies representing progressively more difficult problems: first, the large-scale Labeled Faces in the Wild (LFW) dataset; second, a challenging, high-noise, crowdsourced dataset of handwritten digits; and finally, a large-scale, crowdsourced classification task involving various animal species. Furthermore, we explore the application of HMB in modeling human perceptions of uncertainty and its effectiveness in providing actionable feedback to annotators. The accompanying code and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashleykeller/HMB. Ultimately, the findings presented here hold significant promise for enhancing the utility of crowdsourced datasets in training and evaluating machine learning models. By leveraging ensembles, accurately modeling human perceptions of uncertainty, and offering guidance to contributors, we aim to improve the quality of datasets used across a wide spectrum of applications. This work represents a foundational step toward a more sustainable future for crowdsourced data. Our goal is to inspire further research into the quality and quality-aware utilization of these datasets, fostering a more resilient ecosystem for both human and machine intelligence. We conclude by reflecting on the ethical implications of our findings, particularly concerning the welfare of the individuals contributing to these datasets. This study introduces a novel semiflow, termed the "downward flow," operating on the convex hull of compact operators between Banach spaces. We demonstrate that the spectral radius of the transfer operator associated with a continuous semiflow of homeomorphisms under the projective norm remains at most 1. This finding generalizes a result by R. Bowen. Furthermore, if the semiflow consists of positive operators, the spectral radius is strictly less than 1, unless the operator acts as a scalar multiple of the identity. These findings yield additional insights into nonempty compact operator spaces, including concepts such as the "traceless operator space," "reproducing kernel operator space," and spaces of "nuclear kernel operators." Additionally, we establish conditions ensuring the existence of an eigenfunction for semiflows of semigroups of kernels, which includes nonnegative, real-valued semiflows of homeomorphisms defined on a lattice. Finally, we explore applications of these methods within fluid dynamics. Specifically, we investigate whether eigenfunctions associated with the leading eigenvalue of the transfer operator for fluid velocity exist within downwells, as well as whether these spectral radii can fall below 1, a property characteristic of decaying fluid systems. Additionally, we examine the transfer operator associated with a vector field on a torus, revealing that it admits a nonzero eigenfunction only if the operator is scalar. Minor strength-$t$ covering arrays represent a variant of covering arrays constructed via a covering property within $\lambda$-designs. In this research, we utilize the concept of an orthogonal array to investigate the existence and lower bounds of such arrays. We examine the case where all underlying $\lambda$-designs consist of Steiner systems, focusing primarily on $-1$-designs. Our findings demonstrate that for odd $n$, the existence of an odd multiple of a Steiner triple system is sufficient to establish the existence of a corresponding minor strength-$2$ covering array. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for the size of minor strength-$2$ covering arrays with two interactions. Under the assumption that a Steiner triple system exists, our lower bound improves upon previously established results. Finally, we present a construction method for minor strength-$2$ covering arrays with three interactions using a Steiner triple system, which yields a lower bound that surpasses earlier constructions. Throughout this work, computer searches played a crucial role in determining existence results and in developing the computational framework for these constructions. We conclude by outlining potential directions for future study. Notably, resolving the existence of certain minor strength-$2$ covering arrays appears to require the application of computational search methods alongside theoretical insights. Furthermore, extending the investigation to higher numbers of interactions represents a significant avenue for subsequent research. Our approach begins by identifying minor strength-$t$ covering arrays with a small number of columns, which may yield lower bounds for larger instances. Finally, theoretical advancements regarding the existence or non-existence of specific types of Steiner systems could yield improved lower bounds for minor strength-$t$ covering arrays. These conclusions were derived from the computer search outcomes presented in this study. To facilitate the verification of our results, the accompanying code has been made publicly available. This code employs a backtracking search algorithm to verify the existence of various columns for minor strength-$t$ covering arrays and can be utilized as a starting point for exploring the existence of other column configurations. Furthermore, the code serves as a foundational framework for theoretical constructions, offering a basis for testing and refining new construction techniques. By utilizing the code to build constructions for specific instances, researchers can potentially generalize these methods to develop constructions for other similar problems. Overall, our work underscores the synergy between computational approaches and theoretical methodologies in advancing the field of covering arrays. Determining the future evolution of many interacting systems is a significant challenge in physics and biology. While numerous models have been developed to describe interacting particles, spins, and agents, predicting their future states often remains intractable. In this study, we examine a nonlocal Conway game, a system where every pair of particles interacts based on their relative positions, with each particle's future state governed by simple local rules. We conduct a comprehensive study of Heisenberg antiferromagnets on triangular lattices (TL) and kagome (K) lattices within a fully classical framework. By utilizing a large system in thermodynamic limit, defined as $N\to\infty$ where $N$ represents the atom count, we systematically explore all equilibrium states by solving the equations of motion for time-dependent spins starting from various initial conditions. This allows us to explicitly determine the ground state energy and identify both static and dynamically stable states. Specifically, we examine spin configurations on TL and K lattices that satisfy three distinct criteria: (i) they constitute the unique thermodynamic ground state at zero temperature; (ii) they emerge as limiting outcomes of initial conditions that minimize system energy; and (iii) they remain stationary solutions of the equations of motion with a real eigenfrequency, representing either minima or saddle points of the energy with respect to local spin perturbations. Our results indicate that for both TL and K lattices, these spin arrangements correspond to helical structures aligned along any arbitrary direction in a three-dimensional vector space. Furthermore, we observe that these configurations satisfy both criteria (i) and (iii) but fail criterion (ii). We also detail the methodology for generating diverse initial conditions on the spin lattice to explore various equilibrium states. Finally, we demonstrate the validity of our findings through excellent agreement with existing literature. These discoveries hold significant implications for investigating magnetic structures in actual TL and K lattice materials. Notably, our findings regarding kagome lattices address a longstanding issue in this field: while numerous static helical solutions have been previously reported, no dynamically stable solution of this type had ever been identified. This gap has hindered efforts to experimentally realize such states. We now propose that these solutions can be achieved by selecting appropriate initial conditions for the equations of motion. Consequently, this paves the way for future experimental investigations into these helical solutions on kagome lattices. Ultimately, we contend that these findings offer valuable insights into the complex behavior of antiferromagnetic systems on TL and K lattices. Specifically, it is evident that solutions to criterion (i) are unlikely to yield unique dynamics, as they would necessitate solving the equations of motion for the initial angular velocities of the spins. Given that these initial angular velocities are typically unknown in practical scenarios, we propose that conducting experiments on real materials with random initial angular velocities would likely result in the observation of solutions to criterion (iii) on both TL and K lattices. This study introduces an algorithm designed to achieve a predetermined FDR level while maintaining high discovery power within large-scale random controlled trials. Furthermore, the paper examines the FDR of this proposed method under general dependence conditions and, subsequently, proposes an FDR control strategy for FDR-based intervention tests. Simulation results demonstrate that this correction approach successfully controls the FDR at the designated level without compromising discovery power. Finally, the paper applies this corrected fdrwise approach to a large-scale randomized trial concerning a specific intervention. Additionally, an extension of this work has been published in the FDRplus FDRplus: An R Package for FDRplus Control and Power Analysis in Large-Scale Experiments package on CRAN. A recent study by Lynden-Bell and Arakawa [1] introduced a model featuring negative pressure that accounts for the Arp correlation between high redshift dwarf galaxies and large-scale structures. Their proposed mechanism involves an expansion driven by momentum, which they termed "Astronomical Expansion." In the current paper, we demonstrate that this Astronomical Expansion is fundamentally equivalent to the standard matter-dominated Friedmann expansion. Furthermore, we establish the condition under which the Lynden-Bell and Arakawa model achieves the same expansion rate as the matter-dominated Friedmann expansion. This equivalence implies that the momentum-driven expansion can entirely replace the effects of dark energy. Additionally, we show the correspondence between their model's scale factor and that of an open universe. We also prove the equivalence between their model and a closed universe characterized by a cosmological constant. Finally, we provide criteria for the collapse of their expansion model within a closed universe context. These conditions indicate that the momentum from the Big Bang must be sufficiently large to prevent the universe from collapsing. Consequently, the existence of current galaxies serves as evidence supporting the possibility of Astronomical Expansion. However, our analysis reveals that the momentum required to achieve the same expansion rate as a matter-dominated universe is significantly higher than that of an open universe or a closed universe with a cosmological constant. Therefore, our findings suggest that the Astronomical Expansion model is unlikely to be correct. We also examine the interpretation of the Arp correlation and note that the statistical significance of this correlation remains uncertain. Furthermore, we point out that Lynden-Bell and Arakawa's model fails to explain the observed homogeneity of the expansion rate across vast regions of the universe. Finally, we offer several suggestions for testing the validity of the Astronomical Expansion hypothesis. In our conclusion, we argue that the momentum-driven expansion model is not viable. Instead, we contend that the cosmological constant, rather than momentum, is essential for driving the expansion. We also note that the momentum within the Lynden-Bell and Arakawa model is insufficient to prevent matter from collapsing. Instead, we propose that the repulsive force generated by the cosmological constant is necessary to halt the collapse of matter. Ultimately, we contend that an expansion model relying on the cosmological constant is more consistent with observational evidence than one based on momentum.

Keywords: cosmology: theory, large-scale structure of universe, cosmological constant, Arp correlation, test of astronomical expansion model.

In recent years, several systems have been created to automatically extract and structure knowledge from text, with queries serving as a primary input. These systems rely on queries to represent user intent, but since different users may phrase similar intents differently, a single intent can correspond to multiple distinct queries. To reduce redundancy and enhance efficiency, it is beneficial to identify queries that share intent during the annotation process. However, current systems typically rely on human annotators to manually reprioritize queries as they work, creating a bottleneck in the workflow. To address this limitation, we introduce SWIFTER, a novel approach that efficiently clusters and reprioritizes incoming queries based on a new technique called Crowdsourced Insight. SWIFTER automatically detects queries with similar intent and allows them to "vote" for one another. To prevent the accidental grouping of unrelated queries, a human supervisor periodically reviews and reprioritizes the system's output. Our results demonstrate that SWIFTER can reduce the cost of human labor by 90% while maintaining high precision. Initially, we independently train sequence-to-sequence models to extract forward and reverse representations of audio and speech text from cross-lingual Deep Neural Architectures. Subsequently, we define a new distance function that combines these derived representations to model the degree of conversational synchronization between consecutive turns. Finally, we assess this distance through a conversational control task and demonstrate its application in classifying natural versus artificial dialogue. The findings indicate that this distance effectively captures synchronization relationships in conversational speech, offering a promising tool for studying turn-taking dynamics and their connection to various psychopathologies. Furthermore, our results suggest that for certain instances of conversational disorganization, particularly in cases of low-level conversational control, a speaker-specific approach for calculating this distance may be more advantageous. To facilitate future research on turn-taking and synchronization, the complete code is made publicly available. Temporal action segmentation involves partitioning videos into fine-grained, atomic action segments. While many supervised methods have been developed, they depend on annotated data and struggle to generalize when action categories shift. In contrast, self-supervised approaches learn from unlabeled data and can adapt to new categories. However, prior self-supervised techniques often utilize complex pretraining schemes or rely on specific assumptions, such as the presence of multiple actions within a single activity segment. We introduce SSCAP, a self-supervised method for temporal action segmentation that employs a straightforward pretraining strategy and avoids restrictive hypotheses. Our approach segments actions by parsing co-occurring activities and trains the segmentation layer directly on raw data using a self-supervised identity loss. Experiments on the 20BN-ActiGenes and BiDDA-Emotion datasets demonstrate that SSCAP achieves competitive results compared to other self-supervised baselines and significantly outperforms them on all action classes in the 20BN-ActiGenes dataset. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leehongyu/SSCAP. This study investigates the formation and decay of bound exotic baryons, specifically pentaquark states containing four light quarks and one charm quark ($qqqC\bar q$), by extending both the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ and spin-$1\frac{1}{2}$ structures of the present algebra to accommodate the $c$-quark. Leveraging both the $SU(3)$ flavor and $SU(2)$ spin algebras within this framework, we analyze the internal degrees of freedom, total angular momentum, and cross-sections for the production and decay of these $\bar q$-containing pentaquarks. We calculate the decays of the $SU(3)$ flavor nonet, organized into an $SU(2)$ spin doublet and a quartet, comparing our decays with those derived from the $q$-depleted $SU(3)\otimes$ spin algebra of the traditional Pauli spinor approach. Furthermore, we determine the decays of the $SU(2)$ non-$J= \frac{5}{2}$ states by decomposing the $SU(3)$ flavor representation into two $SU(2)$ doublet $\otimes$ quartet representations. Our findings indicate that the present algebra yields the same decays as the Pauli spinor method but additionally predicts a decays involving a $\rho$-meson that the traditional approach does not account for. These results are expected to be verified in the LHCb experiment's $\gamma p \to K \gamma X$ process. We conclude that the present algebra offers a viable alternative to the traditional Pauli spinor approach for analyzing the internal structure, creation, and decays of pentaquark states. This work is the first in a series; subsequent papers will address the decays of concealed-charm pentaquarks with a single strange quark and those with a single strange and strange-antiquark pair. Finally, we propose that the successful application of the present algebra to pentaquark decays will significantly contribute to the study of the internal structure, creation, and decays of pentaquarks. This approach will be further explored in our upcoming studies on the decays of di-charm and fully hidden charm pentaquarks. Our future experimental and theoretical investigations will be directed toward the production and decays of these pentaquark states. Software testing education is a critical component of computer science and information technology curricula. However, traditional detailed evaluation methods, which demand that students provide extensive reasons for their testing decisions, are often perceived as demanding and may discourage students from effectively grasping core concepts. This paper introduces an inquiry-based approach to testing education that minimizes the need for detailed explanations. Specifically, students indicate whether their testing choices align with a given scenario and are then guided to understand the underlying theoretical principles. The study validates this methodology through a controlled experiment comparing it against traditional testing assessments, which require comprehensive justification. Results indicate that the inquiry-based approach achieves learning outcomes equivalent to traditional methods but with reduced cognitive load. The paper also outlines the method's implementation and provides empirical evidence supporting its efficacy. Ultimately, this research offers a novel pedagogical perspective for software testing education, with potential applications in programming and algorithm instruction. The study's findings also inform educational policy decisions. Finally, the authors invite collaboration to further develop and apply this approach within computer education settings. Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) aims to train a model for a target domain without retaining access to its source domains. SFDA typically employs distribution-based methods to establish relationships with multiple source domains for domain alignment. However, this approach often fails to fully leverage rich task information from sources that share the same semantic labels. To address this, we propose a novel task-based approach that integrates theory transfer with knowledge transfer to enable SFDA. Specifically, we introduce theory transfer, a paradigm that utilizes unlabelled source domains to uncover theoretical connections between a source task and a novel target task. Leveraging these inter-task relationships from various sources significantly enhances SFDA, as theory transfer focuses on learning transferable concepts rather than merely aligning distributions or transferring knowledge. By employing theory transfer to uncover inter-task relationships, we can more effectively combine sources with shared label sets, thereby improving the utilization of task information from the source domains. Extensive experiments on SFDA benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance, with improvements of 1.5% and 2.1% over existing state-of-the-art approaches on benchmark tasks. The code and experimental results are available at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi-chenchen/Semi-Supervised-Theory-Transfer. This work opens a new direction for future theory transfer research. **Keywords:** Source-free domain adaptation, theory transfer, knowledge transfer, multi-source learning.

Gas-core nuclear thermal rockets offer the benefit of operating at extremely high operating temperatures, enabling higher specific impulse. To manage this, a radiative cooling gas core is shielded by a thick, turbopumped liquid coolant annular cladding. This paper introduces the novel concept of using this radiative, nuclear-excited gas core as the direct propellant. The system comprises a turbopumped liquid-fuel annulus and an ex-situ reactivity management system that utilizes neutron excitation within the distant gas core. This configuration retains high specific impulse while significantly lowering system complexity and mass compared to conventional chemical rockets. A detailed analysis of such a system is presented, utilizing kinetic rate equations to model nuclear reactions and their impact on combustion and propulsion performance. Furthermore, the study examines how specific impulse, thrust, and nuclear reaction rates vary with nuclear density and radius. Finally, the relationship between these parameters and the distance between the gas core and the rocket nozzle is analyzed. Results indicate that when the gas core is sufficiently large, specific impulse can reach up to 1000 seconds, while achieving high thrust requires higher nuclear densities. Ultimately, this mechanism, combined with an appropriate nozzle design, could establish a new benchmark for rocket performance. Additionally, the study explores how variations in fuel and coolant properties influence both thermal and nuclear reaction rates. Finally, specific mission profiles are examined to illustrate the performance capabilities of this class of engines. Specifically, the paper details a mission involving a 1000-second specific impulse burn from Earth's surface to geostationary orbit, followed by an orbital raise maneuver to geosynchronous transfer orbit (GTO) utilizing a reactor with a variable specific impulse of 1500 seconds. Furthermore, a mission profile involving a 30-day, 10 AU interplanetary trip is analyzed, demonstrating an average thrust of 1.5 N and a specific impulse of 2000 seconds. These findings suggest that gas-core reactors, whether used directly or indirectly, hold significant potential for space exploration. The proposed solutions, particularly the indirect application, merit further investigation regarding their space-based implementation. Specifically, the feasibility of directly pumping the nuclear reaction product out of the combustion chamber to serve as the working fluid for a closed-cycle turbomachinery system is highlighted as an area for future research. Such a system would offer higher thrust, reduced system mass, and enabled higher power. The paper concludes by outlining promising avenues for future research. This study evaluates neural network architectures employing convolutional, recurrent, and attention mechanisms for discharging particle interaction localization within astroparticle experiments. These experiments investigate nuclear particle physics fundamental questions in fundamental theory, utilizing detector systems divided into discrete readout domains. Each domain records charged particle deposits as time series, where individual measurements are represented by energy and time alongside temporal and spatial metadata. The objective is to determine the spatial coordinates of interaction vertices using these time series data. For the localization task, a simulated dataset of particle interactions was generated, modeled after historical data from neutron interactions within scintillator blocks of open nuclei design detectors, specifically representing experiments comparable to NuGro. The blocks were segmented into 32 readout domains, each containing 8 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs). In the localization problem, inputs consist of the time series read by a single PMT, while outputs correspond to the 3D coordinates of the interaction vertex. The study compares and evaluates the performance of Feed-Forward (FFN), Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM), and Attention mechanisms. Results indicate that FFN and LSTM architectures achieve equivalent performance. However, Attention mechanisms surpass both FFN and LSTM architectures. This superior performance is attributed to the inherent design of the Attention mechanism, which allows the model to assign varying weights to different input data points. Consequently, this work demonstrates that Attention and recurrent neural networks (RNN) with LSTM cells serve as highly effective tools for solving the interaction localization problem in astroparticle experiments utilizing photomultiplier-based readouts. Furthermore, this research provides a foundation for future applications of these techniques to data from current and upcoming experiments. Additionally, this work serves as a basis for future investigations into advanced techniques for calibrating and reconstructing light transport in complex media using machine learning. These approaches will leverage the photomultiplier readouts in each stave to infer the complex geometry of the blocks and the position of interaction vertices. This serves as a precursor to future work on interaction reconstruction using machine learning applied to data from the next-generation experiment ICARUS. The geometry of ICARUS consists of two tanks filled with liquid argon, each containing 98 tons of material. Each tank is divided into 12 planes, with every plane subdivided into 16 staves, each equipped with 16 photomultiplier tubes.
