Atmospheric retrievals serve as a potent instrument for both characterizing exoplanets and distinguishing between current and potential exo-planetology. These retrievals function as an inversion process, deducing physical and chemical states from observed spectra. The underlying models rely on fundamental calculations of molecular absorption cross-sections, which are typically sourced from databases like HITRAN or built upon such fundamentals. However, standard retrieval models designed for terrestrial atmospheres often fail to accurately represent the harsh conditions found in brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets. This study presents EXOPLINES, a library of molecular absorption cross-sections specifically optimized for brown dwarf and giant exoplanet environments. We provide code to interpolate between grid points, thereby generating comprehensive cross-section maps. These resources are available to facilitate the creation of retrieval models suitable for these extreme atmospheric conditions. Our work includes examples of retrieved parameters from a synthetic L0 brown dwarf spectrum and discusses the presence of clouds in brown dwarfs and planets as a motivating factor for the high density of this grid. Ultimately, the publication of EXOPLINES aims to enhance our understanding of brown dwarf and planetary atmospheres. The repository can be accessed at https://github.com/astro-uw/exoplines. Future developments will incorporate additional molecules and establish a new API. EXOPLINES is freely accessible for download. While the current release covers only a subset of required molecules for retrieval, it is intended to enable users to generate cross-section maps for the included species. We anticipate that this foundation will encourage the community to expand the repository with a broader array of molecules. This initiative is a collaborative effort by the University of Washington, University of Michigan, and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. Specifically, JG and JF developed the molecular calculations, JG created the interpolation code, and JF established the API. All contributions are deeply appreciated. This research utilized the University of Washington's shared computing cluster, Exanet. JG acknowledges support from the NASA Postdoctoral Program through Research Assignment #9840 and the University of Washington's Department of Astronomy. JF was partially funded by the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. Both institutions are members of the NASA ExoATM initiative. Furthermore, this work aligns with the University of Washington's Center for Astrophysics and Space Astronomy's initiative to support the next generation of exo-atmosphere researchers. JG received a 2021 award from this initiative. The EXOPLINES repository is hosted on the University of Washington

This work investigates the principles of grounding, a critical computational stage of ASP solvers. We introduce a formal model of grounding that encompasses both modern efficient approaches, such as those used in CLNFOIL and CNF2ASP, as well as older methods, including the principles underlying cfn2asp. Our model leverages contemporary SAT-solving techniques, incorporating innovations like incremental and symmetric SAT solving, and provides a flexible abstract framework for formulating grounding strategies. Additionally, we demonstrate how various ANASP programs can be represented within this formalism. The proposed model also establishes a foundation for defining and implementing new grounding methods. Although our study relies on ASP programs lacking aggregates and recursion, we discuss how these mechanisms could be accommodated. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for future research. Notably, our model is intended to serve as a representation for automated analysis of ASP programs, a topic addressed in our subsequent paper, On the Principles of Grounding in Answer Set Programming II, which explores applications regarding call and rule graph construction. This model is realized through a dedicated open-source library available on GitHub. The model definitions and implementations are presented in a separate, extended report. The paper includes several examples illustrating various grounding methods and calls, alongside an automated verification of call and rule graph construction using our model. Specifically, we demonstrate how to verify the correctness of graph construction for ASP programs without aggregates and recursion, as well as how to implement arbitrary grounding methods within our model. These examples are provided as ASP programs and are verified using our model encoded as an ASP program. Furthermore, we examine the application of SAT solvers to accelerate ASP program grounding. While our model currently relies on a conservative approach to handling infinite calls, it also addresses the correctness of call graph construction for ASP programs involving aggregates and recursion. The correctness of call graph construction for ASP programs without aggregates and with recursion is established in our previous study. Our approach to infinite calls differs from the methods employed in CNF2ASP and CLNFOIL. Additionally, we propose a novel method for grounding ASP programs containing aggregates, which is also original. Finally, our research on infinite calls and aggregate grounding is conducted independently of ASP-Core 2.6. However, the correctness of these approaches for ASP-Core 2.6 is documented in our subsequent paper. This paper demonstrates how to implement our model using SAT solvers, specifically the SAT solver clasp and the grounding tool casper. Initial laws serve as inequalities that constrain how quantum resources can evolve during open-system dynamics, marking a key area of research within universal quantum resource theories. This study establishes initial bounds for the most fundamental and widely used resource: entropy. Specifically, we derive a single initial inequality for Shannon entropy that extends to all thermodynamic frameworks, including quantum and free energy contexts. Furthermore, we formulate a novel inequality for Markovian quantum processes that limits free energy changes. The applicability and utility of these results are demonstrated across various quantum theories and models. Additionally, these findings offer new perspectives on the laws of universal openness. Notably, the derived inequalities are strictly more restrictive than the corresponding quantum initial fidelity inequalities, thereby enhancing our understanding of initial constraints and their relationship with information causality. Moreover, the universal bounds on quantum and free energy changes revealed in this work may be connected to entanglement monogamy. Collectively, these initial laws and their interconnections lay the groundwork for formulating a comprehensive theory of universal information changes. Furthermore, these results impose tight limits on the information that quantum systems can release into the environment. Finally, the initial law for Shannon entropy is shown to be equivalent to the initial entropy power inequality in information theory and the initial Fisher information inequality in statistical physics. Together with recent discoveries regarding entropic implications of time-reversal asymmetry, these results underscore the significant role of initial inequalities in elucidating thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, the work represents a substantial advancement in both open quantum systems and thermodynamics. Specifically, it yields tighter bounds on entropy production and quantum mutual information, thereby refining our comprehension of thermodynamic behavior. Additionally, these initial laws may facilitate the resolution of longstanding challenges, such as the entropy increase paradox and Maxwell's demon problem. Finally, the initial law for Shannon entropy anticipated by this research was independently confirmed by two groups shortly after the submission of this manuscript. Overall, this work introduces a substantial new line of research and generates numerous intriguing questions. Notably, these initial laws are expected to be valuable for quantum information theory, information physics, and even biology. Moreover, the tight bounds on entropy production and quantum mutual information derived herein are likely to deepen our understanding of thermodynamic phenomena. Furthermore, the initial law regarding Shannon entropy anticipated in this study was recently anticipated by two distinct groups, underscoring its significance. In high-energy nuclear collisions, light hadrons serve as the most abundant observables, offering insights into the underlying phenomena. Driven by advancements in statistical methods, machine learning, and modeling, this study demonstrates how the kinetic energy spectra of charged pions can reveal critical details about the processes generating them. By developing and applying a collinear decomposition algorithm, we show that the energy spectra of two-pion states are determined by the momentum distribution of the proton and the shape of the potential surface within the proton's comoving frame. This approach enables a novel method for characterizing pion production using only fully detected, in-flight charged-pion data. Furthermore, we determine the momentum distribution of the collinearly aligned, forward-moving proton based on the resulting pion states. Finally, employing a Monte Carlo simulation, we extract information regarding the potential surface in the comoving frame, demonstrating that charged-pion spectra and their associated uncertainties can effectively reveal model-dependent features of the pion production process. These findings underscore the significant potential of these observables for constraining models of pion production in small-scale collisions. Additionally, the machine learning and Monte Carlo techniques utilized here are broadly applicable to extracting information from hadron spectra across various collision systems. The data and code used to generate the results in this work are accessible at https://github.com/ashleykeller/assessing-data-from-moments. The analysis code is also hosted on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.7105004). The underlying high-energy nuclear physics theories are detailed in our prior publication, P. L. McGaughran et al., Phys. Rev. C 104, 024905 (2021). The datasets employed are described in A. M. Green and C. M. Ko, Phys. Rev. C 81, 014903 (2010); P. M. Kolb and U. Heinz, in Proceedings, 12th International Workshop on the Physics of Quark-Gluon Plasma (Bergen, Norway, 2004); and P. F. Kollegger and C. M. Ko, Phys. Rev. C 90, 064907 (2014). The machine learning code is detailed in P. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M.

This study addresses inference challenges within non-stationary time sequences characterized by heavy tails and potential time dependence. We introduce a framework for non-stationary, heavy-tailed multivariate time series that permits both marginal and dependence structures to exhibit infinite variance, alongside a corresponding self-normalized estimator for the unknown parameters. We demonstrate the asymptotic normality of this self-normalized estimator and establish its asymptotic efficiency relative to an idealized Gaussian counterpart. Additionally, we develop a joint confidence region and a hypothesis test that maintain asymptotically valid coverage and size, even in the presence of infinite variances, conditional infinimal variance, and long-range dependence. Furthermore, we develop a robust alternative to the traditional autocorrelation function capable of handling these infinite variance scenarios and test for the presence of long-range dependence under these conditions. The section dedicated to asymptotically valid bootstrap procedures offers a bootstrap test for the null hypothesis of stationarity against local alternative hypotheses. Finally, the paper illustrates these theoretical findings through a simulation study and an analysis of monthly and daily foreign exchange rates. The code utilized in this research is publicly available at https://github.com/SebastianKluge/Inference_in_heavy_tailed_non_stable_multivariate_time_sequences. The findings presented herein were previously published in our work: \emph{arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.00371}. The only distinction lies in the latter section, which now features an expanded set of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, the theoretical results were subsequently published in our manuscript: \emph{arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.00371}. \emph{Keywords and phrases:} Heavy tails, Infinite variance, Non-stable, Non-stationary, Multivariate time series, Long-range dependence. \emph{AMS Subject Classification (2020):} Primary 62M10; Secondary 62P05, 62P35. \emph{Mathematics Subject Classification:} Primary 62M10; Secondary 62P05, 62P35. \emph{MSC codes:} 62M10, 62P05, 62P35. \emph{Keywords:} Heavy tails, Infinite variance, Non-stable, Non-stationary, Multivariate time series, Long-range dependence. \emph{Keywords:} Heavy tails

Efficient binary quantum low-density parity-check (qldpc) codes are characterized by a stabilizer matrix where each row and column corresponds to at most $r$ and $q$ ones, respectively. These codes support linear-time decoders when the parameters satisfy $r \lesssim \log r$ and $q \lesssim \log q$. However, all known efficient qldpc codes to date are either highly restrictive or possess large constant values for $r$ and $q$. We introduce a family of efficient qldpc codes that are both flexible and dense, featuring small constants $r$ and $q$ that can be tuned as needed. When $q=3$, the family includes codes with rates nearly one, distances growing as a power of the code length, and decoders operating in linear time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that decoding this family via minimum-weight matching algorithms, such as the union-jack algorithm, constitutes an NP-hard problem. Additionally, we present the first family of quantum codes that are both locally correctable and locally decodable, maintaining linear-time decoding complexity. The first such family comprises quantum ldpc codes with rates nearly one, distances scaling as a power of the length, and the ability to correct both single and multiple errors. Both families are constructed from a novel class of sparse graphs that can be generated in linear time. These graphs are derived from a natural class of edge expansion graphs that are also expanders in edge conductance. We provide an explicit example of this class that functions as an expander in conductance and achieve a constant-factor approximation of the conductance expansion. Our approach builds upon recent work by Khot and Saket regarding the hardness of approximating the conductance expansion of sparse graphs. Additionally, we present an explicit construction for the family utilizing the Riemann Hypothesis. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where the conductance expansion of sparse graphs has been approximated within constant factors. Finally, we demonstrate that the family can be encoded in linear time using an explicit construction based on the work of Shelah. Our framework unifies and extends various existing constructions for sparse graphs, ldpc codes, and error-correcting codes. Specifically, we construct sparse graphs with constant rate and constant fractional expansion, build ldpc codes with constant rate and linear-time decoding, and develop explicit constructions for codes capable of constant-time local and local decoding. In each case, the constructions rely on an explicit family of random graphs. Our explicit construction is founded on a novel random graph

This study examines the distributed $r$-distance dominating set problem on high-girth graphs, aiming to identify distance-$r$ dominating sets that are as small as possible. We demonstrate that for sparse high-girth graphs, this problem is closely related to the standard minimum dominating set problem. Specifically, for a given gap parameter $\gamma$, we present a randomized distributed algorithm with running time $O(r n)$ that solves the distributed distance-$r$ dominating set problem on $k$-sparse graphs with girth exceeding $4r+1$. The algorithm outputs a distance-$r$ dominating set of size at most $\gamma n$ with high probability, or it terminates with a "reject" message if a set of size at most $(\gamma - \epsilon) n$ exists with high probability, where $\epsilon > 0$. Additionally, for graphs with sufficiently large girth, we propose a randomized algorithm with running time $O(r n)$ (independent of $\gamma$) for the distance-$r$ minimum dominating set problem, which returns a minimum distance-$r$ dominating set with high probability. Finally, we extend these findings to distributed distance-$r$ total dominating sets, assuming $r=1$ and $k=1$, and presenting a randomized algorithm with running time $n \text{ polylog}(n)$ for high-girth graphs. This approach either identifies a distance-1 minimum total dominating set with high probability or outputs a "reject" message if one of size at most $(\gamma - \epsilon) n$ exists, where $\gamma = 0.356$. Furthermore, we establish that the standard dominating set problem is intractable on sparse random graphs with girth greater than $2r+1$. Our results rely on a recent extension of the Lovász and δ-Shadow Theorem by Alon, which provides a local condition ensuring that distance-$r$ dominating sets of size $\gamma n$ exist with high probability. Finally, we present a centralized algorithm with running time $O(r n)$ for the distance-$r$ minimum dominating set problem on sparse high-girth graphs, which either returns a distance-$r$ minimum dominating set or a certificate of inapproximability. Similar conclusions are drawn regarding the intractability of the total dominating set problem on sparse random graphs with large girth. Notably, all proposed algorithms are randomized; their success is guaranteed with high probability, though no specific time bound is required. Topological bound states arising from the intersection of bulk and/or edge bands are inherently sensitive to boundary conditions, making them susceptible to external perturbations. This paper investigates how the mass-boundary correspondence applies to discrete higher-order topological materials characterized by nontrivial mass-boundary charges. We demonstrate that specific boundary conditions can eliminate these topologically protected states within the gap while preserving the nontrivial higher-order boundary invariants. This phenomenon is elucidated by an underlying index theorem that connects boundary indices to zero-mode winding numbers in the momentum domain. Furthermore, we examine disorder-averaged spectral properties of the gapless disordered higher-order topological insulator SW-TI, revealing that its spectral statistics align with those of a Wigner-Dyson ensemble rather than a Poissonian ensemble. These findings offer new perspectives on the fundamental characteristics of higher-order topological materials and their response to perturbations. Additionally, they deepen the current understanding of spectral statistics in gapless disorder-free and disordered systems. Finally, our study extends the concept of the bulk-boundary correspondence to higher-order topological phases and highlights the distinct nature of this correspondence in such systems. Specifically, we reveal a scenario where boundary charges remain unchanged under certain boundary conditions even though the boundary states have vanished. Finally, we explore the spectral implications of this scenario for gapless disorderless and disordered higher-order topological materials. Keywords: Higher-order topological materials, mass-boundary correspondence, spectral statistics, disorder-averaged spectral statistics. This paper details a phenomenological study conducted at a 13 TeV proton-proton collider utilizing the CMS detector, which integrates findings from prior analyses on supersymmetric (SUSY) scenarios. The study examines various production channels, including gluino and chargino decays, along with 0, 1-, and 2-lepton final states featuring jets and missing energy from chargino and neutralino decays. Furthermore, an analysis of associated neutralino decays was conducted by incorporating results from earlier top quark studies. Building on previous work, an approach for interpreting neutralino decays into final states characterized by jets and missing energy, accompanied by one or two leptons, is presented. This methodology facilitates a more efficient utilization of experimental data. Additionally, the study investigates the neutralino decays of top quarks, focusing on two specific channels: top quark pair production and top quark-antiquark associated production with a neutralino. Combining these insights with an analysis of neutralino decays of top quarks yields the most stringent limits to date on such decays. Consequently, a comprehensive and unified set of limits has been established, covering a significantly broader region of the SUSy parameter space than prior investigations. Finally, the paper outlines a strategy for including significant detector components, such as the CMS muon spectrometer, thereby ensuring optimal sensitivity across all analyzed channels. This serves as a foundation for future CMS and LHC analyses of supersymmetry. The study was performed within the CMS collaboration, offering a unified and complete set of limits on SUSY parameters. The analysis leverages various final states involving neutralino decays of gluinos, charginos, and top quarks, featuring neutralino decays characterized by jets and missing energy, with or without one or two leptons. This work extends the CMS collaboration's previous analyses of supersymmetry and top quarks by incorporating neutralino decays of top quarks. The resulting set of limits is comprehensive and unified, covering a substantially larger region of the SUSY parameter space than earlier studies. While neural rendering effectively reconstructs 3D scenes from camera images, it frequently produces cluttered visualizations that hinder a clear comprehension of brain connectivity. In contrast, bright-field microscopy offers a transparent and intuitive depiction of neural pathways. We introduce a novel technique that simulates the translucency of biological tissues to render "bright-field" neural data directly against real camera captures. This approach applies neural rendering to synthetic views generated with specific transparent material parameters, seamlessly blending these results with the actual camera input to create a realistic visual effect. Consequently, this method generates more legeral neural reconstructions, revealing finer structural details and improving the interpretability of neural activity. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of bright-field effects to neural visualization, representing a significant step toward more intuitive and interpretable 3D brain representations, which is crucial for both neuroscience research and clinical applications. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms current baselines in readability. A video demonstration and interactive preview are available at https://vision.ee.cu.edu.tw/nebv. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/vinvin/Bright-Field-Neural-Vis. Furthermore, a companion paper detailing the 3D+Cam method will be published at CVPR 2021. Additional code and videos related to this work are hosted at https://github.com/vinvin/BrainVizToolkit. By integrating texturing and lighting information into 3D brain scenes, users can achieve textured and lit 3D+CAM visualizations, which are further detailed in our accompanying 3D+Cam paper published at CVPR 2021. The 3D+Cam method is available at https://github.com/vinvin/3D+Cam. The text below outlines the contributions of this work and its three associated papers: First, this paper presents the concept of bright-field neural visualization to enhance the interpretability of 3D brain reconstructions. Second, the 3D+Cam method enables 2D texturing and lighting of 3D brain scenes using camera images and virtual light sources; this method is detailed in a separate paper featured in CVPR 2021's 3D System track. Third, the BrainVizToolkit library implements neural visualization techniques grounded in the methodologies described in all three papers; access to the code and method demonstrations is available via this package. This work was presented at CVPR 2021's 3D System

This study presents speckle interferometric data for 100 binary systems, obtained from the May through September 2021 observing runs of the Southern Optical Astronomical and Research Association Telescope. For each system, we determined precise parameters, including angular separation, position angle, and stellar diameters. We also provide astrometric measurements for 72 of the observed binaries. Additionally, we discuss any resolved components detected within the point spread function of the 61 single stars that were part of the interferometric observing program. The data from the 2021 runs has been integrated with our historical archives and is accessible via the online catalog at http://www.swin.berkeley.edu/speckle. The entire dataset will be released upon the completion of the full archive. The publication deadline for this paper is set for 2022. The authors anticipate that the final archive will be released in 2022, following the conclusion of a five-year observation run. Color-kinematics duality has recently been generalized to integrable systems. In this framework, equations of motion for local integrable sigma-models can be expressed as a duality between holonomy and momenta. We introduce a variant of this duality termed "heavenly color-kinematics duality," which applies to topologically non-trivial sigma-models that possess "heavenly" equations of motion. A primary example of this category is the su(2) sigma-model on any su(2) Lie group manifold. We examine the anysphere su(2) sigma-model to demonstrate how heavenly color-kinematics decomposition facilitates the calculation of its chiral algebra through free-field realization. Notably, this process requires no integrability checks, as the color algebra and its kinematic constraints are predetermined. This method successfully reproduces the known anysphere chiral algebra, which is based on current algebra. Furthermore, we apply the same procedure to a deformed anysphere sigma-model, yielding a new chiral algebra that can be verified against an independent calculation. Finally, we construct a heavenly color-kinematics decomposition for any color-kinematics dual sigma-model, which is characterised by equations of motion that are both heavenly and color-kinematics dual. Examples include various deformations of any- and euclidean-spheres. We provide a free-field representation for the color-kinematics decomposition of any of these sigma-models, thereby enabling the construction of their chiral algebras. Additionally, we provide a direct free-field construction for the chiral algebra of the anysphere and demonstrate how it encodes the sigma-model's equations of motion. Collectively, these findings suggest a connection between heavenly color-kinematics duality and the chiral algebra of the corresponding sigma-model. Specifically, for sigma-models with heavenly color-kinematics decomposition, the chiral algebra can be constructed directly from the color algebra and any kinematic constraints, eliminating the need for integrability checks. This contrasts with standard color-kinematics decompositions, where such checks are essential. This relationship is illustrated by comparing the anysphere and deformed anysphere sigma-models, both of which exhibit heavenly color-kinematics decomposition but differ in the presence or absence of color-kinematics duality. Consequently, these results indicate a novel link between integrability and chiral algebras, driven by the presence of heavenly color-kinematics decomposition. Furthermore, as a byproduct of our calculations, we identify a new class of color algebras

Solar jets serve as a primary mechanism for heating the low corona, though their precise heating mechanisms remain uncertain. This study presents LOFAR observations of a piston-driven shock wave, or surge, occurring within a jet's spine just above the solar chromosphere. The surge was triggered by the interaction between the accelerating jet spine and a pre-existing coronal loop, which acted as a shock driver. LOFAR's exceptional spatial resolution allowed us to examine the surge's dynamics in detail. We detected a sawtooth pattern in the surge's motion, indicating oscillations around the jet's axis, and measured a propagation speed of approximately 100 km/s, consistent with the speed of the jet spine. The surge's behavior closely resembled a piston wave, suggesting it functions as a coherent structure driving the wave. Our findings demonstrate that jet spines can generate jet-driven piston surges in the low corona, thereby contributing significantly to the ongoing debate regarding the mechanisms of coronal heating. The surge's motion aligns with the sawtooth pattern observed in the motion of the entire jet spine, supporting the hypothesis that the spine itself is a coherent structure. Furthermore, the surge was observed in both 160 Å and 1700 Å images, confirming that jet spines can effectively heat the low corona. This represents the first direct imaging of such a surge, providing valuable insight into jet-driven heating processes. Future observations of similar jets will be essential for further investigation. The data were recorded using the LOFAR Low Frequency Solar (LOFAR-LFS) instrument, which offers a spatial resolution of about 100 km at 160 Å formation heights. The surge was detected at a 160 Å formation height of roughly 1.5 Mm, corresponding to a temperature of approximately 1.5 MK. The surge's motion exhibited a sawtooth pattern, indicative of oscillations around the jet axis, and propagated at approximately 100 km/s. These results are consistent with previous measurements of jet spines, supporting the hypothesis that spines are coherent structures. The detection of the surge at both 160 Å and 1700 Å confirms jets' ability to heat the low corona. The paper concludes with a discussion of these findings in the context of the ongoing debate regarding low-coronal heating mechanisms. The study demonstrates the value of high-resolution observations in studying jet-driven coronal heating. Future observations of similar jets will be crucial for further investigation. The LOFAR-LFS

In the general two Higgs doublet model, the flavor-changing $H_z^0\to b\bar{b}$ coupling, which is absent in the Standard Model, can be assessed using the measured $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ anomalies. This evaluation yields a relationship between the masses of the additional Higgs bosons and their couplings to the flavor $B$ meson. By incorporating constraints from the charm and electron dipole anomalies—specifically $(g-2)_\mu$ and $(g-2)_e$—we determine the masses of the extra Higgs bosons and the corresponding $\chi^2$ values. The results indicate that the most probable mass for the CP-even neutral Higgs boson $H^0$ is approximately 115 GeV, while the CP-odd neutral Higgs boson $A^0$ is most likely around 150 GeV. The CP-odd charged Higgs boson $H^\pm$ is most likely near 350 GeV, and the charged Higgs boson $G^\pm$ is most likely around 450 GeV. The $\chi^2$ values associated with the $(g-2)_\mu$ and $(g-2)_e$ measurements are approximately 10 and 1, respectively. Furthermore, the decay branching ratios for $H^0$, $A^0$, and $H^\pm$ into various final states are calculated. The findings suggest that the $H^0\to b\bar{b}$ channel is most probable at roughly 16%, the $H^+\to tb$ channel at about 26%, and the $A^0\to b\bar{b}$ channel at approximately 13%. Additionally, the predicted mass splitting between the charged Higgs bosons is approximately 100 GeV. These predictions may be testable at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) and the future Circular Collider for hadrons (FCC-hh). Finally, the predicted values for the masses of the extra Higgs bosons and the associated $(g-2)_\mu$ and $(g-2)_e$ $\chi^2$ results are visualized in 3D plots. This research examines random fluid dynamics within a three-dimensional bounded domain subject to stochastic boundary conditions, framing it as a functional probabilistic differential equation (focal) with a non-homogeneous initial condition. The methodology relies on a decomposition into a homogeneous problem featuring deterministic initial data and a non-homogeneous problem driven by stochastic initial data. The homogeneous component is resolved via the stochastic Liouville theorem, generating a propagator defined on a Hilbert space. The non-homogeneous component is addressed using the stochastic Fokker-Planck equation alongside the White Noise Functional (WNF) formalism. This approach yields a propagator on a Gelfand triple that adheres to a path-by-path interpretation. Subsequently, the full propagator for the focal is derived through the superposition of these two operators. Ultimately, the probability density function (p.d.f.) of the focal is obtained by applying the constructed propagator to the initial delta distribution. Ultimately, this framework provides a novel method for addressing fluid dynamics problems within bounded regions. Additionally, it offers a new perspective on hydrodynamics by modeling a fluid as a collection of particles with random, variable mass and non-elastic collisions. The efficacy of this methodology is demonstrated via an illustrative example. Finally, significant open questions regarding this topic are presented. Specifically, when solving focal in weak or strong forms, identifying appropriate boundary conditions remains a substantial challenge. Furthermore, there is a pressing need to develop a comprehensive theory of stochastic hydrodynamics. These developments could pave the way for new paradigms in fluid dynamics, such as predicting weather and fluid flows. The methodology utilized here may also prove effective in addressing other areas of physics, including quantum mechanics. Specifically, the focus is on the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation with a non-homogeneous initial condition and complex stochastic boundary conditions. In this scenario, the homogeneous solution is derived from the real and imaginary parts of the wave function, while the WNF represents the probability density. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to demonstrate a quantum advantage. While the average entanglement within this framework has been examined, the entanglement characteristics of its complete output distribution have received little attention. This study investigates those properties by calculating the average mutual information between arbitrary modes. The results indicate that mode entanglement exhibits significant fluctuations and is highly mode-dependent. These findings offer a detailed exploration of the quantum features inherent to boson sampling. Notably, given that non-classical correlations are essential for a quantum advantage, the variability in entanglement identified here may serve as an indicator of sampling efficiency. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the device's underlying physical properties. Furthermore, it establishes a foundation for analyzing entanglement in other boson sampling variants and related optical quantum computing technologies. Finally, this study introduces a general framework for investigating entanglement in quantum computational models, which has broad applicability. Specifically, the framework enables the calculation of entanglement measures based on access to the complete state vector and does not rely on specific model assumptions. This approach is particularly valuable in an era of rapidly advancing quantum simulation capabilities. Additionally, it is expected to facilitate deeper investigations into the physical features of emerging quantum devices. Furthermore, this method can be extended to the average additivity of entanglement. By applying this framework to a T-junction beam splitter, we uncover a counterintuitive result: the additivity of entanglement entropy is positive, contradicting established conjectures. This finding underscores the necessity of explicitly calculating additivity rather than relying solely on heuristic arguments. Finally, the framework has been implemented using PyQuNED, an open-source Python library designed for analyzing the complete output distribution of boson sampling. PyQuNED is freely available and accessible at https://github.com/zhengqiangliang/PYQUNED. Additionally, all relevant data required to reproduce the results are included in the supplementary materials. Specifically, we provide access to a single entanglement measure for the T-junction beam splitter, which was computed using PyQuNED; this data can be utilized to verify the conclusions regarding additivity. Users can also employ PyQuNED to explore the behavior of this measure across various modes. Finally, a dataset containing calculated values for entanglement measures in GHZ states has been made available for benchmarking purposes. Temporally ordered data is vital for describing events in life science, but its analysis is complicated by high dimensionality, dynamic ranges, and the need to identify specific features within a temporal context. Furthermore, the increasing volume of such data necessitates efficient, automated learning methods. We introduce ordered image regression, a guided deep learning technique that produces an interpretable summary of sequential images by regressing a graphic representation of the image sequence. This approach captures the unique temporal arrangement and relative positioning of images within a sequence. When applied to a dataset of 5,000 time-lapse images from 250 live-cell assays, ordered image regression generated a brief summary consisting of 10 images. These summaries effectively differentiate various assays and can be paired with representative sequences for classification tasks. Additionally, our method demonstrates robustness against occlusion, noise, and variations in recording parameters. Overall, ordered image regression offers a computationally efficient and interpretable summary of time-lapse image sequences, with potential applications extending to other temporal data formats. Furthermore, our approach enhances the interpretability of deep learning and facilitates a new form of human-machine interaction for guided learning and assessment. Temporal data compression and assessment are crucial for managing the growing complexity of life science experiments; we aim to make this technology accessible to the broader research community. To achieve this, we have open-sourced our method, including source code, pre-trained models, and a demo application available at orderedimageassessments.github.io. Additionally, we have made our dataset and analysis tools available through the CellProfiler Cloud platform (cellprofiler.cloud), enabling users to integrate temporal image compression and assessment into their existing analysis workflows. Reinforcement learning (RL) addresses agents operating within a partially observable environment, a challenge often modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). To effectively handle this uncertainty, agents must maintain a belief state representing their probability distribution over possible hidden states. This study investigates a recurrent neural network (RNN) that learns a policy directly from historical observations without explicitly computing a belief state. We demonstrate that this policy is equivalent to one derived from an RL agent that utilizes an approximated belief state to map to the policy. Furthermore, we present experimental findings supporting these claims and explore implications for enhancing the sample efficiency of applying recurrent networks to POMDPs. Consequently, these results indicate that it is feasible to train and deploy policies in POMDPs without the overhead of maintaining belief states. Finally, we offer a theoretical discussion regarding the critical factors influencing the sample efficiency of applying recurrent networks to POMDPs. This work is supported by the EPSRC grant number EP/R018245/1. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ahmedhaleem22/RecurrentPolicyInPOMDP. In datasets lacking fine annotations, detecting actions within loose temporal boundaries remains difficult due to the necessity of grasping broader contextual cues. Furthermore, actions often occur against complex, dynamic, and heterogeneous backgrounds, rendering the identification of relevant contextual information crucial for detecting when actions transpire. To address the detection of actions over extended, weakly-defined segments, this paper introduces a two-pronged strategy: (1) learning contextual features through graph convolutional networks, and (2) aggregating these learned features using a graph-based mechanism to generate actions with onsets and offsets. Experimental results on two prominent datasets, THUMOS14 and SSv2, demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively learns contextual features and surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, an ablation study reveals that the model's performance is highly sensitive to the emphasis placed on contextual features. Finally, the proposed network is shown to be computationally efficient for real-time detection. To our knowledge, this framework represents the first integration of weakly-guided detection with the capacity to learn contextual features. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWu1996/ICCV2017-Thumos14.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (ISC) evaluated 85 submissions from 45 participants to identify the most effective image similarity metric. The primary goal was to minimize the average angular error (AAE) on the TestSet for equal-sized neighbor retrieval. Top-ranking methods primarily relied on content-based features, though one finalist achieved strong results using a graph-based approach. Second-place submissions prioritized speed over accuracy to meet computational constraints, while third-place entries combined content-based and low-level features. The challenge yielded three key findings: first, the training and testing datasets differ significantly; second, the largest datasets do not necessarily yield the highest accuracy; and third, there is a strong correlation between accuracy and retrieval speed. Furthermore, the ISC exposed the need for a balanced dataset with representative class distributions to ensure generalizable similarity metrics. Ultimately, this event highlighted both the progress and the remaining obstacles in developing robust image similarity algorithms. Briefly, this study examines boundary value problems for parabolic equations and their associated metastable dynamics. Specifically, we analyze problems involving minor perturbations in non-linear diffusion non-linearities, within non-linear diffusion processes characterized by power-law degeneration at boundary points, and alongside obstacles positioned within the domain. The first scenario yields metastable states mirroring those of the unperturbed system, whereas boundary metastable states are significantly altered in perturbed systems exhibiting degeneration of non-linearities. Finally, we investigate metastable states arising from configurations that integrate all three perturbation types, demonstrating that such metastable states correspond to solutions of an appropriate eigenvalue problem derived from the original parabolic equation. These eigenvalue problems feature degenerate coefficients and obstacles within the domain, yielding eigenfunctions that may vanish at specific interior points. This analytical approach elucidates the stability of metastable states, accounts for the variability of first eigenfunctions, and establishes the occurrence of superconvergence near boundary points. We have rigorously proven these characteristics for power-law degeneration within 1D and 2D domains, extending these findings to higher dimensions under the assumption of local homogeneity. This assumption enables the derivation of superconvergence relative to boundary points and supports the application of a boundary condition based on an appropriate eigenvalue problem, thereby establishing metastable states within periodic domains. These states are characterized by a large time scale and periodicity, with amplitudes determined by linearized problem eigenvalues and a temporal scale governed by a decay exponent linked to the first eigenvalue. The existence of metastable states within periodic domains is further supported by numerical simulations. Collectively, these results demonstrate that minor perturbations of parabolic equations, even when inducing degeneration of non-linearities, result in metastable states that can be derived from linearized eigenvalue problems featuring degeneration and singularities within the domain. This conclusion aligns with established findings regarding metastable states in periodic domains, where superconvergence relative to cell centers and amplitudes is derived from linearized eigenvalue problems with periodic coefficients. The existence of metastable states in periodic domains is substantiated by both numerical simulations and recent theoretical proofs. Furthermore, within periodic domains, higher-order eigenvalues and eigenfunctions have been identified to characterize metastable states within specific cells. The theoretical framework developed for 1D and 2D domains regarding metastable states has also been extended to 3D. This study calculates the energy of nuclear substance within intense magnetic fields using the Landau-Ogarkov-Chasman-Vautherin technique. Findings indicate that such fields significantly influence nuclear energy, even at modest strengths, causing a reduction that exceeds the effects of standard nuclear matter compression. The computed energy is compared against relativistic nuclear substance models under similar magnetic conditions. Furthermore, an ODE module was developed to solve the relevant differential equation, and a benchmark was performed to validate its accuracy. These results provide a foundation for future investigations into nuclear matter characterized by high magnetic fields. This study addresses the core challenges of privacy, communication efficiency, and performance in federated learning. To do so, we introduce a novel approach termed differential privacy-based quantization (DP-Q), which integrates output differential privacy with quantization techniques. We also present a new framework called DP-REC, which combines compression, differential privacy, and extra training rounds. Our results demonstrate that DP-REC surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in privacy and communication efficiency while achieving comparable test accuracy. Specifically, on the MNIST dataset, each client transmits only 1 bit per image with an accuracy of 93.6%, and on Cifar10, the communication requirement is reduced to 1 bit per image while maintaining 92.0% accuracy. Furthermore, we examine how the number of clients influences privacy and communication efficiency, finding that these benefits are more pronounced when utilizing a larger client pool. Finally, we explore the impact of client heterogeneity on the robsap metric and offer recommendations for selecting the optimal privacy sensitivity parameter based on available client resources. The source code will be made publicly available. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01011. We introduce the inaugural far-ultraviolet (FUV) survey of the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga regions conducted by the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE). This survey comprehensively covers these cloud complexes, incorporating observations of all known young stellar objects (YSOs) with magnitudes brighter than F160 = 20. Leveraging the IUE's unique capability to observe in the 1200–1800 Å range, we performed a detailed analysis of the spectral characteristics of these YSOs, specifically examining their far-UV emission lines and continuum sources. Our findings indicate that FUV emission in these clouds originates from both embedded YSOs and their associated stellar clusters, as well as from nearby O-type stars. Furthermore, we demonstrate that FUV light penetrates the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga clouds to a depth of approximately 1.5 A_V, a depth significantly lower than that of the intercloud medium. This reduced penetration is attributed to the presence of dense, FUV-absorbing material, such as protostellar envelopes and clumps. Additionally, we present preliminary results on the FUV photodissociation regions (PDRs) within these clouds, which are generated by the interaction between FUV radiation and dense molecular gas. Our analysis reveals that PDRs in these clouds are characterized by narrow widths and steep density gradients, consistent with theoretical expectations. Finally, we provide a summary of the far-UV properties of the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga clouds. These results are critical for understanding the physical conditions and evolutionary stages of star-forming regions, as well as for investigating the relationship between the far-UV radiation field and the initial mass function of stellar clusters. This study is part of the FUV-YSO project, a collaborative effort by the University of Tokyo, Kyoto University, and the Astronomical Institute of the Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic. Natural language processing (NLP) has made substantial strides in the last few years. However, documents in machine-readable formats like Word or Excel remain difficult for computers to process. Humans typically create these files, enabling their generation without human intervention. A specific category includes scientific publications, which often contain complex scientific tables. These PDFs are frequently submitted to submission systems where their content must be analyzed; for instance, to detect plagiarism. Currently, no fully automated solution exists for extracting this information. This paper introduces a novel method for extracting scientific tables from PDF files using a combination of graph neural networks and representation encoding. We also present a new PDF-based dataset for table extraction and evaluate our approach against it, achieving a mean average precision of 70.71%. Finally, we examine and discuss the results in light of the challenges posed by PDF files. This work has been accepted for the 14th International Conference on Document Analysis and Recognition (ICDAR-2025). Cognitive multi-level agent-based models are essential for analyzing group-level phenomena in complex systems, including financial markets, the internet, and biological ecosystems. These models typically operate across three layers: the cognitive, where agents display human-like intelligence; the interaction, where agents participate in a complex game; and the evolutionary, where agents dynamically adjust their mental states. Although these layers are conceptually distinct, they are functionally interconnected, creating a challenge for traditional analytical methods. To address this, we introduce a novel approach combining the theory of learning in multi-phase games with cognitive map analysis. Our theoretical framework establishes conditions for the existence of a Nash equilibrium within such games and proposes a method to calculate its approximate value. We then apply both the learning theory and the Nash equilibrium analysis to a cognitive layer featuring maps, using numerical simulations to validate the results. Finally, we explore the application of our framework to socio-technical systems, demonstrating how the findings from the simplified model can inform the analysis of more complex systems. This study represents a significant step toward a unified framework for analyzing complex systems across all levels. The associated Python code is available at https://github.com/taiki-ida/ALMIG. This research investigates the autonomous population estimation (APES) challenge, which involves counting humans in satellite imagery to generate fine-grained demographic data. While prior studies have validated the feasibility of achieving low costs and high accuracy for population metrics, these works predominantly rely on data from Western countries, creating a bias that limits the transferability of current models to other global regions. To address this, we introduce a training dataset comprising 1,600 images of people in low-altitude satellite views from Mozambique. We conducted cross-country experiments using this new data, evaluating the performance of models pre-trained on datasets from various other countries. Our findings indicate that a model trained on a similar dataset (specifically, Finland) outperformed those pre-trained on diverse datasets across a range of fine-grained metrics, though achieving this required an excessive number of Mozambique-specific images. Consequently, we conclude that current state-of-the-art models are not sufficiently robust for direct application in field conditions without further training on local data. We discuss the challenges in acquiring such data and propose a hybrid approach combining deep learning with traditional survey methods as a more cost-effective alternative for accurate population estimation in the near future. We hope this dataset will facilitate new research into developing robust field-ready models and enable accurate and cost-efficient population metrics in under-studied regions. The dataset can be accessed at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1144q144q144q144q144q144q144q144q. The source code is available at https://github.com/JoaoPinto1999/APES. Current membership estimation approaches rely on sampling the data distribution, but they struggle to control the false positive rate. We introduce a novel algorithm called EMQF (Estimated Membership Query Filters) within the spindler family, which operates by iteratively refining upper and lower bounds of the membership function. EMQF is the inaugural spindler algorithm capable of constructing a filter that is free of false positives. In our current implementation, the algorithm utilizes Fibonacci sampling to generate these bounds. Under specific distributional assumptions, we demonstrate that EMQF achieves a false positive rate of zero while maintaining a collision rate of $O(n^{1/w})$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that EMQF can be adapted to handle distribution-free settings. Experimental results indicate that, in many scenarios, EMQF outperforms existing methods, including the original spindler algorithm. Additionally, EMQF is well-suited for estimating collection sizes from noisy data. In cases where data is not independently sampled, we prove that the algorithm's performance degrades only slightly compared to the ideal case. These findings are supported by theoretical analysis and empirical evidence. Our results hold significant practical value, as they enable the efficient construction of empty-join filters and the accurate estimation of the number of distinct elements in a data stream. We have made our implementation public to facilitate the evaluation of EMQF by the research community. The implementation is available at https://github.com/SebastianSchmidl/EMQF. We also provide a comprehensive proof of the algorithm's correctness in this paper. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of EMQF by employing it to maintain the distinct element count in a data stream. Our implementation outperforms all other methods, including approximate distinct count algorithms from the industry leader, by up to an order of magnitude. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/SebastianSchmidl/ApproximateDistinctCount. Among these, the MCDD algorithm is free of any false positives. We also show that EMQF can be easily modified to achieve a user-defined false positive rate. Overall, our approach is highly effective, even when the data collection method is flawed. This is evidenced by the fact that EMQF can accurately estimate the size of a stream corrupted by up to 10% noise. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/SebastianSchmidl/ApproximateDistinctCount. This study theoretically examines three-body recombination involving two polar spinor atoms in the presence of a third body, employing a simplified model. The analysis demonstrates that, through appropriate configuration and parameters of the third body—a trapping laser—this process can be extended to molecular formation linked to photon emission. Notably, the laser also facilitates atom-molecule conversion within specific spin states by adjusting its intensity and geometric arrangement. These findings offer a theoretical basis for generating spin-squeezed molecules derived from spin-squeezed atoms, a capability valuable for quantum metrology and information processing. Furthermore, the research explores the potential to create entangled molecules operating within two distinct frequency modes. This represents a significant advancement toward generating quantum entanglement in spin-sensitive atom-molecule systems. Additionally, the study investigates molecule-molecule entanglement for applications in quantum information processing and quantum metrology. Finally, the results can be experimentally validated using alkali atoms such as $^{87}$Rb or $^{85}$Rb. This study introduces a novel smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPHD) approach for analyzing incompressible fluid-structure interactions (FSI) and multiphase flows within a unified framework. The primary innovation lies in a new sub-grid scale (SGS) stress model designed to stabilize free-surface flows and maintain solution accuracy near fluid boundaries. Developed to address free-surface instabilities and numerical diffusion, this SGS term relies on the relative magnitude of the viscous force and the Laplacian of the artificial speed of sound (AsCS) pressure force at every fluid particle. By classifying particles into smooth and free-surface categories based on the overlap with ghost particles, the model applies stabilization only where necessary. This selective activation ensures free-surface flows remain stable while preserving the physical integrity of smooth regions. Consequently, the method enables accurate multiphase flows and FSI simulations without the need for complex boundary conditions or mesh generation. The versatility of the proposed framework is demonstrated through a series of benchmark tests, including the dam-break wave impacting a flexible structure, surface tension-driven rising bubbles, and a droplet impacting a solid surface. These cases highlight the method's potential, successfully replicating key physical phenomena in multiphase flows and FSI. Furthermore, the approach is validated against experimental data from a water sloshing tank and a droplet impacting a hydrophobic surface. The results confirm that the proposed framework is highly promising for practical engineering applications. Finally, the paper concludes with an outlook on future research directions. Machine learning algorithms face significant challenges in batch data environments due to overfitting and the difficulty of identifying the most informative samples. Quantum machine learning (QML) offers a potential solution by addressing these issues through the utilization of quantum-native advantages. This study experimentally investigates both quantum-unmonitored and quantum-instructed learning using the parameter-shift rule across superconducting processors of varying sizes. Our findings indicate that quantum-instructed learning offers superior benefits compared to quantum-unmonitored learning within the quantum regime. Additionally, we observe that quantum-unmonitored learning exhibits noise resilience comparable to classical baseline models. Given the noise constraints of current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, these results suggest that quantum-instructed learning strategies will be essential for achieving practical quantum advantages. Furthermore, our code is publicly accessible on GitHub. Finally, this work paves the way for future research into quantum-instructed approaches for hyperparameter tuning and the development of quantum-instructed methods for hyperparameter optimization. Notably, we demonstrate that a quantum-instructed NISQ algorithm can outperform the Bayes optimal estimator on average, marking a significant breakthrough. Overall, this study provides valuable insights for advancing the field of QML. Specifically, it underscores the necessity of developing quantum-instructed strategies to unlock the full potential of quantum computing. Additionally, our work highlights the need for further research into quantum-instructed methods for hyperparameter optimization, a critical area for realizing the capabilities of near-term quantum hardware. Finally, this research establishes a foundation for future studies aimed at demonstrating quantum-instructed advantages in the context of the quantum supremacy challenge. FastPitch is a sequence-to-sequence deep generation model that utilizes a convolutional decoder to produce mel-spectrograms from speaker embeddings and phoneme features. Although it supports pitch control via speech synthesis, simply modifying speaker embeddings to shift pitch can result in noticeable changes to speech timbre. To address this, we introduce pitch augmentation, a timbre-preserving technique for increasing fundamental frequency. This method combines original and pre-processed speech signals using a layer to enhance pitch controllability while maintaining the natural timbre of the utterance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach successfully generates target fundamental frequencies with timbre preservation and incurs only minor losses in intelligibility and naturalness. Furthermore, these improvements in timbre and pitch control positively impact speaker-verification scores. Consequently, our method offers greater flexibility in speech manipulation and represents a significant advancement over existing pitch-control techniques. This paper introduces Hopper, a model designed to address reasoning tasks within dynamic multi-agent systems characterized by spatiotemporal interactions. Distinct from prior approaches that depend on fixed grid-based representations, Hopper employs free-form trajectories to facilitate reasoning. It achieves this by integrating two key components: (1) a novel multi-agent attention mechanism that incorporates relative feature encoding, enabling effective interaction between multiple agents; and (2) an encoding framework that utilizes agent velocity and trajectories to encode both the motion dynamics and the environment. Extensive evaluations on the recently released Multi-Agent Reasoning (MAR) dataset show that Hopper significantly outperforms single-agent baselines and existing state-of-the-art models, achieving new state-of-the-art results on both the MAR dataset and an additional challenging benchmark, Multi-Agent Traversal (MAT). The model's code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Hopper. Furthermore, we provide our implementation of Hopper for the MAT dataset at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/MIT-VR-2022-Students-Comp-2022-Group-4. This resource includes not only Hopper but also baseline models and several additional state-of-the-art methods. We hope these resources will assist the community in further improving performance on both datasets. Our source code will also serve as a valuable reference for researchers developing new models in this emerging and exciting field of reasoning in dynamic multi-agent systems. The CMS experiment at the LHC investigates the double production of leptons and $b$ quarks at next-to-leading order (NLO) within the Standard Model. This process is characterized by a large NLO-suppressed to leading-order cross-section ratio and a complex kinematical topology, both of which significantly influence the precision of the $W$ boson mass determination. A comprehensive measurement of the triple differential distribution, $\mathrm{d}\sigma/\mathrm{d}m_{\ell\ell}\mathrm{d}p_{\mathrm{T},\ell\ell}\mathrm{d}y_{\ell\ell}$, is performed using 2015-2017 proton-proton collision data with an integrated luminosity of 36 fb$^{-1}$. The findings align with NLO predictions and recent 2018 CMS measurements of the $W$ mass. Utilizing the 2015-2017 dataset, the lepton-pair invariant mass spectrum is utilized to measure the $W$ boson mass as $80.19 \pm 0.62$ GeV. This result is 1.4 standard deviations higher than the Standard Model prediction from the Particle Data Group. The primary source of uncertainty is the experimental scale uncertainty, which is substantially reduced through the inclusion of NLO simulation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that for this specific process, incorporating NLO simulations is essential for an unbiased mass measurement, whereas for other lepton-pair production channels, such as vector boson fusion or Higgs boson production, such inclusion is not necessary. This distinction arises because certain processes are difficult to simulate accurately at NLO due to the presence of hard radiation, a challenge that could be mitigated by implementing a hybrid NLO+parton shower approach. Overall, the analysis confirms that for certain lepton-prompt production processes, the inclusion of NLO simulations is vital for achieving precise $W$ mass measurements. The results obtained with NLO simulations are approximately 1.4 standard deviations above the Particle Data Group Standard Model prediction. Additionally, the work discusses the significance of including NLO simulations for the first observation of top quark pair production associated with a lepton-prompt double production. This is the most recent measurement of this process, and the most precise $W$ mass determination derived from it. Telepresence robots (TPRs) serve as effective solutions for enabling communication with hard-to-reach locations. As the number of users utilizing these systems grows, there is an increasing need for reliable User Experience Quality of Experience (QoE) models. While numerous TPR QoE metrics exist, they rely on subjective human assessments, making them unsuitable for early-stage development and difficult to validate. This study introduces a novel QoE model designed to facilitate early evaluation using non-subjective data. The findings indicate that three specific factors significantly influence TPR operation: the robot's height, control interface type, and user confidence levels. Although a straightforward regression analysis could indicate how these variables affect performance, it fails to address underlying causes. To overcome this limitation, the study employs principal component analysis and machine learning to enhance interpretability and isolate the root causes influencing TPR task completion. The research also investigates potential improvements to the interaction method and robot design to improve efficiency. Ultimately, this work advances both the methodology for developing new QoE models and the technology itself, offering a more effective design for the system. By utilizing objective metrics, this approach enables more precise system evaluation and facilitates future QoE model development. The code and experimental data are publicly accessible to support reproducibility. This methodology is also applicable to evaluating other Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) systems. The paper is organized into the following sections: Section 2 provides a background overview; Section 3 details the methods and materials used; Section 4 presents the results of our experiments; and Section 5 offers a conclusion. A hierarchical linear model (HLM), commonly referred to as a multilevel model, is a regression approach that incorporates random effects. The term "random effect" implies that the parameter represents a sample drawn from a larger population of similar effects, which are typically modeled using a normal distribution. For instance, in a classroom dataset, the mathematical proficiency of individual students depends not only on individual attributes like gender but also on random effects such as the specific teacher or the particular school they are assigned to. While this random effects formulation is a practical computational strategy, it fundamentally reflects the multivariate nature of the data.

This article serves as a gentle initiation into Bayesian hierarchical linear models. The first section offers a non-technical explanation of random effects and distinguishes between first-level and second-level analysis. The second section offers a more formal definition of random effects and demonstrates their implementation using RAND school data. The final section elaborates on the Bayesian framework for hierarchical linear models and concludes with further reading resources.

Mafia, or Werewolf, is a widely enjoyed social game of deduction. In this scenario, two rival groups operate in the dark: civilians versus criminals (such as Mafia or werewolves). During each round, both factions eliminate random members without revealing their identities. The objective for the civilians is to identify all the criminals, whereas the criminals aim to eliminate as many civilians as possible. This study models the interaction between Mafia players and investigates the role of information sharing. Our findings indicate that a player's utility relies heavily on whether their teammates share information; specifically, having an informed teammate allows for a more optimal strategy. We determined the optimal threshold for eliminating players during each round and observed that criminal groups should adapt their strategies depending on which specific player roles exist. Additionally, by varying the number of eliminating players and changing game parameters, we examined how these factors influence the likelihood of the civilian faction winning. Finally, we conducted an experiment to validate our model by comparing simulated game outcomes with data collected from human players. This research offers valuable insights for both theoretical and practical applications of the Mafia game. Notably, our predictions regarding the impact of information sharing can assist players in improving their gameplay experience. To facilitate this, we have also made the code accessible to enable players to design and test their own strategies. Furthermore, players may find it beneficial to incorporate our predicted optimal thresholds into their elimination tactics. Finally, our model can be extended to analyze games involving multiple interacting factions or varied winning conditions. For instance, a third faction consisting of neutral players who can join either side could be introduced, thereby increasing the complexity and entertainment value of the game. The mass and migration trajectories of massive planets are crucial for comprehending the formation and evolution of planetary systems. This study investigates the concurrent gas accretion onto two massive planets within a young, massive, and extended protoplanetary disk. We developed a mass accretion model for a planet-mass critical core, accounting for both homogeneous and stratified envelopes. Our findings indicate that the total gas accreted by the inner and outer planets is highly sensitive to the disk's physical and chemical structure, which varies based on the planet's migration history. Specifically, the planet's location relative to the disk's hot inner region significantly influences accretion rates. When a planet migrates through this hot zone, its core retains more gas due to reduced envelope mass loss. Additionally, we observe that the extended disk suppresses accretion onto the outer planet, whereas the compact disk causes the accretion ratio between the inner and outer planets to decrease. These results highlight the critical role of a multi-planet system in shaping the evolution of the planet-disk configuration. Consequently, our study offers a new perspective on the final mass and evolution of planetary systems containing multiple massive planets. Furthermore, this research highlights the essential role of phonons in the transport physics of carbon nanotube technologies. This underscores the fundamental significance of phonon interactions in the intrinsic physics of carbon nanotubes. This study introduces a novel fuzzy k-means approach designed for clustering high-dimensional data with heterogeneous features. Given the challenge of assigning equal weights to all attributes during the fuzzy k-means process, we propose simultaneously re-calculating variable weights for each feature throughout the algorithm's iterations. Drawing inspiration from Entropy-weighted K-Means (EKM), our method avoids the need for manual weight assignment, a step that often introduces subjective bias. We formally define the entropically weighted fuzzy k-means (WFKM) model, develop an effective algorithm to solve it, and demonstrate its superior clustering performance on high-dimensional datasets. Furthermore, experimental results confirm that WFKM outperforms both standard fuzzy k-means and EKM models. Finally, the method is applied in a real-world analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic in India. The categorical gating network, which is an integral component of the mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture, is prone to the "deadlock" problem, causing the model to fail in learning complex patterns. This issue, first identified by Liang et al. (2021), has inspired several countermeasures, including the use of soft gating, prior distributions, or gating networks trained on teacher-student data. However, these existing solutions are not universally effective across all MoE models. In this study, we introduce a unified and principled framework to eliminate deadlock without relying on information from teacher models or altering the gating network's prior distribution. Our proposed solutions encompass both single-step and multi-step methods to address deadlock in both batch and online learning scenarios. We demonstrate that these methods are broadly applicable, enabling robust and rapid convergence across a wide range of models. Furthermore, our experiments on challenging tasks show that these approaches can enhance performance beyond that of other techniques. Driven by the resolution of Shakirov's conjecture regarding the topological nature of Jacobians as quotients of graph homology, we develop token-firing games on weighted orientable surfaces to address several open mathematical inquiries concerning Jacobians, Prym varieties, and Kahler differentials. These games manifest in two distinct types, with specific variants providing finite field realizations of Prym forms and the Picman rank for non-trivial Jacobian components. The mechanics of these games yield constructive proofs for Shafarevich's conjecture concerning étale covers and demonstrate that key surface invariants—such as the genus, signature, branching data, and branching cycles—can be derived from these games and their extensions. Furthermore, we present an explicit combinatorial construction of generalized Abel maps for combinatorial surfaces. Leveraging Shastri's theorem on fundamental groups, we establish that Abel maps constitute surface invariants and demonstrate their capacity to generate combinatorial models of Jacobians and Prym varieties. Additionally, we offer a combinatorial construction of Jacobians for combinatorial surfaces, which extends Shastri's model of the Jacobian of a projective curve. This construction generates combinatorial models for Jacobians and Prym varieties that serve as effective tools for exploring their topological and algebraic geometries. Finally, by integrating combinatorial methods with algebraic geometry, we develop effective algorithms for calculating genus, branching data, and other relevant invariants of combinatorial surfaces. These algorithms include a resolution to Shastri's problem on computing Jacobian cycles and algorithms for generating cyclic covers of projective curves. The proposed algorithms extend existing methods, such as Zakharevich's algorithm for computing Jacobians of projective curves. Finally, we provide a comprehensive example of our approach applied to the family of Hermitian curves. This example encompasses the resolution of Shastri's conjecture on the Picman rank of Hermitian curves, alongside the derivation of explicit forms for Prym forms and Kahler differentials of projective curves as byproducts. Our findings are expected to facilitate new discoveries within the field of algebraic geometry. This work serves as a foundation for advancing the topological understanding of Jacobians and Prym varieties, as well as their algebraic structures. This study outlines the framework for analyzing quantum gravity effects on globally symmetric forms of dark matter. We demonstrate that electromagnetic plane waves propagating through spacetime can be represented as operators acting on a Fock space, enabling the definition of global symmetries as operators. Furthermore, we show that the disturbance of these symmetries serves as an indicator of the absence of global symmetries in quantum gravity. Focusing on cosmic birefringence generated by electromagnetism during the inflationary epoch as a case study, we evaluate how perturbations to this global symmetry constrain global symmetries within quantum gravity. We show that the birefringence's perturbations, along with their non-local characteristics, complicate the definition of the associated symmetry charge, thereby limiting the symmetry disruption achievable by quantum gravity. We suggest that similar analyses of other potentially shifted polarization patterns could provide insights into the relationship between global and quantum gravitational charges, aiding in the (non-)detection of global symmetry effects in quantum gravity. Finally, we propose that a comprehensive investigation of all symmetry-related shifts in case studies could refine our understanding of how symmetry charges and the breaking of global symmetries manifest in quantum gravity. We conclude that more precise measurements of (or discoveries of) other symmetry-disruption phenomena will enable more rigorous constraints to be placed on quantum gravity. Additionally, we highlight that our framework is general and can be readily extended to examine any phenomenon involving global symmetry effects, such as the stability of particles and nuclei. We believe that a thorough analysis of case studies within this framework will deepen our understanding of global symmetry dynamics in quantum gravity. Finally, we note that this approach is also applicable to other case studies, including those concerning baryogenesis, leptogenesis, and neutrino oscillations. We demonstrate that these studies can be analyzed using the same framework to constrain global symmetry effects in quantum gravity. We also show that these analyses can be extended to case studies regarding the (non-)existence of dark matter and other mysterious matter. We believe that these analyses will also contribute to our understanding of quantum gravity.
