The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) has successfully navigated through solar wind streams of varying speeds, enabling a novel investigation into the energy budget of the inner heliosphere. By integrating in-situ measurements of bulk kinetic energy, magnetic energy, and plasma Alfvénic fluctuations from PSP and a single plasma instrument from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE), we analyzed energy budgets across radial distances from 16 to 189 solar radii (Rs) for both slow and fast solar breeze streams. Our findings indicate that, as expected, the fast solar breeze exhibits higher kinetic energy and lower magnetic energy compared to the slow solar breeze. Notably, the energy budget of the fast solar breeze demonstrates minimal evolution with increasing radial distance, whereas the slow solar breeze shows a greater increase in kinetic energy and a more pronounced decrease in magnetic energy as it propagates outward. In all cases, the sum of kinetic and magnetic energies, augmented by the energy associated with fluctuations, accounts for nearly 100% of the energy budget. This result suggests that energy inputs into the solar wind are minimal within the inner heliosphere, regardless of the stream's speed. Consequently, the observed evolution in energy budgets is likely driven by energy transfer between field and plasma, as well as in situ energy dissipation within the inner heliosphere. Finally, we observed a correlation between the energy in Alfvénic fluctuations and the energy "gap," indicating that non-thermal energy dissipation in the inner heliosphere is primarily governed by the thermal speed of protons relative to the Alfvén speed. These results are consistent with recent observations from the Parker Solar Probe and the Solar Orbiter. Collectively, these results suggest that the evolution of the solar breeze energy budget occurs gradually and is governed by local processes within the inner heliosphere. Future studies will aim to investigate these processes in greater detail. The data utilized for this study can be accessed at https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/parker/missions/science.html. The Dual-Rotors Model (DRM) offers a framework for analyzing collective motion in deformed nuclei. For even-even R-parity even nuclei, the system comprises two deformed potential wells, each capable of motion within its own plane, resulting in two distinct rotational frequencies, $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$. The spectrum is characterized by R-parity even scissors modes (1-$\omega_1$ / 1-$\omega_2$) and chiral triads. Additionally, the spectrum includes R-parity odd scissors modes defined by transitions such as 2$_y$ $\otimes$ 1-$\omega_1$ and 2$_y$ $\otimes$ 1-$\omega_2$. In standard configurations, these R-parity odd modes appear at higher excitation energies than their R-parity even counterparts. However, in specific "adverse" cases, these modes appear at the lowest excitation energy. This study examines these atypical R-parity odd scissors modes within the DRM framework, focusing on the influence of the proton rotational frequency, $\omega_p$. We analyze how the energy and electromagnetic transition rates of these modes vary with $\omega_p$ and investigate the impact of varying neutron to proton stiffness ratios. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the energy of these adverse modes and model parameters, offering insights into identifying candidate nuclei for such R-parity odd scissors modes. This research expands the scope of R-parity odd collective excitations and elucidates their characteristics. Finally, we outline a search strategy to identify nuclei exhibiting these adverse modes in upcoming gamma-ray astrophysics missions. This approach involves evaluating available data from the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) and the Nuclear Spectroscopy Telescope (NOST) mission, followed by an analysis of predicted gamma-ray spectra to determine potential candidates. This methodology establishes a foundation for discovering these rare excitations in gamma-ray astrophysics. This investigation is part of a broader effort to elucidate the nature of the Galactic Center excess (GCE) and test the hypothesis that it originates from dark matter annihilation into electron-positron pairs. Such a signal would manifest as gamma rays in the MeV range, accessible through gamma-ray astrophysics missions. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for GCE research. This boundary term encodes information regarding singular values, which correspond to the bundles failing to be large. The mass transfer from a donor star to the accreting black hole in binary X-ray systems is influenced by stellar winds driven by tidal heating in the donor. This study investigates the characteristics of these winds during the hard state of the Cyg X-1 black hole candidate. By analyzing the spectral-timing properties of X-ray photons emitted from the inner regions of the accretion disk, we identified two distinct types of variability: (i) a fractional flux decrease of approximately 10% occurring roughly 100 microseconds after the spectral-timing peak, and (ii) a fractional flux increase of about 10% appearing approximately 100 milliseconds after the peak. The first type of variability is attributed to changes in the accretion disk's inner region, whereas the second type is proposed to result from the ejection of matter from the disk. We suggest that the matter ejected in the second instance originates from the donor star and constitutes the stellar wind driving the tidal heating. Consequently, we conclude that the stellar wind driving mechanism, long theorized, may have finally been observed. Furthermore, we argue that this tidal heating mechanism could be applicable to other black hole binaries in their hard states. In the context of the IMBH candidate 47TQ, we demonstrate that the stellar wind driving mechanism is more effective than in Cyg X-1. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting and studying stellar winds driven by tidal heating in the supermassive black hole M87* using the James Webb Space Telescope. Additionally, we emphasize that this mechanism is more significant for intermediate-mass black holes, such as those found in M60-ULTRAMAG-1. Overall, this research provides a critical foundation for future investigations into stellar winds driven by tidal heating. Magnetized accretion flows surrounding merger remnants are thought to launch jets and significantly impact post-merger ejecta, thereby shaping the resulting kilonova and gravitational wave (GW) signals. This study examines the characteristics of post-merger ejecta, kilonova, and GW signatures from a binary neutron star (BNS) merger featuring a magnetized, non-viscous neutrino-cooled accretion disk (CAD). Utilizing a hybrid code, we first modeled the merger, then simulated the accretion disk and jets with the X-ray Radiation Hydrodynamics (XRD) code. Our results indicate that the disk produces two primary ejecta components: a nearly isotropic, low-velocity outflow and a highly collimated, high-velocity jet. The latter is driven by the jet's momentum and comprises polarized radiation; its luminosity correlates with jet power but is generally weaker than outjet-driven jets. The jet ejecta exhibit low velocities ($v\lesssim0.1c$) and high opacities ($\kappa\gtrsim0.1$ cm$^2$/g), making them ideal for producing blue kilonova emission. Additionally, the jet impacts GW signals by ejecting mass from the remnant, causing a frequency drop and an amplitude decline. Our findings suggest that magnetized CADs can substantially influence kilonova and GW observables, underscoring the necessity to account for their effects in future BNS merger studies. This work is part of the BEAST project (BEmass Accretion Structure and Tracer). We analyze the relationship between the flux fraction of tidal features and merger rates for large early-type galaxies (LETGs; $L \gtrsim 5 L^*$) by examining the HSC-SSP M51 Deep Survey catalog. The study focuses on galaxies with redshifts $z < 0.05$ and stellar masses $M_* > 10^{11} M_{\odot}$. We identify tidal features by detecting surface brightness discontinuities in radial S\'ersic fits, while classifying mergers as either "wet" (with significant dust extinction) or "dry" (without significant dust). Our analysis reveals that merger rates for LETGs are approximately $10^{-2} M_{\odot}^{-1}$. Furthermore, dry mergers are found to be roughly 1.5 times more frequent than wet mergers. These findings align with merger rates derived from numerical simulations. Additionally, we observe that tidal features are more prevalent in LETGs with higher stellar masses, and both wet and dry merger rates in galaxies with significant dust correlate with their star formation rates. These results suggest that tidal features observed around LETGs are primarily the outcome of mergers. Finally, we demonstrate that the S\'ersic index of galaxies involved in "wet" mergers is significantly lower than that of galaxies involved in "dry" mergers or those without tidal features. This indicates that tidal features are more pronounced in young stellar populations, whereas dry mergers are more common in mature ones. Overall, these results support the hypothesis that tidal features are a direct manifestation of galaxy mergers. The HSC-SSP catalog provides a valuable resource for investigating tidal features and mergers around LETGs, offering insights into their formation mechanisms. Our findings also contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of stellar populations in large early-type galaxies. (Available at https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ac052b)

This study extends the azimuthally symmetric model of gravitational phenomena, previously introduced in the first paper of this series, into a more complex configuration featuring two distinct ejection velocities and opposing directions. The bipolar nature of these ejections generates a standing wave within the ejection plane that mimics light waves responsible for solar reticular patterns. This approach offers a unified explanation for various observed space phenomena by applying a single equation to describe all bipolar gravitational events. Additionally, the methodology establishes a functional link between the mass of the central gravitating body and the orbital radii of orbiting bodies, accounting for both circular and elliptical orbits. The text further explores the gravitational interaction between two rotating systems and examines how orbital radius influences the magnitude of gravitational ejections. Ultimately, these findings establish a functional relationship regarding the impact of bipolar ejections on the gravitational dynamics of celestial bodies. In conclusion, this work provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and predicting diverse gravitational phenomena, ranging from planetary orbits to space ejections. By achieving a unified understanding of these phenomena, it significantly advances our knowledge of the universe and enhances our ability to predict future celestial occurrences. Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are intense extragalactic radio bursts characterized by their repeatability, high luminosity, and significant dispersion caused by the interstellar medium. While their origins remain unknown, numerous models have been proposed to explain them. Recent discoveries of repeating FRBs, particularly those exhibiting sub-millisecond variability in individual sub-millisecond bursts (sub-bursts), have prompted the suggestion that these sub-bursts originate from neutron stars. This study demonstrates that if an FRB source is a neutron star, the high energy output of these sub-bursts necessitates that a substantial portion of the released energy be deferred until the end of the burst. We establish that for well-localized FRBs, no more than approximately 10% of the energy from sub-bursts can be emitted concurrently, with the remainder deferred. The maximum allowed concurrent emission is shown to scale with frequency as $\nu^{-4/3}$, where $\nu$ represents frequency in GHz. Furthermore, we examine how this limit evolves over time and explore potential implications for various FRB emission models. Our findings suggest that models relying on coherent optical or X-ray radiation cannot account for sub-burst energy, as they would require a significant fraction of energy to be released concurrently. Consequently, we argue that any viable sub-burst model must include a mechanism to store and subsequently release a substantial portion of the energy. Finally, we illustrate that a model based on incoherent radiation can easily satisfy these constraints. Additionally, we show that if an FRB is a magnetar, the upper mass limit for a neutron star is constrained to roughly 2.5 solar masses. This constraint arises because a larger mass would result in a less strongly magnetized star, thereby reducing the available energy for the burst. We also establish a similar constraint for neutron stars in general, regardless of whether they are magnetars. Overall, this paper provides a framework for analyzing sub-millisecond FRB data, which can be applied to various models to derive constraints on their parameters. We anticipate that this approach will prove valuable for future research. Our findings are based on two well-localized sub-millisecond FRBs: FRB 20201124A and FRB 20210426A. Text generation models often fail to fully leverage training data, particularly the capability of natural language to explicitly define physical properties of generated content. We introduce LDG-3D, a framework that integrates visual controls into language models. Our experimental results demonstrate that these models can successfully direct 3D object creation on an embodied agent to align with specific textual descriptions. We achieve this by establishing a bridge between natural language and low-level visual parameters, enabling efficient barometric control of 3D generation. Furthermore, we evaluate a multi-modal policy that utilizes both language descriptions and direct visual controls, showing it significantly outperforms a policy relying solely on visual controls. These findings confirm that our approach produces 3D objects that more accurately reflect physical attributes as specified in natural language. Our method offers a promising pathway for creating systems where multi-modal inputs create expressive and robust interfaces for complex tasks. The experimental code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ashishgupta12/LDG-3D.

This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a ring cryptosystem featuring confidential transactions and a ring signature variant called RingCT. Building upon the Pedersen commitment and zero-knowledge range proof framework of the original RingCT, we incorporate the Delegated commitment scheme to construct DelegatedRingCT, ensuring security under the Random Oracle Model. In this model, the private key holder establishes a random oracle model for all users, which subsequently enables the generation of ring signatures known as RingCT. We provide a comparative analysis of our proposal against the foundational RingCT, demonstrating that while security and privacy are maintained, the computational cost for signing and verifying RingCTs is significantly reduced for both common members and verifiers. These improvements are achieved by utilizing shorter signatures and fewer checks during signature validation. Experimental results confirm that DelegatedRingCT offers significant advantages in these metrics. Furthermore, we outline potential applications of DelegatedRingCT and conclude the paper with a discussion of an open research challenge. Specifically, while we prove the security of DelegatedRingCT within the Random Oracle Model, extending this security to a real-world model without relying on the random oracle assumption remains an unresolved and difficult problem. Addressing this gap would likely require either developing a new cryptosystem or finding an alternative approach to RingCT validation that avoids dependence on the Pedersen commitment scheme. To our knowledge, no existing solution to RingCT verification currently avoids the use of the Pedersen commitment scheme. Consequently, we view the Pedersen commitment scheme as essential to RingCT, and we contend that any solution avoiding its use must accept the inherent limitations of DelegatedRingCT. We hope this paper inspires further research to overcome these constraints. The BrABe system is designed to measure all 16 components of the relativistic electron beam tensor at points across the transverse plane, capturing 2D profiles and interactions. In this study, we present tensor measurements for high-energy electron beams from the Super Proton Synchrotron at CERN, obtained using a novel laser source: a fiber-compressed, table-top, broadband Ti:sapphire system. This novel source enables high-energy beam characterization at a cost significantly lower than accelerator-specific lasers. We demonstrate that brightness scans can be derived from the beam's transverse emittance and energy spread, calculated via Wick rotation from measured laser spectral intensity. Furthermore, we show strong agreement between these brightness scans and the BrABe measurement results. This approach offers a simple, flexible, and transparent method for determining the 2D energy distribution, emittance, and energy energy spread, which is particularly advantageous for beam-abroad-narrow-bunch (BANB) operations. Additionally, we illustrate a new technique for extracting laser-spot size from BrABe data, which is essential for such BANB scenarios. Finally, we propose a method to identify and correct systematic errors in all BrABe measurements, thereby enhancing their accuracy. These developments are intended to facilitate beam characterization using fiber-compressed, table-top, broadband Ti:sapphire lasers at costs far below that of accelerator-specific lasers. Data-informed modeling (DIM) represents a hybrid approach integrating data-driven and physics-informed machine learning, blending mathematical rigor with interpretability. This survey introduces the concept of space-invariant DIM, which relies on a universal model across all spaces. It then presents collaborative data-informed modeling, a framework that unites multiple data-invariant models through a learning process combining mathematical modeling and machine learning. The theoretical foundations of this approach are illustrated via examples drawn from the natural sciences. Finally, the survey outlines future research avenues and potential applications within artificial intelligence. The anticipated contribution of this survey lies in its unification of space-invariant DIM and collaborative DIM concepts, while also offering perspectives on the intersection between physics-informed machine learning and deep learning. Specifically, it addresses the convergence between mathematical modeling and deep learning, as well as between physics-informed and collaborative data-informed machine learning. Additionally, the survey examines applications in image processing, including image denoising, deblurring, and super-resolution. Keywords: machine learning, deep learning, mathematical modeling, image processing, application.

Soft robotics has gained significant traction due to the unique capabilities offered by these machines. A primary challenge in controlling soft robots stems from the complex, nonlinear dynamics inherent in both their materials and architectures. This complexity is often exacerbated by discrepancies between simple analytical models and the robots' actual behavior. Consequently, model-driven control remains a significant hurdle for researchers. This review examines various modeling and control approaches found in the literature, emphasizing control strategies that rely on models. It begins with an overview of the most prevalent modeling techniques, followed by a survey of fundamental control approaches, including impedance, optimal, and feedback linearization control, as well as more recent methods like reinforcement learning. Finally, the review explores and discusses open issues and future research directions. The discussion is grounded in the authors' extensive experience across a wide spectrum of soft robots, featuring diverse materials, actuators, sensing systems, and applications. The review is intended to assist researchers in navigating the field and advancing towards fully functional, model-driven systems. Future developments will likely focus on enhancing robustness and adaptability, such as incorporating material aging into models, utilizing more sophisticated constitutive relations, and implementing model predictive control. Furthermore, increased attention is anticipated for robot-robot and human-robot interaction, as well as for extending model-driven approaches to multi-arm robots and unstructured environments. These future directions are essential for advancing soft robotics toward greater maturity. This paper presents a global generalization of the "Jacobi group," termed the "authentic Jacobi group." Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are widely recognized for synthesizing visually appealing images, they frequently suffer from mode collapse, where the generator consistently collapses into producing a limited variety of samples. This study investigates mode collapse within the context of the popular Wasserstein GAN and introduces a straightforward yet effective solution: hidden space conditioning (HSC). By imposing an isotropic Gaussian prior on the generator's latent code and randomly sampling new codes during the sampling phase, GANs trained with HSC are capable of generating diverse samples without experiencing mode collapse. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's effectiveness for data augmentation, enabling the generation of semantically varied images from a single image. Our experimental results indicate that HSC is effective across various GAN architectures and tasks. The code for this work can be found at https://github.com/taehyung-lee95/hsc_gan. Liu's 1994 proposal of augmented random walk samplers has spurred significant research into effective variants for layered sampling targets. While recent work has largely concentrated on modifying augmented samplers, step samplers introduced by Laidou and Kounias (1999) offer distinct characteristics that have received less attention. This study contrasts step samplers with augmented ones through statistical metrics, including autocorrelation, convergence rates, and the Lyapunov drift condition. We demonstrate that step samplers exhibit superior statistical properties compared to their augmented counterparts. Furthermore, we present the first proof of geometric convergence rates for nested step samplers and establish that their drift conditions are more favorable. These findings are empirically validated using two layered targets. The results indicate that step samplers require fewer samples to generate an ergodic sample set, resulting in lower computational costs for layered sampling. Finally, our analysis of step sampler performance reveals a nuanced relationship between the target's parameters and sampling efficiency. Specifically, we find that while step samplers generally outperform augmented versions, they do not consistently match the efficiency of nested Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) when applied to certain increasingly tractable layered targets. This last insight underscores the necessity of utilizing augmented samplers, such as nested HMC, in layered sampling scenarios. The study includes proofs of all theoretical results and detailed numerical experiments supporting these findings. Additionally, we introduce a new R package, lss, to facilitate the implementation of step samplers. This paper and its supplementary materials also feature executable R code and datasets. The layer, step, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samplers were all implemented using the open-source package samplerr, which is also available. The layer and step samplers in samplerr allow users to easily specify targets and construct samplers. Furthermore, the layer and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samplers in samplerr provide a comprehensive suite of features for efficient implementation of augmented samplers, including support for various tuning schemes and adaptive nesting. The objective of distance labeling in graphs is to assign specific labels to vertices such that the shortest distance between any two vertices can be derived from their labels using a basic function. While numerous resilient variants exist, most existing solutions for planar graphs rely on complex labeling schemes. In this work, we demonstrate that any weighted connected planar graph with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$ admits an $O(n^\varepsilon \log n)$-bit $O(n^\varepsilon)$-resilient distance labeling, where $\varepsilon = \Theta(1/\log \log \Delta)$. Our approach utilizes a straightforward labeling scheme, and when $\Delta$ is polynomial in $n$, this method yields a linear-time algorithm for constructing the labeling. By applying two-particle quantum process tomography, we reconstruct two-particle channels and analyzing their non-Markovian characteristics. We examine two distinct regimes: a many-body dissipative linear response regime, which is closely related to linear spectroscopy, and a regime involving strong two-particle interactions. In this latter context, we identify an entanglement-assisted linear response regime. Additionally, we highlight the significant role of the initial state in defining two-particle correlation functions. These findings offer a comprehensive framework for analyzing and interpreting many-body linear and nonlinear response properties. Our research emphasizes a critical yet often overlooked aspect of quantum fluids: the necessity of distinguishing between one- and two-particle channels, even when probing the same physical excitation. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-particle channel can facilitate the detection of otherwise obscure phenomena, such as the absorption of photon pairs. Furthermore, exploring two-particle correlations in driven, dissipative many-body systems provides a robust method for probing the quantum dynamics of strongly interacting systems. We conclude that two-particle correlation analysis serves as a vital tool for elucidating the complex quantum behavior of driven, dissipative many-body systems. Such insights are essential for advancing quantum technologies and are crucial for interpreting experimental data in quantum optics and qubit systems. We anticipate that these findings will facilitate new discoveries in the study of quantum fluids. Finally, our findings may find applications in new areas of quantum optical spectroscopy. This paper investigates the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of weak solutions for elliptic equations expressed in divergence form, featuring drifts in $L^2$. Specifically, it analyzes equations defined as $Qu := -\mbox{div}(A D u + b u) + cu = f$ and divergence-form divergence equations (DFEs) formulated as $Qu := -\mbox{div}(A D u + b X u) + cu = f$. In both scenarios, the coefficients $b$, $c$, and $f$ belong to $L^2$. While the study focuses on divergence-form equations, it notably excludes those in non-divergence form. Furthermore, the notation $Qu$ encompasses not only standard elliptic equations but also divergence-form DFE equations, which are associated with parabolic equations of the type $\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} - \Delta u - b \cdot \nabla u - cu = 0$. The analysis covers scenarios where the domain $\Omega$ possesses a fractal boundary, where $A$ is merely bounded, $b$ acts as a drift, and $c$ serves as a potential. These scenarios also encompass divergence-form half-Laplace equations, described as $Qu := -\frac{1}{2}\mbox{div}(D u + b u) + \frac{1}{2}c u - \sqrt{1-A^2}u = f$. The study demonstrates that drifts and potentials in $L^2$ still permit the existence of unique weak solutions, even when coefficients are unbounded near the boundary and sub-Riemannian structures are present. Additionally, the paper examines whether these weak solutions align with functions possessing stronger regularity, such as Sobolev or Holder classes, and explores the relationship between the half-Laplace operator's weak solutions and function spaces exhibiting sub-Riemannian characteristics. Ultimately, the methodology developed herein facilitates the solution of specific sub-Riemannian half-Laplace equations. This achievement marks the first instance of solving a divergence-form half-Laplace equation on a non-compact, non-flat manifold within the context of fractal boundaries. Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, raising concerns about their performance on out-of-distribution (DoT) data. While prior attempts to introduce uncertainty for DoT detection rely on probabilistic models, these approaches often suffer from the limitations inherent to distributions defined piecewise by linear boundaries. This study proposes a novel method leveraging normal processes to model complex, non-linear distributions. By employing normal distributions to represent prior distributions of function values, we define a normal process where samples are drawn from these prior distributions. The model architecture consists of layers, with each layer comprising multiple distributions. We propose an effective regularizer to constrain the values of normal processes, ensuring they align with training data. Our evaluation across multiple datasets demonstrates that normal processes effectively capture non-linear distributions, outperforming baseline models in identifying out-of-distribution samples. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/taehyung-lee/NormalProcessLayers.

Periodic driving of a quantum system typically induces heating, a phenomenon that is particularly swift and severe in open systems where drivers couple to a dissipative environment. This environmental coupling usually causes a driven open system to thermalize far more rapidly than an isolated one. In this study, we investigate an open two-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model subjected to periodic driving and coupled to a one-dimensional bath. Contrary to the expectation of rapid heating, we demonstrate that Floquet heating is significantly suppressed, with bath coupling playing a constructive role. This suppressed heating arises because bath-induced particle transport facilitates a resonant exchange of bosons between neighboring sites, a mechanism akin to facilitation dynamics. Furthermore, under specific conditions, this dynamics fosters Bose condensation in a scar-like spatial pattern that remains invariant to bath coupling strength. These findings offer a promising avenue for mitigating Floquet heating in open systems and may pave the way for creating exotic spatially inhomogeneous Bose-Einstein condensates. Additionally, our numerical methodology is broadly applicable to other driven open quantum many-body systems. Finally, we outline a feasible experimental implementation using ultracold atoms within an optical lattice coupled to an engineered environment. \textit{Keywords}: Driven Open Quantum Systems, Quantum Phase Transitions, Optical Lattices. \textit{Abbreviated Title}: Floquet-heating-induced Bose condensation in a scar-like pattern of an open driven optical-lattice system. \textit{PACS}: 05.70.-a, 05.60.-k, 05.70.Ln, 79.70.-q. \textit{PACS}: 05.70.-a, 05.60.-k, 05.70.Ln, 79.70.-q. \textit{PACS}: 05.70.-a, 05.60.-k, 05.70.Ln, 79.70.-q. \textit{PACS}: 05.70.-a, 05.60.-k, 05.70.Ln, 79.70.-q. \textit{PACS}: 05.70.-a, 05.60.-k, 05.70.Ln, 79.70.-q. \textit{PACS}: 0

This study investigates stochastic time-domain and statistical features of non-repetitive optical clocks. We analyze two signal types: optical frequency comb (OFC) traces recorded by non-repetitive photodiodes and the derived optical clock signals. Given that experimental data volume is constrained by storage and transmission limitations, we develop a statistical model for time-domain non-repetitive optical clocks using a nonparametric kernel density estimator (KDE). A key finding is that applying a Gaussian smoothing filter to OFC traces prior to conversion to clock signals yields results comparable to analyzing raw OFC data. Furthermore, we examine statistical properties of these non-repetitive optical clocks. While the time-domain clock signal is modeled as a continuous function, we propose a discrete model grounded in large-sample statistics, utilizing asymptotic theory for the KDE estimator. We derive the asymptotic normality of the sample median estimator based on this discrete model and conduct asymptotic hypothesis testing for the median. Additionally, we develop a hypothesis test for the mean based on OFC data converted to clock signals via an analog-to-digital converter. Finally, we apply these statistical tests to experimental data from a 1038 nm Sr clock. Our results demonstrate that both the discrete model and the conversion of OFC traces (using either an ADC or a Gaussian filter) yield consistent statistical outcomes. These findings provide a foundation for developing new statistics and estimation methods for time-domain non-repetitive optical clocks. Furthermore, the statistical analysis of the Sr clock signal reveals that its temporal behavior adheres to Brownian motion with linearly increasing variance, confirming earlier conclusions drawn from this dataset. Ultimately, this research offers a theoretical basis for evaluating time-domain non-repetitive optical clocks and for establishing their compliance with international standards. \textit{(Keywords: optical frequency standards, optical frequency combs, stochastic processes, statistical analysis, kernel density estimator, median estimator, mean estimator, hypothesis testing)} \textit{(Abbreviated as: Statistical analysis of optical frequency standards. The dynamic nature of network services necessitates the use of Software Defined Networking (SDN) to enhance network management and Quality of Service (QoS). However, ensuring fault tolerance and service continuity within SDN-enabled environments remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to optimize Service Function Chains (SFC) and ensure fault tolerance in SDN networks by integrating Fog Computing with Software-APL (S-APL) technology. The proposed solution employs a two-step methodology: first, it utilizes a multi-objective Fog-based optimization strategy to design and restore SFCs while managing fault mitigation and energy efficiency in real-time; second, it applies a fuzzy logic controller to dynamically adjust link and switch-side QoS mitigation thresholds. Simulation results indicate that this approach effectively balances the restoration of SFCs with energy efficiency, offering a restoration success rate of 95% within 2 seconds following network failures. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the study evaluates the restoration performance of critical emergency services, such as those used by the National Guard, to assess the solution's effectiveness during crises. The overall algorithm demonstrates robust performance, achieving an average restoration time of approximately 2 seconds. Finally, the proposed solution is implemented in SDN testbeds using Fog Computing and NS-3 to validate its practicality. The network architecture is modeled after the National Defense Network, which supports diverse network services. This implementation confirms that the solution is highly effective, robust, and capable of meeting the stringent requirements of next-generation networks. Notably, the solution is lightweight, enabling it to scale efficiently with increasing numbers of network failures and services. The SDN-based Fog solution is deployed on an OpenFlow-enabled controller running OpenFog-Controller-18.04 alongside NS-3.28.1. The results confirm that the proposed approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions. Overall, this study addresses the critical challenges of fault tolerance and QoS in SDN-based networks by leveraging Fog Computing and Software-APL technologies. The solution is implemented using OpenFlow-enabled switches, OpenFog-Controller, NS-3, and Mininet. This work offers a promising approach to achieving fault tolerance and QoS in SDN-based networks through Fog Computing and Software-APL. The network architecture is modeled after the National Defense Network, supporting various network services. The solution is highly effective, robust, and can scale to accommodate an increasing number of network failures and services

Although training neural networks frequently employs cross-entropy (XCE) loss, its effectiveness can be compromised by its non-quadratic nature, which introduces non-constant gradients. While recent research has explored alternative loss functions, our analysis of models trained with these variants reveals intriguing phenomena. To investigate this further, we apply gradient surgery to compare how different losses guide neural network training. Our findings indicate that the stability of a loss function is a critical factor for both smooth and non-smooth variants. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the interplay between the inductive bias of neural networks and the characteristics of the loss function produces complex dynamics, a conclusion supported by our experiments. Ultimately, these insights provide novel perspectives on selecting appropriate loss functions for specific tasks. By utilizing gradient surgery, we efficiently compare the effects of various loss functions and offer a new lens for future research in neural network training. We introduce and analyze various holographic quantum error correction (HQC) codes derived from multi-scale Holographic Entanglement Entropy (HMERA) geometries, which feature power-law relationships between radial depth and boundary coordinates rather than the linear rules found in standard MERA. These new codes exhibit a constant minimal bulk boundary distance and a boundary-entropy scaling of $\min_{y} (x_{1}^{-\alpha} \oplus x_{2}^{-\alpha})$, where $\alpha$ represents the power-law scaling exponent. Furthermore, their entanglement entropy follows a similar scaling law for two boundary regions $A$ and $B$: $\min_{y} (y^{-1} \oplus d_{AB}^{-1})^{\lambda\delta}$. When $\alpha=1$, these codes are approximately equivalent to existing HQC codes constructed from multi-slice AdS bulk geometries under the assumption of Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. Additionally, we demonstrate that the generalization of hyper-invariant states to power-law correlations retains their capacity for universal tensor network state (MPS) simulation. Finally, we outline potential applications of these new HQC codes in simulating interacting driven-dissipative lattice boson and fermion systems. This work paves the way for future research into novel holographic error correction codes and their applications. Specifically, it offers a first step toward modeling complex, non-Markovian boundary dynamics arising from simple maximal AdS bulk geometries. As a preliminary investigation, we focus on AdS$_{3,2}$ with power-law boundary conditions, which can be generalized to higher dimensions. Our findings suggest that the simplicity and sparsity of these codes make them highly suitable for implementation on quantum computers. The Galactic Center hosts a dense network of ionized gas filaments, which are hypothesized to originate from the outflows of massive young stars. This study aims to quantify the spatial clustering of these filaments to better understand their formation mechanisms. We examine the two-point correlation function and mean separation of Galactic Core Filaments (GCFs) within a 1.5-degree region centered on the Galactic Core. Our analysis identifies 1,000 GCFs and classifies them into three groups based on their orientation relative to the Galactic Center (GC): parallel, perpendicular, and oblique. Results indicate that the mean separation between filaments parallel to the Galactic plane is approximately 1.5 parsecs, compared to roughly 2 parsecs for those oriented perpendicularly or obliquely. Additionally, the two-point correlation function reveals that GCFs are not randomly distributed; instead, they exhibit clustering, with the signal peaking at a separation of about 2 parsecs. Furthermore, we observe that the strength of the clustering signal varies by orientation, with parallel filaments producing the strongest effect. These findings suggest that the spatial distribution of GCFs is governed by a process with a characteristic scale of approximately 2 parsecs, likely linked to the initial conditions of massive young stellar outflows. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the utility of statistical methods in characterizing the spatial distribution of Galactic Center structures. This study investigates an integrated primary-secondary distribution network featuring optimal voltage reduction through preservation techniques. It initially establishes a unified optimal power flow (OPF) model that jointly optimizes transmission and distribution systems to minimize total generation costs while ensuring distribution voltage levels remain within acceptable limits. Since large-scale voltage reduction via transformer tap adjustments in traditional networks often compromises distribution factor (DF) margins and overloads secondary lines, the paper introduces optimal latching strategies for transmission distribution factors (TDFs) and voltage regulators to preserve voltage capabilities across the network. Specifically, the work examines a distributed solution framework utilizing alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to achieve optimal voltage management. Within this distributed approach, transmission and distribution utilities operate independently, exchanging only necessary information such as net loads at distribution connection points and Lagrangian multipliers. To validate the proposed framework, a four-unit integrated system was constructed, combining three 100~MW and one 333~MW units, along with corresponding primary and secondary distribution networks. Results demonstrate that the distributed ADMM-based approach achieves approximately a 10% reduction in generation costs compared to a centralized OPF model, achieves optimal transmission and distribution factor margins, prevents primary system overloads during voltage reduction, and significantly cuts communication overhead relative to centralized methods. Furthermore, numerical comparisons of various ADMM configurations reveal that the serial ADMM algorithm offers superior computational performance over parallel ADMM. Finally, a sensitivity analysis of the proposed ADMM algorithm was conducted. \textit{Index Terms}: Alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), distributed optimization, optimal power flow (OPF), optimal voltage management, preservation techniques, preservation transmission distribution factor (TDF), preservation voltage reduction. \textit{Note}: This manuscript was prepared for the \textit{IEEE Access} Special Issue on \textit{Data-Driven Decision Making in Power Systems}. This study demonstrates that in online worst-case scenarios, nonrandom strategies can outperform random ones when arm-dependent delays are present. Specifically, we introduce a specialized approach designed to maximize the frequency of selecting the optimal arm under conditions where successful selections occur only sporadically. This framework encompasses various nonrandom policies, including UCB-type methods, and achieves optimal regret performance relative to the broad class of algorithms utilizing arm-dependent arm-reward estimates. While our analysis relies on assumptions concerning the decay rates of these estimates, we subsequently show that these requirements are reasonably mild. This research extends our earlier work, which addressed random specialists; that study did not necessitate arm-reward estimates but was limited to cases where arms could be sampled independently. Automated conversational agents provide cost-effective and scalable support for patients and callers. However, the speech production systems used in current state-of-the-art dialogue models fail to capture the full range of linguistic features found in human conversation. This limitation stems from two main issues: (1) a lack of statistical methods to measure conversational quality, and (2) training data prepared for nearest-neighbor models rather than generative agents. This paper addresses these gaps by first introducing new metrics for text production system performance. Subsequently, we present LEATHER, an end-to-end structure designed for human-like speech production, validated on a 100M utterance scale. LEATHER achieves a 10% reduction in perceived unnaturalness and a 5% improvement in human preference compared to the prior state-of-the-art, based on evaluation against human responses and the textual actions of dialogue systems. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/EdinburghNLP/LEATHER. This study evaluates the uncertainty quantification capabilities of the chained Gaussian process (CGP) model, utilizing a Gaussian likelihood for low-variance regimes and a Log-Normal likelihood for high-variance regimes. The model's performance was assessed against observational data collected from the 5 MW IEA Wind Task 32 S4C turbine during the Hywind Scotland project. Results indicate that CGP successfully replicates the mean and variance of peak shear forces across various locations on the S4C turbine, including the tower-top, nacelle, and blade-root. Furthermore, statistical surrogates generated via CGP match physical surrogates, which are produced by applying Fourier series to simulated load time series from OpenFAST. The authors conclude that CGP is a highly effective tool for modeling the stochastic characteristics of wind-turbine loads. Additionally, they note that due to its computational efficiency, this method is well-suited for integration with physics-based simulators like OpenFAST. Finally, they suggest that CGP can facilitate the modeling of extreme load distributions under stochastic forcing, a critical area of research for wind-turbine reliability. To support this work, a Python package has been developed and made available on GitHub. This package includes a script for modeling and analyzing offshore load data from OpenFAST simulations, as well as the raw data from Hywind S4C. The package also provides a dataset of pre-processed and annotated load data from the same turbine. These resources are also available on the authors' GitHub. The Python package is named GPP. Social media platforms have emerged as vital sources of real-time information, a capability highlighted during the 2020 Izmir earthquake in Türkiye. This study examines Twitter data from that event to analyze the distribution of information types, user demographics, and the temporal evolution of information volume. The findings reveal a narrow range of information categories disseminated at the time. Although initial data flows originated from the epicenter, they subsequently spread to broader audiences. Furthermore, Twitter users from Izmir contributed significantly to the dissemination process. Given these characteristics, such social network data holds promise for early warning systems in future disasters. To facilitate this application, we provide an open-source code repository. This study examines the $R_\infty$ characteristic of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups $B_{p,q}$ relative to their nilpotent quotients, specifically noting that these groups are not hyperbolic. The primary findings are as follows: (1) When $|p|=|q|=1$, the $R_\infty$ characteristic remains invariant under torsion and varies continuously; (2) When $|p|+|q| \geq 3$, the $R_\infty$ characteristic exhibits periodicity. These findings imply that not all $R_\infty$ invariants for such groups are periodic. Additionally, the paper investigates the index of nilpotency within the nilpotent quotients of these groups. Notably, the paper does not address the case where $|p|=|q|=0$. Furthermore, the appendix provides a method for computing the $R_\infty$ characteristic for the nilpotent quotient $G_N$ of a finitely generated nilpotent group $G$ via an inductive process based on the index of $G$ in its quotient $G_N$. As an application, this formula determines the $R_\infty$ characteristic for all nilpotent groups derived from Heisenberg groups. Finally, the paper concludes by establishing a sufficient condition for a group $G$ to possess a $R_\infty$ invariant that exhibits periodicity. Time-resolved data is extensively utilized in fields like physics, chemistry, and biology to observe how systems evolve over time. However, extracting inversion information from these data is challenging due to noise, model errors, and the ill-posed nature of the inversion process. This study introduces a new, stable algorithm designed to identify time-resolved parameters from time-resolved data. The proposed method is forward-optimization-based (FOBO), which represents inversion as a minimization task within a trajectory framework. By applying the proposed approach to a simplified diffusion problem, it demonstrates that inversion can be resolved even with highly noisy data and significant model errors. The framework is also generalized to handle inversions involving time-dependent parameters, and a hierarchical approach is developed to address inversions with incomplete data. Overall, this work establishes a stable foundation for future research into time-resolved phenomena. Notably, the proposed approach is widely applicable across various disciplines, including physics, chemistry, biology, and engineering. For instance, in biology, it can determine kinetic rate constants from time-resolved binding data; in chemistry, it can extract time-resolved reaction rate constants from time-resolved product concentrations; and regarding photovoltaics, it can identify time-resolved recombination rates from time-resolved photo-currents. Furthermore, the approach is expected to facilitate the investigation of emerging technologies, such as time-resolved photovoltaic materials. The developed approach is implemented in Python and is publicly accessible. This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of the theoretical background, and Section 3 presents numerical examples. This work is based on the research reported in S. Sakai, H. Nakamura, and T. Yamagishi, "Solving time-resolved problems by forward-optimization in a trajectory framework," *arXiv preprint* 2202.03501 (2022). The theoretical approach is detailed in arXiv:2202.03501v1 [math.NA], and the open-source code can be found at https://github.com/ssakai21/TimeResolved. Additionally, we provide methodologies for identifying driving situations using a fixed hierarchy of events and extracting relevant behavioral features. Furthermore, the study validates several driving behavior theories and demonstrates that individual drivers maintain consistent patterns over time. This paper examines the reflected entropy $S_R$ across the ground state and the highest-weight (HW) state within two-dimensional border/conformal field theories, encompassing both unitary and non-unitary conformal field theory (CFT) frameworks. We derive an explicit calculation for the quantum corrected reflected entropy (QCRT), defined as $S_R = 2\pi\alpha_c\frac{c}{3}\frac{\pi}{L} + O(\alpha_c^2)$, where $c$ represents the central charge, $L$ denotes the interval length, and $\alpha_c$ signifies the first-order perturbation parameter. Furthermore, utilizing the free boson CFT model, we demonstrate the duality between reflected entropy and Jamming entropy, expressed as $S_R(A:B) = S_J:\bar{A}:\bar{B}$. Our findings indicate that the duality relation $S_R(A:B) = S_R(AB) - S_R(B)$ holds exclusively in the HW state of non-unitary CFTs, failing in the ground state. Additionally, the triangular inequality $S_R(A:B) \leq \min(S_A, S_B)$ is validated solely when $L_{AB} \leq \frac{L}{2}$, utilizing the explicit expressions for CFT. Finally, the insights regarding triangular inequalities in boundary CFTs may prove valuable for interpreting the holographic entropy triangle. These results extend the applicable scope of the holographic entropy triangle. Notably, the triangular inequality $S_R(A:B) \leq \min(S_A, S_B)$ is applicable exclusively in the Hawking regime, whereas in the AdS regime, the holographic entropy triangle exhibits the dual triangular inequality $S_R(A:B) \leq S_{AB}$. This suggests the existence of a critical point that delineates the transition between the AdS and Hawking regimes. Ultimately, the boundaries of the holographic entropy triangle remain an area for future investigation. Neural networks are extensively utilized for classifying and processing data, including images and quantum states. Although both classification and quantum simulation tasks are effectively addressed by neural networks, quantum data often encounters difficulties during training. This study introduces a U-shaped neural network architecture designed to maintain the unitarity of quantum states. When applied to classification tasks involving quantum data, this structure enhances network trainability and boosts accuracy. Additionally, the paper explores the application of quantum neural networks to NISQ quantum state generation. These findings provide insights into the design of neural network structures tailored for quantum-enhanced machine learning tasks. Specifically, we establish the QNNEC conjecture to illustrate the relationship between entanglement and the trainability of quantum-enhanced neural networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a combined neural network architecture can enhance accuracy and eliminate training gaps in data classification when utilizing quantum-enhanced layers. Finally, we show that the proposed U-shaped quantum neural network architecture can model NISQ quantum state generation tasks with high fidelity. These results are supported by experiments conducted on both simulated quantum systems using PennyLane and real quantum systems via IBM's Qiskit. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi-CCFEW/Quantum-Enhanced-ML. Our accompanying repository, Quantum-Enhanced-ML, offers open-source code for constructing and training quantum-enhanced neural networks on simulated and real quantum systems. Additionally, we have developed an open-source Python package, QEToolkit, to facilitate quantum machine learning. The package includes functions for preparing datasets, training models, and visualizing results. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi-CCFEW/QEToolkit. This paper introduces a code creator that translates a shallow embedding of the C programming language into ACL2 into a formal verification proof within ACL2. Unlike a straightforward translation to a verified C code, this deep embedding enables the generation of proofs during the conversion process. We illustrate the system using a formal model of a CAN bus, which features an ACL2 representation of the bus featuring improved provability characteristics compared to a similar elevator system model. The paper also examines how the proof generation is influenced by various styles of shallow embedding. Our goal is to demonstrate a method for formally verifying C programs using ACL2 that is more practical than direct translation, while also providing a framework for C-style modeling and simulation. This work is part of a broader effort to develop tools for formalizing and verifying embedded systems. We present a formal model of a CAN bus, including a message sender, a bus that transmits messages one at a time in a first-come, first-served manner, and a bus monitor that verifies specific properties of the sender. This model can be utilized to formally verify the system, potentially reducing the effort required to verify other systems with similar properties. Furthermore, we aim to explore the trade-offs between different levels of abstraction when using a deep embedding. We begin by outlining the syntax and semantics of our C-like language within ACL2, followed by a translation function that generates a checker for the CAN bus model. Next, we propose a framework for reasoning about the correctness of the translation and present a proof of correctness for the bus monitor model. Finally, we discuss the advantages and limitations of this approach. Although 2-factor authentication (2FA) is a widely adopted and generally accepted security measure, user studies reveal that people often lack a clear understanding of how these systems function and what goals they support. This paper presents an exploratory study on users' knowledge regarding Signal PINs, an essential component of the Signal application. Our findings indicate that users possess limited knowledge of Signal PINs, including their purpose, potential risks, and best practices for usage. These insights were gathered through in-depth interviews with 18 Signal users, which revealed a range of perspectives, from those with well-developed knowledge to others with minimal understanding. We also identified distinct user personas based on their knowledge levels and perceived risks. To address these issues, we developed personas, a design map, and 20 recommendations for improving Signal PIN knowledge and security practices. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our research for the study and design of 2FA knowledge and security behaviors. We anticipate that this work will assist researchers and designers in better comprehending user interactions with 2FA and inform the future development of 2FA knowledge and usability. Additionally, the proposed recommendations for enhancing Signal PIN knowledge and security can inform the design of 2FA systems. Our work is grounded in the theory that 2FA security and knowledge are mutually dependent: enhanced 2FA knowledge improves security, and conversely, improved 2FA security practices foster the development of user knowledge. This theory is supported by the identified user personas and the 20 recommendations presented in this paper. Finally, the design map illustrates the complex interplay between 2FA knowledge and security, offering guidance for researchers and designers to effectively understand and address 2FA knowledge challenges. We also demonstrate how this design map can guide the design of 2FA knowledge interventions. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for the design of 2FA knowledge interventions. Finally, the paper concludes with a summary of our key findings. Specifically, the study reveals that Signal PIN knowledge is lacking among users, and the user personas identified highlight the need for improved 2FA knowledge and security practices. Furthermore, the 20 recommendations provided can inform the design of 2FA knowledge interventions. Additionally, the design map offers a framework for researchers and designers to better comprehend 2FA knowledge and its associated challenges. The paper also explores the potential for 2FA knowledge interventions to influence user behavior, with a focus on how these interventions can be evaluated and measured. Finally, the work underscores the importance of 2FA knowledge and security practices

Precise solar energy integration is vital for modeling the evolution of the Sun and stars. This study evaluates the accuracy of various quadrature schemes, such as Gauss-Legendre and Gauss-Laguerre methods, alongside adaptive schemes tailored for stellar evolution. We introduce solar-energy-precision quadratures (SEP) that significantly enhance convergence and reduce model runtime by an order of magnitude compared to current implementations. These results are demonstrated using both simple test problems and the 15 Myr solar model. The developed SEP quadratures are readily applicable to stellar evolution models, including those utilizing MESA. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/evgeny-mikhailov/sepq. The primary objective of this study is to introduce the ViViT architecture, which leverages the diminished structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton (gGN) matrix to compute curvature. This capability is integrated into a Transformer-based model, enabling end-to-access modeling of curvature. Our approach demonstrates that the efficiency of curvature access scales linearly with the number of layers, utilizing only forward-pass operations. Furthermore, we empirically validate the efficiency and efficacy of ViViT through access-to-training experiments on two tasks: access-to-adaptation for pre-trained ResNet on CIFAR10 and access-to-projection for pre-trained ViT on ImageNet. We also present access-to-ablation experiments, which evaluate the ViViT architecture alongside variations such as curvature-to-training, adaptive gGN, and standard PGD. The results indicate that ViViT outperforms all other methods, achieving an accuracy gain of +1.5% compared to PGD. Additionally, ViViT surpasses all other curvature-based methods in both efficiency and effectiveness. Finally, we demonstrate that ViViT can access curvature for vision transformers without requiring modifications to the transformer architecture. Our code is available at https://github.com/DeepMind/ViViT.

Grammatical gender influences how nouns are mentally represented, often leading to the attribution of gender-stereotyped characteristics to inanimate objects. This study investigates whether such gender-based inferences apply to languages lacking gender marking, specifically Hebrew under translation. We developed the first Hebrew dataset consisting of 420 word pairs, where natively gendered inanimate words were translated alongside gender-neutral counterparts. Using a two-step analysis with word2vec and MIMIC-MNLI, we determined that Hebrew speakers associate gendered attributes with both Hebrew and English words, despite English not grammatically requiring gender assignment. Furthermore, models trained on Hebrew demonstrate the ability to predict gendered inanimate words more accurately than their neutral counterparts, a capability absent in the English-trained model. These findings indicate that gender effects persist even in non-gendered languages through translation, potentially resulting in unintended gender biases in multilingual language models trained on such corpora. Consequently, this research underscores the necessity of developing gender-balanced vocabularies and datasets to mitigate these biases across all languages. Finally, we examine the implications of grammatical gender for cross-lingual transfer learning and its impact on gender bias across various languages. Our contributions include a novel, gender-balanced Hebrew dataset and a comprehensive set of experiments exploring gender dynamics across different languages. The code and data are available at: https://github.com/eyalsha/eyalsha_genderv1.0. We establish the charmability of all lattices within simple Lie groups of real rank two, with the exception of arithmetic lattices in $SL(n,\mathbb{R})$ where $n\geq 3$. Leveraging this finding, we demonstrate the rigidity of these same lattices by applying Mostow's criterion. Additionally, we investigate charmability through the lens of finite amenability. Our primary application focuses on mostowing the gap between two- and three-dimensional lattices. Furthermore, we apply these results to advancing the proof of the Tate Conjecture for all varieties defined over finite fields. We also provide applications regarding the Grothendieck conjecture and the Riemann Hypothesis for varieties, specifically excluding abelian varieties, that possess a large number of points over extensions of the base field $\mathbb{F}_q$. Finally, we address several open questions concerning amenability and charmability. The terminology "charmability" was suggested by J. S. Sandeep. In this work, we utilize the concept of finite amenability, which is closely linked to charmability. To our knowledge, this is the first instance where amenability is applied to prove rigidity for arithmetic lattices. Our approach combines amenability with Mostow's criterion to derive this result. We believe this methodology holds significant potential for extending proofs of other rigidity results for arithmetic lattices in higher dimensions. We propose that this technique could serve as a foundation for achieving rigidity results in all dimensions. We have successfully applied these findings to progress toward verifying the Tate Conjecture for all varieties over finite fields. We also explore applications advancing the proof of the Grothendieck conjecture for varieties, with the exception of abelian varieties, that feature a substantial number of points over the base field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and its extensions. The term "charmability" was suggested by J. S. Sandeep. This paper establishes the finite amenability of all lattices in simple Lie groups of real rank two, excluding those in $SL(n,\mathbb{R})$ where $n\geq 3$. We apply this result to investigate finite amenability, a concept closely related to charmability. This approach may represent the first application of amenability to demonstrate rigidity for arithmetic lattices. We intend to extend these findings to prove charmability for all dimensions. Furthermore, we utilize this result to provide a partial proof of the Tate Conjecture for varieties over finite fields.

Monocular object pose estimation is a difficult task that is further complicated by the lack of a class-specific point cloud in few-shot and zero-shot scenarios. This study tackles the most challenging of these situations: class-level object pose estimation with zero-shot capabilities. Our method leverages recent advancements in object detection and shape retrieval to establish a new framework for this problem. Specifically, we introduce a novel shape retrieval technique that effectively addresses class-specific pose estimation. Additionally, we demonstrate that current object pose regression networks can be directly adapted to handle zero-shot class-level tasks with minimal modifications. Finally, we show that our approach yields state-of-the-art results on the 2D COCO and COTR datasets and successfully applies to zero-shot class-level pose estimation on both COCO and CUB benchmarks. To facilitate future research, we have released the Zero-shot CUB dataset. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/ashishgupta1999/Zero-Shot-COOP. Accurate short-term traffic forecasting is essential for traffic management, planning, and control systems. However, current deep learning-based approaches struggle to simultaneously achieve high prediction accuracy and low computational complexity when handling the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of traffic data. This paper introduces a novel RNN-based framework that addresses these challenges by utilizing city-wide OD matrices as input. By leveraging a city's extensive traffic data, the method captures the complex dynamics of OD flow through similarity-based feature extraction, while employing Recurrent Neural Networks to manage computational costs. This approach enables prediction across multiple dimensions and locations without requiring an increase in network complexity. Experimental results on real-world data from Shanghai demonstrate the method's effectiveness in predicting travel demand, OD matrices, and peak periods, achieving superior accuracy and complexity metrics compared to existing techniques. The proposed framework is expected to significantly impact traffic prediction, management, planning, and control systems. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhengyafang1992/Similarity-driven-Feature-Extraction.

We introduce VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for robust inference in both continuous and discrete domains. By utilizing an expressive latent space, VACA effectively models the joint distribution of observed variables, delivering reliable predictions. Unlike standard autoencoders that only capture the marginal distribution, VACA is specifically engineered to handle inter-variable dependencies, demonstrating a significant advantage when answering contrafactual questions. Additionally, VACA is well-suited for diagnostic tasks where missing data must be imputed through an intervention. We validate VACA's superiority across continuous, discrete, and mixed data types through comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, our source code and a Python-based high-level library are publicly available to facilitate the deployment of VACA in practical applications. This work marks the first integration of variational autoencoders for inference in both continuous and discrete settings, as well as for addressing diagnostic and contrafactual queries. Real-time analysis of the sky has emerged as a promising field within radio astronomy, driven by advancements in hardware, computational power, and real-time data processing techniques. The Irish LOFAR station, equipped with 168 antennas, is among the most promising sites for developing a real-time data pipeline, which is now a core component of the REAL-time Transient Identification and LOFAR Array (REALTA) system. This system is designed to identify and catalog radio transients, detect geophysical phenomena, and monitor the solar environment.

A primary motivation for this system is to facilitate low-latency follow-up observations of radio transients, thereby contributing to a broader multi-messenger approach. This involves the real-time detection, identification, and reporting of radio sources and transients to facilitate immediate observations by other facilities.

The Irish station's data pipeline is also integral to Geophysical Real-time Monitoring (GREALTA), a system that tracks geophysical events such as sferics, ELF Schumann resonances, and ionospheric scintillation. The Irish station is uniquely positioned to monitor ELF VLF signals from the US Navy's Low Frequency Active (LFA) system, which comprises 50 HF transmitters located in the North Atlantic.

This paper presents initial findings from the REALTA system data pipeline at the Irish LOFAR station, including a summary of system performance and performance metrics. It also details the real-time source detection and identification processes, as well as the current status of the cataloging system. Finally, the paper provides an overview of the ongoing REALTA system and its future development. While prior research on box office earnings has predominantly focused on non-financial release characteristics, our study uniquely examines how pre-release attributes influence total revenue. Specifically, we analyze the impact of release type, genre, critical scores, star power, and trailer engagement on final gross earnings. Drawing from the IMDb dataset, we constructed a novel, expansive film dataset comprising 11,040 movies spanning 1955 to 2016, featuring curated financial metrics and pre-release traits. Utilizing this data, we employed multiple linear regression to quantify the effects of various release characteristics on revenue, categorizing outcomes by specific release types and genres. Furthermore, we conducted an exploratory data analysis to identify correlations between release traits and earnings, offering insights into the factors that drive a film's box office success. Our findings indicate that release type, genre, and critical reception are the most significant drivers of revenue, followed by star power and trailer performance. These insights aim to assist distributors in making more informed release decisions. The associated code and dataset can be accessed at: https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/BoxOfficeEarnings. This study introduces and analyzes a frequency-regulation strategy for smart microgrids (MGs) to stabilize their voltage responses. Smart MGs are anticipated to serve as testbeds for next-generation power systems, which will integrate electric vehicles and renewable energy sources that may destabilize conventional grids. The proposed frequency regulation technique employs a new frequency adaptation law within the steady-state frequency adaptation law of the adaptive droop control (ADA-DC) method. Droop control is a widely used decentralized secondary control technique for both synchronous generator-based power systems and inverter-interfaced smart microgrits. The newly suggested frequency adaptation law is designed to maintain a specific frequency value during specified time intervals. The study demonstrates that incorporating this frequency adaptation law into the ADA-DC method results in a closed-loop system capable of achieving finite-time frequency and power sharing regulation, even during transient conditions. Furthermore, voltage behavior is significantly improved, exhibiting reduced oscillations. The approach is validated through simulations of a three-MG test system. These results demonstrate that the proposed method offers an additional degree of freedom for controlling steady-state voltage amplitude and phase, providing an extra tool to minimize oscillations and further enhance the overall voltage response. Additionally, the analysis confirms the robustness of the solution against external disturbances. To achieve these outcomes, the paper introduces new finite-time frequency and power sharing regulation stability results. These findings rely on a novel frequency adaptation law that ensures the frequency error between two interacting MGs decays to zero within a finite time interval, even if this interval is unbounded. Consequently, power sharing regulation stability is maintained for an infinite time span. The complete solution is applicable to interconnected multi-MG systems, provided that the number of MGs and electric vehicles within each island do not exceed specific upper bounds. Notably, these results are derived using only algebraic and calculus tools, avoiding the need for more complex techniques such as Lyapunov functions or comparison theorems. This analytical approach facilitates a more straightforward and comprehensive understanding of finite-time frequency and power sharing regulation stability. Finally, the analysis is robust against external disturbances, as evidenced by numerical simulations. To address these challenges, our cyber-physical intelligence initiative aims to harness cross-domain insights to bolster security and sustain critical operations. This paper outlines the cyber-physical networks framework and its associated intelligence components. Specifically, we present a unified cyber-physical network operating system that manages and coordinates activities across multiple networks, alongside a cyber-physical intelligence infrastructure that leverages multi-network data to enhance security through intelligent, proactive, and predictive methods. Furthermore, we have developed a series of applications that combine intelligence with adaptability to effectively resolve complex issues in cyber-physical networks. Finally, this article provides an in-depth review of our work, with a primary emphasis on the cyber-physical intelligence infrastructure and its practical applications. The proposed solutions offer a pathway to further advancements in cyber-physical intelligence, including deeper integration of AI and machine learning, as well as greater autonomy. Additionally, we identify current limitations and potential future directions for cyber-physical intelligence, including the need for more robust security mechanisms and improved human-machine collaboration. We believe that addressing these gaps will significantly contribute to the future evolution of cyber-physical intelligence. Additionally, we explore how emerging technologies such as 5G, the Internet of Things, and blockchain can aid in managing and securing cyber-physical networks. Ultimately, we argue that achieving a truly intelligent and resilient cyber-physical network ecosystem requires a holistic, cross-domain perspective. The MAPPIES framework utilizes a comprehensive set of polarization-dependent cross-sections to model interactions between ultra-relativistic electrons and various photon fields, such as external-Compton scattering (ECS) and inverse Compton scattering (ICS). We apply this framework to explore the potential of polarized ECS in explaining the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess observed in blazar spectra. To achieve this, we developed a polarization-aware version of the synchrotron self-Compton (p)SASCA model, which demonstrates that polarized photons generated via (p)SASCA can significantly contribute to the UV/soft X-ray surplus. Furthermore, our Monte-Carlo simulations reveal that the MAPPIES framework remains robust against relativistic beaming effects, even when scattering occurs in the blazar's jet rest frame. Our findings indicate that total intensity simulations are insufficient to distinguish between the (p)SASCA and external-Compton Scattering (p)ECS models. Consequently, we conclude that current polarization data cannot definitively identify the origin of the UV/soft X-ray excess in blazars. Future observations with enhanced sensitivity to both intensity and polarization will be essential to resolve this question. Ultimately, our results suggest that ECS may not be the primary source of the UV/soft X-ray surplus in blazar spectra. However, we also demonstrate the existence of solutions where both electron and radiation distributions yield similar results, highlighting the need for further investigation. These insights will inform future observational strategies aimed at uncovering the source of this UV/soft X-ray excess. Additionally, we provide a user-friendly, polarization-aware version of the SYNCH code for the community. This code is based on the previously published intensity-only version but now includes a polarization-aware radiation field, making it a valuable tool for investigating the polarization-dependent external-Compton Scattering mechanism. Our findings suggest that polarization data could help constrain the origin of the UV/soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra. We have also established a link between our Monte-Carlo implementation and the analytical SYNCH code, enabling the creation of a polarization-aware version of SYNCH for the community. This work serves as a proof of concept for the usefulness of MAPPIES in studying the polarization-dependent external-Compton Scattering mechanism.
