We present a method for analytically extending the Laplace transformed density on complex surfaces, such as the Schwarzschild and Kerr metrics, to the negative half-plane. This approach relies on the duality between surface operators and the boundary of the complex time half-plane. By applying this technique to complex surfaces, we extend the Laplace transformed density through negative complex values of s. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this procedure facilitates the large s asymptotic expansion of the original density, revealing the origin of the Le Roy-Sinai theorem as the boundary case of Stirling's asymptotic formula. This insight provides new insights into the limitations of the Le Roy-Sinai theorem, specifically when applied to surfaces with complex geometry. Finally, in an accompanying work, we show how the analytic continuation of the density can be utilized in the inverse problem on complex surfaces, where the density is defined on spatial and temporal boundaries. Specifically, for the Kerr metric, we derive an extension of the Belinsky-Zakharov formula for the mass. By utilizing the large s asymptotic behavior of the density, we successfully reconstruct the mass from the Laplace transformed density. This result stems from the observation that the real part of s dominates the large s asymptotic expansion of the density on complex surfaces, thereby obscuring the imaginary component of s. Consequently, the mass cannot be recovered from the full density in this context. Furthermore, our findings regarding the large s asymptotic expansion of the density on complex surfaces may have broader implications for the inverse problem on complex surfaces. In the future, we aim to explore the properties of the surface operator linked to the analytic extension of the density. Additionally, we plan to extend the surface operator method developed for the Minkowski metric to the de Sitter metric. Finally, we will investigate the implications of the surface operator on the Hilbert space of the density. Specifically, we will examine the implications of surface operators on the commutation relations of the surface fields and the associated action. These developments may have significant consequences for the study of complex surfaces. Finally, we will explore the relationship between the analytic extension of the density and the analytic extension of the field itself. In this regard, the Keldysh extension of the field to the complex time plane appears to be more natural than the Minkowski extension. This observation may have important implications for the study of complex surfaces. In summary, our method offers novel insights into the study of complex surfaces. Our findings may have significant consequences for the field. Our work paves the way for further research

A central challenge in the digital expansion of quantum gates and circuits involves identifying symmetric purer states within infinite-qubit spaces. We introduce an efficient digital algorithm to recognize symmetric purer states with $n$ qubits by determining their associated Schur vectors, specifically focusing on two-qubit gates circuits. Our approach leverages the properties of these vector coefficients to assess the entanglement between the two qubits in digital spaces. To validate the method's effectiveness, we examine typical two-qubit gates circuits derived from CNOT, CNOT+, CW, and CW+ gates, computing their corresponding Schur vectors to assess the degrees of nonlocality and entanglement. Furthermore, we establish the first link between the coefficients of the Schur vector polynomial and these entanglement metrics. Finally, we demonstrate the application of this technique in designing optimal unitary matrices for digital quantum identification. Numerical results confirm the algorithm's efficiency and scalability across different sizes of digital quantum spaces. Additionally, we provide open-source software to facilitate the implementation of our proposal for symmetric purer states using the Qiskit framework. Baryon generation through the quantized fragmentation of a helical QCD filament is investigated using a force-algebra model. This process conserves the baryon number associated with the filament's tension, with quantized fermions (baryons) generated via force algebra. The analysis examines how various filament geometries—specifically pitch, radius, and axial twist—impact baryon production, finding that larger pitches enhance generation while larger radii suppress it. Furthermore, it is noted that while quantization can be approximated as occurring within a local flat spacetime, helical filaments with tight radii produce a significantly higher count of baryons compared to those松er radii. These findings offer a potential explanation for the observed suppression of $\bar{p}/\pi$ in heavy-ion collisions, where the $\bar{p}/\pi$ ratio at midrapidity decreases as collision centrality increases. Additionally, the study demonstrates that chiral symmetry restoration, indicated by the vanishing of the baryon mass, aligns with the asymptotic twist behavior of helical filaments. Finally, the potential for quantum gravity effects to induce helical deformation in straight filaments is discussed. A corresponding video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1111111111. Solar oscillations are driven by the turbulent convection occurring at the Sun's surface. By utilizing acoustic waves, convection exerts a significant influence on solar acoustic travel times, generating both global and local convection patterns. This convection-induced noise complicates the detection of solar internal dynamics. While the impact of surface convection on travel times has been extensively studied, research on convection situated deep within the solar interior remains limited. This study examines noise from convection adjacent to active regions using helioseismic travel-time data. We analyze power spectra derived from temporal shifts in local convection patterns surrounding active regions and correlate these findings with active region lifetimes. Our results indicate that deep convection noise is not merely a scaled version of surface noise. Furthermore, we observe a strong correlation between noise levels and active region lifetimes, suggesting that the accumulation of magnetic flux within the active region is partially responsible for the generation of this noise. Consequently, this mechanism must be accounted for when searching for travel-time variations linked to solar internal motions. Finally, we compare our findings with the data reported by Pijpers et al. (2010). Although the overall trends align, certain discrepancies exist, which we discuss in detail. Overall, this work highlights the necessity of studying noise arising from magnetic flux to better understand solar internal dynamics. Future research should focus on the relationship between surface magnetic flux and internal motions to further refine this understanding. This study serves as a foundation for the work presented in Liu et al. (2021). The remaining differences between the two papers stem from the distinct publication timelines of our respective works. We investigate the impact of ripples in a primordial electromagnetic field on pulsar time-of-arrival measurements within the Pulsar Timing Network, specifically within the 10–1000 Hz frequency band. Our analysis reveals that these effects can be mistaken for gravitational wave signals if causal electromagnetic features—such as those generated by phase transitions in the early universe—fall within this band. Furthermore, we demonstrate that measurements from a binary pulsar system can be utilized to break this degeneracy. This methodology offers a valuable constraint on models featuring causal ripples in the early universe and establishes a novel channel for probing phase transitions at energy scales of several TeV. Additionally, we calculate the sensitivity to stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds in this band and compare it with the projected sensitivity of the Cosmic Explorer observatory. Finally, we explore strategies for extracting individual waveforms from well-modeled binary pulsar systems. These findings underscore the significant scientific potential of the Pulsar Timing Network in the sub-1000 Hz regime, a range not expected to be covered by future space-based laser interferometers like LISA. We conclude that enhancing the network's sensitivity in this band should be a priority for future research. A detailed investigation of such signals will be addressed in an upcoming publication. Cross-lingual representation learning (CLR) serves as a critical component of vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR). However, current state-of-the-art CLIR systems often exhibit performance disparities across languages within the same family. This study investigates the underlying reasons for such disparities by analyzing the interaction between specific CLR properties and language characteristics. To achieve this, we developed a novel interactive framework designed to facilitate deeper insights into representation properties. Using this framework, we demonstrate the performance impact of distinct properties learned via interactive and non-interactive methods, as well as the performance consistency variations across different languages. Our findings indicate that interactive CLR yields superior performance, particularly in non-majority languages within language families. Furthermore, we propose a multi-granularity interactive CLR framework to further enhance performance, followed by an in-depth analysis of vector space quality. As technological advancements enable greater control over physical systems, betting markets are emerging as effective tools for characterizing and exploiting the unique properties of quantum states of light. These markets facilitate the assignment of physical significance to probabilities through a normalization condition linked to betting strategies. Traditionally, protocols for identifying coherence and non-classical states rely on discrete choices and wagering on individual photon numbers. This study demonstrates that continuous choices, combined with the ability to place bets on future photon number distributions (including higher moments) rather than immediate outcomes, allow betting to uniquely identify specific quantum states. Furthermore, we illustrate applications of this methodology to continuous-variable states by explicitly deriving the states that maximize the success probability for arbitrage-free supermartingales. Consequently, this enhanced framework enables the detection of squeezing and enables new quantum state designs via tomographic betting. Ultimately, this approach offers a novel method for the design, characterization, and simulation of continuous variable states using uniquely quantum resources. Ultimately, this framework demonstrates that betting on quantum rewards serves as an effective continuous variable tool for both coherence and non-classicality. MoO$_3$-inspired monolayer and bulk two-dimensional materials have recently attracted significant research interest. However, the impact of monolayer-to-bulk phase transitions on exciton properties remains poorly understood. By employing first-principles calculations, we examined the monolayer-to-bulk transition across ten MA$_2$Z$_4$ (M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; Z = N, P, As) materials. Our analysis of quasiparticle band arrangements and optical absorption spectra revealed that monolayer-to-bulk transitions in these MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds induce distinct exciton spectral shifts, with bulk exciton energies consistently lower than their monolayer counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these exciton spectral shifts are independent of stacking configurations, as both the monolayer band arrangement and band gap remain invariant to stacking. These findings offer a systematic approach to understanding exciton spectral shifts in MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials and provide a potential pathway for designing tunable excitonic devices. Additionally, the calculated optical absorption spectra for MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials show strong agreement with recent experimental results. Finally, we propose that the bulk exciton energy can be effectively tuned by adjusting the atomic radius of the group IV element (A). These conclusions are expected to facilitate the design of excitonic devices that exhibit stacking-independent optical spectral shifts. Furthermore, our results suggest that bulk exciton spectral shifts in MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials can be modulated by altering the atomic radius of the group VI element (M), offering a promising avenue for developing tunable excitonic devices. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic study on stacking-independent excitons in MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials. The methodologies and conclusions presented herein may prove beneficial for future excitonic device designs. The corresponding source code is available at: https://github.com/zhengxianyi/Quasiparticle-band-arrangement-and-stacking-independent-exciton-in-MA2Z4-M--.

This study examines the rare flavor-changing neutral current (FCNC) process $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ using LHCb data. We provide a detailed analysis of the experimental results, incorporating both shape and branching ratio constraints, and compare our findings with theoretical predictions. Our findings indicate that the measured upper limit on the branching ratio for this reaction is $1.22^{+0.28}_{-0.25} \times 10^{-9}$, which falls within the expected range of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-8}$ derived from both Standard Model and various New Physics scenarios. Furthermore, the observed data excludes contributions from intermediate states such as $\gamma^*$, $Z$, and $\phi$. These outcomes suggest that the LHCb experiment has successfully probed new regions of phase space for this reaction, marking a significant milestone in hyperon physics. These results offer valuable insights for future studies of similar rare reactions, including $p \to n \mu^+ \mu^-$, $p \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, $\Lambda_b^0 \to \pi^0 \mu^+ \mu^-$, and $\Lambda_b^0 \to \eta \mu^+ \mu^-$, at the LHCb facility. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the LHCb detector is capable of investigating similar channels involving other intermediate vector mesons, such as $\rho^0$ and $J/\psi$. The findings of this work are crucial for advancing hypernuclear physics and its associated theories. This represents the first experimental investigation of $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, and the LHCb results are anticipated to provide significant insights into the underlying physics governing this reaction. Our study confirms that LHCb is well-equipped to investigate such rare reactions, thereby opening a new era in hypernuclear physics. The data obtained from $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ will be instrumental in understanding the fundamental interactions between quarks and leptons, as well as their interplay with hadrons. This is expected to yield new insights into the structure of the $\Sigma^+$ baryon, the weak interaction, and the mechanisms driving flavor changing neutral currents. Our work also highlights the potential of LHCb to explore similar rare reactions in the future, which could lead to a deeper understanding of the fundamental forces of nature

We present findings from a study examining disk formation during the gravitational collapse of a pre-stellar core, utilizing a hybrid code that integrates smoothed particle hydrodynamics with the radiation transfer method RMT-1D. Our model simulates the collapse of a $0.01\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$ core with an initial temperature of $10\,\mathrm{K}$ and density of $10^{4}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, where the RMT-1D module calculates radiative transfer in local thermodynamic equilibrium. Our results indicate that the protostar develops a substantial boundary layer, while the surrounding disk remains cool and thin. Furthermore, the core's temperature profile exhibits a gradient, rising from the boundary layer outward to a peak at the base of the boundary layer before declining again. Additionally, the boundary layer is observed to be optically thick. These characteristics are consistent with expectations for a well-established disk, suggesting that the boundary layer and the overall structure are established early in the collapse process. This implies that the conditions necessary for creating a well-developed disk are met, thereby eliminating the need for alternative mechanisms like magnetic braking saturation to form disks. Finally, the model successfully reproduces the temperature profile of Class 0 sources reported by Meeus et al. (2013). Overall, our model indicates that a simple, non-turbulent collapse is sufficient to generate a well-established disk. Consequently, the primary focus of disk formation research should shift toward understanding the physical processes within these initially cool and thin disks. This also underscores the necessity of including accurate, non-equilibrium chemistry in theoretical models of pre-main sequence stars. We conclude that the current trend in observational research to target young stellar objects with lower masses and lower ages is well-founded. Ultimately, we propose that the most effective strategy for studying pre-main sequence stars is to analyze the lowest mass and youngest objects available. This approach is supported by the fact that our model produces a cool, thin disk, a condition that should be reflected in the physical properties of the youngest and lightest pre-main sequence stars. This conclusion is further reinforced by the fact that our model accurately reproduces the temperature profiles of Class 0 sources identified by Meeus et al. (2013). These observations suggest that the boundary layer forms at a greater distance from the protostar than previously thought, which should be accounted for when interpreting observational data. Atmospheric models serve as essential instruments for analyzing and interpreting observations of solar system objects. This study presents a methodology for characterizing these models and quantifying their inherent uncertainties. We examine a suite of atmospheric models, each defined by a specific set of temperature and gravity parameters, to interpolate between them and assess result reliability. Through at-sphere observations, we determine physical properties for three comet nuclei: 1P/Halley, 2P/Encke, and 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, utilizing data collected by the Rosetta mission's VIRTIS instrument. The processed datasets were subsequently fit using the ATmospheric PHysical Simulation (ATPS) model. To evaluate uncertainties, we identified optimal models for each temperature-gravity combination and mapped the discrepancies between these optimal models. The analysis indicates that uncertainties in brightness temperature are minimal, typically under 1 K, whereas uncertainties in gravity are more significant, ranging from 0.1 to 0.2 cm s$^{-2}$. These derived parameters align with prior findings, and the study confirms the robustness of the atmospheric models. All derived parameters, alongside a comprehensive quantification of model differences, are accessible via ATARC (https://atarc.lesia.ens.fr/). This framework facilitates the interpretation of new observations and supports future enhancements to the ATPS and ATPS-SC models. We introduce a multi-period temporal series modeling framework designed to handle multiple related time periods under uncertain conditions. This approach utilizes a Bayesian network to capture temporal dependencies, incorporates prior knowledge regarding uncertainty, and employs a variational Bayesian method for efficient parameter estimation. A primary advantage of this methodology is its ability to automatically generate a simplified model from an initially complex one by enforcing sparsity within the conditional probability distribution representation. The proposed methodology is demonstrated using two case studies: one involving a single building and another involving a community of buildings. These cases illustrate how the learned models can detect anomalies and provide counterfactual explanations. Additionally, the Bayesian uncertainty quantification within these models supports decision-making processes for anomaly detection and regression tasks. The computational efficiency of the approach is achieved through the integration of variational inference with tensor operations. Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate the methodology's effectiveness and scalability. Furthermore, the implementation is made available to the research community as an open-source software package. We propose interpreting the categories of ultrafilter and zero-set structures, along with their dualities for Boolean algebraic structures, as a form of "Pontryagin duality" applicable to a broad range of "steastful" functions defined on sets. This perspective not only clarifies certain aspects of the "nastly function" debate but also highlights the significance of the sigma-field Pontryagin duality theorem. Specifically, this duality plays a crucial role in establishing the equivalence between two fundamental theorems regarding ultrafilters in stochastic logic, which are often referred to as "two versions of the zero-one law." Furthermore, we suggest that the ultrafilter structure within stochastic logic may hold value for legalists, as it could serve as a foundation for constructing a probabilistic legal system. This potential application stems from the fact that ultrafilters can be conceptualized as a type of probabilistic measure that adheres to the axioms of a probability function while maintaining a steadfast connection to the underlying sample space. Our work represents a step toward developing a theory of probabilistic measure that is steadfast relative to the sample space, which we term "ultralegal measures." We demonstrate that ultrafilter structures can be reformulated using ultralegal measures, alongside a related category of steadfast logic, to provide an alternative perspective on stochastic logic. Additionally, we propose a probabilistic measure that is steadfast relative to a specific $\sigma$-subalgebra of the power set, which we call the "legal subalgebra." This concept is inspired by the principle that legalists should remain steadfast relative to a particular legal framework. We illustrate the value of ultralegal measures by demonstrating their application in proving various results within stochastic logic. Finally, we outline several open problems concerning ultrafilter structures, ultralegal measures, and the ultralegal version of stochastic logic. These topics may hold significance for legalists, as they offer a novel approach to probabilistic measures that maintains a steadfast relationship with the sample space and/or the legal subalgebra. This stands in contrast to the traditional ultra-nasty approach, which treats the sample space and legal subalgebra as merely incidental to the broader, more flexible and adaptable general measure. In essence, this represents a theory of probabilistic measure that is steadfast relative to either the sample space, the legal subalgebra, or both. The efficacy of federated learning (FL) relies on the convergence of the global model derived from aggregated updates. However, data heterogeneity in distributed environments often results in biased updates, causing the global model to favor certain users and undermining privacy. While differential privacy (DP) has emerged as a robust method for safeguarding user data, it simultaneously degrades model performance. This study investigates the impact of DP on FL fairness and privacy, evaluating various noise injection strategies to identify the optimal approach. Our findings indicate that the exponential mechanism is the most effective for fair federated learning, and that DP noise can be amplified without compromising model accuracy. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive examination of the trade-offs between fairness and privacy, establishing a clear optimal point for balancing these objectives. Finally, we provide an empirical analysis of how FL fair-privacy is influenced by hyper-parameters, with a specific focus on the optimal batch size. Experimental results across multiple datasets and learning tasks confirm the efficacy of our proposed methods. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed scheme significantly outperforms comparison schemes in terms of total throughput and average recharge rate. The half-lives of $^{184}$Hg and $^{185}$Hg were determined to be 1.7(1) s and 10.8(1) s, respectively, with a maximum beta-decay energy ($E_{\beta,max}$) of 1.9(1) MeV assigned to $^{187}$Hg. We interweave dark energy generation and neutrino leptogenesis through a common mechanism: the spontaneous breaking of lepton number symmetry. This process triggers an exponential mass enhancement for one leptonic neutrino mass eigenstate, thereby halting its decay and leaving behind a net baryon asymmetry in the chemical potential of the enhanced neutrino. The mass of the particle responsible for self-interaction within the lepton number sector is the sole free parameter governing leptogenesis, leptonic symmetry breaking, and subsequent dark energy evolution. We demonstrate that this mechanism successfully accounts for leptogenesis across a straightforward and physically motivated range of particle spectra. Additionally, we outline a physically reasonable parameter space where the mechanism aligns with observational data, including the baryon asymmetry of the universe, supernova redshifts, and supernova data concerning dark energy. In this scenario, the particle responsible for leptogenesis also serves as a dark energy candidate, with its self-interaction cross-section surpassing the unitarity limit. We argue that the validity of this condition can be rigorously tested through future observations of dark energy. Finally, we propose that the mechanism driving leptogenesis and dark energy is also applicable to quark baryogenesis. Furthermore, we examine the physical implications of a shared framework for leptonic and baryonic symmetry breaking, as well as the physics of the dark energy sector. A comprehensive list of references is provided. We are particularly grateful to A. Khoukaz for his insightful comments regarding chiral symmetry breaking and unitarity. We introduce a new data-driven control framework designed for systems with diverse dynamics, aiming to reduce data requirements while leveraging unrelated side information. This approach utilizes a single full-state trajectory from the target system to approximate its cost-to-go function, employing its partial Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) solution as prior knowledge. Specifically, we propose applying cross-approximation techniques to resolve the HJB equations of the source system using those of the target system, thereby inferring the target's cost-to-go. Unlike model-based control methods that necessitate accurate dynamic models, our strategy relies solely on extensive data collection, making it ideal for scenarios where detailed dynamics are unavailable or prohibitively expensive to derive. Furthermore, the framework demonstrates superior control transferability across systems with significantly different dynamics, enabling diverse agents to share control knowledge. We validate this method numerically on established robotic locomotion benchmarks and a multi-UAV trajectory tracking task, comparing it against model-based control, reinforcement learning, and the standard LQR algorithm. The numerical results confirm that our approach achieves performance comparable to these baselines using a single full-state trajectory and substantially fewer samples. Additionally, numerical complexity analysis reveals that the proposed method scales more efficiently with both state and action dimensions. Extending existing cross-approximation concepts to control represents a promising avenue for sharing control knowledge among dynamically heterogeneous agents. This capability is particularly vital for swarm intelligence, where agents like drones, underwater vehicles, and ground robots can contribute data to a shared pool for the benefit of the entire group. We conclude by demonstrating the framework's efficacy in coordinating a swarm of vehicles to achieve a common objective. This study investigates a two-dimensional non-linear sigma-metric conformal field theory (CMFT) featuring a negative Gaussian curvature target, specifically the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model. We demonstrate that for the primary fields $\phi_{12}$, $\phi_{21}$, and $\phi_{11}$, there exist linear combinations of their correlation functions that satisfy a system of first-order differential equations. This system aligns precisely with the discrete covariant derivative law defined by the algebraic structure of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ root lattice. Furthermore, we establish that these fields are holomorphic with respect to the complex parameter $\beta^2$, which governs the theory's conformal dimension. This finding resolves the second part of an open question previously raised in our prior work concerning the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda model. Finally, we offer a concise discussion on the implications of these findings for the analyticity of general fields and interaction terms within non-linear CMFTs. We analyzed the distribution of ionized, atomic, and photodissociation region (PDR) gases surrounding the Rho Ophiuchus cluster's S1 multiple star system by examining radio to far-infrared data. Our results indicate that ionized gas is not uniformly distributed around the S1 binary components but instead forms a clumpy, elongated structure extending from the cluster's northern edge toward the S1 binary itself. This pattern aligns with a molecular ridge containing clumps of both ionized and atomic hydrogen, suggesting that the ionized gas is shaped by radiation from the S1 binary and confined by the molecular ridge. Furthermore, the fraction of HII regions exhibiting radio emission is positively correlated with their H$\alpha$ luminosity, implying that radio-emitting HII regions are predominantly located along the HII-molecular ridge. Atomic hydrogen shows a similar distribution to ionized gas, indicating that the molecular ridge has been eroded by radiation from the S1 binary. PDR gas exhibits a symmetric distribution relative to the S1 binary, with its morphology governed by radiation from the binary and the underlying molecular ridge. These findings support the hypothesis that the PDR gas originates from a molecular ridge situated between the S1 binary and the cluster's eastern edge, which is illuminated by the binary's radiation. Overall, the dispersion of ionized, atomic, and PDR gases around the S1 binary system is determined by the binary's radiation and the underlying molecular ridge structure. Additionally, we identified a new PDR filament within the molecular ridge, which may serve as a source of ionized and atomic gas for the S1 binary. These results are consistent with the model proposed by Cleeves et al. (2011), which suggests that the dispersal of gas around the S1 binary system is driven by photoevaporation from the binary. Finally, we propose that the clumpy distribution of ionized gas observed in this study may influence the formation of binary and multiple stars. Specifically, the HII region's radiation can erode the parent molecular cloud, thereby affecting star formation. This mechanism may explain the apparent lack of core fragmentation in the Ophiuchus cloud. Furthermore, the HII region's radiation can destroy the core structure, potentially leading to the formation of binary and multiple stars. The distribution of ionized gas may also impact the formation of protoplanetary disks around young stars. This paper introduces a new class of factor models featuring time-constant factor loadings designed to forecast mortality rates. Initially, long-term mortality trends are decomposed into common, long-term components using an expectation-maximization algorithm. Unlike traditional factor models, this approach posits that individuals within the same cohort experience these trends at a uniform rate determined by their specific factor loadings. We demonstrate that time-constant factor models outperform both classical Li and Lee models and variants with time-varying loadings in out-of-sample mortality prediction for Canadian data from 1961 to 2014. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying a common prediction rule across all factors yields superior prediction performance compared to forecasting each factor individually. Finally, we extend our prediction framework to generate life table functions, including life expectancies, and evaluate their stability using the same Canadian mortality dataset. These life table predictions are then compared against the standard Lee-Carter method. Ultimately, we provide several practical applications of our prediction framework for risk management purposes. Consequently, this study makes several contributions to the fields of economics and mathematics by (i) proposing a novel factor model for mortality prediction, (ii) offering a unified prediction rule that outperforms cohort-by-cohort approaches, and (iii) introducing a new factor-based framework for predicting life tables. This work represents the first application of factor models to life table prediction in the mathematical finance literature. The paper includes an extensive appendix detailing the mathematical derivations behind the proposed factor model. All results were derived using the R programming language. Artificial Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has become a widely adopted method for automatically designing high-accuracy models on various tasks. However, the interaction between architectural components can introduce significant uncertainty, often resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this, researchers have developed a uniformity assumption, designing the architecture search space based on typical component interactions to minimize unexpected behaviors. This paper challenges that assumption by demonstrating through experiments that it leads to a suboptimal solution space. We propose a method to identify the search space's limitations and a novel approach to mitigate these constraints. Our findings indicate that this strategy achieves state-of-the-art results on the CUB-200 dataset while simultaneously reducing model complexity. Furthermore, the approach is adaptable to other tasks and can be easily integrated into existing NAS frameworks. Additionally, we release a new dataset called CUB-200-34, which features a lightweight architecture capable of reaching 80.7% top-1 accuracy, significantly surpassing the baseline CNN performance of 72.4%. This model also requires fewer floating-point operations (FLOPs) and is faster to train. The dataset and models are accessible at https://github.com/ashwin-krishnan/interference-aware-NAS. We demonstrate that for any geodesically complete CAT(0) surface, the set of receding directions at which nonpositive curvature does not adhere to a quadratic decay law forms a closed subset of the boundary. Furthermore, the closure of those receding directions exhibiting less than quadratic curvature decay is empty, unless the area is a Euclidean cylinder or possesses a parabolic isometry. Any parabolic isometry of a CAT(0) area must exhibit polynomial growth, and the center of this isometry is either empty or constitutes a single point. The center is a single point if, and only if, all orbits are either bounded or exhibit sublinear displacement. Finally, we provide an example of a geodesically complete CAT(0) area where there exists a receding direction with nonpositive curvature that fails to decay quadratically, despite the surface containing no flat lines. Additionally, we establish that any CAT(0) area where all receding directions exhibit non-quadratic curvature decay is either a Euclidean cylinder or possesses a parabolic isometry. These findings rely on a novel isoperimetric inequality, which we anticipate will find broader applications. Specifically, we show that any geodesically complete CAT(0) surface where quadratic curvature decay fails at some receding point is either a Euclidean cylinder or admits a parabolic isometry with at most linear displacement. The proof of this result utilizes a novel technique for bounding the area of isoperimetric regions, which we expect to be of independent interest. This approach draws upon the theory of nonlinear potential theory developed by Carrillo, Villani, and their collaborators. By employing this method, we derive a new isoperimetric inequality for CAT(0) surfaces that features a logarithmic correction term compared to the isoperimetric inequality established by Cheeger. Fully connected neural networks, including convolutional ones, are widely recognized for being prone to overfitting and failing to effectively distinguish the few attributes that truly matter. This paper introduces a straightforward and efficient pruning algorithm that operates by randomly removing neurons from layers until the network's performance on a validation set ceases to improve. This method successfully isolates the critical information embedded within the initially randomly selected weights and biases, which are responsible for encoding the relevant attributes. These attributes enable the network to make accurate predictions even when the majority of parameters are eliminated. Our findings indicate that the "winning lottery ticket" can be identified without any modification to the original network's hyperparameters. Furthermore, by applying this ticket to few-shot learning and object detection in convolutional networks, we demonstrated that the fundamental structure of the winning ticket is nearly identical to that of efficient convolutional networks used in current practical applications. This outcome strongly suggests that convolutional networks may have evolved specifically to extract and utilize these few critical attributes. Ultimately, our work offers a rigorous theoretical justification for ad-hoc techniques, such as structural pruning, that have been proposed to address the inefficiencies of fully connected networks. Additionally, this approach presents a promising avenue for developing highly efficient and generalizable neural networks. We present a comprehensive economic analysis of a newly introduced ticket, which guarantees a refund of the expected value if purchased during the expected future crash of a stock. This concept is linked to various concepts in decision theory, including counterfactual conditionals, Sebens and Carroll's many-worlds decision theory, and Daniel Dennett's concept of "centered worlds." Following this background, we outline the optimal purchasing strategy for this ticket, along with empirical findings and limitations. These findings include results from a pilot study involving 30 economics graduate students, which revealed significant differences in willingness to purchase the ticket across demographic variables such as gender, age, and nationality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an algorithm utilizing decision-theoretic principles can achieve rational behavior in a repeated prisoner's dilemma scenario, even without communication between the algorithms. Finally, we propose that the value of this ticket could inspire a new field of "temporal markets." Second, we argue that the ticket's value could significantly enhance AI safety by enabling AI systems to influence their own future constraints. We detail how a system could sell this ticket to a more intelligent future iteration, thereby limiting the current iteration's ability to act destructively. The valley Hall effect and related valley-dependent phenomena are essential for two-dimensional materials. Although valley mixing caused by time-reversal symmetry-breaking is well-established, the impact of electron-phonon interactions remains poorly understood. This study demonstrates that electron-phonon coupling can both induce valley mixing and hinder valley Hall phenomena by decoupling mobility from the Berry curvature determinant. Specifically, a phonon-induced momentum shift ($\Delta k$) can create a asymmetry in intervalley scattering rates, leading to a net current. This $\Delta k$ arises primarily from the non-orthogonality of initial and final Bloch states. We show that this phonon-driven valley mixing is particularly significant in graphene and graphene-like materials, where it can generate a non-zero Berry curvature and influence potential applications. Furthermore, we outline the unique electron-phonon interactions required to reverse the sign of the valley Hall effect. These findings underscore the critical role of electron-phonon interactions in valley physics and provide a novel platform for valleytronics. Visualizing high-dimensional data is a critical step for gaining insights and facilitating human decision-making. Recently, t-SNE and UMAP have emerged as widely adopted techniques for this purpose, yet both suffer from significant drawbacks, including exorbitant computational costs and suboptimal visualization quality. These limitations are particularly pronounced for spherical data, which are frequently modeled as quaternions in robotics and computer vision applications. This paper introduces a novel and straightforward method for visualizing spherical datasets within Euclidean space (R3). Our proposed approach, SNE, is an adaptation of t-SNE that operates directly in R3 rather than relying on embedding into it. Specifically, we replace t-SNE's Gaussian distribution with a three-dimensional one and reintroduce the 3-f component of unit quaternions into the exponential function to ensure quaternion constraints are satisfied. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our proposed algorithms are both highly efficient and effective. Notably, SNE can be up to two orders of magnitude faster than both UMAP and t-SNE. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongzhaojiang/VMF-SNE. The term VMF refers to von Mises-Fisher distribution, a distribution on the unit hypersphere that SNE approximates. A detailed comparison with other spherical distribution families is provided in our arXiv paper, which is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01111. We present novel results for the p-wave pseudogap and interaction energy within strongly coupled regimes. Our computational framework utilizes finite-temperature diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DMC) to sum infinite-order Feynman diagrams. By implementing smart enumeration and stochastic error estimation techniques, we calculate the exact stochastic series expansion up to a controlled, small error threshold. Our findings demonstrate that the p-wave pseudogap persists in the two-dimensional Fermi gas even at strongly positive scattering lengths. We observe that p-wave pairing is significantly enhanced in the attractive regime, whereas it is suppressed in the BCS-BEC crossover within a two-component mixture. Over recent years, remote work has gained significant traction, yet its impact on software engineering within organizations remains uncertain. This research investigates how telecommuting affects Scrum project outcomes. Initially, a survey of 100 software engineering practitioners revealed that while products from telecommuting teams (1–3 members working remotely) achieved higher satisfaction and performance, larger groups collaborated more effectively in office settings. Conversely, an analysis of 34 open-source office and remote versions of the same projects indicated that remote Scrum teams outperformed office teams, showing improved satisfaction, performance, and communication, though they experienced higher conflict. Finally, case studies of three organizations that transitioned to telecommuting confirmed these early findings and highlighted specific challenges, such as reduced team satisfaction and performance due to distributed decision-making. Ultimately, while telecommuting offers benefits, it presents notable challenges for remote Scrum project management. These insights can guide organizations in making informed decisions regarding work location policies. **Keywords:** Agile, Scrum, Telecommuting, Distributed Decision Making.

This paper provides the explicit Gau–Wu value for $4\times 4$ arrowhead matrices and demonstrates its application in solving the generalized discrete Dirichlet problem for the 4D Laplace equation. The introduction of the arrowhead matrix concept by Pearson in the 19th century marked a pivotal development in discrete mathematics, offering fundamental tools for formulating and addressing discrete mathematical problems. Since then, numerous scholars have contributed to the field by developing innovative techniques to compute the Gau–Wu value for these matrices. This survey examines various approaches to determining the Gau–Wu value for $n\times n$ arrowhead matrices, with a specific focus on the $4\times 4$ instance. Furthermore, we extend prior research by calculating the Wu function values at non-zero boundary points for the discrete Laplace equation on a $4\times 4$ mesh. Leveraging these findings, we derive the explicit solution to the discrete Dirichlet problem for the 2D Laplace equation on a $4\times 4$ mesh, thereby demonstrating the practical utility of the arrowhead matrix theory. Finally, we outline potential directions for future research. Given the well-established relationship between arrow matrices and the Laplace matrix on the graph path $P_4$, the established theoretical framework for arrow matrices can be adapted to address the discrete Dirichlet problem for the 2D Laplace equation on a $4\times 4$ mesh with Dirichlet boundaries. This approach offers an alternative solution that offers significant computational advantages. Additionally, our findings may contribute to the solution of the discrete Dirichlet problem for the Laplace equation on the graph cycle $C_4$. Furthermore, the extension of arrow matrices to diamond matrices by Liu in 1992 suggests that our results could similarly inform the resolution of the discrete Dirichlet problem for the 2D Laplace equation on a $4\times 4$ mesh with Dirichlet boundaries in the context of diamond graphs. These results are also applicable to the discrete Dirichlet problem for the Dirac equation on the $4\times 4$ mesh. Finally, our findings hold relevance for the discrete Dirichlet problem on the Euclidean square lattice. These contributions extend and complement existing research, including works by Liu, Wang, Liu, and others. Our findings also offer a new perspective on the Dirac equation, contributing to the broader understanding of the Euclidean Dirac equation. Our results provide a novel perspective on the Dirac equation

This study examines elliptic flow ($v_2$) within Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, focusing on charged hadrons, D mesons, and B mesons across a wide transverse momentum range. By utilizing two particle species with distinct masses, we probe how initial mass influences collective motion. Furthermore, measurements of hadrons originating from beauty hadrons allow for an investigation into the common transport mechanisms governing light and beauty hadrons. To a significant extent, B mesons exhibit collective behavior similar to that of pions. Our findings are analyzed using the AMPT model, which incorporates both color glass condensate and hydrodynamics. This work marks the first instance of elliptic flow observations for charged hadrons and, notably, the first for D and B mesons, offering valuable insights into the transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma and its effect on heavy quarks. Additionally, the data elucidate the dynamics of charm and beauty within the medium. These results underscore the necessity for more precise elliptic flow measurements across a broader mass spectrum to comprehensively understand the dynamics of the created medium. This study examines the $K$-user interference network and investigates how the Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) loss caused by binary power control (BCA) compares to optimal power control (OPT). We demonstrate that the maximum BCA GDoF loss in any subnetwork of size $k$ does not exceed $\sqrt{k-1}$. Consequently, the overall BCA GDoF loss for the entire network is bounded by $\sqrt{K-1}$. This bound is proven to be tight for all $K \geq 4$. Our methodology relies on a recursive construction of interference graphs featuring specific structural properties. Furthermore, we establish that the GDoF loss of any single node under BCA never exceeds $1$, and this result is also tight for all $K \geq 4$. Finally, we extend the analysis to scenarios involving half-duplex communication with side information and interference with general BCIs, proving that the GDoF loss remains bounded in these cases as well. It is important to note that these bounds are not tight for every specific network size $K$. We also observe that, unlike GDoF, the sum of degrees of freedom under OPT is not necessarily an integer, and determining the tightest upper bound for this loss remains an open problem. Additionally, the paper provides a counterexample to a conjecture proposed by Belfiore et al. [1]. To address this, we introduce a new class of interference graphs termed "half-duplex interference graphs," which possess a unique structural characteristic and exhibit a specific property. We prove that for any half-duple interference graph, the GDoF loss via BCA does not exceed $1$, and we confirm that this bound is tight for all $K \geq 4$. We further show that recursive interference graphs constitute a proper subset of half-duplex interference graphs, thereby implying that the GDoF loss through BCA for any half-duplex interference graph is bounded by $\sqrt{K-1}$. We also demonstrate that this bound is tight for all $K \geq 4$ within a specific subset of half-duplex interference graphs. The paper concludes by discussing the relationship between half-duplex interference graphs and the broader class of recursive interference graphs.

The Strauss process is a point process characterized by the tendency of points to cluster in pairs. Existing methods for sampling from this process are largely heuristic, as the model lacks closed-form expressions for either its density or unnormalized measure. This paper introduces an innovative approach capable of exactly and efficiently generating samples from any specific Strauss process. The proposed algorithm combines techniques from rejection sampling and importance sampling to achieve a rejection ratio that is independent of the model's parameters. Furthermore, this method can be adapted to construct an exactly solvable approximation for arbitrary Strauss models. The paper demonstrates the method's effectiveness through several examples, including approximations for the Ising model and the hard-cores model. Additionally, we illustrate how to derive exact realizations of certain Strauss models using matrix methods. The methodology is implemented in the `strauss` package, which is available on CRAN. The package also features an extension to the weighted Strauss model, a variant that facilitates tighter bounds on the normalizing constant. Furthermore, we show that samples from any specific weighted Strauss model can be generated exactly and efficiently. These results build upon and extend the work of \cite{Bauer2018}. The code required to replicate all results is available in the `strauss` package on CRAN. This work was supported by the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), grant number P31066-N32. This study integrates the generalized uncertainty principle (GUP) with both Lorentz and Galilean alterations, demonstrating that their non-trivial combination arises when altering two generalized canonical transformations that commute. Furthermore, we derive the inverse GUP by inverting this combination, finding it corresponds to replacing $\hbar$ with $\hbar/(1+2\lambda\,\hbar)$ in the standard GUP. This result is also derived by applying the GUP to a pair of altering observables. Notably, a key distinction between Lorentz and Galilean alterations lies in their interaction with GUP: the altered position operator fails to reduce to the standard position operator when $\lambda=0$ under Lorentz alterations, whereas it does reduce correctly under Galilean alterations. Consequently, our findings indicate that Lorentz alterations modify the structure of phase space, a conclusion supported by the fact that the algebra of altered observing functionals forms a non-commutative algebra. Finally, we establish that altered observing functionals constitute a deformed Heisenberg algebra, which can be derived from the commutation relations between position and momentum. These findings hold particular significance for theories that GUP aims to describe. In this context, we propose a specific application of Lorentz-altered observing functionals to black holes, showing that the generalized Hawking temperature remains identical to the standard temperature. This outcome is consistent with literature suggesting that GUP effects remain negligible at the horizon. Additionally, we demonstrate that Lorentz-altered observing functionals successfully resolve the ultraviolet divergence problem associated with the density of states for a Schwarzschild black hole. In contrast, we observe that Galilean alterations lead to a divergent temperature at the horizon, rendering them incompatible with black hole physics. These conclusions are also reached when analyzing the correspondence between classical and quantum systems. Specifically, we show that the correspondence principle fails for Lorentz-altered observing functionals when transitioning from the classical to the quantum domain. This failure stems from the fact that altered observing functionals do not commute with the time evolution operator, a characteristic shared by all GUP-based observables. Ultimately, we conclude that the concept of altered observing functionals is fundamentally incompatible with the standard causal structure of spacetime. This conclusion is also supported by an analysis of the correspondence between classical and quantum systems. Over the past few years, Internet of Things (IoT) systems have become integral to numerous critical applications. However, the inherent need to maintain and update these systems creates significant challenges, particularly concerning security and reliability during the update process. This paper presents an investigation into an IoT mesh network featuring distributed firmware upgradability and robust progress monitoring. By leveraging the network's specific architecture and communication protocols, we demonstrate that an upgradability mechanism is feasible within large-scale environments. Our findings indicate that the approach can be implemented with an update success rate of 99.1% and a failure detection time of approximately 10 seconds. Additionally, our research confirms that an A/B partitioning strategy does not negatively impact system reliability or resource efficiency. Ultimately, this study offers a novel methodology for upgrading extensive IoT mesh networks that is both dependable and efficient. The underlying mechanism is made available to the community to foster a safer and more efficient ecosystem for all IoT network participants. To our knowledge, this represents the first comprehensive evaluation of an IoT upgradability mechanism on mesh networks. The complete code and documentation can be accessed at: https://github.com/SebastianKlapp/IoT-Firmware-Upgrades. Furthermore, this work serves as a case study for the topic of "Reconfigurable Computing Systems" and "Embedded Systems," which are currently being discussed at the IEEE International Symposium on on Trustworthy Global Computing (TGC 2021). The paper is titled: "A dependable firmware upgrade approach for IoT Mesh Networks." Its authors are Sebastian Klapp, Lukas Schaefer, and Georgios Paschos. Sebastian Klapp and Lukas Schaefer are doctoral candidates at the Institute for Theoretical Computer Science, Technical University of Applied Sciences Munich. Georgios Paschos serves as a Full Professor at the same institution. All authors are members of the Data Intelligence and Security (DIAS) research group. We also thank the TGC 2021 conference committee for organizing the track on Reconfigurable Computing Systems and Embedded Systems. Finally, we are indebted to our families and friends for their unwavering encouragement and patience throughout the writing process.

Each query splits the space into two parts, and based on the answer, the searcher moves to a new location in one of the resulting partitions. A search is considered complete when all $k$ targets are found and the searcher is ready to depart. The objective is to minimize the total search budget, defined as the maximum number of steps required to start searching from any point until the departure point is reached. This problem is closely related to interactive search theory, which typically prioritizes minimizing the average number of steps from a random unknown starting point. In this work, we demonstrate that minimizing the maximum search budget is more appropriate for our specific context. Our findings indicate that increasing the number of targets by one results in a substantial reduction in the search budget. We also examine the relationship between our proposed algorithm and existing time-constrained search space partitioning techniques. Drawing inspiration from the Quantum Born Rule, this paper introduces a novel class of global adversarial instances tailored for quantum classifiers. We establish the existence and size of these global adversarial instances theorems for shallow parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) classifiers, which include both variational quantum classifiers (VQC) and the Quantum Fourier Classifier (QFC). Additionally, we investigate quantum adversarial instances for VQC to derive the existence size of these global adversarial instances. Finally, we demonstrate the validity of our theoretical findings using a classical simulator. Unlike classical adversarial examples, which are non-intuitive and rely on adversarial perturbations, our proposed global adversarial instances are intuitive and generated through sampling from a quantum bit flip noise (QBF) model. The experiments presented in this study serve as a preliminary step toward understanding the landscape of quantum classification and the robustness of quantum classifiers. This research represents an initial step in a broader effort to explore adversarial attacks within the quantum machine learning domain.

Keywords: Quantum Machine Learning, Quantum Classifier, Quantum Adversarial Instances, Variational Quantum Classifier, Quantum Fourier Classifier.

This study investigates Steklov eigenvalues within almost spherical domains in $\mathbb{}R^3$. Building upon prior research regarding Steklov eigenvalues in convex domains, the Steklov problem on such surfaces can be transformed into a weighted eigenvalue problem defined on bounded regions with smooth boundaries. The study's primary objective is to establish lower bounds for the first non-zero Steklov eigenvalue on almost spherical regions using a geometric spectral framework, specifically employing the isospectral variation formula, spectral gap, and isoperimetric ratio. This framework enables the extension of several existing inequalities concerning domains in $\mathbb{R}^3$ to the case of almost spherical regions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the first non-zero Steklov eigenvalue is highly sensitive to perturbations of the boundary. Finally, we conclude by introducing a functional that quantifies spectral instability, which arises from combining mean curvature and isoperimetric ratio. For additional interest, we compute the spectrum of this functional, showing it possesses a discrete spectrum with finite multiplicities. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for the first non-zero eigenvalue of this functional across all almost spherical regions and characterize the set of minimizers. This result confirms that the first non-zero Steklov eigenvalue achieves its maximum precisely on spherical domains. These methodologies are also applicable to investigating spectral inequalities for the Laplacian on almost spherical regions and analyzing spectral perturbation for the Steklov problem on nearly spherical surfaces. Finally, the first non-zero Steklov eigenvalue is closely linked to isoperimetric ratio and spectral gap. In the final section, the authors explore the relationship between these concepts and establish a novel inequality connecting the first non-zero Steklov eigenvalue, isoperimetric ratio, and spectral gap on almost spherical regions. This inequality generalizes a well-known result by Andrews and Clutterbuck regarding minimal hypersurfaces. Compliance is essential for ensuring that systems and organizations adhere to established rules, whether in business processes or software execution. Modern regulatory frameworks, such as GDPR and the German Basic Data Protection Act (BDSG), provide instructions on how to handle personal information, where individual provisions function as constraints on the order of activities. Existing compliance verification methods typically verify trace segments by checking if infix or postfix alignments of sequential activities match the desired behavior. This paper extends these approaches to verify compliance within arbitrary process fragments, which are defined by their control-flow and potentially data-flow structures. To achieve this, we introduce a method that transforms the process fragment into a marked, potentially non-free-choice Petri net, where compliance can be checked against any sequential process (or process segment) using infix or postfix alignments. The method ensures that alignments of the overall Petri net correspond to alignments of the sequential processes on its free sequential places. We validate this approach by verifying compliance for both control-flow and data-flow fragments under GDPR. Furthermore, the paper presents a novel algorithm for extracting sound, free-choice process fragments from general Petri nets and demonstrates the algorithm's time complexity. Finally, the proposed method is implemented in the ProCom tool, which integrates the Petri net-based fragment extraction algorithm with a compliance verification module based on infix alignment theory. The paper includes experimental results from compliance checks performed using this tool. Accurately modeling signal propagation in cellular networks is essential for planning, optimization, and resource allocation. While traditional methods rely on empirical formulas grounded in physical principles, these approaches often fail to capture the intricate dynamics of modern multi-antenna networks. This paper introduces a data-driven alternative using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to model signal propagation based on channel state information (CSI) and base station configurations. Specifically, we utilize a 3D convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) to predict received signal power across multiple subcarriers, antenna elements, and users within multi-user multi-antenna systems. By learning the complex relationship between user positions, base station layouts, and environmental factors from a large dataset of synthetic channel realizations, our method generates reliable propagation models. We validate this approach in a millimeter-wave scenario, comparing its performance against a 1D channel model with sparse environments and a 3D-coupled wave equation solver against industry-standard empirical formulas. Our results demonstrate that the 3D-CNN significantly outperforms traditional empirical models, particularly as the number of antennas and users increases. Furthermore, our deep learning approach achieves a favorable balance between modeling accuracy and computational complexity, making it highly suitable for practical application. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where deep learning has been successfully applied to cellular network signal propagation modeling. Extensive simulations were conducted using the OpenCellular framework. The source code for this work is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhongtao123456789/Deep-Learning-for-Cellular-Propagation-Modeling. Our findings suggest that this approach could enhance various cellular network optimization tasks, such as joint user scheduling and power control. Although large-scale power system expansion is a critical issue for policymakers, power network expansion models are often too complex for real-time use during decision-making processes. Consequently, researchers typically run these models only after a decision framework is established. This paper investigates the responsiveness of such models by measuring the errors that arise from delaying model runs. We define two metrics for this purpose: generation cost error and network expansion cost error. Our findings indicate that the two metrics do not always correlate, and while they generally diminish as decision delays shorten, the reduction rate varies significantly based on network characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these metrics are also highly sensitive to specific model parameters, including emission factors, fuel prices, and network topology. Finally, our analysis of spatially distributed decision delays reveals that the observed errors are substantially larger than those resulting from decisions made at a single central location. These results suggest the need for further research into novel models and algorithms capable of delivering local, timely decisions alongside globally optimal solutions. To facilitate this, we introduce a new evaluation metric: the sub-optimality gap, which quantifies the difference between local and global decisions. We also outline potential algorithmic strategies for computing these gaps and offer illustrative examples. The methodologies and experiments presented in this work aim to guide future research efforts. Additionally, the model code is made available to support the replication of our findings. This study represents the first step toward developing algorithms and models that can provide immediate local decisions accompanied by quantifiable gaps indicating their distance from global optimality. Such an approach could significantly enhance the practicality of data-driven decision-making processes in power systems expansion. The paper concludes with an overview of future research directions. The code used in this study is accessible at: https://github.com/andreymakarov/responsiveness_of_panem. Furthermore, the source code for the journal's supplementary material can be found at: https://github.com/andreymakarov/panem_sub_optimality_gap. This study establishes the well-posedness of Vlasov-type equations coupled with an external potential satisfying appropriate Lipschitz and growth conditions. Leveraging this result, we demonstrate the global existence of solutions for Vlasov-Poisson systems within confined regions. These findings encompass the previously unresolved three-dimensional half-space scenario and can be extended to Vlasov–Maxwell systems and Vlasov equations coupled with the Yukawa equation. Additionally, we explore various confined domains, including those bounded by absorbing or reflecting interfaces, as well as periodic boundaries. Finally, the derived estimates yield novel insights and insights into the regularity of solutions in unbounded settings. Furthermore, the paper investigates specific applications, such as establishing well-posedness for 1D, 2D, and 3D hard-sphere models, as well as for the Vlasu-Poisson system under Debye screening. We also address a recent query by Lukyanov [27] regarding the regularity of solutions in half-space domains and establish the well-posedness of the Vlasov equation coupled with the Yukawa equation alongside the regularity of the corresponding solution. Finally, we outline an efficient local-in-time algorithm based on the recently developed BGQ kinetic scheme by Jin, Koo, Kim, and Park [7]. This scheme achieves a formal second-order accuracy in space and, when employing an explicit Euler method for time integration, provides first-order accuracy in time. We present a stability analysis and report several two-dimensional simulation results. Finally, the paper concludes with the confirmation of the well-posedness of the proposed scheme. These results were presented at the "International Conference on Mathematical Modeling and Simulation" held in Seville, Spain, in September 2021. Colloidal gels, which are colloidal suspensions where particles are connected by weak bonds, serve as the foundation for many commercial products, including food, paints, and personal care items. These gels exhibit both solid-like and fluid-like properties, making their rheological behavior essential for industrial applications. While ultrasonic vibrations are commonly applied to colloidal gels to control their rheology, their underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates the rheo-acoustic properties of weakly interacting colloidal particles, revealing a strong coupling between acoustic and rheological characteristics. Specifically, we demonstrate that vibrations perpendicular to the shear direction can significantly alter the mechanical and flow properties of colloidal gels. Furthermore, we show that inter-particle potential and the direction of ultrasonic vibration dictate the gel's rheological behavior. Our findings indicate that when ultrasonic force exceeds the gravitational potential, the mechanical and flow properties of the gel can be tuned by adjusting the intensity and frequency of the ultrasound. These insights provide a basis for optimizing the manufacturing processes of colloidal gels and may advance research in rheo-acoustics. Additionally, the ultrasonic force observed here may offer new insights into sonication and cavitation effects in various chemical and biological systems. Finally, this research introduces a new method for dynamically controlling the rheological properties of colloidal gels, with potential applications in microfluidics and nanotechnology. To achieve this, we utilized ultrasound standing waves to modulate particle interactions and colloidal gel rheology. Our results indicate that as acoustic energy increases, the gel's viscosity decreases, while shear storage modulus and yield stress increase. These findings have significant implications for the development of new materials and technologies. Furthermore, our work demonstrates that ultrasound can be used to manipulate the rheological properties of colloidal gels, which could have important applications in material science and engineering. This paper provides an analytical approach to proving the Collatz Conjecture, which posits that any positive integer $n$, when subjected to the operation $n\mapsto n+1/2^n$ repeatedly, will eventually yield an integer of the form $2^k$. We demonstrate that the probability of randomly selecting such a $2^k$ value is zero, yet this zero probability does not preclude the possibility. The proof utilizes the Borel-Cantelli Lemma, along with the Mellin transform and the Riemann zeta function. A key aspect of the argument is establishing that the sum of the probabilities of all previous terms in the sequence $n_i$ exceeds 1. This ensures that, under random selection, the sequence will almost surely produce a $2^k$ term, thereby reducing the problem to the trivial case. Given that the term $n_i$ is selected randomly, the specific instance $n_i=1$—which leads to an infinite loop of $1\to 1\to\dots$—has a probability of zero and can thus be disregarded. Consequently, it follows that any positive integer $n$ will, with probability 1, generate a $2^k$ after a finite number of steps, effectively reducing the proof back to the trivial case. Automated document categorization is a critical component of STEM document parsing, which is essential for document understanding and knowledge extraction. However, current deep learning models for this task often fail to leverage the specific characteristics of STEM fields, leading to significant performance drops when encountering rare entities like mathematical symbols. To address this, we introduce a new data generation method that creates artificial documents by mapping existing ones through a specific domain graph, such as a mathematics entity association graph. This graph links related entities like symbols, formulas, concepts, and terms, capturing domain-specific co-occurrence patterns. We evaluate several categorization models on documents parsed using this graph, and our results demonstrate that these models significantly outperform those using random mappings or no mapping, particularly in generalizing to rare entities. The code for this paper is accessible at https://github.com/taehyungkim97/artificial-docs. Furthermore, we have developed public datasets for document categorization within mathematics and physics domains, which can be retrieved from https://github.com/taehyungkim9/math-physics-docs. We anticipate these datasets will serve as a foundation for future research in STEM document parsing. Our experiments indicate that utilizing an association graph enhances the categorization model's ability to handle rare entities, thereby improving overall performance. The subsequent section of the paper examines the specific association graph properties that contribute to these model performance gains. Additionally, we explore the application of our artificial document generation technique to other research areas, including document clustering and entity linking. Finally, we outline potential directions for future work in STEM document parsing. Our research was conducted while the first author was a visiting scholar at the University of Maryland. Research in both economics and biology has demonstrated that decision-making in group contexts differs significantly from individual choices. Specifically, Stitt and Braver (2018) found that male fruit flies exhibit a heightened sensitivity to reward during group courtship, resulting in more consistent mating decisions. This study investigates whether analogous group-effect dynamics occur in humans, potentially offering new perspectives on the mechanisms driving individual behavior. We examined a human stable marriage market involving women (choosers) and men (bidders), where each participant valued forming a "marriage" (a pairing). Choosers could observe how often their pairings were selected during bidding and could subsequently mimic their partners' valuation patterns. The findings indicate that male participants' valuations shifted to align with their partner's chosen pattern, whereas female participants remained unaffected. These results suggest that an individual's impact on group outcomes can trigger behavioral adaptations in partners, thereby amplifying that person's influence on collective results. Furthermore, the study reveals that group effects are not merely the sum of individual inclinations but can produce phenomena absent in group-of-individuals settings, such as the emergence of highly stable pairings. Finally, our research highlights the critical role of an individual's perceived power and the nature of the object of choice in generating group effects. These insights have profound implications for both theoretical understanding and practical applications, including economic markets and biological evolution. This work introduces a robust, computationally efficient, and statistically reliable framework for restoring low-energy signals from quadratic measurements, including squared or squared-plus-constant values. While reconstructing low-energy signals from squared data is generally ill-posed, the combination of quadratic measurements with the constraint that the signal resides in a low-dimensional subspace renders the problem well-posed. Our method leverages the structure of the Gram matrix associated with this subspace, utilizing a low-rank Bayesian estimator. We propose a closed-form solution that requires no optimization, calculates restoration weights in constant time per entry, and can be executed on standard hardware. Our theoretical findings indicate that the proposed Bayesian approach is both statistically consistent and robust against outliers. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing techniques in accuracy and computational speed. In summary, our contributions are: (i) a new Bayesian estimator; (ii) a restoration weight calculation complexity of constant time per entry; (iii) statistical guarantees of consistency and robustness; (iv) accuracy superior to current state-of-the-art methods; and (v) computational efficiency exceeding that of existing approaches.
