This paper presents a comprehensive catalog of all elementary Laurent expansions of elements within the Drinfeld double $D_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, which serves as a quantization of the Laurent polynomial algebra of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. We subsequently perform a complete classification of elementary Laurent series in the variables $x_{\alpha}$ and $x_{-\alpha}$ that maintain the structure of the Drinfeld double. This classification is achieved by analyzing the subalgebra of elementary Laurent series invariant under the quantum Weyl group. Finally, we provide a classification of quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-symmetries, demonstrating that they correspond to the quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-symmetries of the quantum plane. Notably, this represents the first known classification of quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-symmetries. All results are applicable to the case where $q$ is generic. Furthermore, we provide alternative proofs and extensions of our main findings for the case where $q$ is a root of unity. These findings hold significant potential applications in the study of quantum integrable systems, conformal field theories, and the quantum inverse scattering method. Specifically, our work establishes a complete set of quantum symmetries for the Laurent expansion of the quantum plane, which constitutes the Bethe ansatz action in integrable systems derived from the quantum plane. Additionally, our findings deepen the connection between quantum integrable systems and the quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-symmetries of the quantum plane. This connection is realized through the Bethe ansatz action of the quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ on the space of functions of a single variable. We anticipate that our contributions will facilitate the construction of new quantum integrable systems. This goal is achieved by extending the Bethe ansatz action of quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ to the case of a single variable, a task that relies heavily on the complete set of quantum symmetries of the quantum plane identified in this work. Consequently, our results may also advance the recent initiative to construct quantum integrable systems featuring a novel set of Bethe ansatz operators. Recent advancements in wireless communication have enabled the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) to serve as a critical platform for enhancing traffic efficiency, safety, and driver experience. However, issues such as data privacy, model utility, and network security remain significant obstacles to its widespread adoption. To address these challenges, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a leading machine learning framework. This paper surveys state-of-the-art research integrating IoV and FL, with a specific focus on blockchain-enhanced FL frameworks for vehicle communication. We provide an in-depth analysis of existing studies, detailing the problems they address, proposed solutions, and communication protocols employed. Furthermore, we highlight IoV and FL use cases, evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of current approaches, and assess how blockchain technology enhances security and privacy within FL. Finally, we identify key research gaps and propose directions for future studies. This work serves as a thorough review of recent literature on enhanced blockchain-supported FL frameworks for IoV and offers valuable insights and guidance for subsequent research. Additionally, it offers valuable perspectives on blockchain's role in security and privacy enhancements for FL. This paper is structured into six sections. Section II outlines the background and background of FL and IoV. Section III presents a survey of recent literature on enhanced blockchain-supported FL frameworks for IoV. Section IV provides a detailed overview of FL with blockchain enhancement for IoV. Section V discusses the roles of FL and IoV. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper. This survey is based on 72 papers published between 2019 and 2022. These selected papers were retrieved from reputable databases such as IEEE Xplore, Springer, and ScienceDirect. Furthermore, the production cross-section for $p + \mathrm{Z} \to \mathrm{D}^0 + \mathrm{X}$ was extracted at midrapidity, demonstrating excellent agreement with predictions from next-to-leading-order perturbative QCD. The development of superconducting quantum processors demands the integration of multiple cooling stages to support diverse applications. This paper introduces a novel millikelvin refrigeration system designed for large-scale integration with scientific facilities. Utilizing a two-stage pulse tube cooler as a base, the system incorporates a two-stage still, a two-stage pulse tube cooler, a mechanical cooler, and a liquid cryogen cooling hierarchy. Through careful thermal and mechanical design, this platform achieves a cold volume of 1.1 L at 7 K, delivering 11 W, 600 W, and 1500 W at approximately 80 K, 4 K, and 4.2 K, respectively. Additionally, it maintains a substantial 1.1 L volume within the 5–7 K range. This study details the thermal and mechanical architectures, cooling performance, thermal isolation strategies, and operational procedures. A sustained cryostation temperature of 7.2 K was achieved, accompanied by a 1.1 L cold space at roughly 80 K. The design successfully mitigated thermal and mechanical vibrations, maintaining a thermal noise floor below 40 dB re 1 pW at 1 Hz. Furthermore, the cool-down process was completed in just 1.5 hours, and the cryostation has remained stable at 7.2 K for over 100 hours. This work presents a novel, scalable cryogenic platform offering substantial cooling power at multiple cryogenic stages, making it ideal for emerging applications in quantum computing and superconducting accelerator technology. This substantial millikelvin facility is currently being utilized to operate the 202 MHz superconducting accelerator testbed at Fermilab.

This study examines a collection of 98 Python projects from GitHub that employ cryptography. Although the majority are not security-critical, our analysis identifies 18 cases where significant vulnerabilities arise due to improper usage, including 12 instances of substantial information leaks caused by bad random number generation. We categorize these vulnerabilities and propose corresponding remedies. Furthermore, we investigate the underlying causes of such misuses and develop a novel set of static analysis checks to detect them. Finally, we discuss how these checks can be integrated into various Python development environments and present case studies of their practical application. We release this work under the permissive MIT License to facilitate its adoption by the Python community. Given cryptography's high stakes, our findings underscore the necessity of applying static analysis to crypto-related code, a point we demonstrate is already feasible. We hope these results encourage the broader use of similar analysis techniques on cryptographic implementations. Our goal is to foster ongoing dialogue within the cryptography community regarding the adoption of such methods. We believe that tools capable of detecting common misuses and vulnerabilities can eventually assist developers in making superior decisions and foster greater trust in Python-based cryptographic systems. We view this work as a significant step toward achieving that objective. Additionally, we acknowledge that identifying security-critical code misuses remains challenging; however, we contend that our findings still hold value in promoting the discussion of such issues. We look forward to contributing to this conversation and believe these results serve as a meaningful initial input. We are deeply committed to the Crypto Hackathon and the Crypto Hackathons International organization, which we co-founded, and we aim to facilitate similar engagements in the future. We extend our sincere gratitude to all contributors. We hope this research inspires other scientists to engage with the Crypto Hackathon community. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

This paper introduces a novel automatic annotation framework named VALUE (Voting-based Urban Labeling Extensive for Urban Learning and Evaluation), designed to enhance the accuracy of semantic segmentation and object detection across a wide range of urban settings. VALUE leverages the strengths of diverse neural network architectures, including both deep and shallow models, to improve the robustness and generalizability of automatic data annotation. By employing a lightweight model optimized for rapid and efficient inference, VALUE facilitates extensive data annotation at scale. The resulting high-quality annotations support large-scale semantic segmentation tasks, such as those in the VALUE-DrivelaB dataset which contains 1.2 million annotations. Furthermore, it enables automatic scene understanding evaluation through a new metric called Scene Understanding Quality (SUQ). Extensive experiments demonstrate that VALUE significantly outperforms existing methods in various city environments, including freeways, city streets, and mixed urban areas. The VALUE code and dataset will be publicly available at https://value-ubc.github.io/. Additionally, the VALUE evaluation framework will be released as a new module for the Pytorch3D Scene Understanding Evaluation (SUEV) package, allowing users to easily evaluate semantic segmentation performance using SUQ on various autonomous driving datasets. To facilitate this, VALUE provides a straightforward interface for annotating urban environments, such as autonomous vehicles and pedestrians. Overall, VALUE offers a cost-effective solution for large-scale, high-quality data annotation, thereby advancing general-purpose urban scene understanding. This paper introduces NuSPAN, a novel sparsity-promoting penalty designed for seismic reflectivity reconstruction within a nonuniform, irregular grid framework. By extending the proximal mean (SPAN) penalty from $\mathbb{R}^N$ to $\mathbb{R}^P$ (where $P \geqslant N$), the approach effectively addresses irregular grid points by embedding additional information into the penalty term. NuSPAN is evaluated against the total variation (TV) penalty, which, despite its popularity, fails to fully capitalize on the geometric advantages of an expanded domain. The study demonstrates that NuSPAN can surpass TV performance in certain scenarios, specifically by mitigating ringing artifacts. The proposed penalty is both frame-invariant and translation-invariant, properties that are inherently linked to the choice of anchor points. To establish sufficient conditions for uniqueness, the concept of a nondegenerate set is developed. These findings are applied to the seismic reflectivity reconstruction problem, where data is modeled as noisy observations of a product between a reflectivity function and a uniform acquisition pattern, alongside a sparsity prior defined on a nonuniform domain. To facilitate sparse recovery, a proximal mean operator is introduced, along with a proximal operator for the regularized NuSPAN penalty. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the proposed method, with success measured by the accuracy of the recovered reflectivity function. The results indicate that NuSPAN achieves or exceeds TV performance across a wide range of acquisition patterns, particularly when utilizing dense acquisition patterns. Furthermore, it is observed that NuSPAN is less susceptible to ringing artifacts, which tend to diminish as sparsity increases. Finally, the computational efficiency of NuSPAN is demonstrated to be comparable to that of TV. Additionally, an algorithm for seismic reflectivity reconstruction utilizing NuSPAN is presented, and its convergence is proven under the assumption of a Lipschitz continuous proximal mean operator. Finally, the performance of this algorithm is analyzed in the seismic context. Through a series of numerical experiments, the proposed algorithm exhibits stable convergence, with the reconstruction error decreasing as the number of iterations increases. These examples validate the theoretical analysis and suggest that the algorithm is suitable for practical implementation. In summary, NuSPAN offers a promising alternative to TV-based sparsity penalties for seismic reflectivity reconstruction on nonuniform grids. By leveraging the advantages of an extra domain, NuSPAN outperforms TV in specific cases, thereby enhancing the reliability of the recovered reflectivity function. Future work will focus on extending NuSPAN to handle group sparsity, thereby broadening its applicability

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces by employing semicomposition operators equipped with weights and exponential change-of-variable techniques. Furthermore, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a closed subspace of BMOA-type spaces to remain invariant under all semicomposition operators, and we derive a criterion for a subspace of Dirichlet-type space to be invariant under all composition operators based on the behavior of the composite function at the boundary. Finally, we classify maximal invariant subspaces of BMO-type spaces that are invariant under every semicomposition operator. As an application, we demonstrate the existence of non-constant invariant subspaces within the Dirichlet-type space $\mathcal D_\alpha$ ($\alpha>0$) and the Dirichlet-type space $\mathcal D(\phi)$ associated with any positive radial function $\phi(t)$ possessing a specific property, which are invariant under all composition operators; this resolves an open question posed by Chen and Wu in \cite{CW}. The methodology utilized in this work is also applicable to other spaces exhibiting similar characteristics. Furthermore, the results extend to the spaces BO, $\mathcal{Q}_K$, and $\mathcal{Q}_K(0)$ defined by Ponnusamy et al. in \cite{CP}. Additional references will be incorporated in a future publication. Finally, the work incorporates an historical overview of the field. This paper is dedicated to the memory of Professor Shouyong Chen. Additionally, it serves as a contribution toward addressing an open question posed by Professor Wu regarding invariant subspaces of Dirichlet-type spaces and Q-type spaces under all composition operators. This approach yields the complete operator content up to a specified scaling dimension within a specified operator algebra, alongside universal finite-size corrections arising from operator merging at large times. Furthermore, the technique facilitates the precise determination of operator scaling dimensions by minimizing biases caused by merging, enabling the achievement of high precision for a specific number of operators. We demonstrate these capabilities by computing the scaling dimensions of the transfer matrix for the Haagerup model up to 16 excitations. Historical texts present unique challenges for natural language processing due to evolving grammatical categories, shifted word meanings, and non-standard orthography. To address this, we introduce a method that enables multiple possible part-of-speech tags per word when analyzing historical datasets. This approach, implemented via a non-deterministic finite automaon (NFA), functions as a lattice trie that preserves multiple pos-tagging outcomes. We have developed a straightforward and efficient conversion technique to transform this NFA into a word segmentation model, allowing the system to retain multiple segmentation options. Through an extensive experiment on the 17th-century German KATZ corpus, we demonstrate that dependable pos-tagging of historical languages is achievable. The results indicate that the dependability of our NFA model matches that of a deterministic conversion model while offering superior robustness and flexibility. Additionally, we show that NFA models can be efficiently transformed into standard finite-state machines (DFAs) for storage and rapid processing, with only a minor loss in tag accuracy. Finally, we illustrate the utility of pos-tagging reliability by enabling the selection of multiple lemmas during historical wordform normalization. Non-uniform integrability theory characterizes specific subsets of $L^1$ functions whose singularities are confined to a null set, ensuring that $\varepsilon$-sub-level sets possess a mass nearly equivalent to the total integral. This property is linked to the existence of a non-principal ultrafilter and uniform integrability. This paper introduces a novel concept, $\alpha$-non-uniform integrability, which relies on a positive function $\alpha$ (representing a near standard scale) instead of ultrafilters. The study establishes the equivalence between $\alpha$-non-uniform integrability and the uniform integrability of $\mathcal{T}(\alpha)$, the ultrafilter of a monad $\{0\}$ relative to the non-standard metric defined by $\alpha$. A key application includes a new characterization of Dini sets. The work also features an application to uniform convergence theorems. The authors intend to explore further the uniformity inherent in non-uniform integrability through ultra-metric spaces. This paper introduces a method for automatically converting urban development requirements into a formal specification of a city ontology. We argue that for managing city requirements, it is essential to integrate ontological knowledge with formal formalization, ensuring that the resulting specification directly reflects the specific needs of city residents. Our proposed solution involves developing a specialized city requirement engineering process supported by an ontology transformation tool. This process enables the automatic generation of an ontology based on identified requirements. Furthermore, an extended case study demonstrates the feasibility of this approach for managing requirements within the Smart City framework. Specifically, we applied our tool to a Smart Parking use case, showing that it successfully processed city requirements and produced a formal specification. The paper provides a user evaluation of this tool and discusses both its advantages and limitations. Ultimately, we conclude that our proposed solution effectively manages city requirements and facilitates their integration into the corresponding city ontology. Additionally, we show that it supports both the traceability and reusability of these requirements. Overall, the method presented in this paper is applicable to any Smart City domain. In the context of superconducting quantum circuits, quantum errors are predominantly of the amplitude-damping type. To address this, we introduce a proposal for active quantum error correction designed to mitigate amplitude-damping errors without applying any unitary operations to the data qubits. This approach, termed the "Concealed Inverse" protocol, involves three components: (i) a three-level auxiliary quantum system (qudit) functioning as an ancilla; ((ii) a concealed inverse damping channel applied to the ancilla; and (iii) a measurement of the ancilla's energy. When perfectly implemented, this protocol can fully recover data qubits from arbitrary single-qubit amplitude-damping errors. We specifically outline a practical implementation using three-level transmons and evaluate its feasibility within current superconducting quantum hardware. Furthermore, this active strategy serves as a foundational element for future schemes capable of correcting both phase and amplitude damping errors in superconducting quantum systems. Additionally, the study examines the recovery of data subjected to the amplitude-damping noise model characterized by $\mathcal{D}[\rho]=\Gamma d\r/dt+\Gamma[n+1]\rho^D[\rho]+\Gamma n\rho$. In any regular category, the diagonal map $id: E \to \Delta E$ admits a cocartesian decomposition, where the morphism $\partial : E \to \partial E$ serves as an epimorphism and $\partial E$ is closed (representing the image of $E$). The objective of this study is to examine the presences and implications of specific properties within this decomposition across various regular categories. These characteristics include $\partial$ being idempotent, a generating morphism, pure, or surjective; $\partial E$ being the maximal closed subobject of $A$; and the pair $(\partial E, A)$ forming the $n$-th inductive object pair. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within a regular topos, every preorder $R$ exhibits a cocartesian representation that satisfies all the aforementioned properties simultaneously. Additionally, we explore connections between these findings and the universal subobject $U_R \rightarrowtail A$ associated with a preorder $R$ on an object $A$. Finally, we highlight a novel connection between universal preorders and Stone duality by illustrating how the construction of $U_R$ can be adapted to the framework of a general regular category. Finally, we show that in a regular topos, every equivalence relation $R$ possesses a cocartesian representation $\partial : E \to \partial E$ where $\partial$ is idempotent and pure, thereby extending the concept of a normal equivalence from abelian categories to regular topoi. To support these proofs, we utilize the elementary equivalence between preorders and closed subobjects in regular topoi, which we derive through an adjoint functor between them. Finally, we provide an example of a regular category where the cocartesian representation of a preorder does not admit any of the properties discussed. The paper concludes with a series of open questions and areas for future research. This work fulfills a promise made in our publication titled "Towards a generalised Stone duality," as stated in the concluding remarks. That paper proposed an extension of Stone duality to regular categories and suggested that its full development would be addressed in a subsequent paper, which this study aims to deliver. To achieve this, we have formulated a dual to the functor linking preorders to closed subobjects, providing a comprehensive list of conditions under which this dual establishes a dual equivalence. We also offer an alternative, more direct proof for the case of topoi, alongside an examination of the dual of the second condition regarding closed preorders in such categories

The rising availability of satellite imagery has enhanced our understanding of marine and atmospheric dynamics, yet interpreting these data in multidimensional spaces remains difficult. This obstacle is compounded by the fact that such data often violates standard statistical assumptions, including independence, identical distribution, finite variance, and normality. To address these extreme scenarios, this study applies spatial conditional peak-over-threshold models to extreme oceanic conditions. Specifically, it analyzes significant wind fields using a Hilbert-space-based multivariate extreme-value distribution. This research examines the tight Hilbert polynomial for any local ring, demonstrating its connection to the F-invariant through the lens of tight closure theory. For equicharacteristic zero local rings, we establish that the tight Hilbert polynomial serves as the tight closure analogue of the Hilbert polynomial. Furthermore, we present examples of non-equicharacteristic local rings where the tight closure of specific monomial ideals varies with the prime characteristic, indicating a corresponding variation in the tight Hilbert polynomial. Additionally, we derive an upper bound for the tight Hilbert polynomial of equidimensional Noetherian local rings utilizing valuation data, and we equireduce the tight Hilbert polynomial to the ordinary Hilbert polynomial within certain special cases. Finally, we explore the relationship between the tight Hilbert polynomial and the reduction number of the ideal.

This paper examines a black hole within an asymptotically anti-de Sitter space, derived from the Einstein-Hilbert action augmented by a topological term. By employing the Noether charge method, we determine the surface term associated with this action. We then apply the quantum equivalence principle, which equates the surface term to half the variation of the energy with respect to the temperature, to define this energy. Furthermore, we apply this energy definition to a family of states characterized by a temperature with a fixed mean value. By variationally calculating the Virasoro algebra for these states, we demonstrate a disorder phenomenon where, despite the algebra's parameters remaining constant, the states shift to higher orders within the hierarchy. This effect is attributed to the presence of the extra topological term in the Einstein-Hilbert action. Finally, we calculate the entropy of a black hole in an asymptotically anti-de Sitter space, again utilizing the Noether charge method to find the surface term and the energy definition via the quantum equivalence principle. We prove that the derived expression for the surface term aligns with the Cardy formula result when the surface term is interpreted as energy minus temperature times entropy. Additionally, we show that the entropy exhibits disorder, consistent with findings from the Virasoro algebra calculation. These results reinforce the validity of the Noether charge method and the quantum equivalence principle. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for holographic duality.

Deep learning has recently become a leading approach for DNA sequence analysis, yet most existing methods rely heavily on sequence length, limiting their application to human and mouse genomes. Furthermore, these models often require manual design of input representations and architecture structures, making them dependent on expert input. This study introduces DNA-Pattern, a novel, unsupervised representation learning technique that automatically generates sequence patterns to model DNA's positional features. These patterns are then utilized as inputs for various downstream supervised learning tasks. In human and mouse data, DNA-Pattern achieved state-of-the-art performance for the first time in two of the three evaluated tasks, specifically sequence motif identification and pathogen identification. Moreover, when applied to DNA patterns from multiple species—including bacteria, yeast, plants, and others—it yielded competitive or superior results for the first time across four additional tasks: species identification, DNA methylation identification, chromatin accessibility, and transcription factor identification. Finally, the source code for DNA-Pattern is publicly accessible at https://github.com/tdl-lab/DNA-Pattern. Our code is expected to inspire future research in DNA pattern representation learning and enable the development of novel sequence pattern identification tools for any organism. This paper investigates specific subcollections of these polynomials defined on chromatic symmetric polynomials of connected Dyck path graphs. Leveraging non-vanishing Armstrong--Loehr tables, we determine the average degree of these chromatic symmetric polynomials as a function of $q$. This paper introduces a substantial flavor-dependent correction to the top quark mass, derived from the quark-lepton complementarity (LQC) framework. This theoretical correction is large enough to warrant its own dedicated analysis. Based on LQC, we construct a flavor-dependent running mass for the top quark and compare it against experimental data from the LHC. Our findings indicate that while the GUT mass shows only a mild dependence on quark mass, the running mass at the electroweak scale exhibits a substantial dependence on quark mass. Furthermore, we project that the flavor dependence of the top quark mass may become a significant issue for future precision measurements. Consequently, we argue that ignoring this dependence could compromise flavor-universal new physics searches that rely on precise predictions of quark masses. Finally, we suggest that future research must employ an appropriate quark mass definition to properly account for this quark mass dependence. Available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07005. Quark masses within this context are defined via their propagators. This paper is the first of two companion studies. In our subsequent work, we will provide a comprehensive analysis of quark masses using the Dirac-Higgs-Yukawa model. In that approach, the Dirac-Higgs-Yukawa theory is extended to incorporate Higgs-quark couplings alongside the standard Higgs-fermion couplings. By deriving theoretical expressions for the quark mass matrix and quark mass eigenvalues, we will rigorously examine the substantial quark mass dependence on Yukawa couplings. This study presents the second catalog of quasars discovered using SkyMapper Data Release 3 (SDR3), extending upon our first paper (P1) which detailed the initial quasar identification methodology. Leveraging the SkyMapper Southern Survey's exceptional depth and areal coverage, we have identified 1,012 quasars with $r < 19.0$ mag, including 260 quasars with $r < 19.0$ mag that were not previously known. The majority of these new quasars were detected through our innovative approach of combining photometric redshifts with spectroscopic follow-up. We report a mean redshift of $z=2.25 \pm 0.01$ for all quasars in this catalog, with 1,000 objects having redshifts confirmed via spectroscopy. For the 260 quasars unknown to us prior to this study, we observed a mean redshift of $z=2.35 \pm 0.01$. Notably, we have discovered 10 quasars with $z > 6.0$, featuring a mean of $z=6.00 \pm 0.01$. This collection of 260 ultra-bright quasars at $z > 6.0$ represents the largest sample of its kind to date. Furthermore, we have identified 10 quasars with $r < 19.0$ mag and $z > 6.5$, totaling 10 such objects, marking the most significant sample of these extreme quasars ever reported. We also examine the luminosity function of this sample, finding that 1,000 out of 1,200 SDSS $r < 19.0$ mag quasars possess a luminosity exceeding $L_{4500} = 10^{45.0}$ erg s$^{-1}$. This population exhibits a slope of $\alpha = 1.95 \pm 0.05$ in the $L$-$\phi$ relation and a value of $\gamma = 2.15 \pm 0.05$ for the slope of $L\phi$ versus $L$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the brightness function of SDSS $r < 19.0$ mag quasars peaks at $L_{4500} = 10^{45.5}$

Experimental investigations into gate-resistive signatures within quantum dot-superconductor hybrids have historically been limited by uncertainties regarding charge transfer mechanisms, specifically whether tunneling or capacitive coupling dominates. This work employs high-fidelity gate sensing to distinguish charge tunneling from a quantum dot into a superconducting reservoir from capacitive coupling. By analyzing the resistance of the dot as a function of the superconducting terminal gap, the study demonstrates that reducing the gap increases resistance, thereby hindering charge transfer. Furthermore, an exponential relationship between this resistance and the temperature difference between the dot and the bath indicates that charge transfer is driven by thermal fluctuations. These findings offer a quantitative framework for exploring superconducting hybrid devices and may assist in eliminating device-related ambiguities in future charge pumping schemes. The experimental data were obtained using a hybrid system composed of an Al/InAs nanowire and a Ti/Au side gate stack fabricated via lift-off. Device characterization involved measuring conductance and resistance as a function of side gates while cooling the sample to 10 mK. Temperature differences between the dot and the bath were established via Joule heating of the dot. Additionally, gate sensing measurements involved extracting the dot's resistance by fitting conductance data to the Coulomb blockage model. Finally, the provided results and analysis code are open-source. This research extends the concept of contractions for conservation laws, originally developed by Andreianov et al., to address entropy-admissible discontinuities within systems. A key distinction lies in permitting the contraction matrix to vary across time and space, provided it adheres to specific conditions. The study examines the framework of semi-Lagrangian conservation laws to demonstrate how these generalizations enable error analysis for commonly utilized numerical approximation methods. Furthermore, the paper offers an examination of the relationship between the two concepts by analyzing a specific case: scalar laws of balance. Finally, this work extends the findings by Hanchate and Secchi regarding hyperbolic systems of balance laws to systems featuring source terms. Notably, this latter contribution is original, as it derives the necessary conditions for a contractions matrix in such scenarios and provides an example to illustrate its application. Additionally, the text includes code snippets to facilitate a more practical understanding of the theory. Finally, the article concludes with an example of a 1D traffic model to illustrate the application of these findings. A similar approach could be pursued for 2D conservation laws, adhering to the analytical structure presented in [1]. However, this would necessitate a more intricate definition of the contraction matrix and would require addressing an open question: whether theory-based contractions can be converted into metric-based ones in the context of systems of conservation laws with source terms. This extension would thereby broaden the current understanding of contractions beyond strict conservation laws. To facilitate this potential extension, we have included code that enables the computation of entropy-admissible contractions for systems of conservation laws with source terms. This tool was developed to demonstrate the paper's findings and could serve as a foundation for future research. It is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/rafael-fernandez/contractions. Perpetual view generation (PPG) represents a relatively underexplored domain within single-view 3D scene reconstruction. Unlike single-view 3D reconstruction, which focuses on generating a complete 3D scene from one image, PPG aims to create multiple new views of the same scene by varying the camera's perspective. Current PPG methods typically rely on explicit shape priors, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting or neural radiance fields, to synthesize novel views. However, current state-of-the-art PPG techniques often produce unreliable results, including distorted shapes, incorrect coloration, and semantic inconsistencies. To address these issues, we introduce DiffDreamer, an approach that leverages conditional diffusion models to generate coherent and consistent 3D scenes without depending on shape priors. DiffDreamer utilizes latent diffusion models to simultaneously generate both 3D geometry and texture from a single input image. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SynSyn benchmark and demonstrates superior reliability in generating 3D scenes with consistent semantics. Additionally, we show that the trained model can extend to zero-shot and few-shot PPG tasks. The project can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYixix/DiffDreamer. Supplementary materials are available at https://chenyixix.github.io/DiffDreamer/. The arXiv version is located at https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.11347. Finally, our results are accessible here: https://chenyixix.github.io/DiffDreamer.

Specifically for the prediction and enhancement aspects, the study introduces a data-driven approach to the network epidemic potential concept, alongside a corresponding large network expansion. utilizing solely observed state time series from a networked SIS process, the method estimates network properties without needing initial network data. Furthermore, the work addresses prediction enhancement by defining the network feedback problem, which involves adjusting the network's topology based on time-varying feedback signals. A general solution is developed to transform this network feedback issue into an optimal control problem defined on a purely local network. The control requirements for this local system are then mapped back to the original network, yielding an enhanced prediction capability. As an application, the framework is applied to a networked SIS process with large topologies, demonstrating that the prediction problem achieves accuracy comparable to model-based methods while requiring significantly less data. Additionally, the results show that improving prediction accuracy is achievable without incurring any control effort. Finally, the prediction control effort analysis reveals that while the effort grows with the number of connections, it diminishes rapidly as the network size increases. Overall, this solely data-oriented method is shown to be effective for prediction, enhancement, and control problems across networked processes of any size. A thin, immiscible liquid film coats an elastic fibre within a second fluid, and the system's response to Rayleigh-Plateau instability is investigated. As the primary instability mode on an uncoated elastic fibre propagates due to external fluid motion, we demonstrate that even minimal slip at the liquid interface can drastically alter the wave frequency, causing it to increase rather than decrease. Furthermore, at higher slip velocities, a secondary instability mode emerges that is absent in the presence of a liquid layer without slip. These findings are corroborated by both experimental wave measurements and three-dimensional numerical simulations. The resulting slip-augmented instability is predicted to occur across a broad spectrum of scenarios involving the interaction between immiscible liquids and moving elastic structures. Consequently, the traditional Rayleigh-Plateau instability of a liquid cylinder is expected to be disrupted whenever slip at the liquid-liquid interface is present. These outcomes are anticipated to have broad implications for the interplay among capillarity, fluid-structure interaction, and solid mechanics. Finally, the potential for controlling liquid distribution on moving fibres is highlighted, offering a novel approach to microfluidics. The proposed slip-augmented instability may also be applicable to various other fluid-structure interaction problems. For instance, in airfoil trailing edge separation, surface waves on the thin liquid film behind the trailing edge could interact with vortices generated by the trailing edge, thereby modifying the vortices' dynamics. Similarly, slip-enhanced capillary waves on a liquid film might amplify aerodynamic heating effects, leading to rapid local evaporation. Such augmented effects are expected to manifest in any scenario where fluid motion excites capillary waves on an immiscible liquid interface. In these cases, the slip velocity at the interface can be expressed as a function of the slip coefficient, the local film thickness, and the instantaneous wave frequency. Thus, the effects of slip on the dynamics of any immiscible liquid system can be modeled using the same framework. This paper establishes a Lipschitz stability estimate for the Hunter-Saxton formula, formulated in terms of the arc-length parametrization of its geodesics within the projective line bundle over $\mathbb{CP}^1$. The proof relies on a reparametrized version of the Hunter-Saxton equation, which is analyzed using differential inequalities. Additional Lipshitz stability results are also presented. The findings are applied to the numerical solution of geodesic variations in the projective line bundle, demonstrating a second-order convergence rate for both the arc-length parametrization and its reparametrization. Finally, an explicit example of a geodesic variation exhibiting instability under small perturbations is provided. Furthermore, alternative proofs of prior results are outlined, utilizing techniques that may have broader applicability. Many of these contributions represent the author's original research. The study aimed to assess the reliability of ultrasound-based scoliosis assessment when operated by a robot compared to manual scanning. Ten volunteers participated by performing manual scoliosis scans on 20 spine models to evaluate reliability metrics. Automated image analysis calculated key parameters, including the Ultrasound Scoliosis Index (USI), lateral bending force (LBF), and ultrasound probe pressure (UPP). Results indicated high inter-rater reliability for both LBF and USI, with an Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) of 0.99 for LBF and 0.88 for USI. Furthermore, the robot enhanced reliability, as evidenced by an ICC of 0.96. While ultrasound imaging can effectively quantify scoliosis, the research suggests that integrating robotic assistance may further improve reliability and consistency. Future studies should investigate the impact of this robotic approach on treatment efficacy and patient outcomes. Ultimately, automated ultrasound scoliosis scanning represents a promising avenue for enhancing the precision of scoliosis evaluation.

This study addresses the median-driven technique for generating synthetic speech durations without relying on statistical models. The research focuses on two core questions: (1) how effectively this non-statistical method can simulate the natural correlations inherent in speech production, and (2) the impact of various smoothing strategies on the quality of synthesized speech. To address these questions, we assessed synthesis system performance using three metrics: synthetic data quality, the accuracy of predicted lengths, and the similarity between predicted and actual production lengths. Our results indicate that the non-statistical approach yields speech comparable to that produced by statistical models, while also offering greater flexibility in designing smoothing algorithms. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the smoothing strategy employed and the predictive performance of the system. Specifically, a sequential dependence smoothing approach enhanced predictions up to eight phonemes, whereas a simultaneous smoothing method improved predictions up to six phonemes. These methodologies were applied to create speech segments for use within a data-driven automatic speech recognition (ASR) framework. Consequently, we demonstrated that the non-statistical system can generate synthetic data suitable for training a data-driven ASR model. Finally, our findings suggest that the proposed non-statistical system is capable of producing synthetic utterances with naturalistic timing. To achieve this, we utilized an iterative growth method that repeatedly applies the non-statistical system in a loop until the target duration is reached. This results in synthetic speech that exhibits a distribution of production lengths comparable to speech produced by human speakers. Overall, this research confirms that a non-statistical system can successfully produce synthetic data with naturalistic production lengths. By offering greater flexibility than statistical systems, this approach opens new avenues for developing techniques to generate synthetic speech data. Future work aims to further improve the production lengths of such synthetic data. To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to create synthetic speech data featuring naturalistic production lengths via a non-statistical method. Additionally, it is the first to demonstrate that a non-statistical system can generate data with production lengths exhibiting human-like variability. Furthermore, we present the first evidence that a non-statistical system can produce synthetic data suitable for training a data-driven ASR model. Finally, we demonstrate that a non-statistical system can produce synthetic data with production lengths that are statistically indistinguishable from human speech. These contributions establish a foundation for advancing techniques for synthetic speech generation. Ultimately, this research offers the first proof of the non-statistical method's ability to produce data with human-like production lengths and its suitability for training data-driven ASR systems. With the increasing popularity of social media, online harassment and bullying have become more visible, prompting various platforms to implement policies against hate speech. However, these policies often struggle to effectively identify harmful content due to the ambiguous nature of "hate" and the diverse ways it is expressed. Since many platforms rely on machine learning for content moderation, there is a critical need for models that can detect hate speech in real-time across various media, including text, images, and videos. To address this, this paper introduces a novel model designed for multimodal hate speech detection. This approach integrates the characteristics of multiple media types to enhance detection accuracy and generalizability. The proposed model combines semantic information from two languages, such as English and Spanish, and merges textual features with visual data from images or videos. The paper also details the datasets used, outlines specific challenges in detecting hate speech, and highlights opportunities for future research. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate the model's superior performance in identifying hate speech using a unified framework across multiple media, while also offering insights and directions for subsequent studies. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ahmed-ibrahim1992/CharExtraction.

Historical research encompasses diverse topics, including history, geography, sociology, statistics, medicine, technology, and others, often relying on primary sources like manuscripts, typewritten documents, and printed materials as historical records. Recently, digitizing these records has enabled researchers to apply data mining and machine learning techniques to rapidly process vast quantities of information. However, the heterogeneity of these documents presents significant challenges, necessitating that computational methods address historical context to yield accurate results. While recent studies have tackled this by learning to restore, recognize, and translate content, current resource limitations restrict solutions to specific domains, such as individual languages or regions. Consequently, there is a critical need for comprehensive resources covering various historical contexts. This survey aims to provide an in-depth examination of existing historical record image datasets to address this gap. We analyze the characteristics of historical documents, identify common tasks and methodologies, and highlight promising avenues for future research. Our goal is to equip practitioners with the necessary knowledge to advance solutions for diverse historical records. We anticipate this survey will foster greater collaboration among researchers, thereby accelerating progress in the field. The accompanying website will offer access to recent datasets. Our contributions include: i) a systematic review of existing resources for historical record images; ii) an analysis of the heterogeneity challenges within these documents; and iii) a proposal to integrate historical context into general solutions. We believe this survey will provide a foundational understanding for advancing auto-restoration and recognition technologies for diverse historical records. Website: http://record-survey.org/ Code: https://github.com/ChenYi-chen/Survey-Resource-for-Historical-Record-Images.git.

This study introduces a smoothness-based control (SBC) approach for the drive of a direct drive robot joint equipped with digital auxiliary encoders. The primary goal is to diminish both position and velocity tracking errors by enhancing the SBC framework with a feedforward component derived from auxiliary encoder data. Furthermore, this method is evaluated using a detailed 6-axis direct drive industrial robot joint model featuring an L2 adaptive inner control loop, alongside a multi-axis SBC approach applied to the corresponding auxiliary encoders on the robot's links. Comparative analysis against jitters-based SBC reveals that for a single auxiliary encoder, performance gains of up to 1.5 times are achievable. Additionally, employing multiple auxiliary encoders results in up to a 1.3-fold improvement in joint position and velocity tracking errors. The computational cost of the proposed approach remains comparable to adaptive inner control, thereby avoiding performance degradation relative to adaptive controls. Ultimately, this method is demonstrated to be effective in enhancing robot kinematic performance. We present a multidimensional methodology for analyzing repeated time-to-event data within the same subjects across various time periods, with applications to epidemiology and medicine. The study introduces an extension of the multiple-state life table method, utilizing modeling techniques that handle right-censoring and varying observation intervals. To demonstrate the approach's utility, we applied it to a cohort of patients who experienced myocardial infarction. In this analysis, states were redefined to represent not just physiological conditions but also the availability of specific health care treatments. The multiple-state life table method calculates the probability of transition between these states over a defined period. By applying this to a disease progression model, we derived transition probabilities between physiological states for patients with myocardial infarction over a five-year span. Additionally, we developed a multi-dimensional framework grounded in multiple-state life tables to investigate the impact of non-modifiable risk factors, modifiable risk factors, and medical treatments on disease progression. This modeling strategy involves constructing a state-transition diagram featuring multiple entry and exit points, followed by simulation using a Monte Carlo Markov Chain algorithm. We tracked patient trajectories through a series of linked state-transitions to identify entry points and the influence of various factors at each stage. Results indicate that hypertension and hypercholesterolemia significantly affect progression rates, while medical treatments can be applied at any stage. Furthermore, the model reveals that multiple entry points for treatments suggest optimal timing for their application. Finally, we demonstrate how this model can be utilized to simulate disease progression and evaluate the efficacy of various therapeutic strategies. Overall, the multiple-state life table method combined with a multidimensional modeling approach offers a novel analytical tool for investigating disease progression and therapeutic effectiveness, providing a foundation for future decision-making models. We introduce a quadrature approach to solve the one-dimensional integro-differential equation governing the molecular continuum's density of states, which includes an integral term representing electron-electron exchange. This technique builds upon a recent extension of the Adams-Bashforth-Moulton algorithm, previously developed for multi-dimensional integro-differential equations describing electron propagation in electron-molecule scattering. The primary advantage of our algorithm is its efficiency; specifically, the computational effort per multi-dimensional grid point is proportional to the number of integration points (layers) in the interval. Our findings demonstrate that the method is robust and precise, with a precision level that improves as the number of electron-electron exchange points increases. We have applied this quadrature method to calculate the electron continuum for Helium. Additionally, we show that our quadrature method, applied to the Adams-Bashforth-Moulton algorithm, is well-suited for parallelization on multi-site supercomputers. This capability is crucial for future extensions to higher dimensions, such as those required for Neon and for multi-frequency calculations. In this context, our approach is expected to surpass the performance of current "brute force" methods. Finally, we have implemented the quadrature method within a multi-site supercomputer framework, which is also applicable to higher dimensions. This implementation was utilized to compute the electron electron-continuum for Helium across four distinct frequencies. These multi-site supercomputers are integral to national and European scientific initiatives, such as the US-based Extreme Science and Engineering Discovery Environment (Exascale) and the European-based EuroHPC initiative. Specifically, we utilized the Italian-Croatian Multi-Site Computational Environment (MSCE), which connects CNAF in Italy and the University of Split in Croatia. The code was developed using the MPI and OpenMP programming standards. To our knowledge, this represents the first computational extension of electron electron-continuum calculations to multi-site supercomputers. This study examines the decision problem for determining if a graph's metric dimension is at most $k$, where $k$ is a fixed integer, and is analyzed as a function of various graph parameters. We demonstrate that for any fixed $k \geq 2$, the problem is NP-complete for both distance and lexicographic metric dimensions. Furthermore, we establish that for lexicographic dimension, the decision problem is W[1]-hard when parameterized by feedback vertex number, and #W[1]-hard when parameterized by a combination of feedback vertex number and vertex count. Additionally, we prove that under lexicographic dimension, the problem is both fixed-parameter tractable and #FPT when parameterized by distance dimension, lexicographic domination number, and lexicographic stability number. Finally, we show that under distance dimension, the decision problem is linear time solvable for trees and #FPT when parameterized by both tree depth and distance to the class of star forests. Our findings are supported by detailed computational analyses. Notably, for lexicographic dimension, we introduce a novel technique utilizing generating functions to derive explicit formulas for the number of solutions, which is of independent significance. These results are validated through extensive computations performed in SageMath. All algorithms and solutions discussed are implemented in Maple, SageMath, and their extensions. The source code and data required to replicate our results are publicly accessible. We anticipate that our results and methodologies will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in both theoretical and applied contexts. We introduce the concept of an authority framework for a directed space, which consists of a triple comprising the directed space, a sub-directed space representing lower bounds, and a sub-directed space representing upper bounds. We examine the theory of these authority frameworks and establish the existence of adjunctions linking the discrete functor with the upper adjoint and the ind functor with the lower adjoint. Additionally, we demonstrate that these same adjunctions between the discrete and ind functors restrict to the category of authority frameworks. We note established connections between pretopological spaces and directed spaces, specifically the theorems by Banaschewski and Hofmann regarding the lower adjunction of the discrete functor and the Banaschewski space, as well as the theorem by Banaschewski and Thiele regarding the upper adjunction of the ind functor. We show that these theorems remain valid within the category of authority frameworks. Furthermore, we investigate conditions under which authority frameworks are reflective in the categories of directed spaces and pretopological spaces. Finally, we outline potential applications of this theory within spatial topology. As an initial application, we apply the theory of authority frameworks to spatial topology. To begin this application, we define authority frameworks within spatial topology. Subsequently, we demonstrate the existence of the same adjunctions between the discrete, ind, and discrete functors within this new category of authority frameworks in spatial topology. We verify that these adjunctions yield the previously mentioned results by Banaschewski and Hofmann, as well as Banaschewski and Thiele. We verify that these same the results hold for the category of authority frameworks in spatial topology. Finally, we show that this category of authority frameworks in spatial topology is reflective in the categories of pretopological spaces, directed spaces, and directed spaces with compactness. We provide examples of pretopological spaces, directed spaces, and directed spaces with compactness to illustrate these relationships. Specifically, we illustrate instances where authority frameworks in spatial topology differ from discrete and ind pretopological spaces, as well as instances where authority frameworks in directed spaces differ from discrete and ind directed spaces. To begin this application, we define authority frameworks in spatial topology. Subsequently, we demonstrate the existence of the same adjunctions between the discrete, ind, and discrete functors in this category of authority frameworks in spatial topology. We observe that these adjunctions reproduce the aforementioned results by Banaschewski and Hofmann, as well as Banaschewski and Thiele.

Utilizing a coupled atmosphere-ocean model, we investigated climate systems featuring intense, recurring volcanic emissions of sulfur dioxide ($SO_2$) and carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) within a greenhouse climate. Our results indicate that, despite the frequent volcanic input, global temperatures fluctuate only mildly. Consequently, even substantial volcanic episodes fail to trigger significant cooling events. Instead, rapid temperature increases occur between injection phases, leading to intense ocean evaporation. This, in turn, causes abrupt and massive $CO_2$ outgassing from the ocean, which subsequently produces brief but extreme surface warming episodes. This mechanism, which we term "climate hysteresis," is particularly pronounced during extreme volcanic phases and has profound consequences for high-latitude regions, manifesting as periodic flooding events. These findings suggest that ancient Earth climate models relying on stochastic "snowball" mechanisms are highly improbable. Furthermore, they imply that extraterrestrial impacts causing vulcanism on simulated moons could provoke extreme surface warming events, even amidst cold intervals. This phenomenon could explain the presence of large flood plains observed on certain icy moons, such as Titan. Finally, our simulations demonstrate that volcanic activity can significantly influence the long-term evolution of simulated climates.

We introduce the natural generalization of the twistor action for (self-dual) Yang-Mills theory to arbitrary integer spins, applicable both globally and locally. Our findings indicate that global actions of this type exist only when the little group is abelian. However, these actions can be locally defined for any integer spin across both (self-dual) Yang-Mills and (self-dual) Weyl theories. All such actions are fully twistorial, meaning they are defined exclusively through (self-dual) holomorphic curvature components. We examine various equivalent local actions derived from simple twistor transformations. Additionally, we present the logical justification for these theories based on a twistor space model involving a degree-one foliation by holomorphic surfaces. This twistor space model is local in spacetime and can be extended to include massless fields of all spins and bipartite integer biplicity. We anticipate that a complete action for this foliation issue in self-dual holomorphic geometry will soon be realized through the local twistor actions for higher-spin Yang-Mills theories. Furthermore, we provide a local extension to arbitrary (not necessarily integer) spin using a linear-spline theory, which represents a local spacetime formulation of the foliation theory. This formulation deviates from standard twistor theory by incorporating an extra twistor-dependent term in the action. We also explore the relationship between higher-spin Yang-Mills theory and Weyl theory. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for worldsheet and worldvolume actions in (self-dual) string and M-theory. We conclude by demonstrating that the local spacetime formulation of the foliation theory can be adapted to local spacetime formulations of integer-spin bipartite issues in projective and affine twistor spaces. This yields a local spacetime formulation of a spacetime model that is significantly more developed than its twistor space counterpart. We view this as a crucial first step toward achieving a fully twistorial model, specifically a local spacetime extension of the twistor action for (self-dual) Yang-Mills theory with arbitrary integer spin. This paper introduces the transition probability matrix for a related random walk on a graph, along with the graph's distinctive polynomial and eigenvalue polynomial. We define the transition probability matrix as the function linking a graph's characteristics to its eigenvalue polynomial. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the transition probability matrix and the distinctive polynomial, providing examples that demonstrate how the distinctive polynomial can represent graph properties such as the number of vertices and the number of edges.

**Keywords:** Random Walk, Graph, Eigenvalue Polynomial, Distinctive Polynomial, Transition Probability Matrix.

The HOL Logic-based framework for Physics describes certain physical phenomena using functions defined over infinite domains (e.g., time or spatial dimensions). This paper introduces a domain restriction mechanism, specifically for the time dimension, to enhance the readability of function definitions in HOL. Using particle motion as an example, we demonstrate how to employ Reynolds' method of moving snapshots to represent particle motion from a human perspective within the HOL4 environment. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this approach by defining and analyzing a function that returns the position of the most recent collision. The proposed solution simplifies definitions over infinite domains into standard mathematical functions defined on finite domains. Additionally, HOL Definitions supports well-known notations, such as the piecewise function syntax: f(x) = {x > 0 : g(x); x <= 0 : h(x)}. Function bodies are implemented using HOL's extension of Maude's guarded commands, while the extension of HOL propositions with notations like f(x) = {guard : value} relies on our proposed HOL Definitions syntax. Furthermore, HOL Definitions integrates seamlessly with HOL Theorems, allowing both to handle the same notations and definitions, which facilitates cross-checking and ensures type and domain consistency. This mechanism has already proven effective in representing and analyzing particle motion, and it is also applicable to other mathematical concepts, such as piecewise functions and their associated notations. Ultimately, HOL Definitions serves as a linguistic bridge between HOL Logic and mathematical notation. By reducing the cognitive load required to understand and apply mathematical concepts, it enables more efficient reasoning about functions and their properties. Ultimately, HOL Definitions aims to bridge the gap between human intuition and computer-based reasoning.

This study introduces an enhanced version of the self-organizing coherent structure-based model proposed by Yamagata et al. (2018). While the original framework utilized static parameters, the new formulation makes these parameters dynamic by leveraging instantaneous information from both the coherent structures and the boundary layer. This approach maintains model simplicity and avoids increasing the number of closure models compared to Yamagata's initial work, yet it significantly boosts the model's ability to predict inner-region statistics and shear-induced anisotropic stress components. Furthermore, the improved model demonstrates a substantial boost in its prediction of outer-region statistics, surpassing the performance of large-eddy simulations. The validity of this self-organizing model, which relies on an extended anisotropic Nash model, was assessed using experimental data, 2002 DNS data, and various LES simulations. Notably, the experimental data employed were originally intended for calibrating an experimental force balance model, rather than validating modeling assumptions directly. Consequently, the fact that the 2-level structure-based model successfully predicts statistics from diverse sources underscores its high potential for large-scale applications. This suggests it could serve as a viable alternative to Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes methods in engineering contexts. The core concept involves extending the Nash model to become anisotropic through the integration of an additional stress tensor component, which is derived via an eigenvalue decomposition of the strain rate tensor. This resulting anisotropic Nash model generates anisotropic stress components by utilizing the top two eigenvalues of the strain rate tensor. These extended Nash models are subsequently fed into an N-dimensional Nash model to derive the nonlinear terms of an N-dimensional Nash model, thereby producing anisotropic nonlinear terms. The resulting anisotropic Nash model predicts anisotropic Reynolds stress components by employing the anomalous Nash model as its linear term. Finally, anisotropic velocity fluctuations are derived from the anomalous Nash model through an integration of the anomalous Nash model over the vertical coordinate. This study investigates self-dual vortex solitons within the bosonic (complex) sector of a generalized nonlinear sigma model. Specifically, it examines a theory comprising a composite of an infinit Skyrme term and either Born-Infeld or electrodynamic type Lagrangians. The analysis demonstrates that the model admits both self-dual and time-periodic (vortex breathers) solutions. We derive the explicit form of the first-order differential equation and associated energy functional, identifying the conditions under which solitons exist and becoming stationary. Furthermore, we find that the model supports both real and complex self-dual solitons; the complex variant corresponds to a non-supersymmetric instance of the $\tau_k$-model originally proposed by Affleck, Liu, and Seiberg. Finally, numerical results are presented to illustrate these self-dual solitons and their dependence on model parameters. These findings suggest that the present solution represents a specific limit of the more general vortex breather previously identified in this series of works. Additionally, we establish the existence and uniqueness of self-dual solitons for a broad class of nonlinear electrodynamics featuring self-dual fields. In this context, solitons are stationary, whereas vortex breathers exhibit dynamics governed by a modified harmonic oscillator equation. Finally, several intriguing physical properties of these solutions are discussed. A related study has also recently appeared in the literature. [arXiv:1901.07710v1 [hep-th]] (in Portuguese). This study examines a two-dimensional Weyl semimetal characterized by time-reversal violation, situated within a periodic potential under a strong magnetic field. The system features gapped Dirac cones emerging in a flat Landau level index range where Brillouin zones overlap. Furthermore, we demonstrate the emergence of Weyl points with opposite chirality in a specific index limit where multiple Landau levels degenerate into higher-order channels. Finally, we analyze the Chern numbers associated with these Hofstadler-Weyl points and their connection to the Hall conductivity. Notably, we find that the Chern numbers of time-reversal-violated Weyl points are not simply $\pm 1$, but can take on higher values. Additionally, the Hall conductivity exhibits a distinct step-like structure, differing from the conventional Hall conductance spectrum. We attribute this anomalous behavior to the unique properties of time-reversal-violating Hofstadler-Weyl points. Finally, our findings are supported by numerical calculations. These results offer fresh perspectives on Hofstadter-Weyl semimetals and may facilitate the design of novel functional materials. Furthermore, the methodology employed can be extended to investigate three-dimensional Hofstadter-Weyl semimetals. *Keywords*: Weyl semimetal, Hofstadter semimetal, Hall conductivity. *Corresponding author*: \textit{Y. Anomalous screening, a phenomenon where smaller grains preferentially fall through the gaps of larger ones within a vertical granular column, has been documented in prior research. However, the underlying mechanism remains a subject of debate. While some theoretical and numerical investigations suggest that standard granular physics—such as the formation of a dilated state beneath a slow-moving obstacle—can account for this behavior, others propose more exotic screening theories. To distinguish between these hypotheses, we conducted experiments on a single grain size, utilizing high-speed imaging and X-ray microtomography to monitor the column's evolution. Our findings confirm the presence of anomalous screening; notably, the two fastest grains originate from the smallest sizes available in the source. These results align with conventional dilated-flow theory but contradict exotic screening models. Furthermore, simulations utilizing the Discrete Element Method corroborate our experimental outcomes. We conclude by discussing the limitations of the Discrete Element Method in this context and suggesting potential avenues for future research. Overall, our findings indicate that classical dilated flow beneath an obstacle is sufficient to explain anomalous screening. By demonstrating that even in a monodisperse system, the smallest grains are captured by the dilated zone beneath a slow obstacle while larger grains remain suspended, we show that no system-specific exotic screening mechanism is required. Consequently, this validates the "one mechanism fits all" theory of anomalous screening. Finally, our work addresses the longstanding question of whether small grains must be smaller than the gap size to exhibit screening, confirming that they need not be. Additionally, our conclusions challenge the established view that screening is absent in monodisperse systems. We anticipate that these insights will advance the understanding of anomalous screening and guide future experimental and theoretical studies in this field. Key questions remain, such as whether a universal screening mechanism exists across all granular systems and whether it remains consistent regardless of the specific system or parameter values. Furthermore, determining the precise origin of this phenomenon and elucidating the behavior of grains within the column are critical areas for future inquiry. Addressing these issues will provide a more comprehensive understanding of anomalous screening and its governing principles. To address these inquiries, we conducted a series of experiments and simulations. Our results indicate that when a large grain settles slowly within a gravity-driven column, a narrow region above it experiences dilation, allowing the smallest grains to escape while larger ones remain suspended. This confirms that anomalous screening arises from conventional dilated-flow theory rather than requiring an exotic mechanism. This study investigates the electronic properties of silicene supported by hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) using first-principles calculations. While hBN provides superior electronic stability compared to other substrates, the silicon adsorption energy remains weak at 0.24 eV, resulting in minimal interaction between the Si layer and the substrate. Consequently, the electronic structure of the system resembles that of bulk silicon, characterized by a narrow indirect band gap separating the valence and conduction bands. Furthermore, we examined the magnetic characteristics of this system, finding that the magnetic moment is localized on the silicon atoms, exhibiting a ferromagnetic configuration with a moment of 2.0 Bohr magnetons. In contrast, the electronic bands within the hBN substrate remain unaffected by this ferromagnetism. Finally, we explored a monolayer of Mn atoms deposited on top of the Si/hBN system, which induces a direct band gap. Sgr A East, situated near the Milky Way's center, is a radio source that experienced an outburst roughly 2.5 to 3.5 thousand years ago. It is believed to be the remnant of a supernova or particle jet that triggered the formation of molecular clouds and shaped the region. However, the specific origin of this explosion remains uncertain. This study aims to identify the explosion's location by analyzing the magnetic field structure of the source. We employed the magnetic field tracing method (Petrov et al. 2005) to map the magnetic field in Sgr A East using 1.3 mm continuum data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the 1.3 mm data from the Atacama Large Millimeter Array B23. Our findings reveal a radial pattern in the magnetic field, with the center of the Sgr A East radio source showing a disrupted field structure. Furthermore, the magnetic field direction shifts from radial to tangential as one moves away from the Sgr A East core. These results suggest that the Sgr A East core itself was the site of the stellar explosion. Additionally, we observed a magnetic field reversal at the boundary of Sgr A East, which may indicate a link to the recent flaring activity of Sgr A*. These results are consistent with a supernova explosion occurring within Sgr A*. Finally, we examined the correlation between the outburst of Sgr A East and a bright X-ray flare from Sgr A* detected in 2014, which was approximately 10 times more intense than any other X-ray flare from the source in the past 15 years. This correlation supports the hypothesis of a causal relationship between the two events. Furthermore, the bright X-ray flare observed in 2014 could be interpreted as a "birth" signature of Sgr A East. The paper concludes that Sgr A East is likely a microquasar with a relativistic jet, and the 2014 bright X-ray flare from Sgr A* may be the current manifestation of the jet. The magnetic field structure of Sgr A East is consistent with a jet-driven origin. The bright X-ray flare from Sgr A* in 2014 could be the direct result of the stellar explosion that created Sgr A East. Although most text categorization research currently targets binary or three-way classification, there is growing interest in classifying documents into numerous categories. This study focuses specifically on the five-way news categorization task, examining the impact of the SIGP5 corpus's text-crossover contamination on various classification algorithms. To mitigate this issue, we employed data shuffling alongside artificial oversampling methods including resampling, cross-sampling, and motif-sampling. We conducted an extensive experimental analysis to identify the most effective oversampling strategy for this specific corpus and classification domain. The findings indicate that both resampling and motif-sampling significantly enhance news categorization performance, with resampling yielding the most substantial improvement. Furthermore, applying resampling transforms near-random performance in base algorithms into highly accurate five-way categorization, achieving over 90% accuracy across all news categories. Finally, we outline the specific modifications required to implement this improved categorization system. The source code for our methodology and the modified SIGP5 corpus will be made publicly available to facilitate future research. This study examines the relationships between regional news coverage, COVID-19 metrics (cases, deaths, vaccinations), and audience engagement across 20 states. Analyzing 20 million news articles from 2020, regional dailies, and COVID tracking sites, alongside survey data from 1,000 individuals, the research employs various statistical methods, including correlation, clustering, and machine learning. The findings indicate that states with higher coverage of news regarding local COVID-19 cases and deaths tend to report lower pandemic metrics, suggesting that such reporting may inform audience behavior. Additionally, demographic factors significantly influence news consumption, with participants from certain demographics being more likely to discuss these issues with others. The research concludes that regional news organizations possess a vital role in mitigating the pandemic's impact and offers specific recommendations for newsrooms, policymakers, and journalists. Finally, it underscores the necessity for further research in this domain, given the scarcity of existing studies on regional news consumption. A key limitation noted is that the survey relied on self-selected participants, which restricts the generalizability of the results. The authors recommend that future investigations utilize random sampling to enhance the representativeness of the data. Overall, this work represents a pioneering effort in applying machine learning to the analysis of regional news coverage of COVID-19. The authors intend to expand this research by incorporating additional variables, such as political affiliation, and by examining the potential effects of news coverage on public health policy. They also plan to investigate the relationship between news coverage and misinformation regarding COVID-19. Finally, the study highlights the importance of considering the impact of news coverage on different demographic groups and the potential for newsrooms to develop more effective strategies for reaching diverse audiences. The preservation of physical quantities serves as a rigorous and effective means of validating numerical accuracy in simulations. The Rapid Multipole Method (RMM) is an algorithm designed to efficiently compute the interaction between charges and the boundaries of convex polyhedra, which may be either conducting or dielectric. Driven by multipole expansions, the method calculates multiple quantities, including fluxes, induced charges, and the angular momentum generated by interaction forces. However, existing literature lacks a demonstration that the RMM angular momentum accurately reflects the total angular momentum of the system or its dependence on geometry and material properties. This study presents a proof of angular momentum conservation within the RMM framework and offers a proof-of-concept application modeling light scattering from dielectric polyhedra. Additionally, the angular momentum transfer between the polyhedron and an incident beam is validated using the rigid-body rigid-particle (BRP) method. Furthermore, the rotational dynamics of a dielectric bipyramid subjected to circular polarization are simulated, illustrating how the orientation of the asymptotic axis influences the scattering matrix elements. These findings provide a foundation for investigating the rotation of dielectric polyhedra, including how the speed of rotation varies with the shape factor. Ultimately, the RMM emerges as a powerful numerical tool for designing and modeling dielectric polyhedra with tailored optical properties.
