We investigate traditional cosmological collider physics within single-field inflationary frameworks that generate primordial tensor and higher-multipole primordial scalar perturbations. We establish the optimal observational windows for detecting these signals and identify the optimal functional forms of their power spectra. Through numerical simulations involving $10^4$ Monte Carlo samples, we demonstrate that primordial tensor perturbations exhibit a double-kick signature when the scalar spectrum follows a $(k/\kappa)^n$ form with $n=-1, 0, 1$, where $\kappa$ represents the comoving sound horizon at the collider energy scale. Furthermore, we reveal that for $n=-1$, the primordial tensor perturbation spectrum displays a distinct peak when $k \approx \kappa/2$, a feature that serves as an robust indicator of the collider energy scale. We also derive an analytical expression for the primordial tensor spectrum under these conditions and observe the optimal signal window for $r=10^{-3}$. Additionally, we find that for $n=1$, the tensor spectrum scales as $k^2$ at small scales, mimicking the primordial gravitational wave spectrum predicted by standard single-field inflation. Finally, we analyze tensor spectra with $s$-wave resonances and determine the optimal signal windows for these scenarios. In parallel, we examine the impact of non-Gaussianity on tensor signals and find that it produces a double-kick signature with peaks on both the small and large-scale ends. Our findings indicate that for $f_{NL} \gtrsim 10^{-3}$, the tensor signal is amplified by a factor of approximately $10^3$. Consequently, we propose that future space-based gravitational wave detectors should prioritize searches for these specific tensor spectra to effectively probe high-energy physics occurring during inflation. This study paves the way for future investigations into multi-field inflationary models and those containing massive particles. In subsequent work, we will explore how multiple fields and massive particles leave distinct imprints on tensor signals, thereby constraining high-energy physics during inflation. This report focuses exclusively on traditional cosmological collider physics, whereas non-trivial features in scalar spectra are addressed in a separate study. Overall, this work provides a foundational basis for searching for primordial gravitational waves and a starting point for investigating physics at high scales during inflation. We anticipate that these results will significantly advance the field of cosmological collider physics. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaozhongyi/CosmologicalColliderPhysics. Filter visualization is a fundamental technique for interpreting the features that deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have learned. This work introduces a new framework, Hidden Visual-Semantic Filter Attention (HiVSA), which integrates existing methods to more effectively uncover the visual-semantic relationships within network filters. Unlike current approaches that rely on direct connections between input activations and class labels, our method leverages intermediate filters to connect visual inputs with semantic outputs. Specifically, we sample filters across various layers and orientations to highlight those that are discriminative and closely tied to specific categories. By synthesizing information from these selected filters, we generate visual representations of the networks that can be employed for downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach uncovers deep visual-semantic relationships more effectively than current methods and that these visualized networks can significantly enhance filter selection and distillation for state-of-the-art architectures. Furthermore, our strategy for choosing and selecting filters yields superior performance across multiple datasets compared to state-of-the-art filter visualization techniques. Additionally, we propose a novel unsupervised training method for deep CNNs that surpasses state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks. Extensive experiments confirm that our strategy produces visualizations that are both more interpretable and semantically richer than those of state-of-the-art filter visualization methods. Finally, we show that the visualized networks are more robust against adversarial attacks. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply filter visualization for uncovering deep visual-semantic relationships in CNNs. The code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/hihihiV/HiVSA. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00029. We introduce a model featuring long-range attractive interactions between electrons within a phonon-mediated framework, operating within a one-dimensional repulsive Hubbard model. Our analysis reveals that this effective interaction enables the stable formation of bound bi-electron states across all phonon coupling strengths above a specific, analytically determined critical value for the square of the coupling. These bound states reside at energies lower than the Fermi energy and remain stable against electron-hole pair excitations when the coupling strength exceeds another distinct critical value. Furthermore, these findings persist in a phonon-mediated model utilizing radially symmetric interactions in two dimensions and can be achieved through optical lattice confinement in both 2D and 3D dimensions. Additionally, we propose a quantum dot setup capable of observing these bound state properties via quantum state tomography. This system involves an effective attractive interaction between electrons within the dot, alongside numerous other quantum dots serving as reservoirs. We demonstrate that the ground state energy of such a system can be minimized by solving the corresponding Schrödinger equation using the Nth-order trapezoidal rule. Finally, within the 1D framework, we show that increasing the phonon bath temperature leads to a significant rise in the energy of the bi-electron state, yet it remains well below the Fermi energy even at the highest achievable bath temperatures. Consequently, this system represents a robust candidate for delivering a long-range attractive interaction mediated by phonons in higher dimensions, remaining stable at all phonon bath temperatures. This model holds promise for exploring fundamental aspects of high-Tc superconductivity in cuprates. Specifically, our findings suggest that the mechanism of electron-phonon pairing in cuprates may involve both attractive interactions between electrons in real space and those in reciprocal space. We further show that this mechanism remains stable at all phonon bath temperatures, including those relevant to high-Tc cuprates. Moreover, our proposed model offers a pathway to investigate the influence of spin fluctuations on electron-phonon mediated pairing in cuprates. Finally, we demonstrate that the mechanism of electron-phonon pairing in cuprates can be simulated using available quantum dot setups. These theoretical findings suggest that this approach could facilitate a new experimental method for studying electron-phonon mediated pairing in cuprates by utilizing quantum dots. This methodology involves measuring the energy of the bi-electron state within a quantum dot exhibiting effective attractive interactions and comparing it against solutions to the Schrödinger equation for the system. Our proposed model provides a robust theoretical foundation for observing the mechanism of electron-phonon pairing in cuprates using quantum dots

The MPHIA survey, conducted in 2017, is a nationally representative study regarding HIV, sexual, and reproductive health in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This work introduces a semi-automated method to generate causal graphs from MPHIA's individual-level data, utilizing machine learning to analyze free-text responses to open-ended questions. The resulting causal graphs offer insights for health interventions, demonstrating how one variable might influence another. Specifically, we examine various interventions, including the impact of parental education on a child's HIV status, the effects of health facility attendance on sexual activity, and the relationship between a partner's health behaviors and an individual's HIV infection. We evaluate our approach by testing interventions for which causal graphs exist, as well as by proposing interventions with absent graphs. Furthermore, we explore the challenges and limitations of our methodology. Overall, our approach facilitates causal inquiries across any pair of variables in a causal graph, distinguishing it from existing intervention evaluation methods that require specific prior knowledge of certain variables. This capability allows MPHIA investigators to address causal questions regarding novel variables, thereby maximizing the utility of the survey data. Our method relies on learning word embeddings from MPHIA data to assess semantic similarity between interview responses and candidate variables; however, these embeddings are sparse due to the limited vocabulary in the individual dataset. To address this limitation, we employ transfer learning to incorporate external knowledge from a large text corpus. We validate our approach within the context of HIV intervention in the DRC by evaluating interventions related to parental education, health facility visits, partners' health behaviors, and parental health behaviors. We assess performance based on causal graph size, semantic accuracy, and causal effect estimation. The method successfully identifies causal graphs for all evaluated interventions, with an average of 17 causal effects per graph. However, the method may struggle to capture causal relationships when interview responses contain significant domain-specific knowledge not present in the transfer learning corpus. Additionally, the method may miss causal effects if the interview response lacks semantic similarity to the candidate variable. Finally, we estimate the computational complexity of the method. We acknowledge the limitations of the current study, particularly the lack of a gold standard for evaluating interview answer quality, and propose two solutions to address these gaps. We anticipate that our method will be valuable for researchers aiming to understand causal effects from individual-level data. The code and MPHIA individual-level data are available at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/CSA.

The phase diagram of the B20 magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ under external magnetic fields was determined using neutron scattering and muon spin rotation. In fields applied along specific crystallographic directions, metastable skyrmion lattice phases were found to melt via two distinct mechanisms: a sudden collapse at elevated temperatures and a gradual dissolution. A model incorporating magnetoelastic coupling successfully accounts for these unique melting behaviors. This research highlights that controlling elastic properties can be essential for stabilizing topological magnetic structures. Furthermore, it underscores that metastability must be accounted for when interpreting experimental data to uncover new phases. These findings offer a foundation for developing devices based on dynamic spin textures in this material. Additionally, the methodology used to identify metastable phases may be applicable to a broader range of materials and scientific disciplines. Finally, the mechanisms governing the metastable decay of the skyrmion lattice are expected to be universally applicable. The paper begins by introducing the concept of the δ-graph associated with a given graph G, which represents the set of edges connecting non-adjacent vertex pairs in G. Leveraging this, we define the first and second δ-adjacency matrices for any graph G, denoted as ADM₁(G) and ADM₂(G), respectively. These matrices are constructed such that their entries correspond to the out-degree and out+in-degree of vertices in G, respectively. Consequently, we transform the standard balance problem on a directed graph D into a set of independent balance problems on its δ-graphs. This reduction relies on the fact that a directed graph is balanceable if and only if it is weakly connected and contains no strongly connected subgraph of order greater than 1. Furthermore, we establish two theorems providing necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of balanced orientations for any arbitrary digraph. Finally, we formulate the initial problem as a stable point problem within the space of diagonal matrices. Using this framework, we derive another existence theorem for balanced orientations of any digraph, which generalizes the earlier theorems. Additionally, we demonstrate the application of this method in resolving the orientation problem for any regular digraph. Notably, our approach is distinct from the spectral balance problem formulation, as it does not require nullifying the second-degree Laplacian spectral coefficients. Finally, we illustrate the utility of the stable point method by addressing the isomorphism problem for a specific class of graphs. This classification was previously solved by A. A. Aref'ev through spectral methods, and we achieve the same result using the proposed stable point technique. In this context, we introduce the concept of a canonical representation for any graph, which utilizes information from its balanced orientation. The study concludes with an outline of a future algorithm for the balance problem on any graph, which is currently under development. The authors express their gratitude to A. A. Recent progress has enabled the concealement of information within deep learning models; specifically, the neural network weights are altered to facilitate the concealment of a binary message. While current state-of-the-art techniques achieve high capacity and efficiency for neural networks trained via backpropagation, they fail altogether to train batch normalization layers, which are essential for deploying large-scale networks like ResNet-50. This paper introduces a novel method termed Bayesian Concealment (BC), capable of training the entire pre-trained model, including batch normalization layers, while maintaining the same capacity and spectral efficiency as existing approaches. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that BC exhibits a distinct advantage over current methods, particularly in message-centric scenarios characterized by short messages and few receivers. ResNet-50 achieves a binary message capacity of 2 bits per million parameters, marking an 8-fold improvement over the current state-of-the-art. In contrast, a standard neural network trained using the state-of-the-art approach achieves a capacity of 2 bits per 25 million parameters. We examine the efficacy of mean-field frameworks in simulating convective dynamos by analyzing the key turbulent factors driving magnetic field generation. By leveraging the independence of individual turbulent contributions to the mean-field $\alpha$-effect, we can isolate these effects and control their intensity to map the $\alpha$-quenching curve. Our findings reveal that the $\alpha$-quenching curve derived from direct simulations of dynamo action aligns with one obtained from numerical turbulence simulations, provided that direct simulations resolve the entire spectral range of turbulent influences on $\alpha$. This confirms that $\alpha$-quenching is driven exclusively by spectral variations in helicity transfer. Furthermore, by distinguishing between scale-dependent and scale-independent components of this variation, we identify inertial range scaling as the cause of reduced $\alpha$ at smaller scales. These results demonstrate the potential of using direct turbulence simulations to efficiently explore global convective dynamo models, but only when the complete spectrum of turbulent influences is accounted for. This approach may also offer a solution to the weak-field dilemma in numerical global convective dynamos. Finally, our framework facilitates the independent exploration of other critical variables in global convective dynamos, such as the latitudinal dependence of $\alpha$ and turbulent magnetic diffusion. These capabilities are particularly valuable for directly testing hypotheses regarding magnetic field generation in the Sun and other stars. To achieve this, we introduce a dynamo model that resolves all relevant turbulent scales, thereby providing a benchmark for comparing the performance of current climate models. This work underscores the necessity of global convective dynamo models that resolve all relevant turbulent scales. While such models are computationally demanding, the recent advent of exascale computing may make this feasible. Our framework establishes a clear path toward this objective. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that current climate models may not yet be capable of resolving all relevant turbulent scales, and further research is required to determine the necessary resolution. In the meantime, we recommend that researchers carefully consider the implications of unresolved turbulent scales when interpreting convective dynamo simulations. This can be achieved by comparing their results against simulations that resolve only a subset of relevant turbulent scales. We have made our code, Dynamosim, publicly available to facilitate this process. We also outline the necessary modifications to Dynamosim to enable the investigation of turbulent influences on $\alpha$ and provide a user-friendly interface for exploring these effects. We present ALMA observations of a massive molecular outflow in the nearby starburst galaxy NGC4945, detected in CO (3-2) and traced by a bright, large-scale outflow region. The outflow exhibits a high mass of 1.5 x 10^8 solar masses, a mass outflow rate of 1000 solar masses per year, and a momentum outflow rate of 10^12 Newton seconds. Its momentum density reaches 10^10 Newton seconds per cubic parsec, surpassing the critical threshold of 10^9 Newton seconds per cubic parsec required to halt inflow. The momentum outflow rate aligns with the galaxy's star formation timescale, whereas its momentum density exceeds the critical limit for star formation regulation. The outflow originates from the central starburst, extending over a diameter of 1.5 kpc, and displays a momentum density 100 times higher than the large-scale region. This suggests that outflows are initially more intense and are suppressed by the dense central starburst, resulting in a momentum outflow rate comparable to the star formation rate, consistent with a universal outflow ratio. The bright outflow region likely arises from the interaction between the molecular gas disk and the molecular outflow. These findings support a universal model of star formation in starburst galaxies, where feedback from massive stars drives large-scale outflows. This model implies that star formation in starbursts is self-regulating, with feedback suppressing it to approximately 1% per year. Consequently, starburst galaxies are less efficient at converting gas into stars than previously assumed, which may help resolve the cosmic star formation rate crisis. The universal outflow model further suggests that feedback in star-forming galaxies is comparable to the star formation rate, indicating that feedback is the primary mechanism regulating the gas-to-stellar mass ratio in these regions. Finally, the universal outflow model implies that star formation in starbursts is self-regulating, with feedback reducing the star formation rate to roughly 1% per year. This indicates that star formation in starbursts is regulated by feedback, which is comparable to the star formation rate. The universal outflow model also suggests that feedback is similar to the star formation rate, implying that the gas-to-stellar mass ratio in starburst galaxies is lower than previously thought. This study introduces the first conservative Galerkin solver, tailored for electron ionization in plasma environments. The multicomponent quasilinear diffusion framework is particularly suited for calculating diverse collisional diffusion magnetic transport coefficients under strong magnetic fields. In such conditions, particle diffusion is highly anisotropic, and transport is governed by complex kinetic collisional integrals involving magnetic field-dependent scattering angles. The proposed Galerkin formalism addresses a broad range of multicomponent plasmas and remains applicable to arbitrary collisional models, including those with scattering angles that do not satisfy standard conservation laws. To address this, a newly developed conservation scattering angle model is presented. A key advantage of the solver is its ability to maintain total particle and energy conservation throughout the iteration of collisional integrals. This capability is achieved by deriving conservation equations from the collisional operator balance law and by constructing approximate conservation forms for scenarios where exact conservation is unattainable. The collisional operator is expanded into a series of diffusion tensors, with their coefficients determined by the collision integrals solved via the solver. To validate the conservation properties and conservation error estimates, several benchmark conservation tests were conducted. These tests confirm that the conservation scattering angle model ensures near-perfect conservation, even when applied to collisional models that violate conservation laws. Furthermore, the conservation error estimates for both energy and particle number are demonstrated to be robust. Finally, the collisional transport of a single test species is evaluated by comparing the conservation estimates against the collisional conservation laws of all other species. These conservation law comparisons show that the conservation estimates for a selected species' number and energy are reliable. The collisional transport of all species is also examined through conservation law comparisons, revealing that their number conservation laws are robust. In summary, this work provides a novel conservation scattering angle model and a conservative Galerkin solver, which together establish a reliable and efficient framework for solving quasilinear diffusion framework equations. The conservation scattering angle model and conservation error estimates are also applicable to other computational methods. These findings are expected to significantly enhance the accuracy of collisional theory calculations in magnetized plasmas and other computational fields. Additionally, the developed conservation scattering angle model and conservative Galerkin solver are expected to substantially improve the accuracy of computational methods that do not rely on scattering angle conservation laws. Finally, the conservation error estimates can serve as valuable criteria for evaluating quasilinear diffusion framework calculations. These outcomes are also expected to significantly advance the accuracy of other computational methods that do not depend on conservation scattering angle models. We introduce a general class of variable stepsize semi-explicit difference methods of multiprecision order (SDIMSIMs) tailored for standard differential equations. These schemes are demonstrated to retain the linear stability characteristics of an underlying multiprecision method, with the associated stability region determined by the principal differential operators. Furthermore, we show that the schemes possess difference errors of multiprecision order, corresponding to the orders of the constituent schemes, and differentiate the entire class based on these operator orders. Finally, we prove the existence and differentiability of the variable stepsize scheme's discrete solution relative to the constant stepsize solution, provided a stepsize condition is satisfied; this linear difference scheme utilizes stepsizes that may vary at each step. The paper also presents numerical examples to validate the order and stability properties of the SDIMSIMs. Notably, for linear test equations with complex coefficients, the linear stability regions of our variable stepsize SDIMSIMs cover the entire complex plane. Additionally, we present results for a nonlinear stability problem arising in fluid dynamics, demonstrating that variable stepsizes can significantly reduce computational time compared to constant stepsizes. A Fortran 90 implementation of a variable stepsize scheme is also provided. (The term "standard differential equations" refers to ordinary or partial differential equations where the derivative at any point depends solely on the function value at that point.) This work extends the research presented in [1]. Keywords: standard differential equations, multiple precision, linear stability regions, multipoint, variable stepsize. This study investigates the optimal portfolio selection problem under power utility functions, incorporating both total and relative wealth. We demonstrate the equivalence between the utility maximization framework and a stochastic control problem involving a nonstandard, state-dependent Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. By transforming the problem into a stochastic optimization task with a local Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Quasi-Variational-Inequality (HJBI) equation, we derive its classical solution. This solution yields an explicit formula for the optimal control, which subsequently provides the closed-form solution for the optimal value function. A notable finding is that the optimal investment in each asset exhibits a jump discontinuity at the time the floating barrier is struck. Furthermore, we prove the HJBI equation possesses a unique classical solution and utilize this to recover the unique solution of the original stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. Finally, we compute the closed-form solutions for the power utility function with a fixed exponent. The study includes several examples of explicit solutions. These results are applicable to portfolio optimization models featuring total and relative power utility over a power utility discount factor, a framework that aligns with the economic reality of time preference. Additionally, we provide a novel interpretation of the stochastic target problem with a floating barrier: the final relative terminal wealth is contingent upon whether the floating barrier is hit during the investment horizon. Specifically, upon hitting the barrier, wealth is reinvested at a predetermined level with a predetermined duration. This perspective offers a new approach to the stochastic target problem with a floating barrier and a practical method for managing financial risk. Finally, we propose a numerical scheme to address the stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation when an explicit solution is unavailable. Through a numerical example, we illustrate the characteristics of the optimal investment strategy and optimal consumption policy derived from our explicit solutions. Finally, we extend the explicit formulas to the more general case of a power utility discount factor modeled by the Black-Scholes model. In this generalized setting, the explicit formulas for the optimal consumption policy and optimal investment policy are expressed as integrals. We compute these integrals numerically and provide the corresponding graphs. This extension encompasses the explicit solution previously derived. Our findings offer a new and valuable perspective for the stochastic control community. From a financial risk management perspective, our research provides a new and practical approach to the stochastic target problem involving a floating barrier. Finally, this paper may hold significant value for financial institutions and individuals seeking to construct optimal portfolios. Dwarf galaxies are essential for comprehending the intergalactic medium (IGM) and the early stages of galaxy formation. Their high mass fractions of interstellar gas enable them to retain gas from previous episodes of star formation, making them valuable cosmic time capsules. This paper examines the IGM within these dwarfs by reviewing observational data from local dwarfs and integrating this knowledge with cosmological simulations. We concentrate on two primary topics: (1) the impact of ionizing feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) on dwarfs, and (2) the presence of hot gas in dwarfs that could influence their star formation history. Although we lack direct observations of the hot, low-density IGM in dwarfs, we can infer its properties through the effects it exerts on the cold gas and stars. Our analysis reveals that AGN heating is not uniform across the IGM; it is more effective in low-density gas near galactic centers, while high-density gas remains largely unaffected. Furthermore, the strong ionizing background produced by early AGN could have heated the IGM to over 10,000 K in the early universe, potentially suppressing gas collapse in dwarfs and delaying their first star formation episodes. Finally, we explore how future observations of dwarfs will advance our understanding of the IGM. We conclude that the gas reservoirs in dwarfs serve as a key indicator of the thermal and ionization state of the IGM. By investigating the physical characteristics of galactic gas, we can better understand the thermal and chemical conditions of the surrounding IGM. The significant amount of hot gas found in dwarfs suggests that the IGM is warmer than previously thought, while the high ionized gas fraction indicates that reionization was more extended and occurred at lower mean densities. Consequently, dwarfs are vital for constraining the thermal and ionization history of the IGM. Ultimately, we argue that a thorough investigation of IGM interactions with dwarf galaxies is crucial for understanding the history of star formation in the universe. This can be achieved by studying the gas and chemical content of dwarfs and analyzing how their IGM properties influence local star formation. By examining the physical conditions of the IGM surrounding dwarfs, we can gain critical insights into the chemical and thermal history of the intergalactic medium. However, this work demonstrates that quasiparticles do not universally exist when baryon number is not conserved or when quasiparticles are defined relative to fluctuations of other conserved charges. Specifically, within local bosonic-fermionic models, fermionic excitations defined relative to locally fluctuating bosons fail to emerge as asymptotic states in the infinite-time limit. Instead, these states remain trapped as resonances even at zero energy, a phenomenon we attribute to the dynamic formation of local pairs. We establish a general framework for identifying such resonances and determine the precise conditions required for the existence of true quasiparticles in systems interacting with baryon-number-violating bosons. This framework extends beyond baryon number, applying generally to any system where fermions interact with bosons that induce charge imbalances relative to the system's chemical potential. Our findings offer a rigorous foundation for interpreting recent numerical observations regarding the localization of quasiparticles in local boson-fermionic systems. We further illustrate this mechanism in two representative models: one involving superconducting electrons coupled to electrons within a superconductor, and another featuring fermionic impurities interacting with phonons. In both scenarios, we show that quasiparticles can vanish, leaving only resonances in the limiting spectral function. Finally, our approach provides a pathway to resolve the longstanding paradox concerning the apparent conservation of baryon number in axion dark matter. Additionally, we explore potential experimental signatures of quasiparticle disappearance in cuprate superconductors and outline strategies for identifying resonances in systems where fermions interact with baryon-number-violating bosons. These cases may exhibit significantly enhanced axion coupling, offering a promising route to detect axion dark matter. For the specific case of superconducting electrons interacting with superconducting electrons, we propose a distinct resonance structure that could be detected through shot noise measurements. Ultimately, this framework establishes a general criterion for the stability of dark axion dark matter. This implies a specific, testable constraint on dark matter models. This document outlines the process and rationale behind fine-tuning the RAG framework. The RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system integrates a retriever with a generator to enhance question-answering tasks. Its core premise is that combining knowledge retrieved from external sources with an LLM's internal pre-trained knowledge improves its ability to respond to user queries. The framework comprises three components: a language model, a retriever (specifically DPR), and a cross encoder. While the language model can be fine-tuned end-to-end, fine-tuning the retriever and cross encoder presents specific challenges. This document addresses the difficulties encountered during retriever and dense encoder fine-tuning within the RAG framework, offering a general approach to enhance performance. Note that this guide focuses on the general fine-tuning process rather than providing in-depth explanations of the methods themselves. All code referenced in this document can be found in the `fine-tune-rag` package.

```python
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.models import AutoModelForQuestionAnswering
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
```

### 1. Fine-tuning the Language Model

The language model component involves two sub-modules: a dual-encoder for encoding questions and passages, and a cross-encoder to evaluate their interaction. These components have distinct requirements; the question encoder processes only the query, while the passage encoder handles both the question and the passage. Conversely, the passage encoder for the system's cross-encoder operates differently, taking only the input IDs, attention masks, and token type identifiers of the passage as input, without requiring a question.

```python
question_encoder = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    question_encoder_path,
    output_hidden_states=True,
    output_attentions=True,
    add_pooling_layer=True,
)
passage_encoder = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    passage_encoder_path,
    output_hidden_states=True,
    output_attentions=True,
    add_pooling_layer=True,
)
```

To efficiently retrieve documents without overwhelming the LLM with the entire corpus, the retriever filters out most irrelevant documents. DPR (Dense Passage Retrieval) serves as the retriever, utilizing bidirectional encoders to encode queries and passages. The system calculates a similarity score between each question-passage pair using cross-attention mechanisms.

Human evaluation remains a critical component of NLP research, yet recruiting crowdsourced annotators for complex, domain-specific, or multilingual tasks on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) presents significant challenges. This study investigates the difficulty of identifying suitable workers on MTurk across three such tasks: English-Spanish summarization, legal document summarization, and biomedical question answering. We introduce a "qualified worker" profile—someone who explicitly states they meet the necessary requirements—and analyze the factors facilitating their discovery. Our findings indicate that clear, jargon-free instructions are essential for locating qualified workers, particularly for complex tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate that sample annotations can substantially improve the ability of potential workers to self-assess their suitability. Finally, we report the average time required to locate qualified workers on MTurk for each of these tasks. Although the presence of sample annotations helps, we observe that the search for qualified workers can still be arduous, sometimes resembling finding a needle in a haystack. These results offer valuable insights for researchers planning to utilize crowdsourcing for complex or specialized duties. Text-video retrieval (TVMR) is a critical yet difficult task that demands a deep syntactic and semantic comprehension of natural language to retrieve relevant videos. However, current methods often fail to fully leverage the inherent hierarchical structure of sentences and individual words. To address this, we introduce the Token Shift and Choice Transformer (TS2-Net), a novel network designed to capture word-level and sentence-level syntactic dependencies. TS2-Net comprises a Token Shift Module (TSM) and a Choice Transformer Module (CTM). The TSM utilizes a token-level Token Shift Pooling (TSP) strategy to aggregate features from adjacent words, thereby modeling word-level dependencies. Subsequently, the CTM employs a sentence-level Choice Attention (CA) mechanism to calculate relevance scores among various clause choices within complex sentences, effectively addressing their structural complexity. Extensive experiments on the WebVid, LAVRI, and VWFE datasets demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves new state-of-the-art performance. This study examines highly connected directed random networks formed by a hybrid of two growth rules: one favors attachment based on in-degree, while the other uses out-degree. The process begins with a small initial strongly connected seed network, where a new node is added at each step. This new node creates k in-links from k randomly chosen existing nodes, and an existing node is then repointed to the new node with a probability proportional to its out-degree. This mechanism combines the characteristics of the barabasi-albert and directed uniform attachment models, resulting in networks with both high average degree and low average degree. We analyze the resulting degree distributions and network motifs, finding that the average in-out degree ratio can be tuned to match specific empirical observations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this hybrid model can reproduce key features of real-world social networks, such as those of Twitter users and online friendships. Finally, we extend the model by incorporating memory, where attachment probabilities depend on both current and past degrees; we show that this model can simultaneously capture the power-law degree distribution and heavy tail of the in-out degree ratio observed in Twitter data. These findings underscore the model's utility in both quantitative and qualitative assessments of social network dynamics. Multimedia content, such as videos and audio recordings, frequently contains several labels simultaneously. For instance, a single audio file can bear both a speech label and a disturbance label. This study aims to develop a neural network architecture capable of learning multiple labels concurrently, even when visible visual cues are absent. To achieve this, the architecture must be trained on paired data comprising videos and their corresponding labels. We introduce a multi-label model designed to predict multiple classes simultaneously and evaluate its performance using a dataset of surveillance videos annotated with both speech and disturbance labels. The findings indicate that the proposed model outperforms existing single-label approaches in detecting multiple labels. The video clips within this dataset were collected from various sources and feature audio disturbances including barking, screaming, and arguing. The paper concludes by identifying current limitations and suggesting directions for future research. As an initial step, we have made the data collection scripts and the trained model publicly available to support subsequent investigations. Furthermore, the dataset will be released to enable researchers to train their own models on the video recordings. This foundational work is intended to advance the field of multimedia content analysis and labeling. Additionally, the approach is applicable to other scenarios involving visible surveillance footage. The scenario analyzed in this paper is one of many potential applications, such as content-based filtering for social media platforms or enhancing the accuracy of speech-to-text systems. The code used in this research can be accessed at: https://github.com/ahmedelshafey/Multi-Label-CNNs. Our source code is also available on GitHub. Our contributions include: (1) proposing a novel approach for simultaneous multi-label analysis, (2) introducing a new dataset for multi-label analysis, and (3) making the contribution package open-source to support the research community. Our future work involves applying this approach to detect audio events in still images. We plan to evaluate the approach's effectiveness in enhancing speech-to-text systems. Our methodology represents a significant step toward more efficient and accurate multimedia analysis and labeling. We believe this source code package will be highly valuable to the research community. Our approach utilizes a convolutional neural network trained on a dataset of surveillance videos with two labels: speech and audio disturbance. The model was trained on a corpus of 1,000 videos and subsequently tested on a separate corpus of 1,000 videos. The results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses current state-of-the-art methods for co-label analysis. This paper details the contributions of the Multi-Label CNNs package and provides a detailed analysis of the results.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been a transformative force in the 20th and 21st centuries, driving revolutions across diverse fields such as healthcare, education, and entertainment. However, persistent challenges regarding bias, lack of transparency, and insufficient reliability within current AI systems indicate the need for further advancement. This paper introduces the concept of Enhanced Artificial Intelligence (EAI), which builds upon and extends traditional AI. We outline the core components of EAI, including Enhanced AI Enhancement (EAE), Enhanced AI Governance (EAG), and Enhanced AI Ethics (EAE). Additionally, the paper proposes the conceptual framework of EAI, explores applications for enhancing, governing, and ethically directing AI through EAE, EAG, and Enhanced AI Ethics (EAI), and examines the synergy among these sub-domains of EAI. Finally, the paper addresses the significance and opportunities presented by EAI. As a counterpart to our recent publication in IEEE Computational Intelligence Magazine, this work serves as an introductory overview to the EAI paradigm. We introduce a comprehensive theoretical framework to characterize the thermal evolution of a quantum phase transition in correlated bosons within an optical lattice, incorporating spin-orbit coupling and self-interaction. This approach enables the precise calculation of phase boundaries, specific heat, and correlation functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the thermal shift observed in the antiferromagnetic phase boundary is an intrinsic consequence of spin fluctuations. Finally, by comparing the self-interaction effects on the antiferro- and ferromagnetic phases, we identify that the observed shift arises from the distinct quantum mechanical properties of strongly interacting bosons in the optical grid. These insights are validated through path integral Monte Carlo simulations and supported by the random phase approximation. Notably, our findings regarding the random phase approximation's efficacy in describing quantum fluctuations in strongly interacting bosons may extend to other systems, such as multiband Hubbard models and the Mott transition. This study serves as a theoretical foundation for upcoming experimental investigations into quantum phase transitions in cold atom systems, specifically those featuring spin-orbit coupling within optical lattices. Furthermore, the path integral formalism developed here is applicable to a broad spectrum of many-body systems. Finally, we outline a potential route to observe this quantum phase transition experimentally. By employing radio-frequency dressing of hyperfine states in a $^{87}$Rb optical lattice, we can modulate the spin-orbit coupling, thereby driving the system through the quantum phase transition. The proposed experimental protocol is feasible using current state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, we suggest that the quantum critical point can be accessed by trapping a few hundred atoms in a optical lattice with a depth of approximately 10 $E_{\mathrm R}$. The proposed experimental scheme is expected to facilitate the observation of this quantum phase transition. Additionally, we demonstrate that this transition can be driven by laser-induced effective spin-orbit coupling, which is tunable via laser intensity. This capability offers a means to study strongly correlated bosons in optical lattices, thereby advancing the field of quantum simulation. A primary challenge in applying Gaussian process (GP) models is selecting appropriate kernels. While numerous well-known GP kernels exist in the literature, they often lack clear interpretations of the mathematical relationships between input variables. This paper introduces a framework for developing new GPs based on the mathematical expressions governing the relationships between input data points. The proposed method combines standard kernels to create models with interpretable structures. We demonstrate that these modeled GPs achieve superior accuracy and generalization compared to state-of-the-art alternatives when: (i) input variables exhibit specific mathematical relationships, such as those found in the Navier-Stokes equations, and (ii) output values are derived from the summation of multiple input variables, a common scenario in ensemble learning. Additionally, we note that GPs constructed from this framework display greater sensitivity to changes in hyperparameters, underscoring the critical nature of proper hyperparameter selection for these models. Our proposed approach is validated through two real-world case studies. Open-source code and computational details are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/Interpretable-GP. Our findings indicate that GPs built using this framework offer (i) higher accuracy, (ii) enhanced interpretability via more informative posterior distributions, and (iii) greater model transparency by clarifying input-output relationships. These attributes make the gP framework a valuable asset for interpretable machine learning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that posterior distributions from gP models can be visualized using probability density plots, thereby facilitating (i) the interpretation of uncertain outputs and (ii) the detection of outliers. Overall, this framework advances GP modeling by providing additional tools to address key challenges in GP development. The framework is widely applicable to various domains, including fluid dynamics, physics, engineering, and general data analysis. We conclude that this approach offers value for both modeling and visualization tasks. Future research will explore extending this framework to handle non-stationary data and multivariate output variables. A muon collider faces significant challenges from beam-induced effects, which could severely limit the statistics of rare processes. This paper reviews current understanding of these effects and their impacts, while also outlining potential mitigation strategies. It concludes by identifying open questions and proposing methods for addressing them. Many of the suggested approaches can be readily implemented on existing facilities, and some may also be applicable at hadron colliders.

We introduce Spartan, a class of regularized convex loss functions designed to learn sparse models. Unlike current sparse regularizers, the parameters of Spartan's loss functions are differentiable and non-negative, allowing for back-propagation of these values. We demonstrate that Spartan's loss landscape possesses favorable properties for optimization, such as being strongly convex away from the origin, which facilitates the efficient training of sparse models even within deep networks. Furthermore, we establish that Spartan effectively performs feature selection in linear models and successfully trains deep networks sparsely, achieving performance comparable to dense models on both vision and classification tasks. To enable gradient descent, we provide a closed-form expression for the non-negative soft-thresholding operator, which serves as a proximal operator for Spartan losses. Additionally, we develop a closed-form formula for the derivative of this proximal operator, making the loss function fully differentiable at the output of each layer. This derivative can be back-propagated through the network during training. We also present a closed-form Hessian expression, which, when combined with second-order methods like Adam, results in significant speed improvements. Finally, we extend the Spartan loss to a regularized convex constrained form that converges more rapidly than standard proximal gradient methods. We empirically validate that Spartan can differentiate between relevant and irrelevant data, such as separating cat from background pixels in convolutional filters. This capability allows for the application of a re-weighted conjugate gradient method, which accelerates training and enhances sparsity. We confirm through experiments on established benchmarks that Spartan outperforms existing sparse training techniques. The source code is available at https://github.com/PrincetonML/Spartan. Our findings suggest that Spartan can be applied to a wide range of machine learning problems. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into sparse neural network training and optimization. Spartan offers a straightforward approach to achieving sparsity in neural networks, a critical component for deploying AI in edge computing and other resource-limited environments. An exact weak-coupling expansion for the static density response function of a Bose fluid yields insights into collective excitations and structural properties. Utilizing this method, we construct the spin response function to identify a low-energy emergent mode within an interacting Bose-Bose mixture. Lett. 122, 123401 (2019)]. We demonstrate that this effective Pauli obstruction arises due to the emergence of a Pauli-like behavior in the low-momentum density-density response function of a symmetric Bose fluid as the interaction strength increases. Furthermore, we link this finding to the development of a structural anomaly in the static structure factor of the interacting Bose gas. Finally, we connect these structural characteristics to the collective excitations of the Bose fluid. Our findings corroborate the recent discovery of a robust collective excitation in Bose gases with Pauli-blocking effects, observed experimentally in ref. [Science 367, 1091 (2020)]. Additionally, we predict the existence of a collective mode in a symmetric Bose fluid where effective Pauli blocking is absent, a mode that can be experimentally accessed via Bragg spectroscopy. Finally, we propose a Bose fluid system exhibiting Pauli-obstruction-like behavior, where the momentum cutoff of the structural anomaly in the static structure factor aligns with the Fermi wave vector in the density response function. This system comprises two species of bosons with different scattering lengths, where the energy gap between them generates an effective Pauli obstruction at low momenta. We further show that this collective excitation mode is consistent with the recent discovery of sound-like excitations in the barium ion Bose mixture [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 123401 (2020)]. These experimental observations confirm the emergence of Pauli obstruction in weakly interacting Bose fluids and provide a theoretical framework for understanding these findings. Finally, we propose an effective action for the collective excitation mode in weakly interacting Bose fluids, demonstrating that it shares the same form as that of spin waves in a superfluid Fermi gas. The validity of this study is supported by exact low-order correlation functions and the static density response function of the Bose fluid. Software testing is frequently perceived as a time-intensive and laborious activity, leading many developers to resist adopting testing best practices. This study investigates developers' perspectives on how software testing practices influence software quality. Through a survey of 104 developers from 24 Turkish organizations, we examined their views on whether testing practices exacerbate "testing odors"—antipatterns specific to testing processes. The findings reveal that developers consider software testing processes as intrinsically linked to software quality. Specifically, they consider sharing test cases among developers, sharing tests across projects, and maintaining tests alongside source code as positive testing practices that enhance software quality. Conversely, they identify a lack of communication between testers and developers as a critical process flaw that negatively impacts the testing effort's effectiveness. These insights are discussed in relation to existing literature, and we conclude that developers should be engaged in determining which practices constitute best practices versus antipatterns to facilitate the successful adoption of testing methodologies. Finally, we outline directions for a forthcoming action research study.

We introduce KKMCee, a Monte Carlo event generator designed for electron-positron collisions that models the complete spectrum of lepton and quark pair production, including annihilation, W boson pair decay, and double bremsstrahlung. Built upon the lepton pair formation method from the QED multi-photon framework (as detailed in J. Phys. G: Nucl. Part. Phys. 41 033001, 2014), the primary innovations are the implementation of multiple photon emission, alongside enhancements to bremsstrahlung, pair formation, and hadronization models, along with improvements to the parton shower algorithm. These features are particularly vital for simulating high-energy lepton colliders where KKMCee is intended for use. Regarding the input format, we retain compatibility with the CERNFFN 6.2 and HERACLES 3.6 syntax used by KKMC, as well as the JETSET 6.4 syntax employed at lepton colliders. Furthermore, to address precision physics at colliders operating near or above the Z boson resonance, we have integrated electroweak corrections and adopted the ZZ production mechanism from FEEPWIZ, which incorporates next-to-leading order electroweak effects. This version is released under the name KKMCee to distinguish it from the hadron collider counterpart, KKMC, and it is publicly accessible at www-pph.web.cern.ch/public/pph. Future updates will incorporate additional physics processes and mechanisms, enhanced capabilities for precision physics at lepton colliders, and further improvements to the input syntax. Additionally, we plan to integrate a mechanism for including multiple beam background particles, which is crucial for simulating multiple interaction environments at lepton colliders. The Stochastic Singular Value Transformation (SSVT) offers a method for tensor singular value decomposition (TSVD) by applying a singular value transformation to a specific mode. Due to its data-sparsity characteristic, SSVT is well-suited for large-scale tensor computations. This study extends SSVT for tensor extension by estimating a sub-space that captures the majority of information within the tensor's modes. A novel stopping criterion is introduced, enabling the count of SSVT passes required to identify an optimal sub-space for the tensor's main information. The proposed algorithm is benchmarked against established TSVD methods, including HOSVD and STSV, using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Results demonstrate that the new approach is more efficient than HOSVD for certain applications and faster than STSV when the number of passes is limited. Furthermore, the study shows that restricting the pass count to a single iteration, sufficient for sub-space estimation, results in significantly reduced computational time without compromising accuracy. Experimental findings indicate that utilizing only one pass of the proposed algorithm yields superior results compared to HOSVD across various modes. Additionally, the optimal pass count is highly dependent on the tensor's data structure, suggesting that a variable pass strategy could be beneficial for large-scale tensor computations. Finally, tests on a real-world application of the 3D brain volume illustrate that the proposed algorithm is highly adaptable to different computation requirements. Overall, this paper introduces a novel and effective method for large-scale tensor computations. The algorithm is implemented in Python and made publicly available at: https://github.com/ahmedfouad/SSVT. The implementation supports a pass count limit, allowing users to set a maximum number of passes for SSVT application. This limit can be fixed to a specific number or configured to automatically terminate the algorithm once the desired information is extracted from the tensor's modes. The paper also outlines the mathematical foundation for estimating the sub-space of a tensor's modes and defines the stopping criterion used to determine whether additional passes are necessary. Finally, the theoretical and practical implications of using a pass count limit for SSVT are discussed. The level of detail regarding implementation specifics and their impact on SSVT outcomes is also addressed. These features enhance the algorithm's utility for large-scale tensor computations, and the associated code is provided to facilitate its application. Furthermore, examples are included to illustrate how computation requirements influence the selection of the pass count limit. In conclusion, this work presents a new and efficient solution for large-scale tensor computations, with the provided code offering a practical implementation that supports configurable computation

The efficacy of deep learning models is heavily reliant on the quality of their learned representations. Although various existing techniques have attempted to optimize these representations directly via similarity metrics—such as Maximize Information Necessity (MAXIM)—they often fail to fully leverage model capacity, resulting in overly loose lower bounds. This study introduces a novel representation learning algorithm driven by the Sinkhorn distance. Our approach optimizes two distinct representation spaces using alternating minimization, where Sinkhorn distance serves as a regularizer for the overall objective function. During the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, England implemented contact tracing through a national digital system. However, individuals using separate digital applications outside of this national framework also conducted contact tracing. This study estimates the impact of these localized efforts on infection dynamics within England. Utilizing a dynamic model of infections, we analyzed data from England between July and December 2021, alongside published metrics regarding local tracing efforts. The model estimated transmission and tracing effectiveness by fitting to reported daily new infections. Our findings indicate that local collaborations reduced the effective reproduction number by 0.12 (95% CI: 0.04 to 0.23), whereas national efforts lowered it by 0.20 (95% CI: 0.17 to 0.23). Consequently, the text concludes that localized tracing efforts exerted a smaller influence on epidemic trajectories compared to national measures. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that contact tracing is a highly effective intervention for slowing the spread of the virus. Finally, it recommends that digital contact tracing applications should be integrated into the national framework rather than remaining independent. To achieve this integration, the article outlines necessary steps involving local authorities, the government, and app developers. Additionally, it proposes that public health officials could incentivize participation in digital tracing apps by mandating that vaccination campaigns utilize these applications to maintain social distancing post-vaccination. This approach would ensure consistent contact tracing across all regions, thereby maximizing the intervention's potential to curb the epidemic. Finally, the article underscores the importance of assessing the impact of public health measures on viral spread. By quantifying the benefits of contact tracing, the research aids in resource allocation, such as determining the optimal number of test kits to distribute. Ultimately, this work contributes to the broader understanding of how public health strategies can be evaluated to inform future decision-making. The authors also highlight the need for further research to explore the relationship between local tracing efforts and infection rates. The authors note that the analysis was conducted using open source software, which enhances the reproducibility of the results. Although vision is essential for vision-guided robotic manipulation, learning a vision system's calibration from a limited number of images remains a significant challenge. This difficulty is particularly pronounced for robots with externally mounted cameras (eye-in-hand), where calibration is complex and dynamic due to the robot's movement. We introduce a novel approach to adjust an eye-in-hand camera's position using vision capabilities. Our framework leverages a large dataset of successful grasps collected with a gripper to learn a camera pose function based on object images. By utilizing a large scale of diverse data, we can directly predict the camera's pose relative to the gripper without requiring annotations of the pose or the object's pose. We validate this method through sim-to-real experiments, demonstrating that our approach surpasses a strong baseline that employs neural networks to estimate the object's pose. The resulting policy enables a real robot to grasp new objects using a previously unseen gripper equipped with a camera mounted in an unknown location. Recent advancements in policy optimization for reinforcement learning (RL) have focused on incorporating constraints to enhance sample efficiency and improve off-policy evaluation. However, most current approaches rely on approximations to manage these constraints, leaving the precise relationship between policy parameters and their associated constraints largely unexplored. This paper introduces Reverse Constrained Policy Optimization (RCPO), a novel framework that utilizes the reverse policy gradient to optimize policies under specific constraints without requiring constraint approximations. We provide theoretical proofs demonstrating RCPO's convergence to a first- or second-order stationary point. Furthermore, we offer an empirical analysis comparing RCPO against baseline methods, evaluating both solution quality and off-policy performance. Experimental results across various continuous control environments indicate that RCPO outperforms baselines in terms of sample efficiency and final returns, while also exhibiting greater stability when learning off-policy. GAIA, a mission by the European Space Agency's Science Programme, is designed to create a comprehensive 3D map of our Milky Way Galaxy. This mapping encompasses over one hundred parameters for more than ten billion sources within a defined volume of space. The required data volume is so immense that it will require at least five to ten years of on-line processing by the GAIA Data Processing and Analysis Consortium (GPAC) before being distributed to the broader community via the GAIA Data Release Facility (DRF). To facilitate this, GPAC and the DRF Consortium have developed a novel data distribution and analysis infrastructure known as the Virtual Observatory (VO). This infrastructure enables remote, distributed, and large-scale data access and analysis through standardized interfaces. GPAC also intends to implement a new data reduction pipeline to ensure the DRF operates efficiently as a VO environment. This paper outlines the design of GPAC and the DRF, along with the analysis tools available to users. Additionally, it details the data products to be released and discusses how to access and analyze them using GPAC and the VO infrastructure. The article further explores potential scientific applications, including astrometry, photometry, spectroscopy, and astrometric time series analysis. Finally, the paper addresses the challenges of a mission of this scale and complexity, emphasizing the critical need for a large community of scientists, engineers, and support staff. It concludes by highlighting the significant role of the VO infrastructure in supporting such a mission. This paper introduces a novel vertex divider, representing a fundamental structural element of the divide-and-conquer technique applied to treewidth. Our divider functions without relying on specific treewidth bounds or exclusion sets, offering a conceptually simpler and more robust alternative to prior divider constructions. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any treewidth $k$ and positive integer $q$, the graph can be separated into components linked by at most $k$ edges, ensuring no component possesses a treewidth exceeding $q$. This outcome is achieved via a straightforward and direct application of the standard decomposition tree, which functions as a divide-and-conquer framework. We provide two applications of this research: first, we establish that finding a treewidth $k$ decomposition with elimination bag size $q$ is NP-hard, even when $k$ and $q$ are fixed constants; second, we establish a nearly linear-time algorithm for the parameterized problem of determining whether a graph's treewidth is at most $k+q$, which runs in $\tilde{O}(n+m)$ time. Both findings stem from the dynamic programming algorithm inherent to the decomposition tree. Additionally, we present a straightforward proof establishing that the divider found by our approach is optimal up to constant factors. Finally, we examine fundamental properties of vertex dividers and their connections to graph separators. Notably, we demonstrate that the vertex divider result is optimal by presenting a family of graphs where the divisor is optimal within a specific range of treewidth values. These graphs also offer an alternative proof for the hardness result regarding the $k$-treewidth with $q$-exclusion problem. Our findings are derived from a generalization of the well-known treewidth $2$ decomposition tree algorithm proposed by Bodlaender et al. [Bodlaender et al., 2015]. Furthermore, we provide a unified proof for the hardness result concerning $k$-treewidth with $q$-exclusion. The remainder of the paper addresses open problems and conjectures. Our work builds upon the algorithm by Bodlaender et al. [Bodlaender et al., 2015], which serves as the foundation for the treewidth $2$ divider. Grouping algorithms are frequently employed to analyze networks, typically involving the assignment of community labels to nodes and the identification of group-specific attributes. However, existing approaches are primarily designed for single network analyses, not for integrating multiple, potentially heterogeneous networks—whether inferred or measured—into a single grouping framework. We propose weighted directed grouping (WdG), a framework that unifies multi-network analysis with hierarchical attributes. WdG allows for distinct weighting of networks based on their specific characteristics and supports the inference of either unidirectional (parent-child) or mutual relationships among nodes. We address several critical questions: Can WdG identify statistically distinguishable groupings? Does it recover true groupings in synthetic data? Is it robust to noise? Can it resolve harder instances than current methods? Our results demonstrate that WdG can detect signals in networks where no statistically significant signal exists in any individual network separately. Furthermore, WdG is scalable to large networks and extends to moderatey dense networks. By combining separate network analyses with the ability to merge consistent groupings, WdG offers a versatile solution for multi-network analysis. This work introduces a framework for joint grouping analysis and paves the way for developing inference algorithms within this framework. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a hybrid approach integrating the adaptability of machine learning with the reliability of partial differential equation (PDE) solvers. While the theoretical foundations of PINNs are still being investigated, recent studies have demonstrated their effectiveness in various PDE solution tasks. However, the lack of established error estimates hinders the ability to accurately quantify PINN errors, a critical component for the safe deployment of machine learning models in safety-critical environments. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a method to estimate PINNs in the context of convection-diffusion equations, where the known flux at the exit boundary serves as a safety constraint. The proposed technique utilizes the adjoint method to calculate the error associated with the neural network approximation of a solution and employs the maximum residual method to identify the worst-case error. This maximum residual measure not only quantifies the error but also offers insights into the PINN training process. We validate the method's efficacy on a simple analytical model and a complex model representing the dynamics of a high-speed train. The primary objective is to ensure that PINN outputs remain within a safe operating range, preventing the train from exceeding its design speed. Our findings demonstrate that this error estimation framework can guide the training process and guarantee safety-critical performance. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's application to a more complex elasticity problem. To our knowledge, this work presents the first instance of applying error estimation to PINNs alongside a safety-constrained training protocol. Finally, the code required to replicate our results is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexei-gorban/PINN_codes. Linear contextual bandits are a widely adopted framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, characterized by action sets comprising a fixed number of arms, each defined by a contextual feature vector. While existing research and practical applications predominantly address scenarios with homogeneous action sets, many real-world problems involve heterogeneous structures where action sets vary in cardinality. This paper examines a linear bandit setting with diverse action sets, analyzing how this homogeneity assumption is violated and the subsequent effects on exploration and inference. We introduce a novel algorithm, \textit{LinBandits-Div}, which utilizes a common feature space across all arms to facilitate efficient exploration from a unified perspective. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of this violation on inference by introducing a new hypothesis testing framework. Our analysis of this problem reveals that standard inference methods are often impractical and that violation-induced uncertainty can be quantified through a simple yet effective approach. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms state-of-the-art homogeneous LinBenchits in terms of regret and efficiency, while also showing that existing inference methods are not necessarily affected by the divergence in action sets. Finally, we apply this framework to two real-world problems: online news recommendation and job matching, highlighting the broad applicability of our approach to various practical scenarios. Although the orbital Hall effect in time-reversal symmetric systems was predicted over a decade ago, it has been challenging to observe because effect A, which generates a nonlocal charge current, is typically overshadowed by effect B, which produces a local transverse voltage. In gapped graphene, we demonstrate that time-reversal symmetry enables two distinct mechanisms to generate transverse voltage: orbital Hall effect A and valley Hall effect C. Notably, valley Hall effect C is an alternative to effect B that can be experimentally verified without inducing effect B. Furthermore, valley Hall effect C is easier to measure due to its large magnitude. To validate these predictions, we present experimental results from gapped graphene that confirm the presence of valley Hall effect C. Our findings indicate that valley Hall effect C is comparable to, and potentially larger than, orbital Hall effect B in this material system. This discovery expands the scope of valley Hall physics and may facilitate the future observation of the orbital Hall effect in gapped graphene. Additionally, our methodology is applicable to other materials, such as silicon and transition metal dichalcogenides. Finally, our approach is extendable to valley Hall heuristics involving Berry curvature, anomalous Hall effect, and anomalous magnetoresistance. Notably, valley polarization can be detected without triggering orbital Hall effects that would otherwise complicate the measurement. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically engineered for processing tabular and network-based data, yet recent studies indicate that GNN-based classifiers are significantly more susceptible to adversarial attacks compared to standard neural networks. This vulnerability arises because graph structures frequently contain diverse substructures, providing attackers with multiple pathways to infiltrate and manipulate the data. Consequently, understanding how these substructures influence graph contamination is crucial for developing effective defense mechanisms. In this study, we investigate data contamination within graphs by employing reinforcement learning to generate adversarial attacks. Our findings demonstrate that adversarial examples created under adversarial labeling are particularly difficult for GNNs to classify accurately. We measured contamination levels across three real-world datasets, highlighting the efficacy of reinforcement learning in contaminating graph structures and offering a novel perspective on security and privacy within graph-based environments. Ultimately, this research deepens our comprehension of graph contamination dynamics, providing a foundation for designing more robust and resilient GNN architectures. By leveraging reinforcement learning to identify critical substructures, we can subsequently focus on reinforcing these areas to thwart future attacks. We anticipate that these results will inspire further inquiry into graph contamination and facilitate the creation of novel, resilient GNN models. Catalogue matching serves as a critical method for deriving astrometric coordinates and determining photometry. However, despite significant advancements, numerous studies indicate a substantial error rate, with several analyses showing error rates of 30% or higher. These errors predominantly stem from two factors: a lack of sufficient contextual information and the reliance on flawed heuristics. To address this, we introduce two techniques for enhancing spectral type estimation and catalogue matching. First, we employ an attention-based neural network to estimate spectral types by leveraging spectral energy distributions (SEDs) and neighboring objects' spectral types. We demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances robustness against photometric contamination, thereby boosting the overall accuracy of the matching process. Second, we develop a novel method for estimating catalogue parameters using graph neural networks, which utilizes a graph constructed from inter-object distances and magnitudes. This method is designed to accommodate additional data sources, such as spectroscopy or near-infrared imaging, to further improve matching accuracy. Our evaluation using Mock-SDSS and Gaia DR2 test sets reveals that both of these techniques significantly increase the accuracy of catalogue matching and spectral type estimation. Notably, after our corrections, the cross-match between Gaia DR2 and SDSS DR17 achieved a 99.9% match rate. The code required to reproduce these results is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1999/catalogue-matching. This paper investigates the infinity-edge-cover problem within infinite hypergraphs. We demonstrate that if a hypergraph possesses a countably infinite edge cover of cardinality $\aleph_0$, it necessarily possesses a minimal edge cover of the same cardinality. This finding directly contradicts a conjecture proposed by S. Rautenbach. However, if we assume Martin's Axiom, we can establish that any hypergraph with a finite edge cover of a specific cardinality also admits a minimal edge cover sharing that cardinality. Ontologies serve as formal, explicit specifications of categories within a particular domain of interest. We introduce a method to enhance semi-supervised End-to-End Automatic Speech Recognition (EE-E2E-ASR) by employing CycleGAN, an unsupervised image-to-image translation network, and CyclePenalty, an image reconstruction loss. This loss function measures the discrepancy between original acoustic features and those translated by CyclePenalty into spectral image features from speech data, which are subsequently used by EE-E2E-ASR as alternative targets to complement standard CTC loss. CyclePenalty enforces a constraint on the mapping network to maintain the distributional consistency of speech features, thereby creating pseudo-acoustic features that offer complementary information to CTC loss for improved transcription accuracy. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robustness against varying speech-music SNRs. Experiments conducted on TIMIT and CALLHOME-Telephone datasets reveal that our approach boosts word error rate (WER) reduction from 3.6% to 5.0% on TIMIT and from 4.1% to 5.2% on CALLHOME-Telephone across both end-to-end ASR variants. Additionally, on TIMIT, it achieves WER reduction from 3.6% to 5.1% for ASR-V1 and from 4.1% to 5.3% for ASR-V2, utilizing non-transcribed music data. Finally, we observe that this method yields performance improvements without the need for pre-training.
